MOVEMENT 2 CARRIED NINE MARKS ON SIX DAYS AND MOVEMENT 3 TEN ON SIX, AND 770 PUBLISHES MOVEMENT 1'S OWN TEN DAYS AS TWO, ONE, TWO, THREE, TWO AND THREE ON SIX DAYS, WHICH IS THIRTEEN, WHILE THE STATE PUBLISHES ELEVEN FOR IT; THAT DISCREPANCY IS PRE-EXISTING IN A MOVEMENT 1 FILE AND IS CARRIED FOR THE VOLUME 16 CLOSE, SO NO REMAINDER IS PUBLISHED HERE. THE COLUMN IS CLOSED ONCE, ON 810, AT THE VOLUME'S PUBLISHED FIGURE OF TWENTY-EIGHT DAYS AND NINETY-ONE MARKS. THE COLUMN OF THE WITHDRAWN STANDS WHERE IT STOOD AT THREE AND WAS NOT TOUCHED ON ANY OF THESE TEN DAYS AND WAS NOT TAKEN AGAIN.**

**THE SHEET. IT STANDS AT ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN THOUSAND AND EIGHTY-TWO PENCE OUT, BEING SEVEN HUNDRED AND NINETY-FOUR MARKS, THREE SHILLINGS AND SIXPENCE, AND ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED AND FORTY-TWO PENCE SHORT, BEING SEVEN HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN MARKS, TEN SHILLINGS AND TWOPENCE, AGAINST TEN THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY PENCE IN, ON ALL TEN OF THESE DAYS. NO LINE WAS WORKED AND NONE SETTLED AND NONE IS OWED. THE THIRD FORM WAS NOT USED AND IS SPENT ON 768. 127,082 / 160 = 794 MARKS AND 42 PENCE AND 42 PENCE IS THREE SHILLINGS AND SIXPENCE; 116,442 / 160 = 727 MARKS AND 122 PENCE AND 122 PENCE IS TEN SHILLINGS AND TWOPENCE.**

**THE HONEST TOTAL AND WHAT IS OWED OF IT. THE HONEST TOTAL IS FOUR HUNDRED AND SIX PENCE, BEING TWO MARKS, SEVEN SHILLINGS AND TWOPENCE, AND ITS FOUR PARTS ARE ONE DAY OF A BOAT AT THE FIGURE IN CHALK AT ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-EIGHT PENCE, BEING ONE MARK AND EIGHTPENCE; FOUR MEN AT TWO DAYS AT SIXTEEN PENCE A MAN-DAY AT FOUR TIMES TWO TIMES SIXTEEN FOR ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-EIGHT PENCE, BEING TEN SHILLINGS AND EIGHTPENCE; COAL FOR ONE DAY AT TWENTY PENCE, BEING ONE SHILLING AND EIGHTPENCE; AND THIRTY YARDS OF LINE AT THREE PENCE THE YARD AT THIRTY TIMES THREE FOR NINETY PENCE, BEING SEVEN SHILLINGS AND SIXPENCE. IT IS ON A SHEET UNDER NINE SHEETS IN THE DRAWER IN THAT RECORD ROOM AND IT IS ON NO PAGE OF THE LOWFEN REED, AND PUTTING IT THERE IS OWED TO MOVEMENT 5. THE COST OF THE WITHDRAWAL IS THREE LOTS OF EIGHTY-FOUR PENCE, BEING SEVEN SHILLINGS, WHICH IS TWO HUNDRED AND FIFTY-TWO PENCE, BEING ONE MARK, SEVEN SHILLINGS AND EIGHTPENCE, ALL IN CHALK ON OTHER PEOPLE'S BOARDS.**

**THE TWO FIGURES THAT CARRY OUT UNRESOLVED, AND THE ARGUMENT ABOUT THEM THAT WAS NOT SETTLED. THE FOURTEENTH-VERSUS-TWENTY-FIRST ARGUMENT WAS TOUCHED ONCE, ON 799, IN THE HOUSE'S OWN FORM, AND IT WAS NOT SETTLED, AND THE FIGURE OF ONE DAY IN ELEVEN IS NOWHERE. THE CINDER BELL'S OWN PAGE CARRIES FOURTEEN DAYS OF THAT COMMUNITY'S OWN BELL AT SIX PENCE A DAY FROM THE TWENTY-SEVENTH, BEING EIGHTY-FOUR PENCE, BEING SEVEN SHILLINGS, WHICH IS A DIFFERENT LETTING ON A DIFFERENT SERVICE FROM THE FORTNIGHT BEING ARGUED ABOUT, AND NOBODY COMPARED THE TWO.**

**AND THE THREAD THAT IS PARKED BY NAME AND WAS NOT DROPPED. THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO AND THE WOMAN OF THIRTY OF NO OFFICE ARE ON THE PAGE OF ALL TEN OF THESE DAYS AND ARE NEVER IN A ROOM TOGETHER ON ANY DAY OF THIS MOVEMENT. SHE IS IN THAT YARD ON 795 WITH A PAGE UNDER HER ARM AND HE IS NOT IN IT; HE IS IN THAT YARD ON 798 AND ON 800 WITH A PAGE IN HIS HAND AND SHE IS UP THAT COAST ROAD OR NOT IN THAT YARD. NEITHER SIGNED THE OTHER'S PAGE, NEITHER SAID ONE WORD TO THE OTHER, AND NEITHER GAVE UP AN INCH OF THEIR OWN WORK. MOVEMENT 4 OWNS THE SIX SENTENCES, WHICH ARE SPOKEN BY THE KEEPER'S ROOM AND NOT BY EITHER OF THEM, AND MOVEMENT 5 OWNS THE MARRIAGE GOING BACK TO ORDINARY WORK.**

**AND THE ARGUMENT OF THE TEN DAYS, IN ONE SENTENCE: THE RIGHT TO WITHDRAW IS REAL AND COSTS MONEY, AND THE COST OF IT IS A BELL THAT IS NOT RUNG AND TWO PLACES THAT EACH PAY EIGHTY-FOUR PENCE MORE FOR A BOAT THAN THEY PAID FOR IT BETWEEN THEM, AND A FIGURE THAT A PERSON CAN LOOK AT IS AN ARGUMENT THAT DOES NOT HAVE TO BE HAD OUT LOUD.**

**WHAT A WRITER OF THE NEXT MOVEMENT SHOULD COPY FROM THE VOICE AND NOT FROM THE FIGURES: a cost is not written down before the day it falls on it; a man who says a thing about himself in about four people has not made a finding and is not written down; a number said aloud in a yard of nine is a number four of them will have differently by the stair; a place's own giving is the one thing on a schedule nobody inland can find out by asking a question; and nobody in a yard of about nine is thanked for anything on any of these ten days, and nobody in one is put on a step and asked anything either.**

---

### 791 — Monday the nineteenth day of September, day 31. Figures 524 / 2,494 / none / 125, hearing 289, tin 204. **A rota day.** The cistern went at about nine in fourteen trips by hand and was walked on by none of them, and the butt stood short and had a skin on it by about one. Four new crews came in at about ten and stood at the back of that shed. The man of about thirty-two told them the thing he had been told himself in the spring three times over and got a different part of it different each time, and at about eleven the man of about twenty-seven of the second lay did the same job on the same bench in about a minute and a half without saying a word. A boat of the Ashtide Run came in over the bar with nothing in her at about half past two and went into no column. The correction and the refusal were standing at that end stall on their twenty-second day and the bell of the Cinder Bell was on its twelfth day out of fourteen.

### 792 — Tuesday the twentieth day of September, day 32. Figures 525 / 2,499 / none / 125, hearing 290, tin 205. **The ninety-ninth wage Tuesday.** The column on the lid of that step was read out at about ten in four minutes and stood at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and did not move, and the chest with the twenty envelopes in it was shut from ten until four. The four new crews are not a line on that column and nobody put them there, and the keeper says out loud why. At about two they were put in front of the man of about twenty-seven and did the two hours of work they had not managed on the Monday. A woman of about thirty-four of that market stands at that door and does not come in.

### 793 — Wednesday the twenty-first day of September, day 33. Figures 526 / 2,504 / none / 125, hearing 291, tin 206. **An ordinary working day, and the man of about thirty-two says it himself.** At about eleven he said out loud, to about four and not to about nine, that he was worse at that work than the men he was teaching, and that he had known it since the Tuesday, and that the man of about twenty-seven had done in about a minute and a half on Monday the thing he had needed a fortnight on in the spring, and that he was not going to be put in front of those four crews again on anything that can be done properly by one of the men standing in it. The four crews were then put in front of the man of about twenty-seven and did in about two hours what they had not managed in three days. The bell of the Cinder Bell was on its fourteenth day out and that was the last of that fortnight this harbor would see.

### 794 — Thursday the twenty-second day of September, day 34. Figures 527 / 2,509 / none / 125, hearing 292, tin 207. **A rota day, and the drawer, and the six sentences.** The cistern was charged at about nine and walked on by none of it. The bell of the Cinder Bell went back into service at daybreak four hundred yards and three fields off and nobody in this harbor saw it seated. At about eleven the drawer in the room over that fish market was opened and there were nine sheets in it above the one underneath, and the man of about fifty-seven lifted the nine off one at a time and charged a penny a sheet and took the money, which was nine sheets at a penny a sheet, being nine times one penny, for nine pence, and it came out of the pocket of the man who keeps the leaf. Under the nine sheets was one sheet with four lines and a figure at the foot of them, being four hundred and six pence, being two marks, seven shillings and twopence, and the four parts are each of them true. At about half past three the man of about fifty-seven stood at the back of that shed in about nine people and said six sentences, and nobody asked him one word before them or during them or after them, and nobody said the word forgiven and nobody said the word ruined, and he went back up those stairs at about four and was not sent for again.

### 795 — Friday the twenty-third day of September, day 35. Figures 528 / 2,514 / none / 125, hearing 293, tin 208. **An ordinary working day, and nothing said twice.** Nobody sent for the man of about fifty-seven and nobody in that shed asked about the six sentences of the day before, and about four of that nine looked all morning for a reason to bring them up and did not find one. The woman of thirty of no office came into that yard at about eleven with a page under her arm and stood at the back of that shed until about half past two, and the man of about thirty-two was not in that yard and was two miles up that coast road. The wall of the room over that chandler's store is bare and has been bare since the fourteenth of August and nothing went up on it. The four new crews did the day's work in about three hours under the man of about twenty-seven and the man of about thirty-two was given the tally slate and the book of hours and nothing else to do all day.

### 796 — Saturday the twenty-fourth day of September, day 36. Figures 529 / 2,519 / none / 125, hearing 294, tin 209. **The treaty defended politically and not in a battle.** A notice came off the tide on the Friday evening naming a sitting of a house inland on the eighth day of October, at which the treaty and the schedule that goes with it are to be spoken to and voted on, the schedule as a whole and one entry of it by itself, and a harbor touched by the schedule may send one person to be heard. At about two a woman of about thirty-seven of that market said out loud that this harbor had to decide before the Saturday was out, and about nine minutes of finding out went into it, and about four said yes and about four said it did not matter and one said nothing. At about four the keeper read that notice out once in about twenty people and did not read it out again, and about eleven of that twenty could not read it at all. There is a name under the seal on that paper and nobody in that harbor read it out. This harbor has decided to be represented, and the person is the woman of about thirty-seven, and she said out loud at about half past four that she expects to lose the vote and that she is going anyway, and that being in the room losing is worth more to that place than being outside it and right. It is not a victory.

### 797 — Sunday the twenty-fifth day of September, day 37. Figures 530 / 2,524 / none / 125, hearing 295, tin 210. **A wipe, the hundred and twenty-fifth, 42/29/42 = 113.** The wall behind that reeve's bench came down at about half past ten and went up at a quarter to one and stood bare twenty-nine minutes, and the three men who do that work took forty-two minutes each way, a minute longer each way again. A man of about thirty-eight of that landing stood at the bare wall through the whole of it and said out loud, on the fourteenth time he has said it, that it is a minute longer each way again and that he has asked twice this year and been told nothing. At about two a line was ruled against that Sunday on the sheet at that end stall and nothing was entered against it, and that sheet has now fifteen gaps in it where it had carried fourteen, and nobody in that market said why and about four people looked at it and nobody put a figure against it.

### 798 — Monday the twenty-sixth day of September, day 38. Figures 531 / 2,529 / none / 125, hearing 296, tin 211. **A rota day, and one person of one community.** The cistern went at about nine and was walked on by none of it. At about one a man of about thirty-six of the Cinder Bell came down that coast road with a page in his own hand in his coat and put it on the flat of that bench stone, and the four words at the top of it are that the Cinder Bell is off that shared stretch from the twenty-seventh of September, and about four of that nine cannot read them and heard them read out once. The keeper said out loud that a community may come off a shared stretch and that it takes one person of that community to say it, and that this yard has never once had a turn given to anybody who has not asked for a turn. Nobody asked that man anything else and nobody put him on a step. Two marks went onto the face of that page against the four words and not against the rest of it. The consequence falls on the twenty-seventh and is not yet on any page.

### 799 — Tuesday the twenty-seventh day of September, day 39. Figures 532 / 2,534 / none / 125, hearing 297, tin 212. **The hundredth wage Tuesday, and the cost of the withdrawal.** The column was read out at about ten in four minutes and stood at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and did not move, and the chest was shut from ten until four. At about one the keeper read out three figures and every one of the three is in chalk on somebody else's board. The first is the boat's hire lost: that shared passage is one boat for one day at the figure in chalk at one hundred and sixty-eight pence and its money was divided so that each of the two places stood at eighty-four pence, and from the twenty-seventh the Saltmarch takes that boat alone and the Cinder Bell hires one of its own, each against eighty-four pence before it, each difference being eighty-four pence, being seven shillings. The second is a bell out of service: the bell of the Cinder Bell is not rung on that stretch from the morning of the twenty-seventh, and that community's own page carries fourteen days of it at six pence a day, being fourteen times six for eighty-four pence, being seven shillings. The third is the whole of it, being three lots of eighty-four pence, which is two hundred and fifty-two pence, being one mark, seven shillings and eightpence. About two people still want the other fortnight entered at fourteen days and about two at twenty-one and nobody settled it.

### 800 — Wednesday the twenty-eighth day of September, day 40. Figures 533 / 2,539 / none / 125, hearing 298, tin 213. **An ordinary working day, and the movement closes with both sheets still on the wall.** That correction and that refusal were both still on that wall at that end stall on their thirty-first day, at the same size and a hand's breadth apart, with the wrong figure left showing underneath the correction and not struck out, and nobody in this harbor has said which of the two of them is right and nobody has taken either of them down. The four heads over that wall are claims, corrections put up in public, refusals and restricted records, and all four of them have been used and there is nothing else on that wall. The wall of the room over that chandler's store is bare and has been since the fourteenth of August. The four new crews were on their tenth day and did the day's work in about two hours and a half under the man of about twenty-seven, and about four of that nine said out loud that they were quicker than the man of about thirty-two had been on his tenth day, which is a thing about four people said and not a finding. The column of the withdrawn was not taken and the column of the second hand carries a figure on five of these ten days and is not added up, and the drawer on that hill was not opened and no digit of the three numbers in that room is on any page.

**AND THE COLUMN OF THE WITHDRAWN, DAY BY DAY, AS IT NOW STANDS AND IS TAKEN ONCE: NOTHING, NOTHING, NOTHING, ONE, NOTHING, NOTHING, NOTHING, TWO, NOTHING AND NOTHING, WHICH IS THREE. THE COLUMN OF THE SECOND HAND CARRIES A FIGURE ON SIX OF THE TEN DAYS, BEING THE FIRST, THE THIRD, THE FIFTH, THE SEVENTH, THE EIGHTH AND THE TENTH, AGAINST ONE, TWO, THREE, ONE, ONE AND TWO, WHICH IS TEN, AND THOSE TEN ARE NOT ADDED TOGETHER IN THAT SHED AND ARE NOT ADDED TOGETHER IN THIS MOVEMENT. MOVEMENT 2 CARRIED NINE MARKS ON SIX DAYS AND THIS MOVEMENT TEN ON SIX, AND 770 PUBLISHES MOVEMENT 1'S OWN TEN DAYS AS TWO, ONE, TWO, THREE, TWO AND THREE ON SIX DAYS, WHICH IS THIRTEEN, WHILE THE STATE PUBLISHES ELEVEN FOR IT; THAT DISCREPANCY IS PRE-EXISTING IN A MOVEMENT 1 FILE AND IS CARRIED FOR THE VOLUME 16 CLOSE, SO NO REMAINDER IS PUBLISHED HERE. THE COLUMN IS CLOSED ONCE, ON 810, AT THE VOLUME'S PUBLISHED FIGURE OF TWENTY-EIGHT DAYS AND NINETY-ONE MARKS.**

**THE SHEET. IT OPENS THIS MOVEMENT AT ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SIX THOUSAND THREE HUNDRED AND NINETY-FOUR PENCE OUT AND ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTEEN THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED AND FIFTY-FOUR PENCE SHORT, LINE FIVE SETTLES ON 782 AT SIX HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-EIGHT PENCE IN FIVE PARTS, AND THE TOTAL AT THE FOOT IS READ AFTER THAT SETTLEMENT AND STANDS AT ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN THOUSAND AND EIGHTY-TWO PENCE OUT, BEING SEVEN HUNDRED AND NINETY-FOUR MARKS, THREE SHILLINGS AND SIXPENCE, AND ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED AND FORTY-TWO PENCE SHORT, BEING SEVEN HUNDRED AND TWENTY-SEVEN MARKS, TEN SHILLINGS AND TWOPENCE, AGAINST TEN THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY PENCE IN, ON EVERY DAY FROM 782 TO THE CLOSE OF THE MOVEMENT. 126,394 + 688 = 127,082 AND 127,082 - 10,640 = 116,442. THE THIRD FORM WAS NOT USED AND IS SPENT ON 768. NO LINE OF THIS MOVEMENT IS STILL OWED.**

**THE TWO FIGURES THAT CARRY OUT UNRESOLVED, AND THE ARGUMENT ABOUT THEM THAT WAS NOT SETTLED.** THE BELL OF THE CINDER BELL IS ON THE ELEVENTH DAY OF BEING OUT OF SERVICE AT THE CLOSE OF 790 AND GOES BACK ON THE TWENTY-SECOND OF SEPTEMBER, BEING FOURTEEN DAYS COUNTED THE WAY THIS VOLUME COUNTS, AND THAT IS ONE DAY OF MOVEMENT 4. THE CINDER BELL'S OWN PAGE CARRIES TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-EIGHT DAYS AS THAT COMMUNITY KEEPS IT AND THE FOOT OF THE REFUSAL CARRIES TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-ONE, THE DIFFERENCE BEING SEVEN DAYS, AND TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-EIGHT OVER FOURTEEN IS SEVENTEEN WHILE TWO HUNDRED AND THIRTY-ONE OVER FOURTEEN IS SIXTEEN AND A HALF. ABOUT TWO PEOPLE WANTED THE FORTNIGHT AT FOURTEEN AND ABOUT TWO AT TWENTY-ONE, NEITHER SAID THE OTHER WAS WRONG, AND IT WAS NOT SETTLED IN THESE TEN DAYS.

**AND THE THREAD THAT IS PARKED BY NAME AND WAS NOT DROPPED. THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-TWO AND THE WOMAN OF THIRTY OF NO OFFICE ARE ON THE PAGE OF NINE OF THESE TEN DAYS AND ARE NEVER IN A ROOM WITH EACH OTHER AND NO PAGE. THEY ARE IN A ROOM TOGETHER ONCE, ON 790, WITH A PAGE IN IT: SHE FROM ABOUT HALF PAST TWELVE, HE FROM ABOUT TWENTY PAST ONE, FIFTY MINUTES, NEITHER SIGNING THE OTHER'S PAGE, NEITHER SAYING ONE WORD, NEITHER GIVING UP AN INCH OF THEIR OWN WORK. MOVEMENT 3 OWNS THE MIDPOINT, WHICH IS SPOKEN BY THE KEEPER ABOUT A COPYIST WHO IS NOT NAMED AS A PERSON, AND MOVEMENT 5 OWNS THE MARRIAGE GOING BACK TO ORDINARY WORK.**

**AND THE ARGUMENT OF THE TEN DAYS, IN ONE SENTENCE: A CORRECTION IS SUPPOSED TO BE FREE, AND ON THIS COAST A THING THAT WAS FREE TURNED OUT TO HAVE A PRICE THAT IS NOT MONEY, BECAUSE A TOTAL IS FOR DECIDING WHETHER TO DO A THING AGAIN AND A TOTAL THAT CANNOT BE SPENT CANNOT DECIDE ANYTHING, AND THE MAN WHO WROTE THE PAGE OUT DID NOT MAKE A MISTAKE, HE WROTE WHAT CAME BACK.**

**WHAT A WRITER OF THE NEXT MOVEMENT SHOULD COPY FROM THE VOICE AND NOT FROM THE FIGURES: a figure is worth what it can be spent against, and a page that has stood for three Wednesdays is furniture; a person who paid his own way has his figure read out loud to about four people so that he does not have to say it twice; a reason given three hours after a thing is done is worth more than a reason given at the moment it is done; and nobody in a yard of about nine people is thanked for anything on any of these ten days, and nobody in one is put on a step and asked anything either.**

### 781 — Friday the ninth day of September, day 21. Figures 514 / 2,444 / none / 125, hearing 279, tin 194. **An ordinary working day.** Line five stands on that sheet with the tenth of September on its face and is not in the foot of it, and the Saturday was named out loud twice before anything was written against it, once to about four people and once to about nine. Three sheets of one yard's own three seasons go on the bench stone with a copy of the page of the crossing beside them, the four figures read first and the three words at the top read last and slowly, because about four of that nine cannot read them. A man of about thirty-four of the second lay stands against the wall all morning and is not asked anything. One mark goes onto the middle sheet against the line heading and not against the coal and not against the oil.

### 782 — Saturday the tenth day of September, day 22. Figures 515 / 2,449 / none / 125, hearing 280, tin 195. **Line five settles and the foot is read after it.** The five parts are read with their multiplications before the sum goes down, and the last of the five is read twice, once into the shed and once out towards the step for the men that came in late. A man of about forty-two of the harbor authority asks out loud what that figure is for, and the keeper puts his pencil down before he answers him, because that man has the standing to take a sentence as an instruction and does not have the standing to take one as an opinion. No mark goes onto the face of anything.

### 783 — Sunday the eleventh day of September, day 23. Figures 516 / 2,454 / none / 125, hearing 281, tin 196. **A wipe, the hundred and twenty-third, 40/27/40 = 107.** The wall behind that reeve's bench comes off at about half past ten, stands bare twenty-seven minutes and goes back up at a quarter to one at the angle it has held since the twelfth of January and not whole. A man of about forty-nine of the west end says in about nine that it is a minute longer each way again and that he has asked twice and been told nothing. Two marks go onto one copy of the page of the crossing, both against the fourth of the four lines and neither against the three words at the top, and the second hand that put them there cannot prove a mark against the three words and does not try.

### 784 — Monday the twelfth day of September, day 24. Figures 517 / 2,459 / none / 125, hearing 282, tin 197. **A rota day, the hundred and eighty-third charge**, fourteen trips by hand and walked on by none of them, the figure written against that rota slate at about one and not read out. A sheet of this yard's own comes down off that end stall board at about eleven and goes back up at about twelve, through the first hole, by the man who put it there himself. He gives his reason at about four and not at about eleven, and nobody in that shed uses the word mistake, because a page taken off a board by the man who put it there and put back on it before the day is out has not been a mistake and has not been a correction, and those two words belong to offices and not to boards. This is the first of three withdrawals of this run.

### 785 — Tuesday the thirteenth day of September, day 25. Figures 518 / 2,464 / none / 125, hearing 283, tin 198. **THE MIDPOINT, IN ABOUT NINE PEOPLE, OUT OF A COPYING BOOK AND NOT OUT OF A SPEECH, AND THE NINETY-EIGHTH WAGE TUESDAY.** The column on the lid of that step is read out at about ten in four minutes and stands at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and did not move; the chest with the twenty envelopes in it is shut from ten until four and a further week is fallen due at the close. At about half past eleven the keeper brings the copying book down out of the room over that fish market and the woman of thirty of no office comes down with him and stands at the back of the shed and does not sit, and the man of about thirty-two is not in that yard. The four parts are read out first and every one of them is true; the fifth line under them is a single figure smaller than the four of them make and nobody in that shed holds it; a note in a second hand against it says the figure was asked for in writing by a place that had read the page and asked for a smaller one. The honest figure is on a sheet in a drawer in that record room and the drawer is not opened. The keeper says out loud, once, with no name on it, that the man who wrote that page out wrote what came back, and that the copyist of that room is a trade and not a person anybody in that shed has any standing over, and that in the whole of his working life he has never once written down a page nobody asked him to copy. Nobody says the word forgiven and nobody says the word ruined, and about four people look for both and neither arrives. Three marks go onto the face of that page before the book goes back up those stairs.

### 786 — Wednesday the fourteenth day of September, day 26. Figures 519 / 2,469 / none / 125, hearing 284, tin 199. **An ordinary working day, and the page that was on the outside copy is not the page in that room.** A man of about forty of the Ashtide Run lays a sheet he has had since April on the flat of that bench stone at about eleven, and at about two the keeper brings the page down out of that room and turns it over beside it, and about nine people stand round two sheets of the same size with the same four lines on them. He says out loud before anything is read that the two are not the same page and that neither of them is false, and that they differ in the first of the four lines and in nothing else, the difference being one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence. The keeper reads the top of both, and the top of both is the same three words, and reads them out loud, and says that the fault is in the three words and that the four lines under them are all of them true whichever of the two pages they are on. At about four the man of about forty rolls his sheet up and says he is taking it up that coast road on the Saturday and is not going to have anybody change one word of it. No mark goes onto the face of any page.

### 787 — Thursday the fifteenth day of September, day 27. Figures 520 / 2,474 / none / 125, hearing 285, tin 200. **A rota day, the hundred and eighty-fourth charge**, fourteen trips by hand and walked on by none of it. A woman of about twenty-nine of the Lowfen Reed comes into that market at about nine with a bundle of her own on her back and nothing at all in the bag on her shoulder, having set out on the Sunday and walked four days, and nobody sent for her, nobody carried anything for her and nobody asked her to stay. She is in that yard from about half past ten until about four, is given nothing to do and asks for nothing. At about one she puts her own page on the flat of that bench stone and about six people come and look at it and nobody reads it out, and a man of about thirty-one of the second lay puts one mark onto the face of it and gives no reason out loud. **At about half past three she asks one question in that shed in about nine people, and asks it once, and nobody in that shed answers it, and the keeper says out loud that he is not going to answer it in that shed on a Thursday.** It is not written onto any page of that yard, it is not entered in any column, it is not in the half-past-five slip, and nobody in that yard used it for anything else that afternoon.

### 788 — Friday the sixteenth day of September, day 28. Figures 521 / 2,479 / none / 125, hearing 286, tin 201. **Two pages of this harbor's own come down off that end stall board on one day.** At about ten a man of about forty-nine of the west end takes down one of his own three sheets, folds it once along the middle, puts it inside his coat against the other two, and does not put it back up at any hour of the day, and gives his reason out loud to about nine. At about two a man of about fifty-eight of the chandler's store takes down a sheet he put up himself at about ten that morning and puts it back up through the first hole at about three with the same figure and the same day and the same hour on it. Both men put those pages up themselves and took them down themselves. At about five the keeper makes a sheet for the harbor authority on the west basin and a man of about thirty-one of the second lay puts one mark on the face of it against the day and the hour and not against any figure. Nobody asked the woman of about twenty-nine anything about the Thursday, and about four people in that yard worked out in under a minute who was going to ask her, and neither of them did. This is the second withdrawal of this run and the only one of the two that is not put back.

### 789 — Saturday the seventeenth day of September, day 29. Figures 522 / 2,484 / none / 125, hearing 287, tin 202. **An ordinary working day with no charge on that cistern, no wipe and no wage movement.** A boat of that route's own is hired at about ten at the figure in chalk and is paid for whether anybody goes out on her or not, and nobody goes, and that hire is a figure in chalk and not a line on that sheet. The woman of about twenty-nine of the Lowfen Reed goes up that coast road at about seven that morning with a bundle on her back and nothing in her bag. The wall of the room over that chandler's store is bare and has been since the fourteenth of August, and the board beside it has stood empty from the same hour since the same day, and nothing went up on either. At about three a woman of about thirty-four of the Saltmarch puts three figures of her own on that end stall, the same three figures in the same order in her own hand as on the twenty-fifth day of August, and stands beside them for about half an hour without handing them to anybody, and says out loud that she has been told three times since the twenty-fifth of August that the bell is going to be seated on a Wednesday and that there have been three Wednesdays. The keeper says out loud that the days the men are off the water are that community's own figure and are not on any sheet in this yard and that this harbor has no column for them and never has had one. At about half past three she folds the three figures once, puts them inside her coat, and about nine people watch her do it. No mark goes onto the face of any page.

### 790 — Sunday the eighteenth day of September, day 30. Figures 523 / 2,489 / none / 125, hearing 288, tin 203. **A wipe, the hundred and twenty-fourth, 41/28/41 = 110, a minute longer each way again and nobody in this harbor has said why.** The wall behind that reeve's bench comes off at about half past ten, stands bare twenty-eight minutes and goes back up at a quarter to one, not whole. The woman of thirty of no office comes into that yard at about half past twelve with a page under her arm and the man of about thirty-two comes in at about twenty past one, and they are in the same yard for about fifty minutes with a page in the room the whole time, and neither of them signed the other's page and neither of them said one word to the other and neither of them gave up an inch of their own work over it. At about two two marks go onto the face of one copy of the page of the crossing, both against the fourth of the four lines, one the hand of a man of about fifty-eight of the chandler's store and the other the hand of a man of about forty-nine of the west end, and a mark on a line nobody can dispute is a mark saying the page is agreed with, and about four of that nine have read that page and about four have not. **At about half past four the keeper takes the page of days off the bench and writes the count of the withdrawn against the ten days of that run, and does not read it out in that shed and does not put it in any slip: the ten days stand at zero, zero, zero, one, zero, zero, zero, two, zero and zero, and the sum of those is three, and the base was zero on every day of it.** The drawer in that record room was not opened on any of the ten days of this run, and the correction and the refusal were standing at that end stall on their twenty-first day at the same size and a hand's breadth apart with the wrong figure showing underneath the correction and not struck out, and nobody said which of the two of them is right.

THE VOICE IS THIS HARBOR'S AND THE FIGURES ARE ITS OWN. **AND WHAT THE THIRD REPAIR PASS CHANGED ON THESE TEN DAYS AND NOTHING ELSE. THE NEXT WIPE IS *ON SUNDAY* ON 773 AND IT IS *NO WIPE COMES BEFORE SUNDAY* ON 779, AGAINST A ROTA DAY NAMED AS A WIPE DAY. THE KEEPER NO LONGER WRITES THE FOURTEEN ON 777; HE RULES THE LINE AND WRITES NOTHING INTO IT, AND THE ENTRY IS THE WOMAN'S ON THE TUESDAY NIGHT. THE ROAD OF THE MAN OF ABOUT THIRTY-EIGHT OF THAT LANDING IS THREE DAYS AND NOT FOUR, IN EIGHT PLACES ACROSS 771, 774 AND 779, AND THE FOUR-DAY FIGURE BELONGS TO THE WOMAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-TWO AND TO THE CINDER BELL AND THE LOWFEN REED, SO THE NEWSPRINT GOES UP ON THE SATURDAY, IS READ OUT AT ABOUT THREE ON THE MONDAY, AND THE CARRIER IS BACK AT ABOUT FOUR ON THE WEDNESDAY. THE BELL IS OUT OF SERVICE FROM THE EIGHTH TO THE TWENTY-SECOND, BEING FOURTEEN DAYS COUNTED THE WAY THIS VOLUME COUNTS, AND IS BACK IN SERVICE ON THE TWENTY-SECOND. THE HOUR AT TEN PAST SIX ON 780 IS TWENTY PAST FIVE, BEFORE THE READING AND AFTER THE SHEET PINNED AT FIVE. 778's CLOSING BLOCK CARRIES THE NINETY-SEVENTH AND NOT THE NINETY-SIXTH. NO FIGURE OF MONEY MOVED, NO DAY MOVED, NO LINE MOVED, AND 777's WORD COUNT IS THE ONLY ONE THAT MOVED, BY FOUR. MOVEMENT 1 CARRIED 2, 1, 2, 3, 2 AND 3 ON ITS SECOND, THIRD, FOURTH, SIXTH, SEVENTH AND NINTH DAYS FOR ELEVEN, AND THE VOLUME'S TOTAL OF TWENTY-EIGHT DAYS AND NINETY-ONE MARKS LEAVES SIXTEEN MORE DAYS AND SEVENTY-ONE MORE MARKS FOR MOVEMENTS 3, 4 AND 5 TOGETHER.**

**WHAT A WRITER OF THE NEXT MOVEMENT SHOULD COPY FROM THE VOICE AND NOT FROM THE FIGURES: a cost that is not a figure of money is entered in the hand of the place that pays it and is carried four days up a coast road rather than written down here; a document is read out once, by a working person, in the yard's own mouth, and everybody who needs it a second time is told to come and take the line off the sheet in that yard; the four heads on that wall stay four, and a correction and a refusal stay at the same size and the same height a hand's breadth apart; a stranger with a pencil is a cheaper clerk than any office four days up a road, and what he writes on the back of a bill belongs to whoever picks it up; and nobody in a yard of about nine people is thanked for anything on any of these ten days.**

**AND THE ONE SENTENCE THAT CARRIES THE WHOLE MOVEMENT, WHICH IS IN ABOUT NINE PEOPLE AT THE END STALL AND NOT IN A SUBTITLE: THE TREATY'S SCHEDULE ARRIVES AND IT IS A COPY, AND THE COPY IS WHAT A HARBOR WORKS FROM, AND IT CARRIES A LIST OF WHAT IS UNCLAIMED THAT IS BUILT OUT OF ENTRIES EVERY ONE OF WHICH IS TRUE, AND NOBODY MAY BE REPRESENTED WHO HAS NOT ASKED TO BE REPRESENTED, AND SO THE LIST STANDS UNTIL THE PEOPLE OF THAT PLACE DO SOMETHING THEMSELVES.**

**AND THE ARGUMENT OF THE TEN DAYS, IN ONE SENTENCE: A FORTNIGHT OF A BELL OUT OF SERVICE IN THE MIDDLE OF A WORKING SEASON IS THE FIRST COST THIS VOLUME HAS PAID THAT IS NOT A FIGURE ON ANYBODY'S SHEET, AND IT IS PAID OUT OF ONE COMMUNITY'S OWN PAGE, AND THE TWO FIGURES THAT MAKE IT A FORTNIGHT AT ALL ARE IN TWO PLACES' OWN HANDS AND DO NOT AGREE, AND THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THEM IS SEVEN DAYS.**

### 751 — Wednesday the tenth day of August, day 51. Figures 484 / 2,294 / none / 125, hearing 249, tin 164. **Line eleven settled into the foot of that money sheet at about four, and a boat of that landing went out over the bar at about six and lay alongside that mole again at about eight.**
Line eleven carried Monday the eighth for the work and Tuesday the ninth for the day the mechanism broke on its face and both were said out loud in about nine people before a figure was written: two times one hundred and sixty-eight for three hundred and thirty-six pence, sixty pence of rope and shackles, nine times two times sixteen for two hundred and eighty-eight pence, forty-four pence of sounding line and oil, being seven hundred and twenty-eight pence, four marks, seven shillings and fourpence. The foot read at the close of the day as it stood before the sum went down and stood at one hundred and twenty-one thousand one hundred and fifty-four pence out, and from the eleventh at one hundred and twenty-one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two. The ninth section of that bell and two of the other eight went down to that landing on that boat for a working reason given out loud at about ten: the frame above that room is coming down in parts under the order of the people of that landing and the ninth section was lying across the door of a room where nine people work, and they wanted it out of the room and not out of the harbor. A man of about thirty-four of the second lay said the crack across the seat of one of the other two would be cut out in that yard and not there, there being a vice and a bed in that yard and neither on that landing. At about one the man of about thirty-two said out loud that a boat had gone and what it had gone for and that he had stayed ashore, and nobody in that nine asked him why he was not on her.

### 752 — Thursday the eleventh day of August, day 52. Figures 485 / 2,299 / none / 125, hearing 250, tin 165. **A rota day, the hundred and seventy-fourth charge. Nine route delegates in that shed from about ten until about two put twenty-one words on the face of a page.**
The twenty-one words are that no one authority stands over nine routes at once, that a route is kept by the people of it, and that a thing kept by nine people is not kept by one person. A working man of about forty-four who keeps a page in a room off the west basin brought the page down and would not read it and stood back from it. The woman of thirty of no office read it out once, about four of that nine being able to read it and about five not. A chandler of about fifty-eight in that shed to buy a fathom of line counted it twice and wrote twenty-one on the top corner, that count being a count of words and not a figure of money and the counter's name on no page of this harbor. Six things went under those words and were read out once by the keeper: a keeping that turns and passes with no turn given to anybody who has not asked for it, a record kept in the place the route is, a bell and a buoy and a line mended by all nine and by nobody standing over them, provenance written where a stranger can read it, an error corrected in the same place and at the same size with the error left showing under it, and one person of a community able to take that community off a route with nobody asking why. **No fifth head went on that wall and nothing went up on account of a warning, a rescue, a dive, a claim, a seal, a refusal, a document or a victory. The assembly decided no contested claim, bound nobody who had not signed, and could not send anybody anywhere. The foot of the money sheet steps from the eleventh to one hundred and twenty-one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two pence out and one hundred and eleven thousand two hundred and forty-two short.**

### 753 — Friday the twelfth day of August, day 53. Figures 486 / 2,304 / none / 125, hearing 251, tin 166. **An ordinary working day with the far bench occupied from ten until four and nothing put on it. The public copy went up on the wall of the witness house at about four.**
The copy went down that lane in an open cart with a man of about thirty-six driving and the woman of thirty of no office at the near wheel and about four of that nine at the far wheel, there being one handle and it being the wrong side for two. The witness house is one room over a chandler's store with a door that stands open and a bench along the wall and nothing on that bench but a board, and a man of about thirty-three who keeps it said a person can come in off the lane without saying anything to anybody and hear what is said in that room and read what is on its wall without asking one of the nine people who keep it. Beside the copy the woman of thirty of no office put up a board in her own hand at the same size as the copy's heading, saying what is not known: that the ferry's manifest was altered and that it is not known whose hand altered it, at whose instance or with what intent, that no person is charged with it and none cleared of it, that the room is not the whole of what is known, and that a person who comes in there is not to take the wall for the coast. **The sealed record stayed under two marks put there by two people on the twenty-seventh of July, was not opened, not moved and not named, no third mark went on it, and nobody went up that hill.** The far bench was occupied from ten until four by a man of about sixty-one with his hands black to the second joint at the nails and nothing was put on it and read as a gift and nobody sent for him and nobody thanked him, and the man of about thirty-two did not go over to it at any hour of that day.

### 754 — Saturday the thirteenth day of August, day 54. Figures 487 / 2,309 / none / 125, hearing 252, tin 167. **Line twelve worked at about two carrying the fifteenth on its face, and all four heads on that wall put to use at about three.**
Glass and frames for a case at two hundred and forty pence, two seats and a bench at fifty pence, a stove and its pipe at one hundred and twenty pence, four men at four days at sixteen pence a man-day at four times four times sixteen for two hundred and fifty-six pence, being six hundred and sixty-six pence, four marks, two shillings and twopence. A claim was brought up by a woman of about thirty-four of the Saltmarch, a public correction by a man of about forty-nine of the Morrow Line with the wrong figure left showing under it, a refusal by a woman of about thirty of the Ashtide Run to have her hours read out with nobody to be given her reason, and a restricted record as the notice of a thing that is not shown. **The refusals were written at the same size as the claim and the correction and nobody in that nine said that woman was wrong.** The keeper named the four heads and that fitting-out sheet out loud and apart and said a claim may not be counted with a contribution and a refusal may not be counted with either. At about half past four the man of about thirty-two said he had read the entry the woman of thirty of no office wrote on Tuesday about a request made on the sixth and a refusal given on the sixth and was not going to ask her to soften one word of it.

### 755 — Sunday the fourteenth day of August, day 55. Figures 488 / 2,314 / none / 125, hearing 253, tin 168. **A wipe and the hundred and nineteenth at thirty-six off, twenty-three bare and thirty-six back, being ninety-five the whole of it, and the last wipe before that wall comes down bare again.**
Thirty-six off and twenty-three bare and thirty-six back is ninety-five and it is a minute longer each way and a minute longer bare than the one before it and nobody has said why and nobody has asked. The man of about thirty-two stood on the stones at about eleven for the whole of the time that wall stood bare and did not go inside and did not go up a ladder and did not go near the water, and said out loud that he had not asked to be asked and was not going to be asked. At about half past twelve the man of about twenty-nine put his left hand flat on that bench stone and found it cold and found it wet and took it away and put it in his coat, and nobody asked him why and nobody asked him to do it again and nobody said his name out loud at any hour of that day, and no figure of money stands against any part of it. At about one the woman of thirty of no office read her Tuesday entry out loud once and said she was not going to read it a second time because a thing read twice in one week is a thing the room has begun to own. At about three a boat of about twenty tons went out of that quay with four men in her for the two sections that came down on Wednesday and was not going for the man.

### 756 — Monday the fifteenth day of August, day 56. Figures 489 / 2,319 / none / 125, hearing 254, tin 169. **A rota day, the hundred and seventy-fifth charge, and line twelve settled into the foot of that money sheet at about four.**
The four parts were read with their multiplications before the sum went down and the thirteenth and the fifteenth were both on the face of the line and had been on it since the Saturday. The foot was read at the close of that day as it stood before the sum went down and stands at one hundred and twenty-one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two pence out and one hundred and eleven thousand two hundred and forty-two short, and from the sixteenth it stands at one hundred and twenty-two thousand five hundred and forty-eight out and one hundred and eleven thousand nine hundred and eight short. Hours came down that road at about two in the hand of the man of about thirty-eight saying the two sections that came down on Wednesday were put on a bed at that landing on the Friday afternoon, that the frame is down to two of nine and both are hung, and that the ninth section is laid on dunnage in a room where nine people work and has not been rung since about half past two in the morning of the ninth.

### 757 — Tuesday the sixteenth day of August, day 57. Figures 490 / 2,324 / none / 125, hearing 255, tin 170. **The ninety-fourth wage Tuesday and the last of those eight, the column unmoved and a further week fallen due.**
The column on the lid of that step was read at about ten in four minutes by a man of about thirty-one of the second lay and came to twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and did not move, and the chest with the twenty envelopes in it was shut from ten until four. The keeper said out loud at about eleven that eight Tuesdays was a run and not an ending, that the ninth would fall due on the twenty-third, and that nothing about that Tuesday had changed since the twenty-eighth of June. The man of about thirty-two said at about one that a wage Tuesday is the day a harbor finds out what it owes and that finding out is not paying, and the woman of thirty of no office said her own figure of forty marks first after food for a person of no office had not gone down either and that she was not going to say it out loud in a yard where nothing was paid so that hers sounded like a complaint. **Hours came down at about two saying the ninth section of that bell was cut into two at that landing on the Friday with a saw and a man of about fifty holding it, that the two pieces were set on two beds, and that nobody at that landing has asked for it to be rung.**

### 758 — Wednesday the seventeenth day of August, day 58. Figures 491 / 2,329 / none / 125, hearing 256, tin 171. **The four sentences, in a working place, and no forgiveness.**
A man of about sixty-one with his hands black to the second joint at the nails came down that lane at about ten, did not go to the far bench and came to that shed instead, and put the original repair log on the dry end of that stone. He said four sentences and did not say a fifth: that he signed that log after the cut and not before it; that he knew the water was already moving under that ground and signed anyway because the yard had a berth to keep and his part of it was the signing; that he has never once in any of the years since said so out loud to anybody at that table; and that he is not asking for anything and is not giving anything. **Nobody said the second and third of those four back to him, nobody wrote them on a board, and the log was not read out and was not entered in a column and was not put on the boards at the back of that market and is not that yard's.** About four of that nine said nothing while he said them, about four looked at the log and not at him, and about four went out and stood in the yard. His wife, a woman of about fifty-eight, stood at the door of that shed for about four minutes and did not come in and nobody stopped work for her, and after she had gone he said one more thing that was not one of the four. **At about half past three the man of about thirty-two said out loud that he was not going to forgive his father and that nobody in that shed was to say whether he had or had not, and that a man who has been silent for years has not bought anything with that silence and has not lost anything by stopping. The far bench was empty all day and nothing was put on it.**

### 759 — Thursday the eighteenth day of August, day 59. Figures 492 / 2,334 / none / 125, hearing 257, tin 172. **A rota day, the hundred and seventy-sixth charge, and line thirteen worked at about two carrying the nineteenth on its face.**
Bell metal and a seat at one hundred and eight pence, line of forty yards at three pence the yard at forty times three for one hundred and twenty pence, coal for four days at forty pence, four men at four days at sixteen pence a man-day at four times four times sixteen for two hundred and fifty-six pence, being five hundred and twenty-four pence, three marks, three shillings and eightpence. At about half past three a boat of about nine tons came in over the bar with a man of about fifty of that landing in her and a piece of bell metal wrapped in sacking in her foot, and he said out loud that the ninth section of that bell had been cut in two on the Friday with a saw and had not been rung since, and that nobody at that landing had asked for it, and that one of the two pieces was going into a new seat and one into a fire. **At about half past ten the man of about thirty-two said he had been on no water since the sixth of August and was not going on any today and that his hearing in the left side was the same as it had been every day since. NO FIGURE OF MONEY IS SET AGAINST THE HEARING IN THE LEFT SIDE, OR THE TASTE THAT DOES NOT LIFT, OR THE JOINT IN THE KNEE, OR THE NIGHTS HE DOES NOT SLEEP, OR THE AFTERTASTE THAT SITS ON TOP OF ONE HE ALREADY HAD, AND NONE WILL BE SET.**

### 760 — Friday the nineteenth day of August, day 60. Figures 493 / 2,339 / none / 125, hearing 258, tin 173. **Line thirteen settled and the total read AFTER that settlement at 123,072 out and 112,432 short. The read-back. The page of routes for the third and last time. The final entry with five named witnesses. A boat out over that bar at about five with no escort and nine buoys of nine shapes answering one another.**
A boat of about eleven tons went out over that bar at about five in the morning with three men in her and nobody on her quarter, no boat following her and none standing off that mole head to see her out, and nobody wrote down anywhere what that boat was for. Between about six and about seven the nine buoys off that mole head answered one another in the order they have always answered in and at the two hours a day those nine have kept, being a barrel, a cone, a spar, a triangle, a can, a spar with a flag on it, a double cone, a round and a square, and the sound came across that water nine separate times and stayed nine separate times and did not come out as one note. At about two the woman of thirty of no office read out the final entry in about nine people with five of them named as having heard it, carrying what nine places agreed, what one man refused, and what was asked for and was not granted, and carrying on its own face what is not known. **The man of about thirty-two read it as it was written, put no word into it, and said out loud that he could not put a word into it that would make the choice of the man who is in the ninth section read kinder than that entry reads it.** At about half past three that leaf was read back in the yard's own mouth and in the open, all four columns including the empty one, read twice because about five of that party cannot read a column, both times in the same words and in the same mouth, with its own derivation on the face of it, being four hundred and ninety-two and two thousand three hundred and thirty-seven at the hour of that reading and four hundred and ninety-three and two thousand three hundred and thirty-nine, none and one hundred and twenty-five at the close of it. **The three counts were not taken again. Line thirteen settled at about four and the total at the foot was read after that settlement. The page of routes was written for the third and last time at four held, two restricted and three dormant, the Orison Descent held and the Tidewatch Channel dormant, the sum written at the foot and not said in a room and not in any slip.**

come away from the Orison headland two days of water and a night down the coast. **747** the reason was written at about half past ten in the same words as the one he wrote in June and again on the second of August, the man of about fifty-six has been on the other line since the thirtieth, and the one name was said out loud once in that room by the man of about thirty-eight, who wrote that he day, and a man of about fifty-six died with that section in that hour, and no body is named and no figure of any kind is printed against it and nobody was called anything and nobody was thanked. **AND ### 740 — Saturday the thirtieth day of July, day 40. Figures 473 / 2,239 / none / 125, hearing 238, tin 153. **Ordinary working day; the scattering begins under a pilot's own order.** A word at the boards at about ten that two ships are standing in about four miles off the mouth and neither is moving. A pilot of about forty-one of a creek three days up that coast road hires this yard's boat for two days at the figure in chalk at 2 × 168 = 336, being two marks and sixteen pence, puts the figure in his own book in chalk, and says the order is his own. At about eleven in about nine he says he will take her between the shoals on the ebb on a set he remembers, that two ships drawing what those two draw cannot follow the deep water in, and that the chart of about nine years standing is a chart of a coast that has moved. She clears the bar at about twenty to eleven. Two bell answers at about half past two and about twenty to three, in hours and not in names.

The eight hours go on a sheet by themselves with no place named. The yard's own instruments are tried afterwards and agree, and a woman of about fifty-eight who lost a roof in the spring says the glass and the water are right and the hour is not. Two small boats in and a second watch from about one, and nobody sent up that coast road.
### 742 — Monday the first day of August, day 42. Six of the eight did something and the six things were not one thing. The eighth gives a time in its own hand for the first time since the spring. At about four a man of about thirty-eight comes down that road with a sheet of hours from the ninth bell above Orison and says a man of an office there is on the line and has asked in writing for a diver and a tender, and that the name under the seal is not on that sheet.

Line ten onto the sheet at about two carrying the second and the fourth on its face, 2,370 in five parts, not settled. The reason for one descent at Orison written at about one in the diver's own hand with the hour against it. The boat away at about four with nine men in her.
### 744 — Wednesday the third day of August, day 44. Figures 477 / 2,259 / none / 125, hearing 242, tin 157. **The Ninth Bell named for the first time in that yard's book; the forced held line.** A man of about fifty-six, thin, who dries his hands before he touches any glass, has been on a line in about nineteen fathoms since the thirtieth. The reason is written at about half past nine in the keeper's hand with no consent on the page. At about eleven he says out loud through the bell and not into the room that a bell answered by nine things would be answered by nine disagreements. At about ten past eleven he puts his memory into the bell and nobody in the room can stop it, because the room is above the water. The limit of twenty-five comes and goes twice and is not met, the cutoff is not pulled, and at the fourth hour he cannot tell what he remembered from what he was given. A question goes up that coast road at about two in Calder's own hand.
### 745 — Thursday the fourth day of August, day 45. Figures 478 / 2,264 / none / 125, hearing 243, tin 158. **A rota day, the hundred and seventy-second charge. The answer comes down that lane at about one in the woman of thirty of no office's hand with the hour against it and no name on it, being that a person who has put himself into a thing without being asked is not to be taken out of it by the people standing round it, and that a person is not a bell. The bell ran at ten, two and four and the man on it was asked nothing and gave nothing and the chain did not move. The boat out at about six.
### 746 — Friday the fifth day of August, day 46. Figures 479 / 2,269 / none / 125, hearing 244, tin 159. **The foot steps to 121,154 out and 110,514 short from this day. The central record is not touched and is not in that market. Read out once at about two. At about three Calder says in about nine that he will not decide which of the six is right and that this yard's name goes on none of them. The four heads and the money sheet are named out loud and apart at about five.
### 747 — Saturday the sixth day of August, day 47. Figures 480 / 2,274 / none / 125, hearing 245, tin 160. **The second held line, about twenty-two minutes against twenty-five, not pulled.** The reason written at about half past nine in the same words as on the third. At twenty-two minutes the distributed routes hold, not in one voice, for about a minute, and he comes up by himself and the tender does not pull the cutoff. He surfaces not fine and is not fine at three and at four. At about two Calder says out loud in about nine that the man on the line is the ninth section and that he is not going to pull him out of it and is not going to ask anybody else to. ### 749 — Monday the eighth day of August, day 49. Figures 482 / 2,284 / none / 125, hearing 247, tin 162. **A rota day, the hundred and seventy-third charge. The woman of thirty of no office says her record carries the request, the refusal, both hands and the hour, and that he is not to speak for her. No body is named, no figure is printed, nobody was called anything and nobody was thanked.

Sheet 116,746 out, 106,106 short; bag twenty-eight pence throughout; no state put on any of the nine.**

### 713 — Sunday the third day of July, day 13. Figures 446 / 2,104 / none / 125, hearing 211, tin 126. **A wipe, the hundred and thirteenth, 30 off, 17 bare, 30 back, being 77 the whole of it, from about ten past ten to about twenty-seven minutes past eleven.** A page comes down the coast road at about two in the hand of a woman of about fifty-eight, being that community's own page and carrying a time in the plain hand of a man who fishes that water. Beside the time there is a second mark, a short stroke laid with a flat brush, sitting where a hand would go. The keeper writes both with the hour against them, writes that the second is not a hand and that this yard will not find out whose it is, and does not write it under the time. The man of about thirty-two comes at about four and says that a mark is not a time and a time is not a consent.

### 714 — Monday the fourth day of July, day 14. Figures 447 / 2,109 / none / 125, hearing 212, tin 127. **A rota day, the hundred and sixty-third charge, eleven trips by hand, walked on by none of it.** A man of about fifty-six comes down the road at about eleven with a bundle of reed and shows the back of the page, where the damp came through two sheets at once, and says a seam shows that two things were different and never which of them was true. He says that channel has cut a new bed about a boat's breadth east of the old one and the reed is the same reed over both, and that both beds are true water and one of them is where the fish are. He is asked one thing, being whether the time would hold, and says about a week.

### 715 — Tuesday the fifth day of July, day 15. Figures 448 / 2,114 / none / 125, hearing 213, tin 128. **The eighty-eighth wage Tuesday, the lid read at about ten in four minutes, twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks, not moved, the chest shut ten until four, the eighty-eighth week fallen due. Line six goes onto the sheet with the fifth of July against it and settles on the seventh.** The woman of thirty of no office begins a second book at about half past three and puts the two apart, one on the bench stone and one on the shelf above the butt. She gives her reason in about nine and the man of about thirty-two gives the objection he gave in June, and about four agree with each and the matter is open. One man takes his page at about five and goes down the road and nobody asks him why.

### 716 — Wednesday the sixth day of July, day 16. Figures 449 / 2,119 / none / 125, hearing 214, tin 129. **An ordinary working day; the pump stops weeping at about eleven and sixty yards of new rope go out and come back wet.** A man of about forty-seven comes down the road at about one in the coat he laid the stroke in and says in the first half-minute that he laid it. He says a paper came to that creek in the spring with a table wanting a time, asking for no person and naming no person and carrying no figure against anything, and that what it went with was a line saying two households would be left alone. He says he put the stroke on because he believed a settled page would be read at the front office as a cooperative place, and that he would do it again on a page of that kind. Nobody in that shed said what would have been said about a man who does that.

### 717 — Thursday the seventh day of July, day 17. Figures 450 / 2,124 / none / 125, hearing 215, tin 130. **A rota day, the hundred and sixty-fourth charge. Line six settled into the foot of the sheet at about four, being 1,348 pence in five parts, and the total goes into the foot of it in the morning at 116,014 out and 105,374 short.** About nine people meet in a room at the Lowfen Reed from about ten and read that community's own page out loud twice, and this yard is not in that room and sends nobody. At about three the woman of about fifty-eight says they have agreed to take the time back and will not be asked why. A man of about twenty-six and a woman of about thirty-one go home by different roads in the afternoon and only the hour of each is written.

### 718 — Friday the eighth day of July, day 18. Figures 451 / 2,129 / none / 125, hearing 216, tin 131. **The Lowfen Reed closes itself in four sentences in its own hand at about two in about nine people.** The time was given by a man who was not free to refuse it. The seam shows a mark was taken off and cannot show which, and a thing which cannot tell a willing hand from a pressed hand cannot show the rest of that coast's pages are good. The route is closed from that morning in their hand and not this yard's. They will not be asked why. The Lowfen Reed puts itself into the dormant column of the page of routes on its own saying, and the three columns of that page are not counted on that day. Nobody in that shed called that route anything, and four stones are their own and will be looked at in the spring by their own people, and this yard offered no boat and sent no hand.

### 719 — Saturday the ninth day of July, day 19. Figures 452 / 2,134 / none / 125, hearing 217, tin 132. **The first of the four heads on that wall are used, being a claim and a public correction, both at the same size as the rest and neither by this yard.** A claim, from the woman of about fifty-eight, that her community's page go up with the seam showing and the flat stroke showing and no explanation attached to either. A public correction, of a sentence said at that end stall on the eighth which said that the Lowfen Reed had never given a time. Both read out twice by a man of about thirty-one. Four holding stones are cut and faced at the third lay from about seven to about eleven and the line paying for them is not written until Monday, because that line carries two days and one of them is not yet past. One person of about nineteen leaves the room over the market at about one with her own page.

### 720 — Sunday the tenth day of July, day 20. Figures 453 / 2,139 / none / 125, hearing 218, tin 133. **A wipe, the hundred and fourteenth, 31 off, 18 bare, 31 back, being 80 the whole of it.** A fisher pilot of about fifty-eight goes out at about eleven with two men of his own community and none of this yard. His water is right on the chart and not on the ground, and both of those are true, and the channel has cut about a boat's breadth east and taken the deep water with it. He came up on the set he remembered at about half past one and found flat and hard and shallow, and stood her up in his own water until the ebb began to run out of it. Then the three of them agreed in the boat that he would hold to what he remembered and they would watch where the water went. Two bells answered at about two on the second try at about a boat's breadth east of the water he was born on. The Cinder Bell's name stands against that hour with nothing against the name.

### 721 — Monday the eleventh day of July, day 21. Figures 454 / 2,144 / none / 125, hearing 219, tin 134. **A rota day, the hundred and sixty-fifth charge. Line seven goes onto the sheet at about two carrying two days on its face, being the ninth as the day the work was done and the eleventh as the day four stones of that creek were let go, and the keeper says the second day out loud before writing the figure.** Four stones are let go before eleven by that community's own people on a slack tide with a barge line under them, and no paper came about it and no man told a man of about twenty-two to do it. Line seven is 732 pence in four parts and settles on Tuesday and is not struck. Three people of that line go home in the course of the day and only the hour of each is written.

### 722 — Tuesday the twelfth day of July, day 22. Figures 455 / 2,149 / none / 125, hearing 220, tin 135. **The eighty-ninth wage Tuesday, the lid read at about ten in four minutes and not moved. The other two of the four heads are used, being a refusal and a restricted record, both at the same size as the rest of that wall.** The refusal is that no hand of this yard shall go into that creek for any work and that a boat will be asked for in words and paid for in chalk like any other boat. The restricted record is that community's page with the seam showing in a folder that is not opened in that room and comes out only when one person of that community says it may, and is not copied into either book. Line seven is settled into the foot of the sheet at about four and the total goes in in the morning at 116,746 out and 106,106 short.

### 723 — Wednesday the thirteenth day of July, day 23. Figures 456 / 2,154 / none / 125, hearing 221, tin 136. **Eight bells come in at the reading on that mole at about ten where nine were due, and no reason is written against the late one, which is the first time since this yard began keeping a page of days.** A sheet of tin is riveted under the seat of that bell off the mole carrying that office's own figures for a seizure in the winter and a column headed with the reason given at the time. It is read out once at about two on the boards at the back of that market in front of about twenty people of whom about eleven cannot read it: eleven boats off that coast, three off a creek and four off a shoal and four off a mole, and the reason that the bells of those three places could not be answered from the seaward side and that the Keel required one voice at each of them. Nobody said the reason was wrong and nobody argued with it. Three of the eleven were off the Lowfen Reed's own water and the keeper writes the creek's name and the figure of three with no word against anybody.

### 724 — Thursday the fourteenth day of July, day 24. Figures 457 / 2,159 / none / 125, hearing 222, tin 137. **A rota day, the hundred and sixty-sixth charge and the last rota day of this movement.** A woman of about thirty-four of that creek comes down the road at about two, stands at the flat of that bench stone without taking her coat off, and withdraws herself from the Lowfen Reed line from that day, having told her own people before she came. One person of a community is enough and the keeper asked her nothing and wrote no name against her. The three columns of the page of routes are not counted today. The tin under that bell seat is this yard's to take down and nobody altered it.

### 725 — Friday the fifteenth day of July, day 25. Figures 458 / 2,164 / none / 125, hearing 223, tin 138. **A cart wheel goes over the corner of the first of the two books at about half past two and two leaves are spoiled beyond reading, being the twelfth and thirteenth of July, and the second was on the shelf and is dry and carries the same figures, and the two spoiled days are read out of it before five.** The disagreement between the two of them is put in the open at about four in about nine people, is answered and not met, and is not settled. The reading of that creek is quieter than it was on the thirteenth, two people did not come down that road, and about nine people waited at the end stall until about ten past six.

### 726 — Saturday the sixteenth day of July, day 26. Figures 459 / 2,169 / none / 125, hearing 224, tin 139. **MOVEMENT 2 CLOSES. The count of those who went home is taken off the page of days at about half past three and written down once and said nowhere, being 0, 0, 1, 0, 2, 0, 1, 0, 3, 0, 0, 1, 0, 3, and eleven is the sum.** It is a count of departures and never of refusals, disagreements or people who were wrong, and a person who put a hand on that page and went home is on it once and on no other sheet. The column of the hands that rang stands at thirty and was not taken again. The bell off that mole answers the bell off a shoal four days down that coast road at about half past ten and again at about three, in hours and not in names. The woman of thirty of no office says out loud that eleven is a small number of people to have lost off nine lines in a fortnight and that nobody in that shed should make it smaller or larger by telling the story twice. Nobody was thanked for the taking of it.
