### Chapter 541 — *Wednesday the Twelfth Day of January, Not a Rota Day and Not a Wage Tuesday and Not a Wipe, a Cart Going Down That Coast Road on Monday the Ninth of December Past and Coming Back Up at About Half Past Eleven in the Morning on the Wednesday With Three Windows and Three Bells Written on the Back of a Page in Three Different Hands, a Page of Hours Read Out Loud on That Bench Stone Before a Word of It Was Written With No Name at the Head of It, Three Crews Asked in the Same Eighteen Words and Three Answers, Eight Slates Carrying a Reason in Each Man's Own Words and the Hour and Twenty-Five Minutes of Air, a Man of About Thirty-Three Who Hires Hands Asking Out Loud Who Is in Charge and Being Answered in About Sixty Words, the Shortfall Said Out Loud Unmoved at Sixty-Five Thousand Eight Hundred and Fifty Pence*

**THE NIGHT OF THE THREE IS ARRANGED AND IT IS ARRANGED WITHOUT A HEAD.** A clean sheet goes on that bench stone at about ten in the morning with three windows and three bells on it, and it is read out loud in full before a word of it is written, and **there is no name at the head of it, and the man who keeps the leaf says out loud, once, that a name at the top of three things is a man who is in none of them by the small hours, and that a page a stranger can take three hours off is a page worth having and a page with his name at the top of it is a page that a stranger has to take his word for.** The three windows are half past eleven to one o'clock, twenty past one to half past two, and twenty to three to about five to four, and the three bells belong to the first, second and third marks on the page that went up on four tacks on the boards of that market on the twenty-sixth of December. At about half past eleven a cart comes back up that coast road and the back of that page carries the three windows in three different hands, being three names and two and three, and the man of about thirty-two is the bottom of the three on the first of them. **Hobb Lee, of about forty-six, who mends nets on the third lay and put that page up, stands at the bench stone and says in about fifty words that three hands and three answers is a page being honest about who is in it, and that nobody in that port was asked for anything.** Eight slates are written at about two in the afternoon, three read out in that shed and five at the boats, and each carries a reason in that man's own words, the hour, and twenty-five minutes of air, and **none of them carries a name, being that a slate with a name on it is a slate an employer can read and a slate with a boat and an hour on it is a slate a man can be held to.** Three named tenders are named: Ivo Sark, of about twenty-four, in a dinghy at the first point; a pump hand of about forty-four with nineteen years of compressors at the second, who is in nobody's crew; and **a woman of about thirty-four of that commonwealth in a boat of her own at the third, who is not in that yard, and whose condition is still on the face of a record four hundred yards from that bench stone and is not settled, and who is given the tender because a person who brought a condition is owed the first refusal of a thing that is dangerous and not the first thanks.** A man of about thirty-three who hires hands asks who is in charge and is answered in about sixty words: a mark not put in means a bell not rung, a bell not rung means a boat stays out, and he is the man who finds things out before Sunday. A woman of about fifty-two at a fish stall says the three bells are the only part of the page she would have been able to hear, and is asked nothing further. Nothing goes onto that sheet. The shortfall is said out loud at half past five, unmoved at sixty-five thousand eight hundred and fifty pence, being four hundred and eleven marks, seven shillings and sixpence.

### Chapter 542 — *Thursday the Thirteenth Day of January, a Rota Day, the Hundred and Sixteenth Charge in Eleven Trips by Hand, Four Lines Going Onto That Sheet at About Ten in the Morning at Four Thousand Six Hundred and Eight Pence, Being Twenty-Eight Marks, Ten Shillings and Eightpence, With the Twelfth and the Thirteenth Both on the Face of All Four, Eight Bottles Charged in a Shipyard Eight Days Under a Roof Because There Is Nowhere Else in That Harbor to Charge a Bottle, Three Crews Asked in the Same Eighteen Words Before Anybody Was Off a Slip, a Pump Hand of About Forty-Four Asking Out Loud What Happens If the Plan Fails*

**THE DAY'S COST IS BOUGHT AND IT IS BOUGHT FOR A NIGHT.** Bread and salt for nine men for two days at eighty pence a head a day, being 2 × 720 = 1,440, being nine marks; coal for two nights for the pumps, 480, being three marks; air for eight men for the one night of Friday the fourteenth at two hundred and eighty pence a man, being 8 × 280 = 2,240, being fourteen marks, with the thirteenth and the fourteenth both on the face of it and no second day on it, and **the figure a day's air came in at on the thirtieth of December for four men divided by four is two hundred and eighty, and this yard has not moved that figure since the thirtieth**; and a coil of line, tin and lamp oil for three lamps quoted by the woman who keeps that counter and not argued with, at 448, being two marks, ten shillings and eightpence. **That is four thousand six hundred and eight pence, being twenty-eight marks, ten shillings and eightpence, and the twelfth and the thirteenth are both on the face of all four lines.** The cistern is charged at about eight in eleven trips by hand and walked on by none of it, the name at the head of that rota board is still off it, and **the figure of that hundred is said out loud once with a clerk's own name and the hour under it and is not said out loud a second time this winter.** Eight bottles are charged at about eleven in the morning in a shipyard on that quay **because that compressor is in that building and there is nowhere else in that harbor to charge a bottle, and a compressor has to run in a building and a building has to have a fire under it** — and that is the whole of what the roof of the sixth, seventh and eighth bought, said out loud on the day and not said again. A pump hand of about forty-four with nineteen years of compressors asks one question out loud and it is not about the eighteen words: **what happens if the plan fails, not what happens to me, and he wants to know what the eight of us do.** He is answered in about sixty words: if a bell at the first point has gone and the bell at the second point has not gone inside a quarter of an hour of one o'clock, and one o'clock is the hour the first window closes, then the eight of them come up and the third point does not start, and it is on the page of hours that was read out in that shed the day before in front of nine people. He says a quarter of an hour is not a plan and that a quarter of an hour is what a man can say out loud in a room. A man of about nineteen of the second lay asks who pays him and is told one hundred and sixty-eight pence a day at the figure in chalk in advance on the day before, out of a fund that pays a day for a day, and **that his name goes in the book the days are paid out of and does not go on that sheet, and that the reason is not given, because a sheet that can be leaned on cannot be checked.** The man of about thirty-two is asked the same eighteen words at about half past two and says yes in one word and is not thanked, and **has not a word of the first window in his own hand, because the first window is in the hand of the man of about fifty-one who crews four out of the first lay.**

### Chapter 543 — *Friday the Fourteenth Day of January, Not a Rota Day and Not a Wage Tuesday and Not a Wipe, Three Crews Leaving a Quay Four Days Down That Coast at About Nine and Ten in the Evening in Three Boats From Three Different Slips, Three Bells on Three Marks, Eight Men Over the Rail Between About Half Past Eleven and About Twenty to Four One at a Time, Two Cutoffs Pulled Without Anybody Asking and One Ascent Asked for and Not Argued With, Nine Boats Inside That Line on That Ebb and Seven of Them Back Before Six in the Morning and Two Found on the Ground on the Morning of the Fifteenth, Both Empty, Both Crews Ashore, Not One Man Hurt*

**THE NIGHT.** The three crews go out at about nine and about ten in the evening from three different parts of that quay, and not one man of one of them is in the same boat as a man of another. Ivo Sark is in a dinghy at the first point and not in the water at any hour; the pump hand of about forty-four is in a dinghy at the second; **the woman of about thirty-four of that commonwealth is in a boat of her own off the third point and is not in that water at any hour.** The bell on the first mark goes at about half past eleven and is not rung again and the first man is over the rail at about half past eleven and is on the bottom at about thirty-five minutes past eleven and his helmet is off at about five minutes to twelve, being four down and nineteen on the floor and two up, which is twenty-five of his twenty-five. The second man of that point is over at about twelve o'clock and on the bottom at about five minutes past twelve and **at about twenty-four minutes past twelve the tender calls for the cutoff because that man has said nothing for two minutes, and it is pulled without anybody asking, and the word comes about four seconds after it is called for, and his helmet still comes off at about half past twelve, being five down and eighteen on the floor and two up.** The man of about thirty-two is third at that point, over at about twenty-five minutes to one, on the floor at about twenty to one, helmet off at about one o'clock, and he asks for nothing and the cutoff is not pulled on him. A boat of about eleven tons goes inside that line at about ten to two in the morning with victual in her and six men in her and is out of it again before three. **The bell on the second mark goes at about ten past one, which is inside a quarter of an hour of one o'clock, which is the hour the first window closed, and that is the condition the pump hand asked for on the Thursday and is the first thing anybody in that port had asked for and been given in writing before it happened.** Two men there, the first over at about twenty past one and up at about twenty to two, the second over at about five past two and **at about twenty-five minutes to three he asks out loud for his ascent to be called and it is called and nobody argues with him about it**, helmet off at about half past two; he asks in the boat for a cup of water and for nothing else. The bell on the third mark goes at about twenty to three and three men go there, the last helmet off at about five to four, with one cutoff pulled at about twenty-four minutes past three without anybody asking; the last of the three is a man of about nineteen of the second lay who was paid one hundred and sixty-eight pence in advance on the day before out of a fund that pays a day for a day. **Nine boats went inside that line on that ebb and seven of them were back inside it before six o'clock in the morning, and the two that were not back were found on the morning of the fifteenth lying on the ground off the outer water about forty yards apart with their bows pointing the same way, each with a hole under the forefoot about the size of a man's two hands, the gear of each in the bottom and no gear on either deck, and there was nobody standing on either and there had been nobody standing on either since about half past four. Both crews were in the other boats and were on that quay at about six in the morning and not one man of them was hurt and no body is named and no figure of any person is printed and a lost boat is a boat and is not a lost man.** There was a fourth mark in that water and it is not one of the five on the page and it is a piece of lead in a hole in a stone under about four fathoms, and nobody at that port has a name for whoever put it in and nobody asked for one. **The man who keeps the leaf is not the tender at any of the three, and there was one man in the whole of that night who could have told any of the other seven what to do and he did not use it, and he says that out loud.** A man of about twenty-nine was in a hut on a shoulder above a street of about forty houses and heard three bells he cannot name and a pump he has never walked up to and himself, and a man of about thirty-three who hires hands wrote down the three hours and wrote down nothing else, and **nobody in that port said one word about any of it which made him anything and no figure is set against it and he is a member of nothing.**

### Chapter 544 — *Saturday the Fifteenth Day of January, Not a Rota Day and Not a Wage Tuesday and Not a Wipe, Two Boats Found on the Ground off the Outer Water at About Six in the Morning With a Hole Under the Forefoot of Each and the Gear of Each in the Bottom and Nobody Standing on Either, Three Bells Not Rung Again, Nine Boats Counted In and Seven Counted Back, Four Marks in That Water and Three of Them Answered For on a Page on Four Tacks, a Man of About Thirty-Three Asking Out Loud Why Two Boats Are Going on a Sheet That Did Not Put Them on the Ground and Being Answered in About Nine Words, a Second Week of a Room Over a Store at Ternwatch at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two Pence With the Twelfth of January Against It and Settled on the Fifteenth*

**THE MORNING AFTER.** A boat that had gone out at first light finds the two of them, and nobody is standing on either and there has been nobody standing on either since about half past four. **A man of about thirty-three who hires hands asks out loud in front of about fourteen people why two boats are going on a sheet that did not put them on the ground, and is answered in about nine words: because I put them there and not them. He says that is not an answer and the man who keeps the leaf says one more thing and only that: the page of hours had three windows on it and no name at the top of it and the fourth mark was on neither, and if those two boats are not on the sheet then that sheet is a book of hours and nothing else, and in a month somebody will put a name at the top of it and there will be nothing in the book to stop him.** The two owners are found on that quay and neither is asked for a penny and neither is thanked and neither is asked what he wants done about it. **The man of about thirty-one, who owns the boat of about nine tons, says one sentence: I have got a boat that floats and I have got a hole in the ground with a boat in it and both of those were mine on Thursday, and I have not got one penny the worse off and I have not been asked for one, and I do not know yet which of those two I am going to be gladder about in March.** The man of about fifty-three, who owns the boat of about fourteen tons, says nothing about it, goes and looks at his boat for about a quarter of an hour, and pays a man out of his own pocket to get a warp onto her, and that figure is on no sheet in any hand. **A woman of about thirty-four of that commonwealth came into that port at about seven and said eleven words on that quay: three of them are mine and one of them is not, and I did not say a word about the one that is not, and I am not going to now.** At about ten at Morrow Quay, four hundred yards and four days' sail from either of those boats, a second week's room over that store goes onto the sheet at six hundred and seventy-two pence, being four marks, two shillings and eightpence, **being eight shillings a day for seven days, and eight times twelve is ninety-six and ninety-six times seven is six hundred and seventy-two**, quoted at the same figure by the same woman and not argued with, with the twelfth against it and settled on the fifteenth. The man who keeps the leaf is back on that quay at about half past four in the afternoon and did not sleep in a bed on the Thursday and is not going to be thanked for it.

### Chapter 545 — *Sunday the Sixteenth Day of January, a Wipe, the Eighty-Ninth Time, the Wall Down Bare at About Half Past Ten and Up Unrepaired at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth, Seven People Walking Past It and Not One Putting a Bucket Under It, a Page of Five Lines Read Out Once in That Room by a Woman of Thirty of No Office With a Sixth Line Not Read Out, the Man of About Thirty-Two Asking Her for Her Help in Front of Everybody and Being Refused One Thing and Given Another, a Man of About Thirty-Five of the First Lay Asking Whether the Three Points Belong to This Harbor and Being Told That a Page Goes Down a Coast in a Cart and Does Not Come Back*

**THE SIXTH LINE, AND WHAT SHE REFUSED.** The wall behind a reeve's bench comes down bare for the eighty-ninth time and goes up whole at the angle it has been at since the twelfth, and seven people walk past it and not one of them puts a bucket under it. The reason a berth-fund day is paid on a wipe is said out loud once at about eleven and is not the reason the last wipe carried: **the choice is always made by somebody who is not the man who carried the water, and the figure in chalk does not know what day of the week it is, and neither does the man on the step, and that is the whole reason the ten of them are sound.** At about two a room over that market is let out with about twenty people up those stairs and about eleven of them who cannot read, and **a woman of thirty of no office, who is not on this party's crew and is not its mouth and is not restored and is not forgiven, puts a page of five numbered lines on the long table and reads it out word for word once with her own name and the hour at the foot of it**: that nine boats of that harbor went inside a line of boats on the night of the fourteenth and seven came back and two did not, and both of those were found on the ground with a hole under the forefoot of each and nobody standing on either; that there are nine hulls off the head of that mole this afternoon and that this harbor is not in a position to say why and is not going to guess at it in a room on a Sunday; that there is no flour and the lamp oil board is at four hundred and fifty pence and the mole head has been dark since the seventh of May and neither of those is because of a line of boats; that the wage column is at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and did not move on the sixty-fifth wage Tuesday and a further week stands fallen due; and that a page carrying four names and five marks went up on the boards of this market on the twenty-sixth of December and that this harbor is one body among the bodies on that coast and is not the body that decides. **There is a sixth line on that page and she did not read it out, and the reason she did not read it out is in the second column in her own words, being that a line not said out loud is not a line, and the six words she gives on the stair to one man afterward are that.** The man of about thirty-two then asks her for her help in front of about twenty people, naming her first, and does not assume it: two bills are going onto his sheet on the Tuesday and the Thursday and he cannot read a figure out loud to a room without making a mess of it and he is asking her to carry both into whatever she is keeping, in her own hand, on her own page, and he is not asking her to put his name on it. **She says no to the first part and yes to the second in about a hundred and sixty words: I will not read your figures out in a room, because a figure a man says out loud with his mouth is his and a figure on a page is anybody's, and I have watched eleven people in this room not be told things for a year; what I will do is this, I will write on my own page that two boats of that port were found on the ground on the fifteenth with a hole under the forefoot of each of them, and I will write the date, and I will not write a penny on it, and if a man wants to know what a boat costs he can go to a bench stone four hundred yards from here and read it off a piece of paper himself, and if he cannot read then that is a fault of his and not of the figure.** He said that was fair and then said nothing else at all, and she said out loud that she had noticed it, and that a man asked for a thing in a room with eleven people in it who then says thank you for it has told those eleven people he was owed something. Nobody was thanked and the refusal is not a favour and is on no sheet. A man of about thirty-five of the first lay asks whether the three points belong to this harbor now and is told that the page went down that coast in a cart on the Monday and does not come back, and a name goes on it by a person writing it there. A man of about thirty-four of the second lay and a man of about thirty-eight are in that room and say nothing and are not asked.

### Chapter 546 — *Monday the Seventeenth Day of January, a Rota Day, That Cistern Charged at About Eight in Eleven Trips by Hand and Walked on by None of It, Three Days Apiece in Advance to the Same Four Men at Two Thousand and Sixteen Pence With the Seventeenth, the Eighteenth and the Nineteenth All on the Face of That One Line, the Person Whose Yard It Is Telling Those Four Men in Fourteen People That the Three Days Are the North Wall and the Sills and the Two Doors and the Glass and Are Not a Roof, a Man of About Forty of That Yard Asking What a Sill Is, a Man of About Forty-Seven Saying Out Loud That He Took Three Men up That Coast at the Figure in Chalk and Is on No Sheet, a Pump Hand of About Forty-Four Saying Out Loud That He Will Not Be Asked for Alone Again*

**THE SILL.** The cistern is charged in eleven trips by hand and the name at the head of that rota board is still off it. Three days apiece in advance to the same four men go onto the sheet at two thousand and sixteen pence, being twelve marks and eight shillings, at one hundred and sixty-eight a man a day for three days at the figure in chalk, **with the seventeenth, the eighteenth and the nineteenth all on the face of the one line, two of which are days the line was not written on.** The person whose yard it is then tells those four men, in about fourteen people, what the three days are for and what they are not for, in about a hundred and fifty words and once: the roof went on in three days on the sixth, the seventh and the eighth, and this is a second three days, and **this one is not a roof, this one is the north wall and the sills and the two doors and the glass, and there is not one sill under that roof and there has not been one since the eighth, and a man who is not told that is going to put his weight on a thing that is not there** — and the figure for it is not on that sheet yet and will be on it on the Wednesday and will not be the figure on it now. A man of about forty asks what a sill is, in front of about fourteen people, and is answered in about forty words and does not ask again. A man of about forty-seven who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons stands at the end of that slip and says out loud, in about eleven people, that on the twenty-eighth of December he was told to go and take three of the men who came up that road, and he did, and he paid them out of his own pocket, and it is in his book on the page with his own fuel in it, and **he is telling the room that he did it and not telling the room that it was a favour, and if that sheet ever wants a line for it, it can have one, and it will be his and not that man's** — and the man who keeps the leaf says the sheet does not want a line for it and never will. **A pump hand of about forty-four says out loud, to nobody in particular and in about eleven people, that he stood off that ground for three hours and forty minutes with his own hand on a chain weight, that he is not a good man to have on the end of a line, and that the next time somebody wants a man on the end of a line two are to be asked for and the second one is to be asked for in the same breath and not after the fact** — and the man who keeps the leaf says that was the correct order of things and did not say it twice and set no figure against it, and has not been asked for a second time and has not asked for one.

### Chapter 547 — *Tuesday the Eighteenth Day of January, the Sixty-Fifth Wage Tuesday, the Column at Twenty-Six Lines and One Hundred and Four Marks Read Out on the Step at Ten o'Clock and Not Moving, Nobody Paid a Penny Out of That Chest, a Further Week Fallen Due at the Close of That Day, a Boat of About Nine Tons Found on the Ground off the Outer Water Priced at About Ten o'Clock at Seven Thousand Seven Hundred and Fifty-Two Pence, Being Forty-Eight Marks and Six Shillings, as Five Figures and a Sum, With the Fourteenth Against It and Settled on the Eighteenth, the Man of About Thirty-One Asking Out Loud When He Is Going to Be Paid and Being Told That the Sheet Is a Record and Not a Purse*

**THE SIXTY-FIFTH WAGE TUESDAY, AND THE FIRST OF TWO BILLS.** A clerk reads the column out on the step at about ten with about forty people in front of it and about twenty of them cannot read the column on the lid, and the column did not move, and the chest with twenty envelopes in it stood shut behind that door from ten until four and nobody asked to have it opened, and the sixty-fifth week stands fallen due at the close of the day. At about ten and about four hundred yards away, the boat of about nine tons found on the ground on the Saturday morning is priced in five figures and a sum and every figure is said out loud before it is written: **a new hull, twenty fathoms of two-inch at two hundred and twenty pence a fathom, being 4,400, being twenty-seven marks, six shillings and eightpence; a mast and a boom at 480, being three marks; a warp and about thirty fathoms of line at 1,120, being seven marks; paint and oil at 240, being one mark, six shillings and eightpence; and nine days of her own hours at 168 a day, being 1,512, being nine marks and six shillings — that is seven thousand seven hundred and fifty-two pence, being forty-eight marks and six shillings, and the fourteenth of January is against that line being the day the boat was lost and it is in the total at the foot of that sheet this afternoon, and the two days are both on the face of the line.** And she says once that the boat of about fourteen tons on that ground as well is bigger, is not priced yet, will be priced on the Thursday, and **will not be a number anybody in that yard gets by adding to this one.** The man of about thirty-one who owns her asks, in about nine people, when he is going to be paid, and is answered in about a hundred words: **neither today, because that sheet is a record and not a purse, and the thing that is worth something to him about a record is that it is portable — any man with a leaf and a pencil can take seven thousand seven hundred and fifty-two off that slip and carry it up this coast to a mill, a chandler, a yard, or a man with a boat, and every one of those five will know what it is for and none of them needs to know a thing about him — and the man who keeps the leaf has not got that money, is short by eighty thousand eight hundred and ninety-eight pence, has not asked this harbor for a penny of it and is not going to, and that figure is on that sheet in his own mouth this afternoon and can be taken away.** He said that was fair, that he had not expected the money, and that he had wanted to know which of the two things was true, and that if it is a figure then he can work with a figure. A man of about thirty-three who hires hands asks whether those two bills were the price of the night and is answered in about fifty words: two of the prices, not all of them, and the ones that are not on that sheet are not on it because nobody in that yard has a figure for them and that is the correct way round and not the lazy way round.

### Chapter 548 — *Wednesday the Nineteenth Day of January, Not a Rota Day and Not a Wage Tuesday and Not a Wipe, Six Sill Beams of Oak Going In Under a Roof That Had None in It Since the Eighth, the North Wall and the Dressing to It and Two Doors With Hangings and a Bar and Fourteen Panes of Glass and Three Days of One Woman's Hours Priced at About Ten o'Clock at Five Thousand Five Hundred and Seventy-Two Pence, Being Thirty-Four Marks and Eleven Shillings, as Six Figures and a Sum, the Whole of It a Second Payment and Not Fifteen Thousand Three Hundred and Twenty Pence, a Man of About Fifty-Three Asking Out Loud Why There Is a Wall Going Up While His Boat Is on the Ground Four Days Down That Coast*

**THE SECOND PAYMENT.** At about ten o'clock in the morning the sixth of six sill beams of oak goes in under that roof and there has not been one in that building since the eighth, and the whole of the three days is priced out loud in about eleven people before a figure goes against any of it, in six figures: **the north wall at eleven fathoms of three-quarter stuff at one hundred and forty pence a fathom, being 1,540, being nine marks, eight shillings and fourpence; six sill beams of oak at six fathoms at two hundred and forty, being 1,440, being nine marks; the boarding dressed to that wall at nine fathoms at one hundred and sixty, being 1,440, being nine marks; two doors with their hangings and a bar at 480, being three marks; fourteen panes of glass and the putty at 168, being one mark and eightpence; and three days of her own hours on that wall at 168 a day, being 504, being three marks and two shillings — that is five thousand five hundred and seventy-two pence, being thirty-four marks and eleven shillings, and a man with a leaf and a pencil can take three days off that one line and find they are the seventeenth, the eighteenth and the nineteenth of this month, and two of those three are days the line was not written on.** And she says once that this is a second payment and not the first one, that the first one was a roof at fifteen thousand three hundred and twenty pence over three days and is in an unlocked drawer under that bench stone with the figure on a slate in it, and **that the two figures are not the same figure and this one is not that one plus something, and that the first one bought a roof and this one buys a wall and six beams and two doors and glass, and without the six beams a man puts his weight on nothing.** A man of about fifty-three who owns the boat of about fourteen tons then asks, in about eleven people, why there is a wall going up while his boat is on the ground four days down that coast, and is answered in about a hundred and sixty words: **there was no roof in that building on the fifth, the sixth and the seventh, and a compressor has to run in a building and a building has to have a fire under it, and eight bottles of air were charged in that room on the Thursday before Friday night, and those eight bottles are the reason the outer point could be worked at all; the choice was made on the eighth of January by a man who was not going to walk up a coast road and ask anybody anything, and the cost of the choice was three days and a roof and the cost of what the roof then let happen is three days and a wall.** He says that was not an answer to his question and it was the closest thing to one anybody in that yard was going to get, and he went off up the quay. In the room over that market at about two, the four heads are named out loud and do not change, and the sheet that carries the money is on no wall in that room and is not in it, and the two were named separately.

### Chapter 549 — *Thursday the Twentieth Day of January, a Rota Day, That Cistern Charged at About Eight in Eleven Trips by Hand, a Boat of About Fourteen Tons Priced at About Ten o'Clock at Nine Thousand Five Hundred and Thirty-Six Pence, Being Fifty-Nine Marks and Eight Shillings, as Four Figures and a Sum, With the Fourteenth Against It and Settled on the Twentieth and Not the First Bill Plus Anything, a Man of About Thirty-One Giving His Account of What the Coast Can Now Do in About Sixty-Five Words, and a Man of About Fifty-Three Saying Out Loud in That Room at About Half Past Two, in Eleven Words, That This Coast Can Be Cut in One Place at a Time, Which Is Not Argued With and Is Not Thanked*

**THE RESULT AND THE HOLE IN IT.** The boat of about fourteen tons is priced in four figures and a sum, every figure said out loud first: **a new hull of thirty fathoms of two-inch at two hundred pence a fathom, being 6,000, being thirty-seven marks, six shillings and eightpence; gear, a warp and about forty fathoms of line at 1,344, being eight marks, five shillings and fourpence; a pot, a funnel and two iron rings at 176, being one mark, one shilling and fourpence; and twelve days of her own hours at 168 a day, being 2,016, being twelve marks and eight shillings — that is nine thousand five hundred and thirty-six pence, being fifty-nine marks and eight shillings, with the fourteenth against that line and settled on the twentieth, and she is bigger than the other one by ten fathoms of two-inch and by three days of her hours, and the other three lines of each bill are not the same three things and are not set against one another, so that the whole of the difference is 1,784 pence and not 2,104.** At about one o'clock in that yard the man of about thirty-one who owns the boat of about nine tons gives his account in about sixty-five words in about eleven people: **nine boats went in past a line of boats on the Friday night of the fourteenth and seven came back, and there was no Crown hull anywhere near the inside of it; eight men went into about four fathoms in three places and three men sat in three boats on the surface and the whole of it was moved by three bells and three hours, and a man with a leaf and a pencil can take the days off that sheet and the crossings off the crossings and check both of them, and there is not one Crown figure on that coast with a day against it.** He stops there and nobody asks him to, and the man who keeps the leaf says out loud that he is not going to write one word of it on that sheet, because a sheet with money on it cannot carry a man's account of what a coast is, and because a page with a voice on it is a page that gets argued with. At about two a room over that market is let out with about twenty people up those stairs and about eleven of them who cannot read. **At about half past two a man of about fifty-three who owns the boat of about fourteen tons stands up in front of all of them and says, once, in eleven words: THIS COAST CAN BE CUT IN ONE PLACE AT A TIME.** Nobody argued with him. A man of about thirty-three who hires hands opened his mouth and did not say anything. A woman of about thirty-one who keeps a fish plate outside said she had been thinking it since the Saturday morning and had not wanted to say it in a room, and he said that was all right and that it did not need saying again. Nobody thanked him and no figure was set against it, and it went into the second column in his own words and not into the first. And the man who keeps the leaf says once, in about fourteen people, that it is on the page now and it is the only thing in four days this yard has got that it would be ashamed of, and **that three points and a page of hours is a coast that can be cut in one place at a time, and he would rather have that on a sheet in a room than have a man find it out on a Tuesday with a boat of his own behind him, and he is not going to argue with him about it and neither is anybody else in that room.** The two bills together are seventeen thousand two hundred and eighty-eight pence, being one hundred and eight marks and eightpence, for two boats, and there is not one man in either of them.

### Chapter 550 — *Friday the Twenty-First Day of January, Not a Rota Day and Not a Wage Tuesday and Not a Wipe, a Leaf Read Back in Full at About Ten Past Five in the Evening on the Flat of That Bench Stone in the Open, All Four Columns Including the Empty One, Read Twice Because About Four Men of That Party Cannot Read, With Both Definitions in the Same Mouth and in the Same Words as Every Other Read-Back and With Its Own Derivation Printed on the Face of the Reading, the First Column at Two Hundred and Eighty-Two at the Hour and Two Hundred and Eighty-Three at the Close, the Second at One Thousand Two Hundred and Eighty-Seven at the Hour and One Thousand Two Hundred and Eighty-Nine at the Close, the Third None With a Boy of Twenty-Two's Hand at the Head of It and His Surname on No Page of That Leaf, the Fourth at One Hundred and Twenty-Five With No Hundred and Twenty-Sixth Line in It and Neither Closed Nor Struck, a Question Asked Once at About a Quarter Past Ten at Night in That Yard in the Open in a Working Woman's Mouth and Answered by Nobody and Entered in a Minute as Asked*

**THE READ-BACK, AND THE QUESTION, AND NO ANSWER.** The shortfall is said out loud at about half past five, unmoved at ninety-six thousand and six pence, being six hundred marks and sixpence. At about ten past five the man who keeps the leaf reads that leaf back in full on the flat of that bench stone, in the open, in his own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, and reads it twice, the second reading at about a quarter to six, **because about four men of that party cannot read it**, and both definitions come out of the same mouth in the same words as on every other read-back, and the whole of his own arithmetic is said out loud and printed on the face of the reading before a single figure in it is believed. **The first column's derivation: two hundred and eighty have gone in on the fifty days from Friday the third day of December to this day, one against each of them, and not one day in two of them has not got an entry against it, which is the first time in fifty-one days that those two things have been the same; and the count at the hour of this reading is two hundred and eighty-two, because the entry against this day goes in after this reading and not before it, and two hundred and eighty-two plus this one is two hundred and eighty-three, which is the count at the close of it. The second column's derivation: five have gone in on each of those same fifty days, three of that day's five before the hour of that day's reading and two of them after it, so that of the two hundred and fifty that have gone in, two hundred and forty-five went in on the forty-nine days before this one and three went in this morning before this hour, and two hundred and fifty less two is two hundred and forty-eight, and one thousand and thirty-nine and two hundred and forty-eight is one thousand two hundred and eighty-seven at the hour of this reading, and one thousand and thirty-nine and two hundred and fifty is one thousand two hundred and eighty-nine at the close of it. The third column's derivation: none — nobody has been appointed to it, nobody has offered for it, a boy of twenty-two's hand is at the head of it, his surname is on no page of that leaf, and he is not on the water. The fourth column's derivation: one hundred and twenty-five — it has no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, it is neither closed nor struck, and the reason it took no line was entered once, in the second column, at about ten minutes past nine in the evening of a day in the summer, and it is not entered again here and it is not going to be.** The four columns are at two hundred and eighty-three, one thousand two hundred and eighty-nine, none and one hundred and twenty-five at the close of this day, and at two hundred and eighty-two, one thousand two hundred and eighty-seven, none and one hundred and twenty-five at the hour of the reading, and a man of about forty-six who mends nets on the third lay stood at the end of the slip through both readings and said nothing at all and went home. **Then at about a quarter past ten at night, with the door of that shed still open on the slip, the person whose yard it is put a plane down on the bench stone before she speaks and asks one question out loud, once, in that yard, in the open, in front of about nine people of whom about four cannot read what is on the bench stone: WHAT ARE PEOPLE GOING TO DO WHEN ONE VOICE SAYS THAT IT IS THE ONLY SAFE WAY TO REMEMBER.** Nobody answered it. A man of about thirty-three who hires hands opened his mouth and shut it again. The man who keeps the leaf did not answer it and said afterwards, in about thirty words, that he was not going to answer it and that there was nothing in that yard that could, and that it is a question and it is on the page and it is not answered. **It was entered in a minute as asked, at about a quarter past ten at night on the twenty-first day of January, in the second column of that leaf and in the minute under that bench stone, and neither of those two places carries anybody's name against it, and it was not asked again on that night and it has not been asked since, and nobody in that harbor has been asked it and nobody in that harbor has answered it.** The lamps in that harbor are lit on the quay and not at the head of that mole. A bell went at that port four days down that coast at about half past eleven on the night of the fourteenth and did not go again. The figure in chalk has not moved since the first of December.


## Volume 11, Batch 0004 (Chapters 531–540), Movement 4, *a shipyard on that quay, a choice, and a sea declared* — as written, 30 September 2026. **THE MOVEMENT IS PAID. A SHIPYARD ON THAT QUAY IS DESTROYED IN CHAPTER 534 AND NOBODY IS KILLED AND NOBODY IS HURT AND NO BODY IS NAMED AND NO CASUALTY FIGURE IS PRINTED. THE CHOICE OF RECONSTRUCTION OVER REVENGE IS PAID ON THE FITTING-OUT SHEET IN FIFTEEN THOUSAND THREE HUNDRED AND TWENTY PENCE AND IN THREE DAYS AND IS NOT PAID IN A SPEECH, AND THE PERSON WHOSE YARD IT IS SAYS OUT LOUD THAT IT IS A BILL AND NOT A WOUND AND IS NOT THANKED. TERNWATCH IS ENTERED IN CHAPTER 536 AND NOWHERE BEFORE IT, AND A MAN OF ABOUT TWENTY-NINE IS AT THAT LISTENING STATION AND IS NOT MADE TO BE MORE THAN HE IS. A PAPER SAYING THAT THE SEA IS UNDER MARTIAL CUSTODY IS READ OUT IN CHAPTER 540 IN A ROOM OVER THAT FISH MARKET WITH THE READER'S OWN NAME AND THE HOUR UNDER IT, AND THE NAME UNDER THE SEAL WAS NOT READ OUT ALOUD, AND THERE IS NO MAN IN THAT ROOM WHO IS ONLY A NAME OR A SEAL OR AN OFFICE. NOTHING WENT INTO THE SHEET IN ANY HAND ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS, NOBODY WAS ASKED FOR ANYTHING ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS, NOTHING ON THE POVERTY LIST IMPROVED, A PRICE DID NOT COME DOWN, AND NOBODY WAS THANKED FOR ANYTHING ON ANY OF THE TEN DAYS.** The word counts of the ten are 3,535 / 3,411 / 3,705 / 4,091 / 3,960 / 3,848 / 3,585 / 3,339 / 3,378 / 5,187, BEING 38, 039 AND THAT TOTAL IS THE SUM OF THE TEN FIGURES PRINTED HERE BECAUSE IT WAS ADDED AND NOT COPIED. THREE CHAPTERS RUN ABOVE THE HOUSE GUIDELINE OF THREE THOUSAND TWO HUNDRED WORDS AND THE REASONS ARE RECORDED IN `state/continuity.md`: CHAPTER 534 CARRIES A DESTRUCTION, FOUR FIGURES, A REFUSAL OF AN OFFER AND TWO PAID DAYS IN IT; CHAPTER 535 CARRIES THE ELEVEN WORDS, THE SECOND READING REFUSED AND FOUR LINES; CHAPTER 540 CARRIES THE ARRIVAL OF A PAPER, A FIVE-LINE DOCUMENT READ ALOUD, TWO CONFRONTATIONS AND NINE ONE-SENTENCE DECLARATIONS IN A ROOM OF ABOUT TWENTY PEOPLE..
