### Chapter 491 — *Tuesday the Twenty-Third, the Fifty-Seventh Wage Tuesday, the Column Not Moved and Fifty-Seven Weeks Standing Fallen Due, Bread and Salt Beef at One Thousand Six Hundred and a Day Apiece in Advance to the Same Four Men at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two, and Three Descents on the Boat's Own Bottles with a Figure of Forty Minutes on Each Slate*

**A bell — a plain riveted thing about five foot across, open at the bottom — goes down onto a ring beside the last of fifteen frames at about half past eight, and three men go down in it one at a time on air out of that boat's own bottles and on no line, because the man who keeps the leaf said out loud before the bell was off the chocks that five fresh days had been ordered and were not aboard and that he was not going to open a line for an order that was not in his hand.** Ivo Sark, of about twenty-four, is the tender on the surface for the whole of the three with his hand on the chain weight and a cutoff he can pull without asking; the pump hand of about forty-four is on the compressor with him and neither of them goes down. **Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, 9.10 to 9.50, comes up with a hole in the middle of a Tuesday in him and says it once, out loud, and is not asked.** *An ordinary Tuesday in that shed in the spring, and I can put my hand on either one of the ends of it and there is about a minute and a half in the middle of it that is not there.* Nobody asked him for a year or for his book and he offered neither. At about twelve minutes past nine the tender says out loud that the man in that bell is not answering and **nobody pulls the cutoff, because a man who has stopped answering has not asked to come up and the whole of the house's rule is that a man asks**; he begins answering again at about thirty-one minutes and asks to come up and the cutoff is pulled without asking anybody anything. **Sabra Loach, of about thirty-one, who crews nothing and sells nothing, 10.10 to 10.50**, says one thing about her own body and not one thing about what is in the room: that it did not hurt, that it took about two minutes off her, that she was holding the edge of the eleventh frame, that her mouth was full of a taste like a penny that had been in a pipe, and that she has not been asked what she gave it and is not going to be told. **A man of about thirty-seven, 11.10 to 11.50**, comes up with a headache and a cold in the back of his neck and works the pump that afternoon. Nobody was thanked. The leaf is read back at half past nine in the evening with both definitions and its own arithmetic; the fitting-out sheet is **sixteen thousand two hundred and forty-eight pence short**.

### Chapter 492 — *Wednesday the Twenty-Fourth, Four Days of Coal at Two Thousand Three Hundred and Fifty-Two and Five Days of Air at Nine Hundred and a Second Pair of Hands at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight, and Eleven Minutes in Which a Man Holds a Crew to Shore With His Own Body*

**Three lines go onto that sheet at about eleven in the morning and are read off it out loud as they go on, and the man who keeps the leaf says the whole of what each one is before he writes it**, including that the line for the air bears the twenty-fourth of November and no other date and that every descent from this day onward is on that line and on nothing else. **The figure on the sheet goes to nineteen thousand six hundred and sixty-eight pence short.** **And then, at about ten past one in the afternoon, in front of all nine of them and before anybody has said a word to him about it, the holder of that writ says out loud what he is going to do and how long for and gives the hour twice:** he is going down into that bell at about a quarter past one and is going to be in the eleventh one from about half past one until about forty-one minutes past one, that is eleven minutes and he is going to count them and not round them, his air is the line of the twenty-fourth and the limit on his slate is forty minutes and he is going to be out of that water in about thirty-five of them, the man of about thirty-seven goes in that bell ahead of him, Ivo Sark is the tender and is on the surface, and he is telling the nine of them in front of Ivo Sark that he is not going to ask him for the cutoff. **And the man who keeps the leaf says the one thing that was said out loud about it, once, and nobody else on that deck says it after him: that a person who is asked whether he will be used as a piece of equipment has already been used as one.** Nobody asked him, nobody put a figure on him, nobody named what he did, and nobody thanked him.

**The bell goes down onto that ring at about ten past one with the man of about thirty-seven in it, on a slate of his own, and he is out of it and on that floor at the front of those frames at about half past one. The holder goes into the same bell at about a quarter past one. He sits down in the eleventh frame with his back against the iron of it and his hands on the ring, and the man of about thirty-seven at the front of those frames is about nine foot off him, and the thing on that floor takes from both of them, and what it took from the man at the frames came through that frame and into him, and that is what holding them to shore is.** At about thirty-five minutes past one the tender says out loud over the wire that the man on that floor is not answering and the hour goes in against the line. At about forty-one minutes past one the holder says one word, which was the word, and the cutoff is pulled without asking anybody anything, and the bell is up in about six minutes and he is out of it at about ten to two, and the man of about thirty-seven comes up in the same haul and had not asked to come up either. **Four clocks close: a quarter past one, the half hour, forty-one minutes past one, and ten to two.** He could not get his knees to work on the ladder, sat down on that after deck until about half past two, and was put a can of hot something into his hands at about a quarter past two by a man who said no word and was not thanked for it. **And from about two o'clock to about four o'clock he cannot tell the order in which three things happened**, and Nessa Pike has all three in that minute with the hour against each, and he read them at about four o'clock and they were right and he could not place them, and has not been able to place them since. His hands were not steady for two days afterward and on the second day of December he could not get his cup down off the counter without putting two fingers on it. **No figure is set against any part of it anywhere, he is not a casualty, nobody has named him one, nobody thanked him and he is not an example of anything and was not made one.**

### Chapter 493 — *Thursday the Twenty-Fifth, a Rota Day, the Hundred and Second Charge Walked on by None of It, a Man of About Thirty-Two Leaving the Best Evidence This Party Has Ever Had in Its Hands on the Bottom of That Trench, and a Crate That Goes Down Full and Comes Up Empty*

**At about eleven in the morning on that after deck, in front of all nine of them, before he has said a word to anybody about it, once, in about four minutes, the holder of that writ says it and nobody interrupts him and nobody asks him a question at the end of it.** I am going to leave it. **The first thing is that it is the best evidence this party has ever had in its hands, and he is leaving it in the dark on the bottom of a trench in a room behind a machine that three of them cannot agree about. The second is that it is the only thing in that room that holds a route together — any man alive can come back to that room with that paper in it, and the day that paper is in a crate on a boat that room is a hole in a floor with nothing in it, and the next party down here is nine men with a line and a bell and no reason whatever to come back twice.** So the paper goes to the room and not to the boat, and the crate on that deck comes up empty, and the brown page under the weight on that tarpaulin comes up flat and goes on no sheet of any kind. And he is telling all nine of them that **he is not using that room to decide where this boat goes tomorrow or the day after, and the boat sails on the morrow at about four in the afternoon whatever is on that floor and whatever is on that deck**, and that he has not looked at a line of it this morning and is not going to this evening. Nobody argued with him, nobody thanked him, nobody was asked to agree with him and nobody was asked whether he had thought about it, and the whole of it went into the second column with the hour of eleven o'clock against it.

**The crate, battened since the thirty-first day of October past, is taken forward off that after deck at about half past eleven and set down by the fore hatch.** **At about ten past one in the afternoon the man of about fifty-one, out of a coast town four days down, and the man of about thirty-seven go down on air of the twenty-fourth, forty minutes apiece, one man in that bell at a time, with the crate roped to a line and the three baskets roped inside it, and both of them are out of that water at about ten to two. On that floor the batten comes off, the three baskets come out one at a time, and they go back onto the second shelf of the rack against the back wall on the north side of that room, in the dark, in the places they had been in.** A line is added to the end of one of the two slates left inside that doorway on the eleventh of November, being that the room behind the wall and the paper in it stay as they are and that the party is not coming back for them, with the hour of the twenty-fifth against it and nothing else, and nobody told either man what to write. **The batten goes back across the lid before the crate is hauled up and the crate comes up empty and goes into the forepeak.** **The holder of that writ does not go down at all that day and says so out loud once:** he would go down if he put the reason in front of him and asked him to write it himself, but he got up off that deck with two hands at about ten to two the day before and is not a man who goes into twenty-two fathoms this week, and the man who has been in holds nineteen years is going down because he carried the paper up and he is not going to pretend he sent him because he could not be bothered. Nothing went out on that sheet and nothing went into it and the figure has not moved.

### Chapter 494 — *Friday the Twenty-Sixth, a Man of About Fifty-One Going Down at About Ten Past Ten and Coming Up at About Ten to Eleven with One Whole Sheet Out of a Bundle of About Forty That Was in a Case About Four Foot Off That Room, a Date and a Place and a Broken Impression and a Name, and Four Things Said Out Loud That It Does Not Show*

**One sheet, not cut and not wet, folded twice, about nine inches by six, taken out of a bundle of about forty sheets tied with a cord that had gone to a hard grey colour under a lid about four foot off the room with the racks in it, on the other side and against the north wall, and the other thirty-nine put back and the cord put back and the lid shut.** On the face of it: a head with a rule under it and six short strokes ruled down the left of the body; a place, being the name of a port and not the name of that harbor; a date, being the fourteenth day of a month that the clerk of that office called by a name this coast does not use; **no year at all, and that is not a thing that has been taken off it**; a line ruled about two inches long with nothing on it in ink and, beside its middle, **an impression pressed into the paper about the size of a thumbnail, broken at the top edge by a fold that goes through it so that the two sides of it do not make up into one another**, and nobody on that deck said the name of the thing that made it and nobody has said it since; at the foot, in a second and larger hand in an ink brown where the first is black, an endorsement of one line and a rule under it and a name, being **Ilya Serr, an examiner of that office**, the office being the one whose engineers rebuilt the frame on that floor three hundred years after a man of about thirty-four said out loud that the frame under the fittings was six centuries old; and down the left margin, in a third hand in a green ink, four words and a short stroke, being that the sheet was received into that port's ferry file. **Three hands and three inks and three dates, and a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can take all three off the face of the paper in about a minute and find that they are three and not two.**

**And at about two in the afternoon the man of about fifty-one says the one description of that sheet that was going to get itself into a record — *that is a Crown signature on a transfer out of that ferry's file and that is the end of it* — and Calder Marr stops it and puts four lines under it and the man of about fifty-one says he will not argue and has the whole of the four read back to him word for word off the holder's own slate before he goes below.** The four: **it does not show why, and there is no line of writing anywhere on that sheet with a reason at the head of it; it does not show that the man whose name is on it knew what was in the case, and there is nothing whatever on the face of that paper about what was in the case; it does not name anybody as the author of a lie and it is not a confession; and it is a piece of paper, it does not consent, it cannot be asked anything, and it does not testify.** It shows that the office that rebuilt the mechanism also signed the transfer of the evidence out of that ferry's file, **and nothing else.** **At about four in the afternoon that boat gets under way, eighteen hours ahead of a figure of two days, with the chamber with a stove in it standing where it has stood since the thirty-first day of October past with its stove drawn out and its hatch shut and nobody going back for it and nobody given a key to it that anybody else does not have.** The leaf is read back that evening as it is on every reading night and there is no other reading on that boat for six weeks.

### Chapter 495 — *Saturday the Twenty-Seventh, Under Way Since about Four o'Clock on the Friday and Moored off the Third Lay at about Ten o'Clock in the Morning, Eighteen Hours Out of a Figure of Two Days, a Case and a Lock and a Lining of Oilcloth at Three Hundred and Twenty, and a Sheet of Paper Into a Case in a Room over a Fish Market*

**A case, a lock and a lining of oilcloth at three hundred and twenty pence, being two marks, with the twenty-seventh against it, and before he writes the line the man who keeps the leaf says out loud that it is the case and not the crate, that the crate is a different thing and is not on this line and is not coming into that harbor in anybody's hand, and that nobody is to write a second line under it that week saying what is going to be put in it, and that whatever goes in it goes in it in that room over that market and is not put in it in a shed.** **At about two in the afternoon the sheet of paper goes into that case in a room over that fish market**, with the lock shut afterward and the key in the keeping of the woman who wrote the minute, and **nobody in that harbor read it, nobody was shown it and nobody was asked what it said. Sabra Loach, of about thirty-one, who crews nothing and sells nothing, did it and said one sentence while she was doing it: a case is a thing that can be carried and a case is not a hand, a thing in a hand is a thing one man has, and this is a thing a room has.** The brown page did not go into that case and was not cut and was not folded; it went up to a room over that market flat on a board with a weight on it and a second weight on the board, it is on no sheet in that boat and on no sheet in that harbor, and a woman of thirty of no office is the only person who knows exactly where it is and has said so out loud once. **The master of that boat comes ashore with his two men and his boy and is not thanked, nobody asks him why he came, nobody asks him to have come, nobody asks him for a date and he gives none, and his boat is not put to sea again on any day of that trip.** A roommate of about thirty-eight is told on that quay that there is a sheet of paper in a case in a room over that market and says he will not go and look at it and will not be told what is in it, and says he has got a thing of his own that he is not going to be asked about and is not going to hand over, and that if you put a second paper in a second box in a second room four hundred yards from that that is two boxes and not one fact, and that he has not been in that room and is not going, and that he was asked nothing and has told them nothing. A man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a chart in a bag is not asked for it and does not produce it. **The best evidence this party has ever had in its hands is still in the racks in a room on the bottom of that trench, and a machine six centuries old is still on that floor with a Crown man's marks set around it under a chamber with a stove in it, and nobody in that harbor has been given the machine and nobody in that harbor has been stopped from knowing about it, and the word that would name the seal on a warrant is in no mouth in that boat and in no mouth in that harbor.** The sheet is **nineteen thousand nine hundred and eighty-eight pence short**.

### Chapter 496 — *Sunday the Twenty-Eighth, a Wipe, the Eighty-Second Time, a Room over a Fish Market at About Two o'Clock With About Twenty People in It and About Eleven of Them Who Cannot Read, a Sheet Read Out Twice With the Rule on Its Face, and a Figure Corrected in the Second Reading and the Wrong Figure Left Where It Was*

**The wall behind a reeve's bench comes down bare for the eighty-second time at about half past ten and goes up unrepaired at the angle it has been at since the twelfth, and four people walk past it and not one of them puts a bucket under it.** **At about ten minutes to two the man who keeps the leaf stands where the long table is and says out loud that the sheet that carries the money is not in that room and not on that wall and is not going to be read out to them that afternoon, and that the first column of that leaf and the second column of that leaf are two other things and are not in that room either and have never been on that wall, and that anybody in there who wants either of those two things said out loud can ask him for it and it will not be that afternoon.** Nobody asked. A woman of about fifty-eight with an end stall and a slate said, out loud, that a thing being off a wall was a thing that could be got at in a week and a thing being read out was a thing that was heard once, and that the harbor had a great deal of the second kind of thing in it and had never once had the other. **The room was let out on that Sunday with a bowl on the step and about twenty people went up in the half hour after two o'clock and about eleven of them could not read. Hobb Lee, of about forty-six, who mends nets on the third lay and has done since he was nine, read out twice a sheet written the day before in the hand of Nessa Pike, of about twenty-seven of that yard, being the account of what was done in that harbor on the twenty-seventh and what was not done in it**, with the rule on the face of the paper above the account: the reader's own name goes under what he reads and the hour under his name, and anybody in that room may stop him at any word and put their own words against his, and what goes into the book afterward is what is on the paper. Readings at **two o'clock and twenty-five minutes past two.** Nobody stopped him in the first.

**In the second, at about half past two, at one word in the ninth line, a man of about fifty-one out of a coast town four days down said *that is fifty* — that is fifty in a hand that was not in that hatch and he was in that hatch, that he counted them on the hatch head on the Tuesday before they came away and counted them twice, and that there were about forty of them in the bundle and not fifty.** Hobb Lee stopped, put his thumb against the ninth line, let the man finish, and read the ninth line again exactly as it was written including the figure of fifty, so that the people at the back heard the wrong figure a second time and knew what was being argued at. He then asked for a name to go against the correction and was given the trade and the years and the hour instead, **and was not asked for a name**, because the man would rather a man who thinks the figure is wrong came down that hatch and counted them himself than had his name on a paper in a harbor where he has never worked. **The wrong figure was left where it was — not rubbed out, not scraped, not taken off with a knife — and the corrector's refusal to give a name was written on the face of that paper under the ninth line in the reader's own hand.** Nobody thanked him. A man of about thirty-one who keeps a chandler's store on the second lay said out loud that a figure corrected in a room of about eleven people who cannot read is a figure corrected eleven times over, and Hobb Lee said that was a fair thing to say and was the reason the wrong word was left on the paper and not taken off it. **And then he read the whole of that sheet out a third time from the top, with the rule at the head of it and the ninth line in it as it stands with the correction under it, and about eleven people in that room heard all of it.** The sheet is **nineteen thousand nine hundred and eighty-eight pence short** and nothing standing in that harbor was paid, advanced, reduced, improved, struck or closed.

### Chapter 497 — *Monday the Twenty-Ninth, a Rota Day, the Hundred and Third Charge Walked on by None of It, a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Five Days Under Way at One Thousand Two Hundred and Fifty as a Settlement and Not a Hiring, and a Roll of the People Who Put Nothing In Proposed in a Room and Refused in About Four Words*

**The cistern is charged for the hundred and third time and walked on by none of it, and the figure of that hundred is not said out loud a second time.** **A boat of about nineteen tons, five days under way at two hundred and fifty pence a day at one thousand two hundred and fifty pence, goes onto that sheet at about eleven in the morning with the twenty-ninth against it**, and the man who keeps the leaf says the whole of what that line is before he writes a figure against it: that it is the settlement of five days she was at sea and it goes on the twenty-ninth because the twenty-ninth is the day the boat's owner came and stood at the end of that bench and asked him for it, and not because the twenty-ninth is the day it was hired; that she is going out again when her master says she is, that he has not asked him and is not going to, and that if he sails on Thursday he shall be here paying a day at the figure in chalk and putting it against his name like anybody else. **The room over that fish market is let out three days running that week, and on the Monday nobody put a bowl on the step, because there is nobody in that harbor who has a bowl on that step for a Monday. About twenty people went up and about eleven of them could not read.** At about ten past three a man of about fifty who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons, who wrote a thing on the wall of that room on the tenth of October past and has not said the name of it since, proposed out loud **that there be a roll of the people who put nothing in, not to move them but to stop them being asked again.** **A ropemaker of about sixty-one, who is not in her room on a Sunday and has not been in one for two years, said no in about four words from about nine feet back, and the man who wrote on that wall on the tenth of October did not answer her: *there is no roll.*** Somebody said then somebody will be asked twice. She said yes, and that a man in this room in six weeks will be able to say to that person, you said no to me once, in a room, and I have a paper, and it will be true, and it will be worse than being asked cold, and it will be worse for them than it is now because now it is one man with a bad memory and afterwards it is a room with a sheet — **and *I put nothing in*, and not one penny of hers is on that sheet on any line and nobody asked her for one and nobody asked her twice, and she came up those stairs this afternoon anyway, because a man who wants a list of us ought to be made to stand up in the room with the rest of you and be told no to his face rather than go home and write it out.** **And then the holder of that writ said the only other thing that was said about it: no, and he wants it written down that it was no in this room on this day and not in a shed, and that the two of them are the holder of that writ and a ropemaker of about sixty-one, and that is all that goes in the minute about it, and it is not going to be the fourth thing on that table, and he is not going to ask this room to hold a list of the people it has not got anything from. Nobody wrote anything. There is no such roll in that room, there is none in that harbor, and none is going to be.** At about twenty past four a man at the front of that room put one question to the man of about thirty-four of the second lay about whether the thing in a case is going on that wall, and got *no*, and a second question about why not, and was told that there was not going to be a why, that he had said no to the putting of it on the wall and that was the whole of it, and **ask me about the rope.** Nobody asked him about the rope. The sheet is **twenty-one thousand two hundred and thirty-eight pence short**, said out loud in that yard's own mouth at about half past five and not answered by anybody.

### Chapter 498 — *Tuesday the Thirtieth, the Fifty-Eighth Wage Tuesday, the Column Not Moved and Fifty-Eight Weeks Standing Fallen Due, a Day Apiece to the Same Four Men at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two, and the Holder of That Writ Told No in a Room and Sitting Down Without Answering*

**The fifty-eighth wage Tuesday comes and the wage column in that harbor stands at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with twenty envelopes in a chest and does not move, and a further week stands fallen due at the close of it, and a wage Tuesday is the day a harbor finds out what it owes and the finding out is not a payment.** A day apiece to the same four men at six hundred and seventy-two pence goes on the sheet with the thirtieth against it. At about half past five the man who keeps the leaf reads that sheet back in full with the day against every line and says the deficit out loud in his own mouth and stops there: **twenty-one thousand nine hundred and ten pence short, being one hundred and thirty-six marks, twelve shillings and sixpence, against that yard's book and nobody's else, not answered, and he is not going to ask anybody in that harbor to answer it, and if the rest of it is wanted it is wanted in a room over that market and not in a shed, and there is a bowl on the step there on a Sunday and there is not one there on a Tuesday.**

**And at about two in the afternoon the holder of that writ stood in that room in front of about twenty people, about eleven of whom cannot read, with a sheet of four lines in his own hand in his coat, and he was told no in about a quarter of an hour by a man of about forty-six who mends nets on the third lay and has never argued with him about anything.** He said it first, before anybody asked him anything: he is going to read the four lines himself, he wrote them on Saturday night in a shed, **the man who got the thing they are about is a man of about fifty-one out of a coast town four days down who is in that harbor and is not at that table and did not write a word of them, and what he is claiming is not that he carried it up out of that room** — he sat in the eleventh frame on that floor on the Wednesday for about eleven minutes and held a man there with his own back, and if a man in that harbor hears four sentences about a floor that was twenty-two fathoms down read out by the man who sat in it, those four sentences carry something they would not carry out of a man who mends nets. **Hobb Lee put his thumb between the pages of the long table's own book and said no, and it was the first no that had ever been given to that man in that room and it was given without any argument at all:** then no, and he will tell them why in one sentence and then read them. A man who reads out a thing he has a stake in cannot be stopped by anybody standing in the room. In this room there are about eleven people who cannot read, and their whole of the power to stop him is one word, and the word is that you are reading it straight, and that word is not a stop. It is you asking them to trust you, and asking a person who cannot read to check you is asking them to do the thing they came because they cannot do. **In September a page in an office on a hill was worth a room. That is the whole of what a page is worth and it is not nothing.** The holder said that was the hole in the rule, that he said it out loud on the sixth of November and said he would stand in a room with about eleven people who cannot read and be told no, and here it is and here he is and he is not going to argue with a man who has never argued with him about anything. Hobb Lee said: **I know you are not going to argue. That is the reason it was easy to say it.** **He sat down on the bench at the back of that room at about ten past three and put the sheet on the long table face down, and he was not thanked for standing in that room and the room was not satisfied and nobody in it said that anything had been settled.**

**Hobb Lee wrote his own name and the hour under each of the four lines as he read them, being the hours of ten past three, of a quarter past three and of twenty minutes to four, and stopped after each one and looked round the room, and nobody put a hand up and nobody said a word against any of them, and about eleven people who cannot read heard all four** — one, that the office which rebuilt the mechanism standing on the floor of that trench also signed the transfer of the evidence out of that ferry's file; two, that the sheet it signed does not show why; three, that it does not show that the man whose name is on it knew what was in the case; four, that it does not name anybody as the author of a lie, that it is not a confession, and that it is a piece of paper which does not consent and cannot be asked anything and does not testify — **each with Calder Marr's own name and the twenty-seventh day of November and a shed in this harbor in his own hand under it. A woman at the back who cannot read put her hand up about halfway through the second and had it read again exactly the same.** **The name on each of the four is his own, there are four of them and they are the same name, and he was sitting at the back of that room and was not thanked and was not restored by any of them and did not ask to be**, and a man of about fifty who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons looked at the sheet for a while and said out loud that the four heads on that wall had not changed by any of it and that a fifth head was not going to be added to that wall by anybody on account of a Tuesday. **The four questions people in that harbor asked a man in a hall on the west basin in the spring are not asked in that room and were not asked in it on that afternoon and are not answered there.**

### Chapter 499 — *Wednesday the First Day of December, a Case and a Lock and a Lining of Oilcloth Opened at About Ten Past Two in a Room over a Fish Market and Not in a Shed, a Sheet Read Out Twice With the Four Limits Read Out With It, a Record Written of What Was Read and by Whom and at What Hour, and the Paper Going Back Into the Case*

**The case is opened in a room over that fish market at about ten past two in the afternoon and not in a shed, by the woman who wrote the minute, who had had the key in her keeping since the twenty-seventh and who had not had anybody ask her for it in the four days between.** She put the case on the long table with the lining of oilcloth folded back and the lock open and **did not lift the paper out**, put her hand flat on it for a moment and then took her hand off. *A case is a thing that can be carried and a case is not a hand. It has been in a room over that market since Saturday and it has not been read by anybody in that room and it has not been shown to anybody in that room. There are about eleven people in this room who cannot read it and I am opening it in front of all of you, and there is no man at the head of this table and no man in this room who is the name on it.* **Nobody at the head of that table said anything, because there is nobody at the head of it.**

**Hobb Lee read it out at about twenty past two and read it out again at about half past two, with his own name and the hour under both readings in his own hand, and nobody stopped him at any word, and about eleven people who cannot read heard it twice** — the head and rule and six short strokes, the place being the name of a port and not the name of that harbor, the date being the fourteenth day of a month that the clerk of that office called by a name this coast does not use, **no year on the face of it at all and that not being a thing that has been taken off it**; the line ruled about two inches long with nothing on it in ink and, beside its middle, the impression pressed into the paper about the size of a thumbnail, broken at the top edge because the paper has been folded once across it, the two sides of it not making up into one another, and nobody in that room said what made it and he is not going to say; the endorsement in a second and larger hand in an ink brown where the first is black with a name at the right of it, **and that name is a name on a paper, and that man is not in that harbor and is not in that room and nobody in that room is that name and no part of that name is standing at the long table this afternoon**; the four words and a short stroke down the left margin in a third hand in a green ink, being that the sheet was received into that port's ferry file, and that is three hands and three inks that a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can take off the face of that paper in about a minute. **And the four limits were read out with it and not after it, and about eleven people who cannot read heard the paper, then all four of the limits, and then the paper again, and the order went into the record that room keeps with the hour against each of them.** **It does not show why. It does not show that the man whose name is on it knew what was in the case. It does not name anybody as the author of a lie and it is not a confession. And it is a piece of paper, and it does not consent, and it cannot be asked anything, and it does not testify, and nobody in this room can put a question to it and get an answer out of it, and anybody who tells you that a paper has told them something is telling you about themselves.**

**And then a man of about forty at the back asked out loud whether the man whose name was on it was a bad man, and the woman of thirty of no office answered him, and was not thanked for answering him, and about eleven people who cannot read heard every word of it and none of them said anything.** *No. And I am not going to tell you he is not, either, and that is not me being careful. A signature on a transfer is a signature on a transfer. I have spent eleven years looking at documents made to sound certain, and the whole of my trade is that a document which settles a question is a document somebody has settled on purpose, and this one settles nothing. It says that a man signed a thing on a day. It does not say what he thought when he signed it, and it does not say what was in the case, and a man who signed a transfer of a case that he had not opened has done something this paper cannot tell you about, and it may be the worst thing a man can do and it may be the ordinary way that office did its work in that year. **I am not going to hand a room of people who cannot read a worse man than the paper has got.*** At about half past three a sheet was written of what had been read in that room and by whom and at what hour and was entered in the book that room keeps, the paper went back into the case, the case was locked and the key went back, and **no figure is set against the paper, the case, the lock, the oilcloth, the day of the woman of about twenty-seven who wrote it, or the reading of a man of about forty-six who was paid nothing for it.** The third column of that leaf is empty and nobody has been appointed to it and the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it and has not been scratched out and his surname is on no page of that harbor and that boy is not on the water. The fourth column stands at one hundred and twenty-five and has taken no line and is not closed and is not struck. **The man of about twenty-nine did not hear out of the left side of his head on that day and nobody has said when it will.** The sheet is **twenty-one thousand nine hundred and ten pence short**.

### Chapter 500 — *Thursday the Second Day of December, a Rota Day, the Hundred and Fourth Charge Walked on by None of It, a Leaf Read Back at About Ten Past Five With Both Definitions and Its Own Derivation, the Sheet Twenty-One Thousand Nine Hundred and Ten Pence Short, and a Question Asked Once at a Mole Head and Answered by Nobody*

**At about ten past five in the evening, on that after deck, in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, the leaf is read back and read twice because about four men of that party cannot read, and both definitions come out of the same mouth in the same words they came out of on the twenty-second of October past and the first day of November and the eleventh and the twenty-second of November, and the reading prints its own arithmetic on its own face so that anybody with a pencil can take it and find that it agrees.** **There are two hundred and thirty-two entries in the first column at that hour and two hundred and thirty-three at the close of the day, and there were one hundred and eighty-three at the close of the twelfth day of October past, and fifty have gone in on the fifty days of the fifty-one from Wednesday the thirteenth of October to this day, one against each of them, and not one day in two of them, there being one day in between that is the twelfth day of November and that is a day nobody is in.** The second column has one thousand and thirty-seven at that hour and one thousand and thirty-nine at the close, and the reading prints that five have gone in on each of those same fifty days, three before the hour of that day's reading and two after it, **so that of the two hundred and fifty that have gone in, two hundred and forty-five went in on the forty-nine days before this one and three went in this morning before this hour, and two hundred and fifty less two is two hundred and forty-eight, and seven hundred and eighty-nine and two hundred and forty-eight is one thousand and thirty-seven.** The first column's two hundred and thirty-two and the fourth column's one hundred and twenty-five at that hour are a count of entries and a count of lines and both of them can be taken with a pencil. **Those are the two definitions and they are said out loud in the same words and in the same order every time this leaf is read back, so that a man with a pencil taking either figure off a page knows which of the two he is holding and at which of the two moments.** The third column is empty and nobody has been appointed to it and the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it with a name beside it that is not that boy's and is not the holder's, and that boy is not on the water and nobody has asked him why. The fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines at that hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, has taken no line in these fifty days, has no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, and **that is not a closure and it is not a strike-out and nobody has closed that column and nobody in that yard is going to.**

**The sheet that carries the money is read back after that in full with the day against every line, carrying no count of persons, the three who said no at the same size as the figures, and none of the three asked a second time in any of these fifty days: ten thousand six hundred and forty pence in, thirty-two thousand five hundred and fifty out, twenty-one thousand nine hundred and ten pence short, being one hundred and thirty-six marks, twelve shillings and sixpence, and eight lines went out in these ten days and nothing went in on any of them** — bread and salt beef for nine men for ten days, sixteen hundred, the twenty-third; a day apiece in advance to the same four men, six hundred and seventy-two, the twenty-third; four days of coal for the pump, two thousand three hundred and fifty-two, the twenty-fourth; five fresh days of air off that same supply boat, nine hundred, the twenty-fourth; a second pair of hands for a day, one hundred and sixty-eight, the twenty-fourth; a case, a lock and a lining of oilcloth, three hundred and twenty, the twenty-seventh; a boat of about nineteen tons, five days under way, one thousand two hundred and fifty, the twenty-ninth; a day apiece to the same four men, six hundred and seventy-two, the thirtieth — **seven thousand nine hundred and thirty-four pence, being forty-nine marks, seven shillings and tenpence, and a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can take all three of those figures off that sheet in about a minute and find that they agree.** And one hundred and sixty-eight pence came into that yard and one hundred and sixty-eight went out of it on each of those ten days, being one thousand six hundred and eighty pence each way, and twenty-eight plus one thousand six hundred and eighty less one thousand six hundred and eighty is twenty-eight pence, and **not one penny of the whole of that trip came out of that bag, out of the owner of any boat, out of the man with two papers, or out of the Crown.**

**And then, at about twenty to six in the evening, when it had gone dark enough for the mole-head light to be missed and it is out anyway and has been since the seventh of May, about eleven people of that harbor were standing at the head of that mole, and the wind was off the land and cold, and a woman of about fifty-eight with an end stall and a slate put her slate against the parapet and asked a thing out loud, once, and nobody answered it.**

* I have got one question and I have had it since Wednesday and I am going to ask it now and I am not going to ask it again.*

Somebody at the back said ask it.

> **If they are putting that old thing back together on that floor down there, how many harbors have to be joined up to it before a man can make it work?**

**Nobody answered it.** The holder of that writ was about nine feet off her and did not answer it. The woman of thirty of no office did not answer it. The man of about fifty with the boat of about twenty-two tons did not answer it. A man of about thirty-four, who has a hole in the middle of a Tuesday, did not answer it and was not asked it. A man of about twenty-nine stood at the front and did not hear it asked and nobody told him he had. **Nessa Pike entered it in that minute as asked, with the hour of twenty to six in the evening of the second day of December against it, and read it back to the woman who asked it, and the woman who asked it did not ask to have it read back and did not ask for a word of it to be changed. It has not been asked a second time in that harbor and it is not going to be asked a second time, and there is no answer to it anywhere on this coast tonight, and the person who asked it did not ask it to be answered tonight.**

**AND THE CLOSING BLOCK IS INSIDE THE WORLD AND SAYS NOTHING ABOUT WHAT IS COMING.** A case stands on a table in a room over a fish market with its lock shut and its key in the keeping of the woman who wrote the minute. **The crate that went down off that boat on the twenty-fifth with three baskets in it came up out of that water empty with a batten back across its lid, and there is no word on any page of that harbor for what was going to be in it.** A slate leans on the bench stone in a shed at the head of that third lay with a figure of twenty-eight pence under a figure of six hundred and forty. The cistern at the back of that market was charged at about eight in the morning and was walked on by none of it, and it is walked on at every charge. There is a mole head in that harbor and the light on it is out and its lens has been out since the seventh day of May, and there are about eleven people standing at it in the dark. A man of about twenty-nine is standing at it and cannot hear out of the left side of his head and will not be able to until the fourth day of December. A boat of about nineteen tons is lying off that third lay with her master in her and his boy in the forepeak and that crate put down beside him. A man of about thirty-four has a hole in the middle of a Tuesday that a week ago he could put a hand on either end of and not on the middle of, and a question he asked at the head of that slip in October that nobody has answered and that he has not asked again. **And on the bottom of a trench in about twenty-two fathoms there is a machine six centuries old with a Crown man's marks set around it and a chamber with a stove in it standing over the top of it with its stove drawn out and its hatch shut, and nobody in that harbor has been given that machine and nobody in that harbor has been stopped from knowing about it, and the word that would name the seal on a warrant is in no mouth in that boat and in no mouth in that harbor.**

### The six rulings a Volume 04 writer must not re-derive

1. **LOCK L5 IS AMENDED: THERE ARE FOUR RETURNS AND THERE IS NO FIFTH.** The fourth, Friday the fourteenth of July, on the day, out of a finding of Monday the tenth, caught by the first limb by itself. **The day of a finding is not counted and the return falls due on the fourth day after it. Nothing is recalled, corrected, un-said or re-sent.** The clerk's own page has said four since the fourteenth of July. Full form at `outline/volume-04.md` lock L5.
2. **The condition's onset is the FOURTEENTH of October 2025 and there are THREE different things on that date that may never be fused: the dive was the night of the THIRTEENTH, the onset is the FOURTEENTH, and the order and the seizure were the FOURTEENTH at half past six in the morning.**
3. **The sentence — *both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other* — is a shape, not a sentence, and its origin is settled: Calder Marr's, in a hearing room, Volume 02, Chapter 97. No fisher in Volume 02 said it. In Volume 03 Nessa Vale of the Sill said it FIRST, on the mole's steps on the tenth, and the holder yielded the first saying to her in front of forty people, and Elias Voke said it last in a market on the thirteenth and would not say it twice.**
4. **The calendar.** 15 August 2026 is a Tuesday and is the last day of Volume 03. **1 SEPTEMBER 2026 IS A FRIDAY.** The Mondays in the rest of August are the 17th, 24th and 31st and the Mondays in September are the 4th, 11th, 18th and 25th. The wage Tuesdays are the 18th and 25th of August and the 1st and 8th of September. **The slate wall's own counter restarts at zero, because the first Monday this volume reaches is the seventeenth of August and that is the first Monday and not the sixteenth.**

### The six open threads, and no more

**Mara Venn's break with the Registry, which is Volume 4 and a different event from her leaving this crew** · **the third column, the boy, and the pencil** · **the nine-line mark, which closes in Volume 5** · **the question about who changed the rule, asked in a market and not answered** · **the second season of the writ and the first of March, and the first of September, and the unpaid wage and the three marks owing** · **the five bells at about five and a half fathoms and the four people of the Sill who own them and have no boat.** The full statements are at `state/open-threads.md` § *Volume 03 close* and at the audit's § 23, and the carried material that is not a seventh thread is written into `outline/volume-04.md`.

Each entry is two to five sentences and records: what the chapter's scene changed, what new canon it established, what it cost, and which thread it closed or opened. Entries appear in chapter order under a volume heading, and the most recent twenty chapters stay available for voice continuity.
