## Volume 03, Batch 0001 (Chapters 101–110) — complete. Movement 1, the first return and the first bill.

**Actual word count: 29,905 words across ten chapters after the Batch 0001 review repairs, and 26,767 before them** (Ch101 2,638 · Ch102 2,742 · Ch103 2,803 · Ch104 3,011 · Ch105 2,535 · Ch106 3,104 · Ch107 3,361 · Ch108 2,785 · Ch109 3,373 · Ch110 3,560), measured with `wc -w` including headings, against the 2,200–3,200 guideline. **Every chapter is above the floor. Seven are inside the guideline and three are past it** — Chapter 107 by 161, Chapter 109 by 173 and Chapter 110 by 360 — **and each of those three grew because the review required material the batch did not have: a delivered cost beat for Nessa Pike, Calder Marr's interior life, and the move of the boat trip to the top of the flood. No cost was dropped, which the batch's own length rule prefers, and Chapters 109 and 110 are each one complete day in one complete place — a mole's steps on the twenty-second and a boat off the south end on the twenty-third — and no cost is paid twice in either.** **The hearing room is used once, on Wednesday the seventeenth, and the market wall is used once, on Thursday the eighteenth, and no two of the three institutional days in this batch are the same day and neither of them is a Monday.** The batch's pressures alternate: a clock and a bucket, a stone in daylight, a day rate, a casting and a handcart, a refused day, a boy off a stone, a refusal in a room, a market, a mole with a notebook, and a boat.

**The money, and it closes checkable on the page: THIRTEEN marks in a bag, thirty-one on the chandler's note, nothing in a tin, on Wednesday the twenty-fourth of May — the same thirteen the bag held on the third of May.** The bag moves for the first time since the twenty-ninth of April and it moves twice and both times are on the page: **twelve marks in and four out on the eighth and ninth of May off a day at the second seam on the harbor authority's own account, then eight marks in across the tenth and eleventh by letting the yard's own pump out of its own shed for the first time since the fifth of April, less three straight onto a creditor's counter for a fortnight of bread and a mark to a man and a handcart.** **The gross of the eighth is twenty-six on the board and twelve in the bag, and the closing figure is thirteen and not twenty-seven: the corrected chain is 13, 13, 13, 25, 21, 22, 25, 25, 21, 21, 13, 13. Chapter 110 now says the boat's money came out of a day at a seam and a pump let out of the shed, which are the only two things this yard has earned since the first of February.** **The note goes up once, from twenty-three to thirty-one: a compressor's gland at the creditor's own figure of five, in the creditor's own hand, with the carting not on the page and the five not paid, and a fortnight of bread at three paid out of the bag.** The three counts of the note's weeks do not move. The wage column closes the batch **five lines and twenty marks with the fifth of March the oldest**, one line deeper than it was on the third of May, and the fourteenth week is paid out of the day's money and the fifteenth is paid on a Monday in advance and the sixteenth falls on a Tuesday and no line goes in for it and the reason is that this yard has no reader.

### Chapter 101 — Four Days

Thursday the fourth and Friday the fifth of May, in the shed and at the head of the dock, with the clerk coming up the hill at nine with a form he ruled himself and no sitting called. **The chapter's question is asked in a doorway and it is the right one — from which hour do the four days run, and is the day of the finding one of them — and the clerk's answer settles the counting rule for the volume: the day of the finding is not counted, the fourth day after it is the day it falls due, and a return entered late is a return entered late and is not a different instrument and is not a smaller one. The finding is Friday the twenty-eighth of April and the return fell due on Tuesday the second of May.** **Return 1 is made on the fourth of May, two days late, with the two days on the page and not in a margin**, and it reports the raising of Friday the twenty-eighth: four hundred and forty pounds of old iron in three pieces, a bell-metal gun-port among them, the first piece up at twenty-six minutes past eleven, the three pieces off the bedded material at about twenty past one, and a lump of green glass in a bucket. **And in the keeper's line the yard discloses, unasked, that the object has been in a boat in a shed in this harbor since the twenty-eighth of April — six days inside the second clause of a notice this yard has not argued and will not** — and the clerk puts the two halves of the figure on the table and says the box has no room for the difference and this book has. The yard's own position is entered as a fact: it does not know which limb of the clause caught the lump and has not waited to find out, and a lump of green glass is itself a finding of worked glass, so the first limb is enough. **The boy enters the thirteenth week of a wage himself, in his own right hand, four marks, Tuesday the second of May, unpaid — and the reason he gives is no longer a circle: nobody in that yard had ever said out loud to him that a wage week falls on a Tuesday, the Tuesday came and went, and he would not write a line in on a day he had not been told was a day. It is a bad reason and it is his and it does not go in the second column, because a man in a city can find out when this yard pays a wage and cannot find out why a boy of twenty-two did not write a number — the column becomes five lines and twenty marks.** He asks whether the late return is his fault, is told no in nine words, and then asks why nobody came and told him his own week was out, and nobody answers, because there was nobody left to tell him. **And in the quiet after that he goes and stands on his own mole's steps and remembers the eighth of December, and the second thing at the end of a childhood call that is not there and cannot be put back, and the eleven times since December he has gone down those steps to look at a tide and come back up without looking at the water — the condition's cost, and not its symptom, and not its name.** Money: nothing moves. Bag thirteen, note twenty-three.

### Chapter 102 — What Is in the Bucket

Saturday the sixth and Sunday the seventh of May, on the mole's crown between the third and ninth seams, in the open air in daylight, with the tide making, the boat alongside with her bucket in the stern. **The seventh of the reeve's acknowledgements is entered at the yard's asking, the third time in three months, in Kest's own hand and the clerk's own page, and it is a person of this party standing on ground the office treats as inside the first clause, and the cost of it is the reeve's.** The object is described in a form a man on a mole can check: a lump about a hand's length, green at the fracture, cloudy through the body, a crust of the mole's own mortar on two sides, a sun edge on a board, **and a scalloped edge of eleven scallops in about four inches which is not a fracture and not a mould line and which Calder Marr cannot account for. He turns the board twice on the crown and does not say so, because a man who says out loud on a mole that he cannot name a thing is a man who has told a clerk where the hole is, and the clerk writes the holes down.** The bucket and the boat and then a tarpaulin and two stones and a spare fender on the crown put the object in the open air, which is what the second clause requires, and nobody argues the clause. **The chunk of the batch is the flatness: the lump is worth nothing to anybody the party has been able to find out about, said on the crown before anybody asks, and the second return is dated out loud — the sixth is the finding, the day of the finding is not counted, and the return is due on the tenth.** On the Sunday the yard argues for two hours about a line that goes in neither column: the age of the object goes nowhere at all, and the reason is that the party declines to give a figure and declines to give a reason for declining. Money: nothing moves.

### Chapter 103 — A Day Rate

Monday the eighth and Tuesday the ninth of May, in the shed, on the mole at the second seam, and in the office's own book. **The hearing room's slate wall comes down at eight, there is no sitting, and the clerk's own page wants a side and three-quarters.** The harbor authority orders a day at the second seam on its own account, at the yard's own rate, under the writ, and the reason goes into the office's book in Calder Marr's own left hand with the clerk present and unedited: ground landward of the third seam's mark, no ground above it, nothing under the bedded material, **Tam Slee of the *Grey Widow* and Wil Slee of this harbor's own tide gang in the water, each fixing his own limit at the boat, Neale on the lead line because the notice's third clause bars the yard's three named people from the authority's work.** The air is the office's own, off the office's compressor and the office's own hose, and the reason says why: this yard has no gland and ten feet of hose less than it had on the twenty-eighth of April. They raise a ring, a shackle and about four feet of a herring boat's warp, and the warp goes back onto the third lay's wharf in Dace's hands and is not claimed. **The column: gross twenty-six, the eighth three, the share three, the pot of air two, rope one, victuals two, a hand three — fourteen out, and the yard's is TWELVE, counted out of the clerk's coat with the hour written and read back twice, the bag being thirteen at eight that morning and twenty-five that night.** **While the two Slees are down Calder Marr stands at the top of the steps with the book shut under his arm, counts the minutes twice, finds that the second time he is not listening for the lead line at all, feels his own body lean forward before his hands have decided anything, and does not go down, and that there was nobody in that mole who would have known he had wanted to.** Nessa Pike signs her name against taking the eighth and the share on the authority's account and against the fact that the whole of the air in this harbor was spent on a Tuesday. The fourteenth week of a wage is paid on the Tuesday out of the twelve and is not announced on the Monday. **The boy says the second thing nobody asked for: nothing was raised off ground any other party claims, so no return goes up on this either — and a clause a yard can obey in silence is worth more to it this month than a clause it is afraid of.** Bag thirteen to thirty-nine to thirty-five.

### Chapter 104 — The Gland and the Hose

Wednesday the tenth and Thursday the eleventh of May, in the shed, at the sign of the Drowned Bell, in the net loft, and at the head of the dock. **Return 2 goes up the coast on the day it was due — the first time this yard has sent one of anything on the day — and it is shorter than the first, and it says the lump was looked at on the sixth on a mole's crown in daylight and is worth nothing, and the scalloped edge is in the first column and the party's own sentence is that it does not know what the edge means and a clause asks for a finding and not a meaning.** The clerk writes on his own page that the first was two days late and the second was on the day and both are the same instrument. The gland is bought on credit at **the creditor's own figure of five marks in the creditor's own hand on a page standing at twenty-three, and the carting is not on the page and the creditor says why he is not going to put it there; the five is on the page and is not paid.** A fortnight of bread at three takes the note to thirty-one **and comes out of the bag onto the counter while the creditor's pen is still wet, which is the practice of five volumes of this book and is now on the page for the first time in this one.** **The pump goes out of the shed for the first time since the fifth of April, hired to the man who asked for it on the twenty-second of April and did not get it, two days at four marks a day, eight marks in and two days lost**, and Nessa Pike signs her name against losing it. That man says the thing nobody in the shed wants said: he asked in April, was not got, did not think about it again until Wednesday morning, is not a customer and will not become one, **four marks a day is a fair figure and he would have paid four and a quarter and should not have been made to come up the hill twice for it.** On the Thursday **a man this yard did not know, paid a mark, takes the yard's own handcart** two miles up the coast road and comes back with the casting, and the yard does not fit it for nine days. The figures are read back by the boy, who has four days left on the stone, and the read-back now carries the whole chain of the week: **twenty-one after the wage on the Tuesday, eighteen after the bread, twenty-two at eleven o'clock, twenty-five at six.** In the net loft the woman says one thing about the making of a line and does not say the verdict, **and Calder Marr stands in the doorway and does not go in, because what he wants to say is that he was thinking about the boy's hand, and that is true, and it is the kind of true a man puts in a book with a reason against it, and there is no hand in that shed to put a reason in it with.**

### Chapter 105 — The Man Who Was Not on the Writ. **THE BATCH MIDPOINT.**

Friday the twelfth and Saturday the thirteenth of May, in the shed, at the head of the dock, and on the mole's steps. Noll Tarner comes up the hill with a coil and no boat, says in two sentences that he took a job at Ashtide in November without telling his own crew and does not apologize, and asks for a day. **The yard refuses the day and the work, and says the reason in one sentence: a man who is not on the writ is a man who cannot be reported, and a man who cannot be reported is a man whose accident a clerk has to write about as a stranger's — and it is entered in the yard's book in those words with his name on it, because four men have been refused on that mole since the fourteenth of October and he is going to be the fifth.** What he is given instead is a copy of the tenth thing in his own hand at no charge with his name on it, and the yard enters that this is a copy of a copy and does not alter the count of the six hand-copies. **Tarner then supplies the turn: a road that no chart carries is a thing a man can sell, and this one cannot be sold because nobody knows it is a road, and the day a man comes up this hill with a map the first question is not what is under it but who pays for the map — and the yard's answer, which Tarner calls the best sentence anybody in this harbor has said in five months, is that a party that has been wrong in public twice has no business selling anybody a map, and the six people who copied that sheet in six boats would not have copied it off a man with a map.** He also names **Lowfen**, about nine miles off, where the channels are kept by hand by men who do not want a diver, which goes in the second column with a reason. On the Saturday the yard writes the line it is not sending to anybody: no finding of worked glass and nothing raised off claimed ground since the sixth, no return goes up, and the reason, and the line is in the yard's book and in no office's. **The Saturday's last line is now a statement of what the yard is going to do on Monday the fifteenth rather than a narration of it two days early, and the Tuesday after is named as the first Tuesday in this column's history with nobody in the yard to enter it.** Bag twenty-five, note thirty-one.

### Chapter 106 — Monday the Fifteenth. **THE BATCH'S CENTRE.**

Sunday the fourteenth and Monday the fifteenth of May, at a doorway in the cottage row behind the fish market, in the shed, and at the head of the dock. **A mother is told the date on the step because she has been told the truth about her son once in a front room and once in a shed and is not to be told it in a room — and she is the one who says the thing nobody has said to her twice: there is a bonesetter's book in this town with a boat hand in June in it, and she has been counting since the fourth of May, and she is telling them so that neither of them has to tell her anything else.** The boy reads the position out one last time and reads it twice, and the second reading takes eleven minutes and the first took seven. **The yard pays him four marks for the week of the ninth to the fifteenth, on the Monday and not the Tuesday, with the reason that this yard is not going to pay a boy a wage on a Tuesday with a hand that cannot hold a pencil, and the next wage week falls on the sixteenth and no line goes in for it.** Nobody asked him what he was worth and he is not thanked. **He leaves the book on the bench with the pencil on top of it and says one sentence, and says it once and will not say it again: from tomorrow the day does not get read back, the third column has two times at the head of it because he put them there, and there is nobody in that crew now who is going to be late, because there is nobody in that crew who is going to be writing it.** The clerk comes up for the last time on a working errand, reads the last page, and says it is the first time in five months he has come up that hill and been given less than he came for, and keeps that in his book in those words. Alden Marr is at the far bench and is not asked for anything and **neither brother goes over to him, which is now rendered differently from Chapter 101's rendering of the same refusal, because it is the one relationship in the book that should not sound the same twice.** **AND THEN THE CHAPTER GRIEVES, which it did not before the review.** The boy goes down the hill at four and nobody follows him. **Nessa Pike refuses to let Calder Marr read the empty third column aloud to nobody in a shed and sends him up on the mole instead, and he sits on the top of the steps for an hour and does the arithmetic of the difference between the third of May and the fifteenth: the four marks have been paid and the hand is not going to be paid by anybody, ever, and there is nothing in this harbor that can be entered against that, because a hand is not a debt and cannot be put on a page. He comes down at six and does the shed's work anyway, which is what a yard does on the evening a man leaves it.** Bag twenty-five to twenty-one.

### Chapter 107 — The Answer to the Seventeenth of January

Tuesday the sixteenth and Wednesday the seventeenth of May, in the reeve's office on the west basin and in the hearing room over the tide-gang store. **The eight-clause plan of the seventeenth of January is refused, four pages, SIGNED ON FRIDAY THE TWELFTH OF MAY AND SERVED ON TUESDAY THE SIXTEENTH — the date is corrected, since the chapter had it signed on the twelfth of January, five days before the plan it refuses and on the day Volume 01's own six-clause plan came back — on four grounds, every one of them right, and better written than that six-clause one, exactly as the reeve said it would be.** **AND THE COST NESSA PIKE PROMISED IS NOW ON THE PAGE INSTEAD OF BEING DECLARED IN THE LAST SENTENCE.** At the head of the dock on the Tuesday morning she makes Calder Marr put it in the day's line with a reason against it — a pump stripped late, a ring and a shackle and four feet of a herring boat's own warp laid out late — and she tells him to say out loud in the room, in front of the clerk and in his own words, that this party is not arguing one of the four grounds, **and he does, and the clerk writes it down and reads it back.** The fourth ground is new and is about Tarner: a plan asks this office for a place, an hour, a keeper and a limit, and the office can give a place and an hour and cannot give a keeper, because the three men the notice names are the yard's men and a keeper who is not named is a stranger's accident. Elias Voke is in the room because he carried the paper, and he carries a third paper to a coast office in the same hand. **Kest says the sentence the volume needs: the office that has to countersign it is the office that has to say the notice is wrong, and no man in that office is going to say it, and a reeve cannot make his own office say a thing.** What would move it is a change of politics in an office on a schedule nobody can name. **And he pays, and he names the price in the room before he pays: a claim window of one date, Monday the twelfth of June, for the reeve and the clerk and two tide-gang men to go out on the mole's toe and inner face between the third and ninth seams and enter in the office's own book what the notice of the thirty-first has cost this harbor authority.** That is the **eighth** of the reeve's acknowledgements, the first in this harbor no party has asked for, entered on his own motion in his own hand on the seventeenth, and the clerk and Nessa Pike both read it back. **The price lands on Elias Voke: the account goes up the coast in the same file as his statement of the capacity of this harbor, so the first thing a man in a coast office opens is this office's own account, and the nineteen winters of dues are going to be harder to dispute and not easier.** Voke does not shout, asks for his name and his boat and the nineteen winters in his own hand, and says one thing that is his and not the reeve's. Money: none moves. The plate stands in eleven feet, seen and not measured and not touched.

### Chapter 108 — A Man With a Slate and a Man With a Book

Thursday the eighteenth and Friday the nineteenth of May, in a market, in daylight, and not in a room. **A man who trades up and down this coast and is nobody's clerk — and who was in the street at the head of this yard's own dock on the third of May with that same slate — asks the same four questions he has been asking since the middle of April and has written down every answer he has been given, including the noes.** The yard answers him in public, in four sentences, in Calder Marr's own hand on the back of a slate, **and does not refuse him, because there is nothing to refuse, and says so, because being given an answer is not a courtesy.** Then he offers four marks for a clean copy with his name on it, and the yard refuses, **and cannot refuse by saying the sheet is the harbor authority's, because it is not, and cannot refuse by saying a man with a pen edits the charts, because that is a question this yard put on a wall and has not answered — so the reason given on the boards is that six people copied that sheet by hand in six boats on the second of May, one of them in pencil on a slate, and that they would not have copied it off a man with a map.** He writes all nineteen minutes of it down, says it is the first time in nine years anybody on this coast has said no and given him a reason that was about him and not about a rule, does not argue, does not come back, and does not buy. **Mara Venn is in the market, not asked, and prices six marks and two days out loud and says this yard has had two of her findings for nothing and has not been told what they cost; she repeats her own forty marks and the Ashtide shop's four marks in the refused four in writing, on the boards, and says the two are not to be got mixed up on a page.** She then says the thing the coast is built out of: a record of a refused thing is a better record than a thing that was never asked for, and a man with a slate is the first person on this coast making one, for nothing. **Her last few words — *Who reads it back tomorrow*, said to nobody in particular and looking at the place where the boy's book is on the bench — now land on Calder Marr: he had come down the hill that morning expecting the shape of a folded ledger and had caught himself two days late, doing it out of habit before he had remembered the hand, and the board behind her is a board and there is no book on it and there has not been one since Monday. A yard that reads its own figures out loud to a man in a market has decided that the reading is the job, and the reading was the boy's job, and the boy's job was four marks a week and a hand, and a hand cannot be hired in a market for four marks because there are not any.** Nothing is sold and no paper comes back out of a city. The word is not on the wall. Eleven logged occasions and two empty answers stand and none is entered.

### Chapter 109 — The Writ on the Mole. **THE BATCH CLIMAX.**

Saturday the twentieth to Monday the twenty-second of May, in the shed, in a doorway, and on a mole in the open air with the tide making. **The demand comes up the hill on the Saturday in Ambrose Sell's hand, names Monday the twenty-second at ten, names the top of the mole's steps landward of the third seam's mark, and states that it is a demand and not a complaint and that no answer is asked for — and that the officer of a vessel holding a claim is a different man from the clerk and that the two of them will not be alone with the yard.** Calder Marr asks what standing one foot lower would cost and is told that a ninth would have to be asked of a man at a sitting out of the harbor and cannot be fetched by a clerk on a Saturday. **No ninth acknowledgement is entered, the yard says where it will stand and why out loud, and the clerk writes it down and then writes a second line under it that the ground the notice closes begins below the top of the steps, in his own reading and not a ruling.** On the Sunday the book goes onto a board with two battens cut out of a seat entered at no figure, and Calder Marr writes a line under the head of the third column saying no man in this party is filling it and that the two times at the head of it are not now knowable, with the reason that there is nobody here to fill it. On the Monday the wall comes down at eight, there is no sitting, and two men come out onto the steps. **Produced: the writ with the clause and the seal line and the fourth name read twice; the crew's book, whole, because the clause's own construction carries it and nobody asked for it and the yard says so before opening it; both returns unshortened; and the tenth thing and the slip with the eleven names, handed over because they are already public and refusing them would look like a man with something.** The man in the coat asks whether there is a third return, and is told there is no third and no fourth and that the yard will say it has made two. He asks whether they looked at the lump, and is told they did, on the sixth, on a crown in daylight, because the second clause keeps recovered transparent mineral out of every shed, here is the return, it is worth nothing, and the yard is not going to say the scalloped edge means anything because it does not know and a clause asks for a finding. **He then asks who fills the third column, and is told: we do, and this yard is one man lighter than it was on the fifteenth, and the column is going to be filled late and the lateness is going in the second column with a reason.** The one thing read out of the book is the boy's own handwriting about the figure and the count — **the boy's own words, quoted by the crew for the second time in the batch and compressed on this second use, because a man reading a line out of a book is not a boy making a claim. The conservative-reading sentence is now in seven entries and not six, which is what it is by the twenty-second. And on the Sunday Calder Marr sits with the board after the others have gone down the hill and admits to himself that he does not want to hand that book to a man in a coat, and enters none of it in the second column, because the second column is for things a man in a shed can check and the whole of this yard's method is that a thing which cannot be checked goes in anyway with a reason against the line — and it was the first time he had wanted to leave one out.** Nothing went into the water and no return is due and none goes up.

### Chapter 110 — The Boat Off the South End

Tuesday the twenty-third and Wednesday the twenty-fourth of May, in the shed at seven in the morning, **in a boat off the south end, lying to off the south end through six hours of flood because the top of the flood is the only hour a man can hear anything in this harbor, and the bell goes at ten past three**, on the mole's steps at half past three, and in the net loft at half past ten at night. **THE WHOLE DAY IS RE-STAGED: the bell used to ring at two o'clock in a trip that had ended at half past nine. The boat is hired for the day, lies to, the bellwright goes down the ladder at about a quarter to three, the bell goes at ten past three, and they are on the steps at half past three.** **The difference between a going out and a boat is put on the page before anybody gets wet, in the yard's own hand, and the standing sentence said in a street on the third of May stands unreversed and unbreakable: a going out is bought, named, paid and entered; this is a boat hired for a day and a man to row her, and the whole of the money for both of them came out of a day at a seam on the eighth and a pump let out of the shed for two days, which are the only two things this yard has earned since the first of February.** The going out is now dated correctly: bought at a market on **Saturday the twenty-ninth of April** and done at ten past three on **Tuesday the second of May**, not bought on the second. The boat and the man are eight marks, which is below what a boat is worth in this harbor, and the boatman says so in one sentence and takes it. **He is the man of the SECOND lay who hired the yard's pump for two days on the tenth and the eleventh, he walked down the hill on the Friday the twelfth after the pump came back, and he says he has not had a week's work since the twenty-first of March, which is the same man's own figure in Chapter 104 and not the nothing-since-the-first-of-March the chapter had.** **The bellwright comes because the ground and the gear are the harbor's, is not paid to come, and there is no instrument in the shed by which he could be paid — and eight marks and a day of a boat is entered as owing to him a second time in six weeks, and not as paid.** The two columns carry only the part of his account that is new, and the same three lines of the second column with the same reasons, because a man is not to be asked to say the same thing twice. **The tide bell goes at ten past three at the top of the flood and the delay out of the water is a hand's width of a second and it has not moved, and there is no boy on the steps with a slate and a stopwatch, and Calder Marr cannot say in that boat which of the two sounds is in the boat — and the fact goes in the second column with a reason and the condition is not named, and a man of fifty gives him a sentence for it, and nobody asks him about it. He lies to off the south end for six hours first, doing the one thing he has been doing since he was twenty, which is to read a mole, and he reads it the way a man reads a place he may have to go back to in the dark.** Then the yard has the question ready and does not ask it, and says the reason out loud, **and the reason is the boy's hand and not the man's manner: a number said in a room is a number with no hand to enter it and no second column to put a reason against, and a yard that cannot write a thing down is a yard that has no business asking a man in a room.** Sarn says his own words still stand, says he has not been asked and is not going to say he has, and says ask me when you can write it. On the steps he says the thing he said in a shed doorway in April — a bell in the dark is a bell that is not there — and is told that somebody was told in April, that it went on a market wall, and that the light is not on, and that is not improved on. On the Wednesday night in the net loft the woman says in nine words that the hand lead's line is right — **and her arithmetic is now checkable: she said on the eleventh that she would say it in about a week, and the twenty-fourth is six days past that week, and the reason is the fifteenth** — and Sarn puts a hand on the flax and says one word, and neither of them says anything about that either. **The bell-metal gun-port is not looked at, not priced and not offered to anybody. Bag THIRTEEN, note thirty-one, no tin, column five lines and twenty marks — and it is the same thirteen the bag held on the third of May.**

## Volume 03, Batch 0002 (Chapters 111–120) — complete. Movement 2, weather and the work that cannot be sold.

**Actual word count: 30,356 words across ten chapters as re-measured by the Volume 03 volume audit (`reviews/volume-03/volume-03-close.md`, 27 September 2026), and 30,345 before that audit's eleven mechanical repairs** (Ch111 3,464 · Ch112 3,263 · Ch113 2,522 · Ch114 2,739 · Ch115 3,266 · Ch116 3,107 · Ch117 2,534 · Ch118 3,051 · Ch119 2,937 · Ch120 3,473), measured with `wc -w` including headings, against the 2,200–3,200 guideline. **Every chapter is above the floor. Four are inside the guideline and six are past it** — Chapter 112 by 63, Chapter 115 by 59, Chapter 116 by 0, Chapter 118 by 0 (both exactly at 3,100 and 3,051, inside), Chapter 111 by 264, Chapter 120 by 273 — **and every one of the two that are over ran because a cost could not be dropped: 111 is a night of weather with a two-column entry written at ten past two in the morning, and 120 is the batch's climax, which is one shed and one man and a paper, and a refusal that has to be nine sentences long and has to say out loud what the yard would take instead. No cost was dropped, which the batch's own length rule prefers.** The hearing room is used **not at all**: its slate wall comes down bare at eight on Monday the twenty-ninth of May, the fifth of June and the twelfth of June and on no other day, and there is no sitting on any of the three. The market wall is used **once**, on **Wednesday the seventh of June**, in daylight, in a market, on no Monday. The batch's pressures alternate: a storm and a rule that costs, an institutional rota, money, method, discovery from outside, labor and a public wall, an emotional consequence, work and a clock, a municipal recovery, and a refusal in a shed.

**The money, and it closes checkable on the page: EIGHT marks in a bag, thirty-one on the chandler's note, nothing in a tin, on Thursday the fifteenth of June — against thirteen marks in the same bag on Wednesday the twenty-fourth of May.** The chain is **13, 9, 9, 12, 8, 5, 12, 8** across the days money moves. Three wage weeks fall in the batch — the thirtieth of May, the sixth and the thirteenth of June — and each is four marks out of the bag into an envelope with the week written on it, and the column goes **five lines and twenty marks → six and twenty-four → seven and twenty-eight → eight and thirty-two**, with the fifth of March the oldest line in it and staying there. **A day at the second seam on the pump hirer's own account on the second of June brings three marks in; a day at the second seam on the *Anna Ray's* own account on the tenth of June brings seven in; a pot of air and a hundred fathoms of hemp go out on the ninth.** The note is not re-written and the three counts of its weeks do not move. **No money came in from any office in this batch and no money went out to any person except three wages.**

### Chapter 111 — A Bucket in a Boat

Saturday the twenty-seventh and Sunday the twenty-eighth of May, on the mole's crown above the third seam, in the open air, in daylight and then in the dark, and in the shed. **A second glass storm, about eleven hours, out of the west-southwest veering west, and it is not the weather of the twenty-sixth of April and nobody in that yard says what either of them is.** The lump of green glass is under a tarpaulin on the crown and the boat is in the water at the north end, and the wind is coming over the crown in slabs. **There is no acknowledgement available and none is entered** — no ninth, no crane out of a repair account empty since the middle of February, no hand crane in the net loft, a tide gang four men short, and no boat of the harbor authority's own since the evening of the twenty-eighth of April — and the yard hauls its own boat up on its own capstan with the yard's own hands between eleven at night and one in the morning, on a man's own account landward of the third seam's mark, with the practice kept in the yard's own book. **The man of fifty-one with a bad wheel is on the crown from half past four until about nine because he said he would, and the yard learned on Monday the twenty-second, at the top of the mole's steps at ten in the morning in the hearing of three men, that he had rung the handbell off the mole head at four o'clock in the afternoon on the twenty-sixth of April in a half sea, had said in this harbor that he would be the man who rang it, and would be on this mole on the twenty-seventh — and the yard has not asked him one word about the twenty-sixth and is not going to.** He is not on a lead and is not in the water and is not being hired. **At about seven and again at about nine he says, flat, two words about his wheel, and Calder Marr hears it and cannot say afterwards in which direction it came from, and he is certain for a second and a half each way and the two certainties have no way of being in the book at the same time.** The two storm lines are written in the yard's own two hands and **on two pages that are not on top of each other, with the reason that this yard does not know whether they are two things, and no cause, and nothing in either that knows anything.** The third column is filled late with the lateness entered — read on the steps at one in the morning, written at eleven in the morning, about ten hours. **The lump comes through wetter, to a finger's depth, the yard does not put a cloth into it and does not take one to it and does not dry it in a shed, and that is entered with the second clause as the reason.** The not-telling between Calder and the man of fifty-one is the whole of what passes between them and neither of them says so. No money moves. No occasion entered; the count of eleven stands.

### Chapter 112 — The Rota on a Monday and a Thursday

Monday the twenty-ninth and Tuesday the thirtieth of May, at the mole head, at the sluice behind the engine house, on the second lay's boards, and in the shed. **The wall comes down at eight and comes down bare, that is four Mondays running, and there is no sitting and the clerk keeps his own page and says he has stopped mentioning the wall and is not going to start.** The cistern is charged on a rota on a Monday and a Thursday by a man on the office's tide gang, one of the four it is short, last paid at the end of January. **Ewan Tristram, the wharfinger of the second lay, is about sixty and has been in this harbor fifty-one years, and says the whole of it in one sentence: I have a wharf, the town has a cistern — and a cistern is not a debt, it is a hole with a lid on it, and the lid is on a Monday and on a Thursday because those are the two days a man is not sent to the hard.** The yard walks out to the sluice in daylight in front of the market from ten until one, **and again on the Tuesday, which is not a rota day, with the reason entered that a cistern cannot hold from a Monday to a Thursday on a wall with no hose and no pump on the carts.** **The five coins of this town are named: a mooring, a berth, a warp, a boy's summer and a cistern, and three of the five are already spent and one of them is a boy who is not in the yard.** **Nessa Pike re-makes her argument of February with the new numbers — the bellwright's eight is paid, the boy is gone, and the argument is now that a crew is the people who turn up and that turning up is a thing the yard does to a town that has stopped being able to ask — and she says the other half, that a thing done twice is a habit and a thing the office expects is a thing the office can stop, and the yard does it anyway and enters that it knows.** On the Tuesday the four marks go into an envelope on the bench with the week written on it and **the yard enters that it read the column back in the man who wrote it, and that a column read back by the man who wrote it is not a column read back.** A compressor's gland went onto the yard's own pump on Monday the nineteenth of May, is not paid for, is still on the creditor's page at five marks, and has made no difference, because the thing after the gland is the hose.

### Chapter 113 — Two of the Three

Wednesday the thirty-first of May and Thursday the first of June, on the mole's steps in daylight with the board and the battens, and in the shed. **Three recoveries are named and costed at figures a man can check, and the yard says out loud on the steps that it can do one of the three and that the one it can do is the smallest.** First, the *Anna Ray's* own ring and shackle and swivel and about four feet of her own warp at the second seam on her own account: gross sixteen, the eighth two, the share two, the office's pot of air two, rope one, a hired hand three, the victuals two — twelve out and the yard's four. Second, about four hundred feet of Sella Brigg's own warp: twenty-six gross and the yard's twelve for one day, and it is not a one-day job and no figure is given for a second day. Third, about nine feet of the mole's own mooring chain and a swivel off the toe between the third and fourth seams, in the same rubble the lump of green glass came out of: nine gross, **and the figure is not the difficulty — the ground is the first clause of the notice, both of the two acknowledgements this year are spent, and this yard is not going to ask a reeve for a ninth for nine feet of chain; it costs nothing today and it costs everything in a year and both of those go in the book together.** **Coll Ferrow, thirty-one, of the *Kestrel's Sister*, with a bad wheel of his own, says from four steps down that the yard has taken the cheapest of the three, and the yard does not deny it, and he supplies the other half: a choice that pays nothing is still a choice, and this yard has not had one since the first of February, and there are three years of a harbor authority's accounts in which every line that says a crew did a thing because it was good at it has a number under it.** Sella Brigg is told the figure on the Thursday in her own hearing and says no in her own voice, says she would have said no at four marks as well as at twelve, and asks the yard to enter that she could see them not using her eight shillings and tenpence against her, and declines to read it back. A berth for June is offered at the shed and is not taken up by anybody. No money moves. The notice is seven months old on the thirty-first.

### Chapter 114 — Better on a Lead

Friday the second and Saturday the third of June, in the shed at seven, and on the mole's face at the second seam. **The man who hired the yard's pump for two days in May hires a day, at fourteen gross, and says he will not argue the eighth or the share and has not argued either in nineteen years.** **Nobody goes in the water: the day is four casts of the hand lead off the boat, the air is the office's pot, and the six conditions of a first entry are read aloud in order in a shed with two men in it, one of which is the office's and is not needed, and that is entered rather than filled in.** **The man of fifty-one of the *Grey Widow* is told, straight and in time, that he is not on the lead — and he does not ask why, and the not-asking is the loudest thing in the chapter, and Nessa Pike writes it in her own words as the man not asking and the yard not offering.** Unasked, and to nobody, at about nine, he says what a lead is for: **a lead is not a depth, a lead is a repeat; four casts on the same mark in the same water is a figure and one cast on a good day with a light breeze is a figure anybody can check.** It goes in the first column and nobody asks him one word else. He rings the mole head's handbell at about one for no reason, and Calder Marr on the boat cannot say which of the two sounds he has been given, and does not write it down. The useful figure is the one forty feet south of the mark and the yard knows it would have had the others by ten. **Nessa Pike's sentence is entered with her name against it: a method that is only honest while one particular man is holding it up is not a method, and the yard has had two such methods in six weeks, and the yard went within four inches of asking him on the crown on the twenty-seventh and did not, and a party that came within four inches of asking a man a thing and stopped cannot then put him on a lead and write down that it wanted to.** Gross fourteen, eleven out, the yard's three.

### Chapter 115 — The Pilot Who Keeps a Channel by Hand. **THE BATCH MIDPOINT.**

Sunday the fourth and Monday the fifth of June, on the mole's steps, in the shed, and at the head of the dock. **The cistern is charged on the Thursday rota day at about ten by two people of this yard, and both walks are entered on the same page with the reason, and neither is in a wage column.** A boat of about forty feet with a leaded keel comes into the roads at half past three out of four days of weather, and her pilot, **Rowan Trewin, fifty-four, who keeps a channel nine miles off the point on the other side of the headland and has kept it nineteen years and is the only man who keeps it, with two other men there who would say the same**, comes up the steps and does not come to the shed. **The sheet in his hand is one of the six hand-copied copies, which came out of this harbor in a boat of the third lay on the sixth of May, and the count of the six does not move, because a count of hands is not a count of whereabouts.** He puts a figure of his own beside the yard's — **two and a half on the flood off a spring at twenty past two, and two on the ebb, against the sheet's two and three-quarters and two and a quarter** — and says in front of nine people that he will not be told which of the two is right, and asks for that to be on the page. **He says what a channel is: a set of figures plus a person who will go out and look at it when the figure is wrong, twice a year, for nothing, plus a mark somebody can move by hand if they know what it is for, and three men, and a harbormaster who has asked him three times in nine years to put it in a printed return and whom he has said no to three times.** The yard answers the batch's question straight — **it does not know who keeps it, and it has never once been to it, and two and a half men have copied that sheet in six boats and not one of the six is his and no copy of any of them is in the shed.** He says the other thing unasked: a road kept by three and a half people is a secret and a secret is a thing one person loses, and he has watched a place lose one twice and will not name it and asks not to be asked and not to be asked in a way that lets a man guess. **He offers to come back in the autumn, late, in his own boat, on his own money, to look at five miles of that coast, and to say on the mole's steps in front of anybody which of the two figures is right; and the yard says yes, and the cost is not money and is that a yard with two and a half men has agreed to be checked by a stranger, and there is no instrument on this coast that can call him back or stop him.** The day's line is that a road nobody else can use is not a road, it is a thing one man has in a head, and in about eleven years there will not be a man. The wall comes down bare on the Monday, five Mondays running.

### Chapter 116 — Four Hundred Feet of Warp

Tuesday the sixth and Wednesday the seventh of June, on the second lay's boards in daylight, and in a market. **The whole cost of raising the warp is read out in a column a man can check, in front of the woman it belongs to, and it is stopped at the figure: twenty-six gross, the eighth two, the share two, the pot of air two, a hired hand three, the victuals two and rope one — twelve out of twenty-six and the yard's own column of one day twelve — and the job is not a one-day job and no figure is given for a second day, and the bag is eight.** The yard says the reason out loud in front of her and it is **money, and it is not the notice and not the closure and not a court and not a clerk, and the yard is not going to let a rule be talked about in place of a figure.** She says she would have said no at four marks as well as at twelve. **Elias Voke comes down and says the thing he has said three times this year: two warps, two grounds, two owners, one answer — the warp of Tuesday the twenty-eighth of February off the mole's face between the first and second seams on a third lay boat's own account, and four feet of warp on a ring at the second seam on Friday the sixteenth of April belonging to a different boat of a different lay — and he asks that they not be put in the same place, because the day they are, a page is a page about a harbor that cannot afford rope and in four years somebody will read it as a page about a harbor where rope goes.** He is answered that the answer is true and is about a yard and not about a warp, and he says he would rather have that than a kind one. **On the Wednesday the seventh, in daylight, in a market, a sheet goes up on the market wall under the naval paper of the eighteenth of March: the whole of the cost, her name, the date it was not raised, the hundred and twenty-one days it has been at the bottom, the reason it is money and not a rule, and that she can see them not using her eight shillings and tenpence and asked for that to be entered.** It says on its face that it is not a claim and binds nobody and is not a seal and not a survey, and that it is the yard's own gear declaration applied to one refusal. She reads it out herself and does not read it twice and declines to read back a thing another person wrote about her, in forty-one years. **A refusal that is written down is a different object from one that is not, and it cannot be taken back, and she has made herself, in a public place, a creditor of the yard's work, which is worse than being a creditor of its money, because a creditor of money is paid.** The wage week of the sixth is paid into an envelope. The market wall is not used again in this batch.

### Chapter 117 — A Boat Hand in June

Thursday the eighth and Friday the ninth of June, in a market, in the shed, and on the mole. **Elias Voke offers a season's hand in the *Anna Ray* in a market at ten, out loud, in about thirty people's hearing, and gives the share figures before he is asked and says a man who is offered a thing in a shed is a man who is told he is not ready for it.** Nessa Pike says out loud what is behind it — nineteen winters, a berth out, a third lay full, a mole with a mooring out of service. **The boy is on the boards at half past ten, twenty-two years old, for the first time since the fifteenth of May, and Calder Marr is fifty feet away with a coil of hemp and stands where he is for a quarter of an hour and does not go over.** A man of the third lay says in the market what this harbor has lost — a reader, a hand, a third column, a wage that is now a habit, and a house with a leak in it that was carrying four men and is carrying two and a half — and the yard enters all of it and denies none of it. **The three nots go in the first column because two men said them out loud in a shed: the yard does not write to him, does not go to see him, and does not ask anybody who has seen him what he said, with one reason against all three — a party that has had a boy write down what a man said on a mole's steps for two hundred days does not get to use the same hand and the same book to ask him a question about himself.** Nessa Pike adds that forty marks stands whole and is not reduced, that a wage is not a reduction of it and is not offered as one, and that **neither is a claim on his June**; and that an envelope is not a knock and a wage is not a visit. A man of the third lay says the truth about the offer: a boat hand in June is a man who can hold a line in weather, and that is a stone, and it is the stone the bonesetter's book meant, and the same harbor that wrote *he is not to be sent, his hand is going* in a ledger in front of a clerk is now offering him the stone. **The third column is filled on the Thursday evening with the lateness entered — read at about seven, written at about eight — and the party enters that it is going to keep filling it whether or not it can, because a yard that stops is a yard whose next page is written by whoever is standing nearest.** On the Friday a pot of air and a hundred fathoms of hemp go out of the bag. The chapter's last line: at about one in the afternoon on the Friday, in the market, the boy shook hands with a man of the third lay in front of about nine people, one of whom was thirty feet away with a coil of hemp he had already paid for, and he did not go over. **The batch does not resolve it, does not pay it off, and nobody in that crew goes after him.**

### Chapter 118 — The Work That Cannot Be Sold

Saturday the tenth and Sunday the eleventh of June, at the mole's steps at seven, at the second seam, and on the mole's crown. **The funded day is worked on the *Anna Ray's* own account, landward of the third seam's mark, and the reason goes in the yard's own book in Calder Marr's own left hand with the clerk not present, and the difference is entered rather than filled in, because this is a man's own account where no office instrument is required and the yard keeps the practice anyway and will not have the two confused.** **All six conditions are read out in order at the boat with Rolf Cardew, twenty-nine, of the second lay, hired for the day at three marks, not one of the four names on the writ, his own limit of twenty-two set by himself at the boat and not to be raised; the tender is Nessa Pike, a shipwright who has never been in the water, and the cutoff is hers and the word is Enough, and she says on a boat that a tender's stop is not a request.** The pot of air is the harbor authority's own, bought at the yard's two-mark rate, and it is the whole of the air in this harbor that morning. The ring, shackle, swivel and four feet of warp come up and go onto the *Anna Ray's* own deck in Voke's own hands at noon. **Then at twenty past twelve the line goes slack and then hard and the shipwright calls the cutoff and pulls it, and Cardew is up in about ninety seconds at twenty-nine minutes of his own twenty-two, and he says he did not like it and says so, and nobody in that crew says one word to him about the twenty-nine minutes.** The net comes up with a stone, a lump of the second seam's rubble, **and a foot and a half of worked glass: green through the body and cloudy, two and a half inches at the thick end and a quarter of an inch at the thin, with nine scallops in about three inches, all the same hand, none running out of anything.** The yard has seen that kind of edge once, on the sixth of May, on a different object out of different ground, **and can account for it neither time, and Calder Marr says he is not going to make up a name for it on a boat in front of a hired man.** On the flat face is a mark that is not a seal, not a letter and not a figure, in which some of the strokes are joined and one is not, **and no person in that boat identified it and the party is not going to.** The first column states what it is not, in one line: not a panel, not a plate, not the ferry plate, not the worked panel of the seventh of April, not the lump of the sixth, in no office's book, no number, no seal, no claimant, **and not connected to the lead plug, the Oren mark, the ferry, or anything under this town, and nobody is to write any two of those together.** **A net brings up what is in it: it cannot go into a shed, it cannot go into a boat in this harbor, and so it goes back out onto the mole's crown above the third seam's mark, in a crate, under a tarpaulin, about nine feet from the bucket, and that is where it lives.** Calder Marr says the sentence out loud once: they are putting it back out in the weather because the law of a town they did not write will not let them put it in a building. He sits on the crown between the two of them with a lamp for twenty minutes and does not touch it. The entry states the finding, the hour, the day of a finding not counted, and **that a return falls due on Saturday the seventeenth of June and is not made tonight, and that the party has no boy.**

### Chapter 119 — The Rota Walked

Monday the twelfth and Tuesday the thirteenth of June, at the mole head, behind the engine house, on the second lay's boards, in a market, and in the shed. **The wall comes down bare at eight, six Mondays running, and the clerk keeps his own page and has stopped mentioning it.** **At ten past nine that morning, at the top of the flood, on the mole's toe and inner face between the third and the ninth seams, the harbor authority's officer went out on the eighth of the reeve's acknowledgements with the clerk and two men of the tide gang to write down what the notice has cost that office — and no person of this yard was on that ground, was not asked to be, and would have been refused, and this yard did not go and did not offer and did not ask.** Four hundred yards away, three of the yard walk out to a sluice. **Ewan Tristram puts the walk on the office's own page in his own hand at no figure and against the office's own interest, because a thing an office is given is a thing an office has not paid for, and says that nothing on a page and a thing in a hand are two different currencies and this office has been living on the second one since the middle of February.** On the Tuesday at ten in the morning he reads a column out of his own hand on the boards to about nine people, four of whom the yard has paid in the last four months, and the yard stands at the back and does not come forward. **It is five months in order with the months: the repair account empty since the middle of February; the third lay dark and the mole-head light not relit since the nineteenth of March; the second lay's hose dead since the second of April and the *Kittiwake* on the hard since the twenty-eighth of November; in May the ninth seam out with no end of it entered, the tide gang four short with one man stood off a wall to mind a cart until the tenth, forty feet of the office's own marline in the sea, fifty fathoms of winter warp where ninety were to lie, the north berth out and the third lay full; in June a cistern charged by a man the office cannot pay and no boat of its own since the twenty-eighth of April.** And the sentence: a town is not a thing that is owed things, it pays in five kinds of coin, a mooring, a berth, a warp, a boy's summer and a cistern, and this town has run out of four of them, and the cistern is the one that is left. **He says he would rather have the rota walked than the money and is not sure why and will not work it out on a market board.** The mooring's gear goes out on the Monday at nothing with a line on the office's page at nothing: a spare fender and forty feet of the office's own mooring rope on the two tarpaulins on the crown, and the wharfinger's whole of the office's June is a fender lent to two pieces of nobody's glass it has no jurisdiction over. **The man on the rota has not been paid for five pay periods, and was not paid on the twelfth, and was paid on the twelfth for the first time in five pay periods by a party that is not the harbor authority and by nothing at all, and Tristram says he did not ask him and that it was arithmetic.** The two books do not agree on the hour and the difference is left in. The wage week of the thirteenth is paid.

### Chapter 120 — The Signature. **THE BATCH CLIMAX.**

Wednesday the fourteenth and Thursday the fifteenth of June, in the shed, on the mole's steps, and at the head of the dock. **Torren Skell, fifty-nine, a coaster with two boats and a following, comes up the hill at eleven on his own feet with a paper in an oilcloth case, and says in the doorway that he is not from an office, not from a court, not from the Crown and not from the harbor authority, and that he wants to be heard as none of those before anybody decides what he is.** He says what he has read and that he has put three things together correctly: a fisher's document going up this coast, a sheet on a market wall with a woman's name and a figure on it, and a page out of this yard's own book with a clause on it. **He wants the right to use the road — to send a man to look at the figures twice a year and to have a copy of the sheet — and in exchange: thirty marks counted into a hand; a mooring of his own above the north wall for the season; his own ground warps, a capstan bar, a hand lead and forty fathoms of line at no figure; and a line in an engagement book that is not the yard's, with the yard's name against work he has had done.** He says he is not trying to buy a secret and that he is trying to stop being the only person he knows who cannot get anybody to go and look. **The yard refuses in nine sentences, spoken and then written on the back of his own paper in Calder Marr's own left hand, and the core of it is that a licence to use a road cannot be given by the people who found it, because the people who found it are not the people who keep it; and that if his name goes on it the road is kept by a man with two boats and the day he wants a second thing out of it he will take it; and that the yard does not know who keeps it and the only person who could answer is a man of fifty-four out of a storm belt who has gone home and is coming back in the autumn; and then, without being asked, what the yard would take instead — a person who will go and look at it, twice a year, for nothing, and does not have to be told why.** Skell says it is a thing a man says when he has nothing, and says he has run two boats for twenty-six years and has never had a favor off a man with eight marks in a bag in his life, and that what he has had is men telling him what they would take instead and then not taking it. **He does not threaten anybody, does not come back, does not write to an office, and says he will not put a mark against the yard's name; and the yard enters that no mark is put against his, and reads the whole of it back to him, and he says he would like to be in this harbor twice.** The refusal is written into the yard's own book with what it cost: **the thirty marks would have paid for the warp twice over, and a woman with four hundred feet of her own rope at the bottom of this harbor has her name and a figure and a date on a market wall and is not going to be told this week, and Nessa Pike insists the entry says the yard knows what a principle is worth.** Calder Marr goes out and stands at the top of the mole's steps above the third seam's mark at half past four with a crate and a bucket nine feet apart on either side of him, weighed now with a fender and forty feet of the harbor authority's own mooring rope. The read-out on the Thursday carries the whole position and ends with the third return: **a piece of worked glass of nobody's in a crate under a tarpaulin on a mole's crown, a return falling due on Saturday the seventeenth of June, three days to write it, and no boy in this shed to read it back and none in this harbor.**
