THE REPAIRS ARE DISPOSED OF IN FULL IN `state/continuity.md` § *Batch 0004 review repairs*, WHICH IS THE AUTHORITY FOR THEM. No chapter was restarted, no scene was cut, no cost was dropped and no planned plot was altered. The batch is 30,890 words after the repairs and 30,635 before them.** **The four that mattered most: the Monday the tenth's day account did not add up — the pot of air is struck out of that gross, the day closes at nine out of thirteen and the yard's four, the bag is six and not four, and the false *nothing has come into it since the first of July* is gone, so that the published chain `4, 2, 6, 2, 7, 1, 4, 0` is now what the chapters say; the slate wall's *N Mondays* counter had been restarted at *three* in Chapter 122 and this batch continued it, and the tenth, seventeenth and twenty-fourth of July are the **tenth, eleventh and twelfth** with Chapters 122, 125 and 129 corrected at source and Chapter 129 retitled *Nine Mondays, and a Wage*; the six conditions were not read aloud on the eighth of July, the batch's one dive of the holder's own, and they now are; and the hour of the top of the flood ran backwards and now moves forward — about eleven on the eighth, half past twelve on the fifteenth, twenty past one on the seventeenth, ten past two on the nineteenth, half past two on the twentieth.** Also corrected: the onset of the condition is the fourteenth of October in every chapter that states it and the dive is the thirteenth; the six joint spacings agree with the builder's day-book and the string is three hundred and fifty-one feet; there are three thicknesses of fouling and not five; the conservator has been in this harbor about a fortnight; the market wall's two Monday references are Saturday; a duplicated crown scene spanning Chapters 131 and 132 is re-staged; and the closing read-out is broken up in the two chapters that were long for it.

**Actual word count: 30,916 words across ten chapters as re-measured by the Volume 03 volume audit (`reviews/volume-03/volume-03-close.md`, 27 September 2026), and 30,890 before that audit's eleven mechanical repairs** (Ch131 2,899 · Ch132 3,210 · Ch133 2,403 · Ch134 3,526 · Ch135 2,635 · Ch136 3,347 · Ch137 3,149 · Ch138 3,576 · Ch139 2,317 · Ch140 3,854), measured with `wc -w` including headings, against the 2,200–3,200 guideline. **Every chapter is above the floor. Five are inside the guideline and five are past it** — Chapter 140 by 654, 138 by 376, 134 by 300, 136 by 147, and Chapter 132 by 10 — **and every one of the five that ran ran because a cost could not be dropped: 134 is the fourth return written out in full with its disavowal line and its second column, the clerk on the steps, and the full read-out at the head of the dock; 138 is four books out of a press, a line of three hundred and fifty-one feet on a shed floor, a public disagreement in a market and a nail; 140 is the batch's close and carries the whole labor spine, an office's entry, a price in a market and the forward pull; 136 is the day the seam is read and the wrong is said and both have to breathe; and 132's ten words are the cost of a required arithmetic repair, because the pot of air was struck out of that day's account and a sentence had to be written saying so.** The hearing room is used **not at all** in this batch. The market wall is used **once**, on **Saturday the twenty-second of July**, in daylight, in a market, on no Monday and on no hearing-room day — **and the sheet that goes up on it is the yard's own fourth return, over the rival's printed one, with no scale and no price on it.** The batch's pressures alternate: a market and a figure, labor and a snag, a bench and a debt and a letter, an office and a return, a conservator, a working day and a public error, a disproof and a word in a book, a press and a wall, a sentence and a departure, a close and a forward pull.

**The money, and it closes checkable on the page: NOTHING in a bag, thirty-one on the chandler's note, nothing in a tin, on Wednesday the twenty-sixth of July — against FOUR marks in the same bag on Thursday the sixth.** The chain is **4, 2, 6, 2, 7, 1, 4, 0** across the seven days money moves. Three wage weeks fall in the batch — the eleventh, eighteenth and twenty-fifth of July — and each is four marks out of the bag into an envelope, and the column goes **twelve lines and forty-eight marks – thirteen and fifty-two – fourteen and fifty-six**, with the fifth of March the oldest and staying there, and **nine envelopes on a bench and not one of them anywhere.** Two pots of air at two marks apiece go out. The note is not re-written and its three counts of weeks do not move. **No money came in from any office in this batch and no money went out to any person except three wages and two pots of air.**

### Chapter 131 — A Lead and a Slate, and a Thing Under the Mole

Friday the seventh and Saturday the eighth of July, in a market, in the shed, on the second seam's own face. **Sella Brigg has been to the man from Ashtide and has a figure and a date — twenty-six marks and a day, and the twenty-eighth, and she has not told him about the eighth of March because that is between her and her own rope — and she says out loud on the boards that the yard's own sheet is not on that wall any more and that there is a man from Ashtide over the top of it with four marks at the head of it, and she is not saying it to be cruel.** The pot of air goes out of the bag at ten, two marks, at this yard's own rate, filled at the office's compressor on the office's own hose, and **two marks in a bag.** Saturday: a westerly of four hours, four casts of the hand lead's line at the top of the flood, **eleven and a half on the mark for the third time this summer and it agreed with itself, and ten forty feet south and forty feet down, which is a different bottom and not the same bottom** — and then the lead snags, all at once, with no weight in it, and he works it up by hand for eleven minutes and it comes up on the ring at about twenty past eleven. **A piece of metal about the length of a hand from the wrist to the middle knuckle, not rusted through after a hundred and forty days in four fathoms, with three blows cut on the head of it with a chisel and not stamped with a die, of which the third is a different depth from the first two.** The shipwright says in her own hand that it is not a thing this harbor casts, and a smith is not asked this week. The six conditions are read out in order at the boat with the limit at nineteen set by the diver himself, and **the second column gets the bare fact that he could not for about four minutes tell which of his two hands was holding the line, with a reason and no cause and no name.** At about four in the afternoon Calder Marr walks down past the chandler's to the door of a smith's shed with the piece of metal in his coat, stands in it for the better part of two minutes, does not go in and comes back up the hill, and the reason is on the page: a first-column line says a smith of this harbor has not been asked and is not going to be asked this week, and a man cannot un-ask a thing by standing in a door.

### Chapter 132 — Nine in About Seven Feet

Sunday the ninth and Monday the tenth of July, in the shed, on the crown, and at the second seam. **The two of them do not agree about what the metal is made of and both of them are half right and neither of them knows it, and a person of no office's price — six marks and two days — is put into the book by the shipwright without that person being present.** Sunday they go up on the crown and look at the two tarpaulins. Monday: **the wall behind the reeve's bench comes down bare, ten Mondays, and the cistern is charged for the ninth time at no figure**, and a day at the second seam on a hirer's own account, gross thirteen, the eighth two and the share two and a hired hand three and the victuals one and rope one, that being nine out of thirteen, **with the office's pot of air not charged to the day at all, because it went out of the bag on Friday the seventh and was spent in the water on the Saturday, and two marks in a bag on Monday morning and four more in at about two in the afternoon and six at the close, which is the first money this yard has had in the bag since the first of July.** Both men in the water are hired and paid at the mole by the man who hired the day and neither is of this party. At about half past eleven a lump about the size of two fists comes up on the ring, not stone, not oakum, not lime, not pitch, with a skin on the outside of it a quarter of an inch thick and the inside a different color. **At about ten past four in the afternoon a chip of green glass about the length of a thumbnail comes up in the tallow of the lead, and that is the finding.** Nobody touches it; the ring comes up with it on it and it goes on a cloth and the compound goes on a different cloth. The reason goes in at ten past six with the clerk absent. **The first limb of the clause catches the chip by itself and the party has not needed the second limb.** The disavowal line is in full and includes the lump, the shard, the panel, the plate, the ferry plate, the plate at the fifth seam, the plug, the compartment in three steps, the run under this town, the road, the bar, the cairn, the stem — **and it says the chip is not a mark of nine joined lines and the party is not going to write one.** The clock is named out loud: the day of the finding is not counted and a return falls due on **Friday the fourteenth**.

### Chapter 133 — The Count of Four, and the Figure of a Hand

Tuesday the eleventh and Wednesday the twelfth of July, in the shed and in a market. The wage goes in, four marks, **seven envelopes**, twelve lines and forty-eight marks, and two marks in a bag. **THE FORWARD BEAT CHAPTER 133 OWED IS PAID: at about half past eleven on the Tuesday morning the shipwright writes in the FIRST column, in her own hand, the count of four, with the four dates and the four weathers, and the reason she gives is that the second column is a page of things this yard cannot check and a count is a thing this yard can check, and she refuses to put a name against it for the reason she gave on the third of July and has not improved on it.** And then **she prices a hand at eight marks a week, says in words that she is not going to say the reader thing a third time, says it once in a different sentence that means the same thing, says she is not sorry they put the boy on the stone on the fifteenth of May, and says it is in the first column because she said it in a shed.** Wednesday: **three lines go to J. Hesketh in Veyr in the ordinary post at no cost, telling him a return is coming and that it is not for sale and has no price on it and that if he prints it he is to print what it says and not what it is about** — and Calder Marr says out loud what changed his mind, and it was not a principle, it was that a man with a press who has already written once is the only person in nine hundred miles who is going to be obliged to look at a paper of this yard's. **Edric Pringle comes up the hill, says the cause out loud before the figure, warns them the day she is booking is a day of looking and not a day of work, and says eight shillings and tenpence in the same breath, and says that if the two debts are ever in one sentence she will come back up the hill — and she checks the book on Thursday and it is right.** Alden Marr is at the far bench on both days, is asked nothing, asks nothing, neither brother goes over to him.

### Chapter 134 — The Fourth Return, and a Clerk Who Comes Up the Hill

Thursday the thirteenth and Friday the fourteenth of July, in the shed, on the steps, and at the head of the dock. **THE FOURTH RETURN IS MADE ON THE DAY**, out of a finding of Monday the tenth, the day of the finding not counted and the fourth day after it, one sheet unshortened with place, hour, keeper and limits, a copy for the harbor authority's ledger in the clerk's own hand, and the clerk's own page with the hour it was written and not the hour it was done. **The whole Thursday is spent arguing about one sheet of paper and the argument is about whether to put the word *joint* in it, and the shipwright wins by a better rule: leave it out and put the leaving out, in the second column, where a reason is required.** The disavowal line goes in whole. The clerk comes up the hill at half past seven, does not go to the shed, and says for the seventh time that he cannot enter what a thumbnail of glass is, and writes on his own page that a party with no boy in it has now put four returns up this coast in ten weeks and every one has been on the day except the first. **And then he says the thing nobody had thought of, on the steps, in one go: the vessel has withdrawn its objection to a claim window of this office inside the harbor line until the first of March, so there is nobody to seat, and the only reason that is true is a reeve who sold a herring skipper's nineteen winters for a chart in a room in June, and in four years that will be the only reason anybody could not take the thing out of that mole, and it is a reeve's price and not a party's.** The full read-out runs at the head of the dock with about eleven people in the street.

### Chapter 135 — Six Marks and Two Days, and Six Things She Can Prove

Saturday the fifteenth and Sunday the sixteenth of July, on the mole's steps, in the yard's own boat, and in the shed. **Mara Venn has been in this harbor since about the thirtieth of June, staying above the chandler's, and nobody in this yard knew and nobody asked, and she says so at the top of the steps before anybody has said anything at all.** She prices herself out loud before she does anything, and she puts the conditions of her own finding in words she has chosen — a finding of no office in a yard's own book, unsigned, with a reason on the page, on her own account, not to be paid, not to be thanked, not to be treated as a favor — and she will not say *useful* in a yard's book. She asks one question all day, **what the packing is made of**, and she answers it herself: *I do not know, and I can tell you four things about it and not one of them is what it is made of. Do you know what your weir is made of.* **On the Sunday she gives six findings in the order she finds them convincing and will not give a seventh.** Two ends cut to each other, so a shipwright can check it in ten minutes with a rule. The packing and the fastenings one age. Both went in over three inches of fouling on the seaward side and not on the landward side. The packing came in from the seaward side, with a runnel of it thinning seaward. **Nine fastenings in about seven feet at a hand's breadth apart, three chisel blows each, the third a different depth from the first two, and the same three blows on all nine.** And a chip of worked glass in the packing, the same glass as the chip out of the tallow, put there on purpose, with her reason for it in a conservator's own words. **And what she cannot say is who, and she says it in the trade's own boundary: a joint is made by a body and two hands and a decision, a decision is not a mark, a body does not leave anything on a thing that a trade can read, and anybody in this coast who tells you a conservator can tell you who made a thing is selling you a thing.** She enters it unsigned with the reason on the page. **At the head of the dock on the Sunday evening she makes the shipwright read the line about her forty marks, twice, and puts the figure on it herself: nine months, and she would like the ninth month said out loud in nine people's hearing, because in about two years there is going to be a page in a city that says what a conservator of no office costs a town that owes her money.**

### Chapter 136 — Two Talks at Once, and the Wrong Thing Said at the Head of the Dock

Monday the seventeenth and Tuesday the eighteenth of July, on the mole's face, in the boat, and at the head of this dock. **The wall comes down bare, eleven Mondays, and the cistern is NOT charged, and the reason is on the page in the yard's own hand: the gate takes four hours with three men and the same three men were on the second seam from seven until about two.** **Edric Pringle's day: gross seventeen, the eighth two, the share two, the victuals two, a hired hand three and a second hired hand three at the mole, that being twelve out of seventeen and the yard's being five, two marks less than the same day of work brought on the twenty-fourth of June, and the two figures written side by side on the mole's steps in front of everybody without saying which one it hoped for. Five marks in a bag.** On his second call down, with his hand flat on the cut where the two ends of the joint meet, **he reads a seam for the first time in his life**: not a scarf, not a clamp, but a break where two cuts of different ages have been forced into one pattern, a cut made once and a cut made on top of a cut that was there first. **And then, sitting at four fathoms with his hand on it, he does the thing that takes the rest of his day: he makes the old mending into a fact — not the mending, the age of it, the number of mendings, and the hand that made them — and he supplies all three, and the hand on the wood told him none of them.** He is in the water four more times, seventeen minutes each, the limit is his and he keeps it four times out of four, and he loses the count of the boat: the shipwright says four, he says three, twice. **The boat comes off the face at eleven, two hours and a quarter before the flood, and the day is charged whole at seventeen with the crevice half cleared, and there is one top of the flood a day and there are two more floods.** Tuesday: the wage, four marks, **thirteen lines and fifty-two marks, eight envelopes**; a second pot of air out of the bag; the six read out in order again in the same words because a man who reads his conditions differently on Tuesday than on Monday has a reason for it and does not know what it is; **the first two fouling readings, the two at the root end, a quarter of an inch each**; and at about half past three in the afternoon, at the head of this dock, in about eleven people's hearing, **he says the wrong thing: that the six joints are a chain, that they were made once, in one time, by one set of hands, from the north end down, and that whatever it is for it is not to keep two boats off the bottom in a blow.** **The shipwright does not stop him, and enters the reason she did not, in the second column: a man saying his own trade in the open air is not doing wrong, he has been right in public four times this month, and a shipwright who contradicts a man in a market is a person who has decided that a man's mouth is a thing to be managed.** And **Tam Slee of the *Grey Widow*, the fourth name on the writ, not hired, not paid, not of this party, says in the boat that he went down because he was told to and is not doing it because of Tuesday, and asks that the difference be kept as a difference.**

### Chapter 137 — What the Fouling Took Apart, and a Word in the Book

Wednesday the nineteenth and Thursday the twentieth of July, on the second seam's face, on the boards, at the foot of the dock, and in the shed. **The six are read out in order at the boat before anybody is wet on all three of the days, in the same words, with the clerk's absence entered three times.** Wednesday, on the top of the flood: **the third joint reads three inches and a quarter and the fourth reads three inches and a quarter, and the two thin ones are the two at the root end, and the holder said on Tuesday at half past three in a market that the newest was the first — and it is the last, and he got it backwards, and he says so on the mole in about nine words and asks for it in the book in the words he is about to use: fouling goes on in order, a quarter of an inch is a fortnight and three inches and a quarter is a season, and a quarter and three inches and a quarter is not a morning but at least three different days in three different seasons.** A boatwright of the second lay, forty-one years in the harbor, comes down for nothing because somebody he never met asked him, and confirms the nine fastenings and the spacing with his own rule and says the spacing is not a spacing anybody on this coast works to and that a man who says a hand's breadth is telling you about two men with two hands, and that men who lay out by hand are men working in a hurry or where there is no batten — **and says he has not said a word about where it came from and does not know who, and the yard enters all of it in the first column because a man said it in a shed and has given his name.** **Edric Pringle comes up on the Wednesday evening and says the cause out loud: the tide was there at seven and at two, the boat came off the face at eleven because the man in the water could not say whether the basket had gone up four times or three, and he is of the yard — and she will not be told it was the tide, and she was told a thing about the job and not about her money, and she is owed eight shillings and tenpence and is not going to ask, and the two debts are in no sentence together.** Thursday: the cistern is charged for the eleventh time, at no figure, and the entry gives the hour of the flood against the yard's own account. **The fifth joint reads nine inches and is the fifth of the six and the second from the seaward end, and the packing in the fifth is a different color to a depth of a quarter of an inch with the same color under it.** And at about a quarter past nine that night, in the shed, with a man of the *Grey Widow* awake on a net loft floor and nobody pretending he was asleep, **THE ONE NAMING VOLUME 03 IS ALLOWED IS SPENT, IN THIS CHAPTER, IN THE YARD'S OWN BOOK, IN HIS OWN LEFT HAND, IN THE SECOND COLUMN, WITH A REASON.** He says the word *a tide-sickness*, says he got it from and that he produced the word himself, out loud, in the *Grey Widow's* cockpit on the thirteenth of May, says it is not a cause and no cause is written, and says he will not be asked to take it out and will not fight anybody who wants it out — **and the reason he breaks his own line of the second of June, which says there is no name in it and there is not going to be one this year, is in the reason against the line: a man who can lose a quarter of a second out of an ordinary conversation in a shed is a man whose account of a seam under four fathoms is a thing that can be asked about, and the party has decided it can be asked about in this book, on this page, on this date, by anybody who comes up this hill, and the only difference between that and a man with a seal is that it can be argued with.** The shipwright reads the whole of it back and does not improve on it, and the count of the four lines above it is still four and they have no name in them and are not being struck out.

### Chapter 138 — Nine Places, and a Sheet of Paper With No Price On It

Friday the twenty-first and Saturday the twenty-second of July, in the market office press, on the mole's face, on the shed floor, and in a market. A day at the second seam on a hirer's own account, nobody in the water, gross fifteen, the eighth two, the share two, two hired hands at three apiece, the victuals one and rope one, that being twelve out of fifteen, **four marks in a bag, and it is the last money this yard has coming in before the twenty-eighth.** **The market office keeps four books in a press under a stone slab and unlocks it on a Tuesday and a Friday morning while the counting is going on, and the party has never once been in it in five months.** **A builder's day-book of the port of Ashtide, in that press since a year nobody names, with six places in six entries — forty feet, and seventy-three feet, and one hundred and forty-one feet, and two hundred and ten feet, and two hundred and seventy-nine feet, and three hundred and forty-eight feet, each at the second seam — and the six places are the six joints, and the builder's name is cut into a stone at the mole head, and the last entry says that in thirty-one years he was never once asked what the joints at the foot are for and he is not asking.** **A weir-book with nine pages in a fisher's own hand and a night in a westerly and eleven hundred and forty fish and a lost boat and a repair four years later, and the third joint is a foot and four inches below that weir's own sill stone, and the repair is signed by the man whose grandfather built the weir.** **A poor-book with one line about twenty-two children put out of a village and nine of them named, and the place is not on this coast and is not on any chart anybody in this harbor has seen.** **A tide-gang's step book whose column for the foot of this mole's face stops, and after it the name of a sand and shell lay of this coast that is not on any chart in this harbor, and the party has entered that it did not match it and is not going to guess.** And a string laid on the shed floor with two pins in it: **the six joints stand in a straight line, three hundred and fifty-one feet, with nothing in the string's way, and a man can walk it in about eleven minutes.** **And the party declines the word: nine places is nine places, a line is a line, and a builder who wrote down where he worked because he was paid by the foot is not a man leaving a message — and the word *chain* is disowned, because it was said in a market on the Tuesday by a man who was wrong in three parts out of four of the same sentence.** The second column says, in full, that the party will not join the two halves: **the account is about the sea, the finding is about the glass, and neither of them is a reason to believe the other.** **On Saturday at eleven, in daylight, in a market, the yard nails its own fourth return up on the market wall, over the rival's printed sheet, with no scale and no price and nowhere to write a letter to, and a shilling changes hands at the foot of the dock for the printed sheet and is not this yard's income. Perry Ollett reads it three times, says it is the only paper on that wall anybody in a city is obliged to look at, and says he will be standing there on Monday with a better sheet and is not going to pretend he would not be. And at ten past twelve, in the open air, in front of about forty people, Mara Venn says out loud that Calder Marr is wrong, and that the yard has made it public and cannot un-print it, and that she does not think he is wrong and that she thinks he is a man who has run out of money and a man who has not — and her objection goes onto the sheet on the same Saturday, on the same nail, unsigned at her own request, with the reason, in her own hand.** His answer, in fifteen words, in the same market: **both, and I will not be able to tell you which was right in October.**

### Chapter 139 — What She Said Before Anybody Asked, and the Calipers She Took With Her

Sunday the twenty-third and Monday the twenty-fourth of July, at the top of the mole's steps, at the market office door, and in the shed. **Mara Venn says the thing that ends her time on this crew, in her own words, before anybody asks her for it, on the steps, in the wind, in nine people's hearing, and she has written it herself the night before and hands it over.** Her sentence: **a yard that cannot pay me asks me whether I can be useful; I have been useful four times since the twenty-seventh of January, not asked once, not paid once, and the fifth time I was not asked and I was not paid and I did the work, and I am not going to do that again; six marks and two days is my price and it does not come down, and I would rather be owed at the rate I am owed than be had at the rate I am had, and I have been had since January and I did not know that was the word for it until this morning; and a trade that says yes to nothing is not a trade.** It goes in the first column because she said it out loud, and nobody disputes a word of it. **Then he tells her all of it — the day-book, the weir, the poor-book, the step book, the nine places, the string — and she calls it the best thing anybody has found out in this harbor in five months, and then says it is worth nothing to her: not because it is thin, but because she is not being paid for it, and a thing a person is given because she is owed money is not a gift and not a trade and not a finding, and she will not be it twice again.** **So the disagreement is not settled by him giving her the evidence, and it is not repaired, and the party enters it whole, and neither half was settled by anything anybody handed to anybody.** And he says the yard's half out loud, and it is the sentence the movement is owed: **a conservator I cannot pay is a conservator I have to keep asking, and asking her to be useful is asking her to be cheap, and I have been doing the second thing since the twenty-seventh of January and calling it the first.** Monday: the wall comes down bare, twelve Mondays; the cistern is charged for the twelfth time; **she is not on the mole and not in the shed and the brass calipers are gone off the bench, hers, bought out of her own apprenticeship money in her second year, and she was not parted from them for a boat and was not parted from them on the Monday.** The entry says the party will keep asking her and will not ask her to be useful, and that those are two different things, and that her finding of the fifteenth and sixteenth stands unsigned and can be used and cannot be checked and cannot be paid for and **cannot be got done again.** **And she is at the market office door on the Monday afternoon with her book under her arm and does not come up the hill, and the standing arrangement is entered: a conservator of no office in Morrow Quay is to be found on a Friday morning at about ten in a room that is open to anybody, and the party did not arrange it and would not dare to.**

### Chapter 140 — Four Days of the Third Lay, and Nothing in a Bag

Tuesday the twenty-fifth and Wednesday the twenty-sixth of July, in the shed, in a market, on the mole's steps, and at the head of the dock. **The wage goes in at about eleven, four marks, and the bag is nothing, and the party enters the figure and the reason in the first column, and the reason is not the reason the bag stood at nothing for five days in April: in April this yard was living on a creditor's page and in July it is living on a wage, and a wage is not a page, it is a man's four marks for six days' work he has not been told about and that has not been carried to him, and there is no man in this harbor who can be asked about it because he is on a herring boat. Fourteen lines and fifty-six marks, the fifth of March the oldest, nine envelopes on a bench and not one of them anywhere, and the next of them is four marks on Tuesday the first of August.** Alden Marr is at the far bench, is asked nothing, asks nothing, neither brother goes over to him. **On the Wednesday the reeve enters, in his own book and at his own cost, that the footing of the mole from the third seam to the twelfth is to be examined on the second of August and the moorings of the third lay are to be closed for the four days of it — and the repair account of that office has been empty since the middle of February and the money is not coming and the entry is made nevertheless, and the reason is on the face of it: an office whose instruments nobody contests can enter an instrument with nothing behind it, and that is worse than no instrument.** **The price lands on the third lay and a man of the third lay says the number out loud in a market in about forty people: four days, the second to the fifth of August, the tide right on the second and the third and wrong on the fourth and worse on the fifth, the north berth out, the third lay full, and the rest of it in the order that matters — a cistern that holds and a mole's footing that is going to be looked at, one of them a lid and one of them a hole, and he said the word *town* in a market on the sixth of July and is not going to say it again, and is not angry, and is not asking anybody for anything.** **And Mara Venn, on the boards, at no figure, says the one thing none of the others in that market can say: four days with a lay shut is four days with a hull's bottom out of the water and nobody on it, and if the weather comes in on the fifth of August there is a boat in this harbor with four days of fouling on her bottom and nobody able to scrub her, and that happened here twice in the year before she was born, and she knows it because the men who were in it are still standing in that market.** And at about four in the afternoon the holder asks the reeve, on the steps, in nine people's hearing, whether any of it is about the plate at the fifth seam, **and the answer is thirteen words: it is not and I will not tell you what it is about** — and the party enters both halves and does not know what the entry is about and has not asked. The full read-out runs at six with the whole labor spine, **dated lines for the seventeenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, twentieth and twenty-fourth of July saying that no finding of worked glass was made and nothing was raised and no return goes up on any of those days, and there is no fifth return and there is not going to be one out of a day that produced nothing**, the third column's two entries and the party's refusal to make a trend of them, and the autumn visit of a man of fifty-four with a figure of his own for the bar and no instrument in this harbor that can call him. **And at half past six a man of the third lay says a boat's name out loud in the street: there is a working boat with people in her lying off the outer marks, the tide gang has walked past her every day since the ninth of July and has been told nothing, her name is the *Hearthwake*, and a man of a boat of his says she is one of the nine, and he has said her name out loud in a market because if a man in this harbor has a boat off the outer marks with people in her then a man in this harbor should be the one who says it and not a man in a city.** **And the yard writes it down where anybody can check it, which is a page in a book in a shed on a hill, and does not go and look, and does not send anybody, and does not ask that man one question about her, and says out loud that the outer marks stand where the writ of the first of May says they are and that the party is not going past them this season and has not tried and is not going to — and that is not nothing, and it is not enough, and both of those are on the page.**

---

## Volume 03, Batch 0005 (Chapters 141–150) — complete. Movement 5, the cutter and the bell-archive. **THE VOLUME'S CLIMAX AND ITS RESOLUTION.**

**No card file existed for this batch. `outline/batches/volume-03-batch-0005.md` is not in this repository and none was invented, reconstructed, or written. The batch was shaped from `outline/volume-03.md` alone — its Movement 5 section, its Volume climax, its Concrete resolution, its New-volume question, its Final chapter image, its Reveal discipline, and its twenty-eight locks — and out of the four state files Batch 0004 had just written. That is the third time this volume has been built that way and it is recorded in its own first line so that a reader of the state files is not left guessing.**

**Actual word count: 29,823 words across ten chapters as re-measured by the Volume 03 volume audit (`reviews/volume-03/volume-03-close.md`, 27 September 2026), 29,814 before that audit's eleven mechanical repairs, and 29,688 before this batch's own review repairs** (Ch141 2,666 · Ch142 2,615 · Ch143 2,743 · Ch144 2,704 · Ch145 2,363 · Ch146 2,795 · Ch147 3,640 · Ch148 2,999 · Ch149 3,213 · Ch150 4,085), measured with `wc -w` including headings, against the 2,200–3,200 guideline. **Every chapter is above the floor. Seven are inside the guideline and three are past it — Chapter 147 by 440, Chapter 149 by 13 and Chapter 150 by 885 — and all three ran because a cost could not be dropped.** 147 is the climax: the six conditions, the approach, three calls down, the case half out of the water, the boy in seven fathoms, the choice, nineteen minutes in the water, four people off, and the second-column entry that puts the price of the choice in the yard's own book. 150 is the volume's close and carries the market wall, the sheet, the wage that is not paid, the third column, **the chandler's note said out loud as un-re-written**, and the whole labor spine of the batch. The hearing room is used **once**, on **Saturday the twelfth of August**. The market wall is used **once**, on **Tuesday the fifteenth of August**, in daylight, in a market, on no Monday and on no hearing-room day. **The *Vigil's* own notice is on that wall twice, on Friday the twenty-eighth of July and Friday the fourth of August, and neither is this party's use of it, and the chapter says so.** The batch's pressures alternate: a day of work and a Crown notice, a mole with a glass and an arithmetic, a wage and a boy and a public sentence, a grounding in four minutes, a room open to anybody and a second nail, a reeve's last entry and a cost entered in advance, the working day, a testimony with a limit on it, a man in a coat and a question in a market, and the close.

**The money, and it closes checkable on the page: NOTHING in a bag, thirty-one on the chandler's note, nothing in a tin, and three marks owing to a man of Ashtide, on Tuesday the fifteenth of August — against nothing in the same bag on Wednesday the twenty-sixth of July.** The chain is **0, 3, 3, 7, 3, 7, 7, 11, 0, 0** across the days money moves: a day at the second seam on a hirer's own account on Thursday the twenty-seventh, gross fifteen and the yard's three; a day on Monday the thirty-first, gross thirteen and the yard's four; the wage on Tuesday the first of August; a day on the dump on Wednesday the second, gross thirteen and the yard's four; a day on Monday the seventh, gross thirteen and the yard's four, which is the first time the figure has been eleven since the fourteenth of June; and then Tuesday the eighth — **the wage, four marks; two pots of the office's air at this yard's own two-mark rate, four marks; and the master of the *Sallow Reach* at six marks of his own naming, of which three is paid at the mole and three is not — which empties the bag exactly.** **Three wage weeks fall in the batch, the first, eighth and fifteenth of August. The first and the eighth went into envelopes; the fifteenth was NOT PAID, and the envelope was not made, and that is the batch's cost and it is in the first column with the figure against it.** The column goes **fifteen lines and sixty marks – sixteen lines and sixty-four marks** and stops, with the fifth of March the oldest and staying there, and eleven envelopes on a bench and not one of them anywhere in twelve weeks. The note is not re-written, its three counts of weeks do not move, five marks of compressor's gland stand on it unpaid and useless, and the tin is empty. **No money came in from any office in this batch and none went out to any person except three wages, two pots of air and a day of another crew's boat.**

### Chapter 141 — Four Days in Somebody Else's Hand, and a Sentence in Our Own

Thursday the twenty-seventh and Friday the twenty-eighth of July, at the second seam, in the shed, on a quay, and at the head of the dock. A day at the second seam on a hirer's own account, nobody in the water, gross fifteen and the yard's three; **the cistern is not charged, with the reason on the page in the yard's own hand, the gate taking four hours with three men.** **A tender comes inside the line and a man in a coat nails a notice to the market wall on the outside of whatever is there** — and the notice is quoted in full: the *Hearthwake* is claimed by the Crown as Crown material, being one of a formation of vessels described in a schedule held elsewhere and not produced to this harbor; any person who boards, works upon, takes from or renders assistance is to report in writing to the harbor authority within four days; and no assistance will be rendered by the officer commanding. **THE NOTICE HAS FOUR DAYS IN IT AND THE SAME HAND ON IT AS THE REPORTING CLAUSE, and the shipwright says that in about nine words and it is in the first column because a man said it in a market.** And Calder Marr reads his own sentence of the fifth of July back on the quay in nine people's hearing and says it is now the reason he cannot help. **Nell Ardery, of the second lay, sixty-odd, says the boat has been pumping for nine days, gives her name, says her mother was on the Sill, asks for nothing, and is in the first column in the shipwright's hand with the hour.** And a crew of Ashtide takes four hundred feet of Sella Brigg's own warp off the bottom of this harbor for twenty-six marks and a day, and she is paid by him and is owed eight shillings and tenpence by this yard, and the two figures are not one.

### Chapter 142 — A Compressor of His Own, and Ten Marks We Do Not Have

Saturday the twenty-ninth and Sunday the thirtieth of July, on the crown, in a shed, and in a doorway. **A man of the tide gang, Tam Rundle, thirty, four men where there should be eight, stops on the crown and gives nine days of his own watching: her pump going since about the time the gang started walking her, upright on the twenty-first, a foot of list on the twenty-second, two foot on the twenty-fourth, four foot and about seven fathoms this morning, and he has said nothing to nine people in his office and is saying it and is not going to say it again.** **The shipwright then says the thing the whole argument turns on and it is checkable: the outer marks are two stones, the bar of four hundred yards is a line off them on the officer's own chart, the *Hearthwake* is inside that line and about three miles inside the imperial line, and every one of those three lines is a line about paper and not one of them is a line about water.** And Calder Marr, on the crown, finds the half of it nobody had said: **there is no writ past the outer marks and no clause past the outer marks and no instrument and no keeper and no return, and if we go we go on our own account, and he has been trying to make that sentence into a reason not to go for four days and it is not one.** Sunday, Perry Ollett comes up the hill in daylight and names six marks for the *Sallow Reach*, the day and two men, the air at no figure because it is his own, and says out loud that he is not doing it because he is a good man and that he will say the figure himself if anybody gets it wrong. **The shipwright's four reasons the plan fails, given out loud in a shed with the date of her last asking of it said out loud, and a note that she did not say the fifth thing.** And the arithmetic on the back of a slate: ten marks at the outer marks, three in the bag, and the only way this yard has ever made ten marks is four days of work it is not doing.

### Chapter 143 — Thirteen Mondays, and the Thing He Was Kept For

Monday the thirty-first of July and Tuesday the first of August, in the shed, on the steps, and at the head of the dock. **The wall comes down bare for the thirteenth time; the cistern is charged for the thirteenth time by strangers and not by this party.** A day at the second seam on a hirer's own account, gross thirteen and the yard's four. **THE RESOLUTION'S SENTENCE ABOUT THE BOY IS ENTERED HERE, IN THE FIRST COLUMN, IN THE HOLDER'S OWN LEFT HAND, AND IT IS NOT A LESSON AND NOBODY LEARNS ANYTHING FROM IT: the thing Bevin Rook was kept for is reading a position back into a slate for a man in a boat; he did it for two hundred days; on the fourth of May he read four figures and got all four right and on the eleventh of May he read two and got one wrong; he was put off the stone on the fifteenth on a date the party named before anybody asked; he has not done it since and is not going to and cannot; the party has entered that he cannot, has not asked him, is not going to, and is not going to hire a boy to do it and call that the same thing; a column in that book is not a wage; and the head of the third column carries two times in his hand and they have not been scraped out and a request to scrape them out is refused in the same words it is refused for a line in any column.** The third column is filled at about four hours' lateness, the ninth entry since the second of May, and the party refuses to draw a figure out of nine. Alden Marr is at the far bench on both days, is asked nothing, asks nothing, neither brother goes over to him. **The argument the holder loses: the shipwright says they should say her name in a market on Saturday and then says, after a full day, that the end of that is a form, and that a thing said in a street about people in a boat is a thing that can be used against the people in the boat, and he agrees and asks for the date on the rule.**

### Chapter 144 — Seven Foot of List, and a Tender That Came Alongside to Hold Her Down

Wednesday the second and Thursday the third of August, on the dump, on the crown, in a doorway, and at the head of the dock. **The third lay's moorings shut at seven in the morning on a board, and the man who pays for the four days read the date out loud.** A day on the dump — ground the writ of the first of May names in its own ground — gross thirteen and the yard's four. **And at about half past two in the afternoon, from the crown, in nine people's hearing, in about four minutes, a boat with people in her comes up half a fathom on the flood and takes the ground by the head and settles with about seven foot of list, and the *Vigil's* own tender, at two hundred yards, puts a grapnel on her anchor cable and holds her there.** The entry is in the first column with the hour, and the hour and a half it took to write it is entered, and the reason is that a party which has said out loud in a market that it is not going to ask a man one question about a boat has to be able to say it about a woman too, and it said it about a woman on the twenty-sixth of July. **The *Vigil* is sighted at anchor two and a half miles off and four minutes of glass is spent on her and one sentence is entered: a man who writes down what he has seen of a vessel of the Crown from a mile and a half with a glass is a man who has begun to keep a watch, and this yard is not going to be a party to the keeping of a watch either, and the second of those was not in the entry of the fifth of July and is now.** The cistern is charged for the fourteenth time. And at about five Nell Ardery comes to the doorway and gives the figure nobody in the shed can get: **they can pump her with what is in her until about the fourth day of August, and after that the water comes in faster than two men and a boy and a woman can shift it**, and it is a figure they have because they have been doing it nine days and can see what is left in the pump's own well. And the day booked for Friday the seventh is not cancelled, because a tide at the second seam's face at about ten past one and a tide at the outer marks at about two on the fourth of August are two different tides and a man has to be on the water at the first one.

### Chapter 145 — Six Marks and Two Days, Asked by a Woman in a Room, and a Second Nail

Friday the fourth and Saturday the fifth of August, in the market office, on a market wall, and in a shed. **Mara Venn is at the long table in the market office at about ten on a Friday morning because that office is open to anybody and this party did not arrange it, and a woman of the second lay asks her a question out loud in a room of nine people, and not this yard.** She prices herself first, says she would have said the same figure if the yard had asked, says she has said she would not do a thing at nothing again and is going to do this once and says so in front of nine people so it cannot be said for her later, and then gives **six things and no seventh about the Crown notice: it is a second original and not a copy; it is guillotine-cut office paper; the first two paragraphs are a clerk's hand and the third and fourth are a naval officer's; the first notice said *any part of her* and this one says *any part of her and everything in her*, and that is the only line in either paper that reads like a man writing to himself; the fold is a wet naval fold; and the seal is a stamp struck in ink and off by about a sixteenth of an inch.** And then the seventh, which is the one she does not have: she cannot tell anybody what is in that boat, the trade that can is six marks and two days, and there is no instrument, no money and no trade on this coast that reaches five and a half fathoms inside the four hundred yards. **A tender comes in at two and a man in a coat takes the first notice down and nails a longer second one up on the same nails, and the party does not go and read it.** Two people of the third lay bring a copy up the hill. And on the Saturday a man comes up the hill and says her pump stopped for an hour at about ten, and a lamp went up in her rigging and was answered from a boat on the inner shoals, and he does not know what three short and one long means and is going out on his own tide at twelve. **The shipwright's entry refuses to learn a code because a boat is going down, and the refusal is entered, and the sentence is that a code is the only thing a community keeps that a stranger cannot read off a book, and this yard has been here five months and has learned nine places out of four books and not one practice of anybody.**

### Chapter 146 — An Office With Nothing Left to Put In Its Book, and a Cost Entered Before It Is Paid

Sunday the sixth and Monday the seventh of August, on the mole's steps, in the shed, and at the head of the dock. **The officer of the harbor authority is on his own steps at ten on a Sunday and reads two entries out of his own book and neither is softened: that a vessel of this coast went on the ground inside the four hundred yards with four persons in her while the third lay's moorings were shut on the authority of an examination he entered on the twenty-sixth of July, the two being eleven words apart in his own book and he put them there; and that a notice of the Crown is nailed over a return made under a writ this office granted, so that the paper of this office is what a Crown paper is nailed over in this market, and this office cannot take it down and has no power to. And then: there is nothing in my book that will put a boat of mine past the outer marks, and nothing in yours either, and that is not a failure of either book, it is the design. HE SPENDS AUTHORITY A THIRD TIME, THE PRICE FALLS ON THE THIRD LAY AGAIN, NOBODY THANKED HIM, HE HAS NO SECOND SEASON IN HIS KEEPING AND A SPENT LEDGER, AND HE IS NOT A FRIEND. Calder Marr asks him nothing about any of it and enters all three not-askings with a date, and refuses to thank him for the second entry and says that in four years a man reading that wall will read it as a reeve's price. Monday: the wall down bare for the fourteenth time; the cistern charged for the fifteenth time by strangers while the party is on the second seam; **a day at the second seam on a hirer's own account, gross thirteen and the yard's four, and the string laid out along the foot of the face again for no reason the party could give and did not write one; ELEVEN MARKS IN A BAG.** **THE DECISION IS ENTERED IN THE FIRST COLUMN AT NINE O'CLOCK ON THE MONDAY NIGHT, BEFORE THE DAY AND NOT AFTER, and it costs four paragraphs: that the party is going past the outer marks on its own account with no instrument of any office; that the sentence of the fifth and twenty-sixth of July is broken and that this party broke it and the breaking is entered in advance; and that the cost is the air, the *Sallow Reach* at six marks part paid, the wage of the same Tuesday, and the sentence itself, which cannot be said again, with the reason — a yard that has said a thing in a market and has not done it is a yard whose saying is worth nothing in any figure it puts on any wall in any year after this one — and that the forty marks and the eight shillings and tenpence and the eight marks are not paid either way and are not in the cost and are not mentioned in it; and that the party knows the price of the third lay's four days and is not going to look at it; and that nobody goes near the imperial line, that the Second Bell license is not granted and is not approached and would not be known what to do with, and that if anything were raised out there it would not be reported to any office and the yard knows what that will look like in a file in five years. ALDEN MARR IS AT THE FAR BENCH AND THE HOLDER DID NOT GO OVER TO HIM, and neither brother has said why.** And Nessa Pike says one thing that is not in the book and tells him not to write it down, and he does not write it down.

### Chapter 147 — What Was on the Gunwale, and What Was in the Water

**THE CLIMAX. Tuesday the eighth and Wednesday the ninth of August. A working day, not a room.** The wage goes in at about eleven, four marks, the sixteenth line and the sixty-fourth mark, the eleventh envelope. Two pots of the harbor authority's own air at this yard's own two-mark rate go out at about a quarter past twelve. **At the mole at ten past one Perry Ollett comes alongside and takes six marks off the board for the boat, the day and two men, the air at no figure because it is his, and the yard pays three of the six at the mole in the way it pays every other man at the mole, and three marks is a debt to a man of Ashtide with a date on it. AND HE SAYS THE THIRD THING BEFORE HE GOES, so that he does not have to say it at six: that if a boy comes off her foredeck he is going in after him on a line off his OWN bow and will refuse the yard's line, because a boat of his alongside a boat of theirs with a pot in it is a thing that has gone wrong in other waters.** **THE SIX ARE READ OUT IN ORDER AT THE BOAT IN DAYLIGHT AT TWENTY PAST ONE, in the same words, the limit at seventeen set by the diver and not raisable by the holder, the cutoff hers and the word *Enough*, and the stated reason entered in the yard's own book with the clerk's absence entered rather than filled in AND WITH THE FURTHER FACT ENTERED THAT THERE IS NO CLERK TO BE PRESENT BECAUSE THERE IS NO INSTRUMENT TO BE PRESENT FOR, the writ being bounded by the outer marks and the clause being on the writ.** They are on the water at four minutes past two; the outer marks go by on the port bow at about a quarter past; the shipwright says the time out loud; the two men of the *Sallow Reach* say nothing. **Three calls, seventeen minutes each, kept three out of three. The hatch is under about five and a half feet at the top of the tide and the pins on the grating are seized. There are five bells in a case about four feet by two, not a set, a line cut in the lip of each that is not a letter in any hand on this coast, the largest about a foot across the mouth, and HE PUTS HIS HAND ON IT AND IT IS COLD AND IT SAYS NOTHING AND HE DOES NOT STRIKE IT, and the reason he did not is that a bell is not a thing you find out what by making a noise on.** In about six feet of water in the dark he reads a seam on her garboard — a plank cut and let go and mended over, mendings under mendings — **and it tells him nothing about when or in what order or by whose hand, and THIS TIME HE DOES NOT SUPPLY THE REST, and the reason is that a man who has been wrong in public in a market once about the word *chain* does not get to be the man who supplies the rest of a sentence about a boat with people in her.** Four of the five in a bight of the *Sallow Reach's* warp come up to the gunwale and stand on end in about three feet of water with the lid against her own rail. **AND AT ABOUT TWENTY PAST THREE THE GRAPNEL COMES TIGHT AND SHE GOES OVER ANOTHER THREE FOOT AND A BOY OF SEVENTEEN GOES OFF HER FOREDECK INTO SEVEN FATHOMS. He shouted, and for about a second and a half Calder Marr could not tell whether the shout came from the water or from the deck, and that second and a half is the whole of what is entered against him for it.** **HE LET GO OF THE LINE. The case went down straight and the grating lid was the last of it. One of Ollett's men said a word in his own language and the other said nothing. He was in the water in about a second and a half.** Nineteen minutes; the *Hearthwake* rolling a foot and a half on a seven foot list; the boy twice under the *Sallow Reach's* counter; the woman on her own doorway with a boathook holding him on while Ollett's man takes his own line off his own bow and gets a bight round the boy's chest from the outside; the fourth man off her on his own account with a line round his own waist that the boy of seventeen had put there before he went over the rail. **Nessa Pike never said the word, and it is entered, and the reason is that a man of thirty-two going to a boy of seventeen was not going to be stopped by a woman in a boat in about nineteen minutes, and if it had been twenty-five she would have pulled it, and she has entered that too.** On the Wednesday the *Sallow Reach* takes four people off at about two, the pump handle left in the pump, and they come up the mole's steps at about six in the afternoon in front of about forty people with the mole head's light not on behind them. **THE SECOND COLUMN IS FILLED ON THE WEDNESDAY NIGHT WITH THE WORD NOT IN IT, and the reason for the line is that a man on a mole cannot check which of his own ears a sound came in through, and the party has made that line twice now and is not going to make it a third time for the same thing and is not going to stop making it.** And nothing was raised: a basket half out of a hatch in a boat is not a raising, the clause does not reach that ground, there is no fifth return, and a dated line says the party was past the outer marks on its own account, raised nothing, told no office and will tell no office. And the third column was not filled on the eighth, and that is entered in the first column with the reason, and with the further fact that the party does not know who will fill it next and has not appointed anybody.

### Chapter 148 — What a Bell-Archive Is, and the Limit a Person in a Doorway Is Wearing

Thursday the tenth and Friday the eleventh of August, on the mole's steps, in the market office, and in a shed. **Four of the Sill come up the steps and stop, and the woman names them and herself without being asked: Nessa Vale, thirty-eight, Awn Proude, Tom Kittow, and Ewan Kittow, seventeen, who went into the water on the Tuesday and a man of this yard came after him, and she says it once in front of forty people and will not say it again and will not say it to him.** And then the thing this harbor has been looking at: **the Sill is the weir at the south end of this mole, its sill stone under four feet of stone at the south end, and they have been in this harbor since the second of June and put her over the shoal inside the four hundred yards because they had to, and they pumped her for nine weeks and did not put a lamp up and did not go to the officer and did not send a letter.** What a bell-archive is, in eleven minutes and a good question: **not a book; a thing you open. Five bells with a line cut into the lip of each, read out — not written down — by whoever has the turn, on a fixed day, in the hall, in front of the whole community, saying what they did, when, how many, who was in it and what it cost. The oldest is about a hundred and forty years by the sound of it. The other four are the ones they could not leave behind. The rest went in a fire in a year she will not name in a market, and one of their own saw that fire and she is dead nine years and there is nobody left who heard it and one of the bells that went into it. IT IS WORTH EVERYTHING THEY HAVE AND IT IS WORTH NOTHING WHATEVER TO ANYBODY STANDING ON THAT MOLE, AND BOTH OF THOSE ARE TRUE AND NEITHER IS TAKEN BACK.** **The limit is written by them, in their own words, signed by four people, and it is real: they will not say it in a shed, they will not say it into a book that goes out of this harbor, they will not say it to a man with a seal, they will not say one word about who took her off them, they will not give their names to any office in any city — because a bell-archive is not a thing that is read out, it is a thing that is struck, in a hall, in front of the people it is about, and there is nobody in this town it is about.** **AND THE HOLDER SAYS OUT LOAD, IN FORTY PEOPLE'S HEARING, THAT HE WANTED IT LIFTED, THAT HE CANNOT LIFT IT, THAT HE IS NOT GOING TO ASK TWICE, AND THAT THE WANTING IS ON THE PAGE WITH A DATE ON IT.** On the Friday the page is written out in the market office, which is open to anybody on a Tuesday and a Friday morning, and **Mara Venn is at the long table as a person who uses the room and is asked nothing by anybody, and gives six things about the bells — a maker's mark on the sound bow of each, the line and the lip cut with the same tool, two shallow cuts of different ages inside the lip of the largest of the same order as the two cuts at the second seam — and then says the thing that is the point: five bells at five and a half fathoms inside the four hundred yards under the after hatch of a vessel claimed whole by an office in a city, and no instrument here that reaches that water, no money here that reaches that water, no trade on this coast whose work it is, and she is not going and is not asking anybody to send her, and the not-saying costs her and not the boat.** Forty copies go out at no price, and a shilling changes hands for the *Sallow Reach's* sheet and is not this yard's income. **Nothing in the bag, and the reason is that a yard of two and a half that spent three days in a boat past the outer marks and three days writing down what it did there has not sold a day in ten days, and the men who hire a day want a Monday or a Tuesday and there has been no Monday and no Tuesday in the ten days.** And four people of the Sill have no boat, no wages and about nine marks between them, and have asked this yard for nothing, and are not going to be given anything, and the yard has entered that it would have liked to and had nothing.

### Chapter 149 — A Man in a Coat With a Paper, and a Question in a Market Nobody Answers

Saturday the twelfth and Sunday the thirteenth of August, in the hearing room over the tide-gang store, and on the boards. **THE HEARING ROOM IS USED ONCE. A man comes in who has not been in that room before and is not going to be again: Amos Trewhella, of an office in a city whose name the clerk wrote down and this yard has not repeated, with a paper, and he does not sit down for ten minutes.** He reads four things: **the *Vigil* is not to be employed upon this coast; Captain Veyra Holt is relieved of that vessel and of the command of this coast from the fifteenth of August and is posted from the first of September to the making up of the coast's wreck lists, in a city, at a table, with every vessel reported, claimed, entered and closed upon this coast for the year — SHE DOES NOT COME TO THIS HARBOR AND HAS NOT BEEN IN IT AND IS NOT GOING TO BE, and she is described from a distance and appears in no room; the second season of the writ of the first of May is not granted, refused or dealt with by the paper, is not before the office it comes from, and the holder will be told when it has been decided and not before, WHICH IS THE WRIT'S OWN LAST LINE GIVEN BACK TO HIM BY ANOTHER OFFICE; and he asks for the writ, the crew's book and the four returns.** **THE YARD PRODUCES ALL FOUR INSIDE ELEVEN MINUTES, WHOLE AND UNSHORTENED, and says out loud why it is opening the book, and the reason is the clause's own construction and has been since the second of May. The shipwright does not open the book. He points at the lead plug's line and says he is not going to say one word about that number to you or to anybody and never has. He names the eighth of August and the seventh of August out loud, with no softening, and the man in the coat reads the seventh twice and does not comment on it.** Four questions and four answers: they went for four persons and nothing else and are not going to say they nearly had it; no, they will not claim it; if it were raised it would go to four people of the Sill by their own hand and not by his, under a limit they wrote and he asked to have lifted; then produce the writ. **And the standing sentence is said out loud without softening — has not been told, has not asked, does not want to know this month, will read a paper about the second season, will answer it on the day it comes, and will not treat the man who brings it as a friend or as an enemy — and the yard adds that a man in a coat was let up the stairs BECAUSE of that standing arrangement, which is the point.** The clerk enters what a box can hold and says for the seventh time what he cannot enter: a person of no office having five bells at five and a half fathoms inside the four hundred yards on a vessel claimed whole, when the officer of this harbor authority has entered that he has nothing that will put a boat of his past those marks. **THE POSTING IS ENTERED IN THE YARD'S OWN BOOK WITH ITS DATES AND CHECKED AGAINST THE FOURTH THING OF THE FIFTH OF JULY, and the check is on the page: it is not a command in this harbor, not an inspection of or over the harbor authority, not a commission, puts nobody past the outer marks and nobody past the imperial line, and the check holds. And the second season is not granted and the writ runs to the first of March and its ground is not widened and its four names are four.** On the Sunday, in a market, in about forty people's hearing, **a man of a boat of the second lay, sixty, forty-one years on this water, asks the volume's question: WHO CHANGED THE RULE. Nobody answers for half a minute.** He does not want a letter, he wants the answer or the not-answering said out loud. **Calder Marr says he does not know, says that a man who has never heard the question says *what rule* and a man who has heard it says *I do not know*, says he has thought about it for five days and is not going to go round the side of a limit four people put on their own account, and cannot give a name because he does not know what the rule was called or what it changed from, and because in four years somebody would be standing on a mole in another town with the name in his hand and no lead in his water — and that is a thing this harbor has already had done to it once.** **And he is the one who says it out loud, in the yard's own hand with a date on it, so that a man can come up this hill and ask whether it was put and whether it was answered, and the answer is that it was put on the thirteenth of August in about forty people's hearing and was not answered and the not-answering is on the page with the reason against it. THEN ELIAS VOKE SAYS THE SENTENCE THE VOLUME CLOSES ON AND WILL NOT SAY IT TWICE: nineteen winters in a naval file because a reeve of this harbor sold a chart for them and did not have to and said afterwards in a letter of four lines that he would have asked and would have done it anyway — and that is one of them true and it is not that the other one is not true, both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other, and he has been saying that shape of sentence for forty years and has never had anybody write it down. WRITE IT DOWN. I AM NOT GOING TO SAY IT AGAIN. And Calder Marr writes it in the first column and Voke makes him read the last sentence back twice.** And nothing in that market answered the question, and the entry says so.

### Chapter 150 — Under a Naval Paper, and the Wage of the Fifteenth

Monday the fourteenth and Tuesday the fifteenth of August, in the market office press, on a market wall, in the shed, and at the head of the dock. **THE VOLUME'S FINAL IMAGE. THE SHEET GOES UP ON A MARKET WALL UNDER A NAVAL PAPER, ON TUESDAY THE FIFTEENTH OF AUGUST AT ABOUT ELEVEN IN THE MORNING, IN A MARKET, IN DAYLIGHT, ON THE SAME NAILS, ON THE OUTSIDE OF WHATEVER WAS THERE — and what was there is the *Vigil's* notice of the fourth of August with the Crown stamp off by about a sixteenth of an inch to the right, which is over the *Sallow Reach's* printed sheet, which is over the sheet of the seventh of June, which is over the yard's tenth thing, and the yard's own fourth return of the twenty-second of July has been under four papers since the twenty-eighth of July and is still on that wall and can be read if a man stands at the side of it in the right wind. THE ARRANGEMENT IS THE ARRANGEMENT AND THE YARD DID NOT DECIDE IT AND THE SHIPWRIGHT SAYS SO OUT LOUD AND REFUSES TO PRETEND A SHEET UNDER A NAVAL PAPER IS A SHEET ON ITS OWN.** The sheet carries, in its own words: **the place of every copy of it** — copied at the foot of the dock at no price on the day, forty out of the press on the eleventh, one up the coast, about sixty boats, one copy in a city going to press that cannot be stopped, four of the eleven copies of the public sheet of the fourteenth of October not reached and not going to be; **the nine places, as this yard is able to state them, with a date against each, and it does not call them a chain and it does not call them a compact and THE WORD *HARBORS* IS NOT ON IT ANYWHERE** — six by a builder's own figures at this harbor's own second seam, forty, seventy-three, one hundred and forty-one, two hundred and ten, two hundred and seventy-nine and three hundred and forty-eight feet, the builder's name cut into a stone at the mole head, the day given and the year not on it because the book gives no year in any hand this yard can read; and three as the books give them, this harbor's own weir called the Sill with the third of the six lying a foot and four inches under its sill stone, a village not on this coast and not on any chart anybody here has seen with twenty-two children and nine named, and a sand and shell lay not on any chart in this harbor; **and it says that this yard does not know why the three are there and is not going to guess, and that one of the nine is under the south end of this mole and four of that nine were living in this town on Friday last, and says nothing else about them; and the two columns, nine lines of the first and five of the second, each of the five carrying its reason in full, both standing, neither scratched out, a request to strike one out refused; and the limit, and the five bells at five and a half fathoms, and the going past the outer marks and the broken sentence with the breaking entered in advance and the cost on the page for anybody who comes up the hill.** **AND THE WAGE OF THAT WEEK FELL ON THE SAME MORNING AT ABOUT ELEVEN AND WAS NOT PAID, and the bag was empty and had been since the evening of Tuesday the eighth, and the envelope was not made, and the whole of it is in the first column at about ten past eleven in the morning with the figure against it: four marks, four marks short, spent on a pot of air and on a man of Ashtide, not borrowed, not asked of the harbor authority or any office, not paid in part.** The third column is filled at about an hour's lateness — the shortest since the fourth of April — in the ship's hand, and **nobody reads it back to anybody, and it is the only entry in nineteen days that was not read back twice, and the entry above it says why and the reason is hers and was given in advance.** And the read-out runs at about five in the afternoon with about nine people in the street and the mole head's light not on, and **the chandler's note is said out loud, in nine people's hearing, as NOT re-written and going to stay un-re-written, with its three counts of weeks standing at twenty-two, thirteen and eleven as last written on the fourth of January, the refusal of the thirty-first of March unreversed, and the reason that re-writing a note with nothing in the bag is not a payment, said in a market on the third of May and said again today.** The delayed note has not moved, the delay is a hand's width of a second and was not taken and **nobody in this yard has said why and nobody in this harbor has ever said why and this party is not going to be the first.** And the last three lines: **in about four years a bell is going to be out in a boat at eight marks and a day of a boat then as it is now, and the whole of the craft is the going out, and it stands unreversed; and the boy who used to read the day back is not on the stone and has not been on it since the fifteenth of May; and there is a pencil in this yard tonight and it is in somebody else's hand.**
