### Chapter 181 — A Day to Be Named, and a Paper Served in the Doorway

Thursday the twenty-second and Friday the twenty-third of October, at the mole's steps, in the doorway of the shed, and on a wharf on the boards. **The cistern behind the engine house was charged at no figure by strangers on the Thursday morning, the twentieth since the third of August, and this party walked none of the twenty. Alden Marr is at the far bench on the Thursday and is not asked for anything and asks nothing.** At about eleven on the Thursday **Ambrose Sell, clerk of the circuit office, comes up the hill and gives his name and the name of his office, and says four things: that a day is to be named and that he is not going to name it in a doorway because a day named in a doorway is a day a man can refuse before he has heard it; that a paper will be served naming it; that this yard's book is to be read whole and unshortened from the first of May to the last page and that this office has decided that and has not asked whether the party minds, and that he is saying it a day early so the party has a night to think about the parts it would have left out; and one warning, given once, that whatever goes into the record is what a clerk can enter and not what a clerk can be asked about afterwards.** Calder Marr answers in about two hundred words — that the second column is the only place this party has written down what it could not check, and that it is not going to leave a line out and is not going to soften one — and the clerk reads it back and enters it. And a party may be represented, and this party has said in September that it is not going to be, and he does not ask again. **On Friday at a quarter to eight in the morning the same clerk serves a paper in the doorway in about two people's hearing and does not read it out of it, and the party enters the day and the room — the twenty-eighth and the twenty-ninth of October, the hearing room over the tide-gang store — in the first column and enters why.** And then the day of work: a pump hired by a man of the third lay for a vessel with a started plank, **gross on the board ten, the yard's being three**, and at about half past two **a copper union on the discharge lets go under pressure and the pump's handle comes round through the quarter turn that is in it and strikes the left forearm of this yard's own shipwright across the bone about two inches above the wrist, and she says, before anybody has said anything, that it is the bone and not the joint, and asks that it be said on the boards in that order.** The man finishes the pumping himself with the pump on a bar and pays the day's figure at the figure without anybody arguing about the quarter of an hour that was left on the boards. **Four marks and twelve shillings is in the bag, and three shillings and sixpence goes out of it on the Saturday.**

### Chapter 182 — Three Shillings and Sixpence, and What a Clerk Can Enter

Saturday the twenty-fourth and Sunday the twenty-fifth of October, in a room at the back of a chandler's shop off the market, and in the shed. **At about ten on the Saturday afternoon a bonesetter comes up this hill on foot, looks at an arm in a shed for about eleven minutes, and charges three shillings and sixpence, which is paid out of the bag at ten past four at her own counter in her own hand.** **Hessa Barlow, forty-four, of this harbor, with a room at the back of a chandler's shop off the market, and a name on a painted board over that door since before either brother in the shed was born.** She says the joint is all right and everything one can do with a joint goes on, that the bone wants to be in one position for six weeks, that the forearm is not going to be a hand that takes a pump handle in a month, and that it is a quarter of the year gone out of the left side of a shipwright and there is nothing in the world she can do about any part of it; and she says the word *quarter* is to go in the book in the ship's own hand, because a quarter is a figure and a month is not. **And on the Sunday the two of them do the thing neither of them had thought to do in nine weeks, which is to go through the second column and find out how much of it can go into a record: a line, a date and an hour is what any clerk in any office on this coast can enter, and a reason is a paragraph and there is no column for it.** Five checkless lines, four with no name against them, one of the fourteenth of August of which the man who wrote it can bring up the first four words, and not one reason. **AND THE CLERK'S OWN WARNING OF THE THURSDAY AND THEIR OWN DISCOVERY OF THE SUNDAY ARE THE SAME FACT FOUND FROM TWO DIRECTIONS, AND THAT IS ENTERED.** The bonesetter says the return on the fourteenth day, Saturday the seventh of November, will not be charged and that she would be annoyed if anybody tried to thank her. **Four marks and eight shillings and sixpence is in the bag, and a wage of four marks falls on Tuesday the twenty-seventh and there is enough to pay it.**

### Chapter 183 — The Twenty-Fifth Wall, and a Wage That Goes In

Monday the twenty-sixth and Tuesday the twenty-seventh of October, at the mole's steps, at the head of the dock, and in the shed. **The wall behind the reeve's bench came down bare at eight, the twenty-fifth Mondays since the first of May, the clerk kept his own page and did not mention it, and the next sitting is on Wednesday morning at ten and is not in this party's keeping. The cistern was charged on the Monday, the twenty-first since the third of August, walked on none. Alden Marr is at the far bench.** And there is a man on the mole's steps who is not usually on it: **Fenn Ardle, forty-three, of the second lay, with a boat of about seventy tons and a boy of seventeen on the second hand**, who says two days, Wednesday and Thursday, and that the officer of that office came up on the Friday and told him before he told anybody else, and that he is out of a Tuesday on the water on the twenty-seventh and has told him that and it is written nowhere he can see, **and that a thing nobody has written down is a thing that did not happen in about four years.** Calder Marr says he is not going to ask that office for a tenth thing in that ledger and has not asked it for anything since the fourth of October, and is asking the man what his Tuesday is worth, and is not going to be thanked for it and is not going to say sorry, because a man who says sorry in a market for a Tuesday he did not take gets a Tuesday back for nothing. **And at a quarter to eleven Ors Kest says one thing in the open air, in about four people's hearing and about eleven people's near enough to hear it: that he put the man on those steps and told him on the Friday and not on the Monday morning because a man told on a Friday has a Saturday to be angry about; that the loss is not in his ledger because that ledger is spent; that a thing which cannot be entered cannot be produced and a thing which cannot be produced cannot be argued about; and that the repair account of that office has been empty since the middle of February and he would rather say that out loud to about eleven people than have it found out in a market in March.** The yard took nothing, was given nothing and asked for nothing. **And on the Tuesday the wage of four marks goes in at about eleven, the column is twenty-four lines and ninety-six marks, eighteen envelopes, three weeks fallen due, and eight shillings and sixpence is in the bag.** And at half past eight that night the two of them say out loud, once, what is coming on Wednesday and Thursday: the book goes down whole, and five bare lines are going into a record in a city with no reason against any of them, and the reason does not travel and the line does, and the third column is at the top of a page in a boy's hand and nobody fills it.

### Chapter 184 — The Whole of It, Whole and Unshortened, in a Room Over a Tide-Gang Store

Wednesday the twenty-eighth and Thursday the twenty-ninth of October, in the hearing room over the tide-gang store on the west basin, and on the boards. **THE VOLUME'S MIDPOINT. The wall behind the reeve's bench has been bare since Monday the twenty-sixth. About nine people are in the room on the first day and about eleven on the second, the tide-gang store is shut behind them, and no copy of any record is made in that room and none is given to any party and none is asked for.** The party is not represented. **Ambrose Sell writes the date and the hour before he says anything, says the book is to be read by the man who keeps it because a book read out by a stranger is a document, says he will enter a line, a date and an hour and NOT a reason, and gives the reason in his own trade's words: a record has a column and the column is the width of my page, and if I take four words out of a man's paragraph then in about four years a man in a city thinks the man wrote four words and he did not.** **AND THEN THE HOLDER READS HIS OWN BOOK OUT LOUD FOR THREE HOURS AND FIFTY MINUTES, WHOLE AND UNSHORTENED, FROM THE FIRST OF MAY TO THE LAST PAGE, IN THE ORDER IT IS IN, INCLUDING THE FOUR RETURNS WITH THE DAYS AGAINST THEM, THE COUNTING RULE, THE SHEET OF THE TWENTY-FIFTH OF AUGUST, THE DAY OF THE EIGHTEENTH OF AUGUST, THE ELEVEN WORDS OF THE TWENTY-NINTH OF SEPTEMBER, AND THE FIVE CHECKLESS LINES OF THE SECOND COLUMN AS BARE LINES.** The clerk asks twice for a thing to be read a second time and both times it is read a second time. **THE THIRD COLUMN AT THE HEAD OF A PAGE, FOURTEEN LINES IN THE RIGHT HAND OF A BOY OF TWENTY-TWO DATED FROM THE SECOND OF MAY, IS NOT READ BY THE HOLDER. He says read it. The clerk reads it in a flat voice, because it is a page and a clerk reads pages, and says in the room that this office cannot make that boy come and cannot make anybody ask him, and enters that the three nots of the eighth of June stand and that this office is not going to act on them.** And at four o'clock the clerk asks the holder what a second column is; the holder begins an answer and stops; the answer is entered as not given; **and the clerk then asks the ship's hand, and she answers it in one sentence, and it is entered that the answer was given by the ship's hand and not by the holder of the writ, and about eleven people look at the two of them, and the holder says nothing at all.** And on the Thursday the cistern is charged at no figure and this party is in a room and does not walk it, the twenty-second since the third of August. **AND THE SEAM.** The clerk asks whether the party says anything about the notice of the tenth of September, which is the paper the whole sitting is built out of, and Calder Marr says: there is a join in it, and gives four grounds — the colour of the ink in the first three paragraphs and the sixth against the fourth, the fold of the sheet at that paragraph the other way from the others, the opening and shutting of the paper at that fold, and the head of that paragraph starting a third of an inch lower than the head of the third, which is what a clerk does at a different sitting with a different nib, and he has watched about four hundred men do it — **and then says, in the same breath, that it does not say which of the two hands is right, or why, or whose the two hands were.** **AND THE CLERK SAYS THAT HE HAD THAT PAPER SINCE THE TENTH OF SEPTEMBER AND COULD SEE THE TWO INKS AND DID NOT NEED THE HOLDER OF THE WRIT TO COME UP A HILL AND POINT AT THEM, AND ENTERS THE FACT IN THAT ORDER, THE CLERK FIRST AND THE HOLDER SECOND, AND GIVES HIS REASON: that if it is left out of the record then in about four years the only thing in the bundle anybody is proud of is a thing a man of this harbor put there.** Calder Marr says write it. **Then the question — what does it mean — is asked, having been written in the clerk's own page first, and the answer is *I do not know*, three times, with the reason: that his trade finds out that two things were not made at one time and does not find out which of the two is the true one, and he has never once pretended to anybody that it did.** And then **the entry of the second column of the eighteenth of July is read out of his own book in a flat voice by a clerk who is not doing a part, and the line of the twenty-third of July with it, that the party did not stop him and has not shortened it and was wrong in three parts out of four and has not taken it back — and he does not deny it.** Nothing was decided. Nobody was convicted. **And on the boards at half past two on the Thursday afternoon the shipwright says the one thing she says about the woman: a form with her hand on it was in that room and she was not in that room, and it is the same as the eleven words of the sixteenth of October and it is not the same as the eleven words, and she wants the difference written down while the two of them can both still remember the room.**

### Chapter 185 — The Most Dangerous Column in This Harbor

Friday the thirtieth and Saturday the thirty-first of October, in the shed, and on the mole's steps. **Alden Marr is at the far bench on the Friday and is not asked for anything and asks nothing. Nothing happened on the Saturday and the party entered that, with the reason against the line, that a day on which nothing happens still happened.** And at about eight in the evening on the Friday the ship's hand puts her forearm on the table in a sling and says the thing she has been carrying since eleven o'clock on the Wednesday morning, and says first that she has been trying since Wednesday afternoon to find a way of saying it that does not sound like a frightened woman and cannot, and would rather say it badly than say it well and be listened to in the wrong tone. **THE SECOND COLUMN IS THE MOST DANGEROUS COLUMN IN THIS HARBOR, and it was not in September, and the yard wrote on the sixth of June that it is the only place a man in this harbor is allowed to say that he does not know and mean it, and on Wednesday a man said it in a room and a clerk wrote it down and it is in a record in a city and it cannot be got off.** And the half of it she did not see coming: the crew is two and a half and one of the two and a half has a bone cracked about two inches above her wrist and a figure of three shillings and sixpence and a quarter of a year out of the left side, and she is the tender and the pump and the fall and the board and the slate and the standing shutdown and there is nobody in this harbor the yard can hire to do any of it. **AND FOUR PEOPLE OF THIS COAST ARE ALIVE IN THIS TOWN WITH NO BOAT AND NO WAGES AND ABOUT NINE MARKS BETWEEN THEM, AND THEY WROTE A LIMIT THEMSELVES AND SIGNED IT, AND THE LIMIT IS NOT IN THE RECORD, BECAUSE A LIMIT IS A REASON AND REASONS DO NOT GO INTO A RECORD, AND IT CANNOT BE PUT THERE, BECAUSE THIS YARD HOLDS A WRIT AND A WRIT IS A CHANNEL AND A MAN WITH A WRIT IS EXACTLY THE THING THEY WROTE THE LINE AGAINST.** And she says there is a third thing and it is that he is going to keep saying it, that he is right to, and that in about four years a man in a city is going to read five bare lines and is not going to know whether they are the work of a man who was careful or the work of a man who had somebody to be careful about, and that the reason is not that anybody lied to him. **And the shape of the sentence is said about it: both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other, and there is no third thing to say and she has looked, and nobody improved on either half.** And she will not fill the third column and will point at the page of the seventeenth of October if somebody asks her in a room in four years. **And then she puts a slate and a piece of chalk on the table: three nights on the mole's steps, every pump that goes off and every boat that goes out and every boat that comes in, with the hour, and no reason against any of it — because that is the first thing anybody learns about a listening buoy and a buoy is a book of hours and a man who will not write the hours down, and the rest of it needs a crew that keeps them and there is no crew and she is not going to let him have the other thing.** He does the three nights: nine pumps, four boats out, three in, sixteen lines, no reason against any of them.

### Chapter 186 — A Man at the Head of a Dock Who Did Not Say the Yard Was Wrong

Sunday the first and Monday the second of November, at the head of the dock, at the mole's steps, and in the shed. **And on the Sunday, with the market gone in and about eleven people in the street, Gwil Lasker, thirty-six, of the first lay, with a boat of about a hundred and twenty tons and a man of forty on the second hand, who has crossed this bar twenty-one springs and has never once said out loud that the yard's figure was wrong, says that a yard which has been in a room and come out with a clerk saying that a clerk could see what the man could see is a yard whose figures are worth what the clerk's are — and says first, and says out loud, that he is not saying this yard was wrong, and that he is not the man of the third lay who has been waiting since the ninth of July for something to be wrong with.** His reason in full: a man in a city is going to read two lines on the same page and take the first off and leave the second on, and he does not know what he would do if he were that man with a book of his own, and he would do it in about four seconds and would not be lying when he did it. **And he says he has crossed this bar twenty-one springs and has never once said out loud that the yard's figure was wrong, and that at twenty-two he took a sounding off it off a master's own figure at that master's own asking and was a foot and a half out in a slack water and did not tell him, and that the said master had it himself inside a month off a man out of a city, and that neither of them has said one word about it to the other since — and he gives his name before he is asked for it.** **THE ERROR HE CONFESSES IS HIS OWN. Until the Batch 0004 review this entry gave him the holder's own error — the word *chain* and three parts out of four in one sentence — which is Calder Marr's, at `chapters/volume-03/chapter-0138.md:27`, and is the line the clerk reads back in the room at `chapter-0184.md:137`; two men carrying the same mistake is the one thing the volume's reversal turns on, and `chapter-0186.md:17` and its first-column entry are corrected.** Calder Marr does not thank him, does not let eleven people hear him say that a man who has crossed this bar twenty-one times has come about on the figures, **and says the other half: the figure is not withdrawn and is not going to be, the pilot's figure is not withdrawn, neither can check the other and neither has ever pretended to — and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other. He answers in about two hundred words, and the first column now says so.** Nobody in the street said anything, which is what about eleven people say about two men who have both told the truth about the same thing. **The wall behind the reeve's bench came down bare on the Monday, the twenty-sixth Mondays since the first of May, and the last thing that was ever on that wall was a sitting two days ago that is now a bundle in a city. The cistern was charged, the twenty-third since the third of August, walked on none. Alden Marr is at the far bench.** And the whole of the two days goes into the first column against itself, with the reason: **that a yard which has spent four volumes saying that its own record is the only kind anybody can check has come out of a room less able to be checked, and that it happened by the party's own method, in public, in about nine and about eleven people's hearing, and that nobody was convicted of anything and nothing was decided and no office was a villain in it, and that a man who is the best reader of joins in this harbor was made less credible by a thing he is good at and said so himself in a room and cannot unsay it, and that the yard is not going to be told it is sorry about it in a market and is not going to thank anybody for it and is not asking.**

### Chapter 187 — An Envelope Not Made, and a Column Nobody Is Going to Fill

Tuesday the third and Wednesday the fourth of November, in the shed, and at the head of the dock. **THE WAGE OF FOUR MARKS DID NOT GO IN ON TUESDAY THE THIRD AND NO ENVELOPE WAS MADE, and the number of weeks fallen due this year with no envelope standing against them is now FOUR — the fifteenth of August, the fifth of September, the sixth of October and the third of November — entered in the same breath and not one after the other.** The column stands at twenty-four lines and ninety-six marks, the fifth of March the oldest, eighteen envelopes on a bench, and **eight shillings and sixpence in the bag, which is one hundred and two pence, and a wage of four marks is six hundred and forty pence and the yard is **five hundred and thirty-eight** pence short of it (**the figure of six hundred and thirty-eight that stood here and in two chapters was arithmetically wrong and is corrected; the full account is at `state/continuity.md` § *Batch 0004 review repairs*, item 2**), and this party entered on the sixth of October that it would enter the day of a working Tuesday unpaid in the first column with the figure and the reason rather than wait for a day it does not know is coming, and has entered it again because it came.** And at half past seven on the Wednesday evening the two of them have the argument the third column has been waiting for since the seventeenth of October. **He says then somebody has to be appointed. She says no, twice, and the second no is not the reason of the seventeenth of October.** Hers: that the column is a page where a man wrote down what he said when he was not in the boat, that it has been worth what it is worth because nobody ever filled it but him, that on Wednesday a clerk read fourteen lines of it out loud in a room in a flat voice and entered that the office cannot make the boy come and cannot make anybody ask him, **and that there is no more of that column in this harbor that anybody can add to, and whatever goes in it now goes in it after a room has been in it.** And when he suggests that she put her nine sentences in it, **she says that is the worst thing anybody has said in that shed since the first of May, and that she has already said out loud in this yard in her own hand what the nine sentences are and why they are not going in a page, and that if the column is going to be filled by somebody then somebody is going to be reading it and is going to be deciding what goes in and what does not, and a page one person decides is a page one person owns, and that is a man with a book and not a column.** And then nobody is appointed, and the reason: **a column nobody fills is a column somebody else fills, and the somebody else is a clerk with a pen, and a clerk with a pen is not a bad thing and is not a villain and is the only way a record gets made at all, and the day he fills it is the day this yard stops being able to say that the one honest column in it is his.** The first column says plainly that the party does not know where the boy is and has not asked and is not going to send for him, and the three nots of the eighth of June stand.

### Chapter 188 — A Name for a Reason, and Five Marks at the Second Seam

Thursday the fifth and Friday the sixth of November, at the wall outside the market office, on the mole's steps, and on the face of the second seam. **The cistern was charged on the Thursday, the twenty-fourth since the third of August, walked on none.** And at about eight in the morning, before the market was off the boards, **a man of the first lay, about fifty-five, with a coasting boat of his own and a letter from a city in his coat, is standing in front of the unsigned finding on that wall reading the reason on the page out loud, and asks this yard for the name of the woman who wrote it.** He says he has been at four doors in three days and this is the fifth and it is a wall, and that a thing on a wall with no name on it is a thing he cannot be made to answer for, and that he has a letter that a man in a city is going to act on the strength of that sheet. **Calder Marr says no in about four minutes and gives the whole of it: she is not on this crew and not of this yard and not a holder and not on the four names, and the reporting clause does not reach her and never did; she left this crew in her own words on the twenty-third of July and that is a different thing from anything that has happened to her since and he is not going to put the two together in a street; she is owed forty marks first after food since the fifteenth of October and not one mark has been paid and the six marks and two days have not been offered and have not been reduced and he is not going to offer them in a street in November because it is the same price and it has not moved; the sheet is unsigned because she asked for it to be unsigned and he is not going to have it signed or taken down; and this party was refused by her in a room open to anybody on the twenty-ninth of September and has asked her nothing since, because a party which has been refused once and then tells a man in a street where the woman is has decided that a person is a door.** And the man's answer is the cost of the whole month: **that in July the same answer sounded like a yard being careful and that on the fifth of November it sounds like a wall, and that he knows a page in a city is a sheet he can be made to answer for and a wall is not, and that he would rather have the page, and would rather have it from this yard than from anybody else, and is not going to pretend he would rather have a yard than a wall because he has been in four rooms in this harbor this month.** And Calder Marr says he has got it the right way round and has not got a better version of it, and adds the one thing that is against this yard and not for it: **a sheet with no name on it is a sheet a man cannot be made to answer for, a page in a city is a sheet a man can be made to answer for, this yard has spent four volumes saying the second one is the only kind of record anybody can check, and it went into a room on the twenty-ninth of October and came out with that, and he is the man who put it there, and he would rather have the wall than the page and has not got a reason for that which is worth anything.** And on the Friday **a day at the second seam's own face, gross seventeen, the yard's being five, with the jobs swapped: the holder runs the pump, which he has not done since the second of May and did badly for the first hour, and the ship's hand keeps the book and the count and the times and hauls the line over with her right hand; and the hirer knew about the arm and did not ask about it and said the day went slower than a day with three on it, and the holder said that it did, and the man said he knew it did and had had a yard of two before.** The first column re-enters as a carried fact that the yard now holds two documents and not one, and that a form is a form whichever office writes it.

### Chapter 189 — The Fourteenth Day, and a Wharf Day Refused

Saturday the seventh and Sunday the eighth of November, in a room at the back of a chandler's shop off the market, and in the shed. **And at about ten on the Saturday morning a bonesetter comes up this hill and looks at an arm in a shed for about nine minutes, on the fourteenth day, and does not charge for it, having said on the twenty-fourth that she would not, and says so again before she has looked at it.** She will not touch it: there is a thing in a bone that has to be left alone for fourteen days, and if anybody puts a thumb on it today that is the day it does not knit. **The strapping comes off on the twenty-first of November and not before**, and the figure of the three shillings and sixpence is paid and is not going to be charged again by her this winter, **and the figure of the rest of it is a quarter of a year out of the left side of the only shipwright on this coast who can hold a pump on a wharf for six hours, and that is not her figure and she does not want it in her book.** And she says a day of work this yard has refused is the most expensive thing anybody can hand you and nobody hands it to you for nothing. And Nessa Pike says the three shillings and sixpence and the quarter of a year go on the same line in the first column and not in two places, in her own hand, **and that a bone is not a bill and a bill is not a bone and a man who has the two in one line will end up arguing about the wrong one** — and adds that on Wednesday a man read her hand out of a book in a room for about an hour and a half and she sat in that room the whole time and could not check one figure of it. **And at about half past four on the Sunday afternoon a man of the first lay comes up this hill and offers a day, and it is about three marks on a wharf, and this yard refuses it and says the reason in nine words: a pump on a wharf takes two and one of them is her, and her forearm is strapped, and a hand that will not take a handle until the twenty-first of November at the earliest, and this party is not going to book a day it cannot work.** And the other half of the reason, which is in the same breath: that on the ninth of September a man of the first lay of about ninety tons asked this yard to look at a thing on his stem and this party said no and he said he had not expected it in October and would come again in the spring, and this party is entered that it is not going to be the yard that says yes to everything from November and then cannot do the February ones. He says that is a good answer and not a cheerful one. **And the second column carries the body's time: a man stood in a room for two days in the last week of October and read out of his own book for three hours and fifty minutes, and on the Wednesday night he did not sleep and on the Thursday night he did, and the party entered both halves of that on one line and is not going to name what it is in a shed, and that the four lines above the named line of the twentieth of July are still four and are still nameless and are not struck out.**

### Chapter 190 — The Twenty-Seventh Wall, and a Reason Against the Line

Monday the ninth and Tuesday the tenth of November, at the mole's steps, at the head of the dock, and in the shed. **The wall came down bare, the twenty-seventh Mondays since the first of May, and the last thing that was ever on that wall was a sitting four days ago that is now a bundle in a city. The cistern was charged at no figure by strangers and this party did not walk it, and no figure is entered against that charge. Alden Marr is at the far bench, the sixth and last of the three weeks.** And on the Tuesday **the wage of four marks goes in at about eleven, the column is twenty-five lines and a hundred marks, nineteen envelopes, four weeks fallen due, and a mark and eight shillings and sixpence is in the bag, which is two hundred and sixty-two pence, and the same bag held three hundred and four pence on the twentieth of October, and the whole of the difference is three shillings and sixpence and it is a bonesetter's bill on the twenty-fourth and it is the only money this yard has spent on itself in twenty-one days.** **And at about six, with the market gone in and about eleven people in the street, the two of them read the three weeks out at the head of this dock in about nine minutes — and that is what a reading at the head of a dock is, and nobody was asked to be quiet.** The shipwright says the figures: the bag, the column, four weeks fallen due, nineteen envelopes, three shillings and sixpence and a quarter of a year, five marks off the face of the second seam, three marks refused on the wharf on the twelfth of October and three marks refused again this week, nothing on the twenty-eighth and nothing on the twenty-ninth, the cistern charged twenty-four times since the third of August and walked on none, the wall twenty-seventh time, **the far bench occupied on the twenty-second and the twenty-sixth and the thirtieth of October and the second, the sixth and the ninth of November, and on no other day of the three weeks, and neither brother went over to the other on any of the six; a man of the second lay out of a Tuesday that is in no ledger and is in this yard's book; the thing none of them can check, which is a record in a city with five bare lines of the second column in it and a clerk's entry that he could see a join before the man who keeps the book pointed at it, and a market of the eighteenth of July read out in a room by a stranger; and a man of the first lay of about fifty-five at the wall outside the market office on the Thursday morning who said he would rather have the page than the wall, and was right, and whom neither of them is going to unsay.** **THE READ-OUT NAMED THE WRONG MAN UNTIL THE BATCH 0004 REVIEW: it gave the *page rather than the wall* sentence to Gwil Lasker, thirty-six, at the head of the dock a week ago, and it is the man of fifty-five at the wall, and `chapter-0190.md` is corrected in the read-out, in the holder's speech and in the first-column entry. THE READ-OUT ALSO GAVE THE CISTERN TWENTY-FOUR CHARGES AND THEN SAID IT WAS CHARGED AGAIN THAT MORNING, WHICH A READER COUNTS AS TWENTY-FIVE; IT NOW KEEPS THE TWENTY-FOUR AND SAYS THE PARTY IS NOT GOING TO STAND IN A STREET AND SAY WHETHER THAT MAKES IT TWENTY-FIVE, BECAUSE IT DID NOT SEE THE DAYS THOSE MEN COME ON. The full account of both is at `state/continuity.md` § *Batch 0004 review repairs*, items 3, 4 and 5.** And she says she is not going to read one line of the second column out and is not going to be asked to in a market and will point at a page in their own book if she is asked in a room in a city in four years. **And at about half past nine in the shed, with the lamp lit and the read-back done from the top by the ship's hand and after her by the holder and nobody else in the room, the whole of three weeks goes into the first column and four lines of it into the second, and the ship's hand stops the read-back at the Thursday of the twenty-ninth of October and says: a man of this yard was right about a thing in a room on the twenty-ninth of October, and the same man has been less believed in a market ever since, and both halves of that go on one line in the first column with a reason against it, and the reason is that a man in this harbor can get off a mole tomorrow and walk to that room and ask a clerk whether it is in his page, and can ask any man on that quay on the fifth of November whether a man of about fifty-five said at that wall what he said he was going to say, and that the cost of what happened in that room is public and is not a thing either of them can hold in a shed.** And the forward pull: **the question standing on the table is a document this party has never seen and has never asked for, a copy of a record about an object with the limits the record itself carries printed on the face of the copy, which would show that a manifest was altered and would not show who altered it, and which a man of the first lay of this harbor cannot check, and the party is not applying for one this month and has entered why and is not saying no to it in four years and is not saying yes either, and the release of that copy is not in this yard's keeping and has never been in it.** A working harbor is poorer at the end of these three weeks than it was at the start of them, and nothing this yard has done in three weeks has made it better, and nothing this yard published on a market wall in October has made it better.

### Chapter 201 — The First Morning, and a Counter at Thirty-One
Sunday the sixth and Monday the seventh of December, in the shed, and at the mole's steps. **No day of work booked on either day, and the reason against the line is that a day on which nothing happens still happened, and that this is the first day of a month in which this yard is going to have to be able to be checked on any day of a week by anybody who can get off a mole.** Three sheets are on the bench where the pump used to be and none has been put away: the copy of a record of the twenty-fourth of November in six heads and about a page and a half, dated the date of a counter and not the date of a record; the acknowledgment of the twenty-ninth; and the half sheet of a court in a city of the fourth of December with the **fourth of January** on it. **Twenty-nine days, of which four are Tuesdays.** The holder enters, in his own left hand, with the date and the hour on it, that this party will do nothing in aid of the fourth of January, and gives the whole reason: **a thing done in order to be ready is a thing that arrives with a date on it**, and in about four years a clerk in a city would have a piece of paper with a date on it and this party's name at the head of it, and it would be in a file whatever happened to the yard. **The writ runs to midnight on the first of March and the two dates are not being joined.** The ship's hand puts the standing question once: it is standing, it is not going away because nobody asked it twice, and **if somebody asks it in a market in January the answer is the answer already on the page and it is not going to be a better one.** On the Monday the wall comes down bare for the thirty-first Monday since the first of May, the clerk keeps his own page and does not mention it, the cistern is charged on the rota day at no figure and walked on none, and the far bench is occupied from ten until about four and neither brother goes over. The read-back runs. **No money in and nothing out on either day; 717p in the bag, seventy-seven pence short of the wage, six weeks fallen due with no envelope standing against them.**

### Chapter 202 — A Form With No Date on It, and a Man Who Is Not the Man Who Directs It
Tuesday the eighth and Wednesday the ninth of December, in the shed, and on the mole. **The wage of four marks does not go in, no envelope is made, and the number of weeks fallen due with no envelope standing against them is SEVEN, all seven given in the same breath, and the bag was seventy-seven pence short of the wage.** At about eleven on the Wednesday morning a man comes up the mole on foot in a coat that has been in weather, with nothing in his hands until he is in the doorway, **and he does not give his name.** He gives the name of the office at the foot of the sheet and the reason he is not giving his own: a man's name at the foot of a thing is a thing a man in a city can hold for four years, which is the reason a clerk of that circuit office gave at this bench on the twenty-third of November and which the yard has in its first column in two hands. **The sheet is a sheet and a half with no signature anywhere and no date at the head, in the body or at the foot, and at the foot there is the name of an office; the name of that office is not on any page of this yard's book and is not printed here, and the reason is on the page and is not a defect. It is the form of an office in a city of the same kind as the form that acknowledged the discrepancy on the twenty-ninth of November and signed nothing, and it is NOT the circuit office, NOT the Court of Wreck Claims, NOT the harbor authority and NOT the coast office.** It proposes that this yard hold a copy of a record for the coast and be named in an entry as the person who holds it, and says the party is not to be examined, licensed, enrolled, paid or asked to find anything and is asked one question; **it says nothing about what follows an answer of no, and the date of the answer is the only date on it.** **He says the Crown's position in one sentence and one sentence only: testimony is safe in one place and nowhere else, and this harbor is not that one, and that is not an opinion, it is what three hundred years of an office is. Nobody in that shed said it was a lie and nobody said the man was anything at all.** He said he is not the man who directs it, and that he did not know what picking up a sheet off a bench is and the office does not say, and left the sheet on the bench and went down the mole and nobody followed him. The ship's hand reads it out once more and squares it and says: **the whole of the sheet is for a name; a room is a building and an address is a name; and a party which holds a copy of a record becomes the address of that copy, and that is true, and she tried all Wednesday to make it not true and could not.**

### Chapter 203 — The Harbor Authority Agrees, and Says What It Cannot Do, and Names the Price of the Rest
Thursday the tenth and Friday the eleventh of December, on the mole's steps, and in the shed. **The cistern is charged on the rota day and walked on none.** At about eleven, in the open at the foot of the mole's steps in about eleven people's hearing, the holder asks the officer of the harbor authority one question and says first what he is **not** asking: not an instrument, not to seat anybody, not to hold anything, and he gives the reason, including that the third lay of this harbor lost four days in June for the want of a room and that it will not happen again. **Kest says his office's view is that a thing kept in Morrow Quay is a thing kept in Morrow Quay**, and gives the reason: no office on this coast can get at a copy of a record kept in this place; a record in a city can be asked for and got at by a man with a carriage and a record in Morrow Quay can be got at by about four people, two of whom are the men on that mole; **and a man in a city who wants a thing in a fortnight will not send a carriage and will write to this harbor authority first, because that is the name a man writes first when he does not know any other, and that office will answer him and cannot tell him a thing about a record, and that is how a man in a city finds out where a thing is.** Then he names **what his office cannot do**: it cannot certify a copy of a record, cannot hold a record for the coast, **cannot enter this in his ledger because the ledger is spent and the ninth acknowledgement is spent and a tenth may not be entered and will not be**, cannot renew the writ of the first of May and is the only office that can, cannot overrule a seizure, cannot certify a glass witness — and he is not going to do the rest of it and pretend afterwards that it was part of it. **The price is named before he says yes, and it is not a morning of the tide gang and not a day of the third lay and not anybody's body: it is that his office becomes a name in this business, and every party who comes up that hill about anything at all is going to be told at the foot of those steps that this office has an opinion about a copy of a record, for years, including the ones who have nothing to do with this party.** He puts it on a page of his own and not in the ledger, **because a page of his own is not a record and cannot be produced on demand by anybody**, and says again that he is not a friend of this party and that the yard agrees with him. On the Friday the far bench is occupied from ten until about four, not asked, asking nothing, and **he was not at that bench on the Thursday at any hour**, and at about four a man comes up the hill about a day at the second seam on the Saturday at about three marks and the yard takes it. **THE FAR-BENCH LINE OF THE ELEVENTH IS NOW IN THAT CHAPTER'S FIRST COLUMN AND WAS NOT AT FIRST, AND IT IS ONE OF THE FOUR DAYS OF THE BENCH IN THIS BATCH; THE REPAIR AND ITS REASON ARE IN `state/continuity.md`.**

### Chapter 204 — Three Marks on a Board, and the Thing After the Gland Is the Hose
Saturday the twelfth and Sunday the thirteenth of December, on the face of the second seam, and in the shed. **The board for the day is twelve gross, and what comes off the top of a day rate comes off the top of it in the order it has come off since the third of May: the eighth, one. The share, one. The victuals of the day, one. A hired hand, three. A second hired hand, three. Nine of twelve paid at the mole and the yard's being three, which is four hundred and eighty pence, and the bag held seven hundred and seventeen on the Friday morning and the sum of the two is one thousand one hundred and ninety-seven, which is seven marks, six shillings and five pence.** A hand lead's line went over the side and back four times, nobody in the water, the count and the times onto a slate in the ship's hand and the slate into the book in her own writing and the holder reading it back after her. The hirer was of the second lay with a boat of about seventy tons and brought the pump and a man and **said he had asked for a yard**, and she tells him the day is going slower than a day with three on it and that the reason is in the book in the holder's hand and not in hers and that he would only have an opinion; he says he has not got one. **The day is booked by this party with a person in it and not a person short, and the cost of that is a day that went slower, and a day that goes slower is a day not earned whole and is entered as a day not earned whole and not as a day at a figure.** On the Sunday no day is booked, and the second column carries the gland and the hose: **five marks of compressor's gland standing on that page since the nineteenth of May, unpaid and useless, and the thing after the gland is the hose and this harbor has no hose**, and the yard is not going to price it and not going to buy one out of a day at a seam, and she said the rest of that sentence once and is not going to say it a second time in a December. **The form is still on the bench under the pump and has not been answered and has not been put in the stove.**

### Chapter 205 — Eleven Lines Beside a Form, and a Reason That Cannot Be Written Down
Monday the fourteenth and Tuesday the fifteenth of December, in the shed. **The wall comes down bare for the thirty-second Monday and the cistern is charged on the rota day and walked on none.** In the shed the ship's hand takes down the sheet of the twenty-second of November, folded once, and reads the eleven aloud: the place of the case of five bells; the four people it belongs to; **the limit they wrote themselves**; the plate at the fifth seam; the two objects on the crown of this mole; the boy; the forty marks standing whole to him; the forty marks first after food to a person of no office; the delay; the letter that was coming up this hill on the Saturday; and the two figures for the bar of gravel and the Kettle, which was not looked at. **Item ten has happened and came back no.** She reads the limit out once and it is that **the account is not to be read out, is not to go into a book that leaves this harbor, is not to be said to a man with a seal, and not one name to any office in any city**, and the holder says the fourth paragraph back as a sentence: a party which agrees to hold a copy of a record is a party that has put its name in a record. **THE DISAGREEMENT IS THE BATCH'S DISCOVERY: the yard cannot put the limit in the answer because the answer carries the name of the party, the place and the date, and a reason does not go into a record; and the yard cannot put its name to an answer without the limit in it, because that is what an answer is. And a place a copy of a record is kept in IS a room, and the eleven lines are a list of what does not go into a room, and every one of them is a thing this yard would be right to keep out of a room — so the eleven lines are the answer to that form, and the answer to that form is eleven lines this yard cannot put in an answer. NOBODY'S NAME WENT NEAR A PIECE OF PAPER ABOUT A FORM.** She is not going to write a no sentence this month, because a bare sentence in a form with a name at the foot of it will be read in about four years as a man who had somebody to be careful about. On the Tuesday the wage is not paid and the number of weeks fallen due with no envelope is EIGHT, all eight in the same breath, and the bag is five hundred and fifty-seven pence short. The read-back runs. **Item eleven has not been moved off that list in three weeks and is not going to be moved in a December.**

### Chapter 206 — A Sentence in a Street, and a Reason That Does Not Travel
Wednesday the sixteenth and Thursday the seventeenth of December, at the head of this dock, and in the shed. **No day of work booked on either day, and the reason against the line is that a day on which two things happened and neither of them was work has to be entered twice and the second time it says so.** At about half past eleven on the Wednesday, at the head of this dock in about eleven people's hearing, a man of the third lay asks what the yard is going to do about a thing on a bench up the hill and says he is not asking it for anybody and that he has had it from three people since Friday and has stopped repeating it back. **The holder answers in the street on purpose, and gives the reason: a thing said in a street is checkable by anybody who was in it, and a thing said in a shed is checkable by one other person.** He gives the whole shape of the sheet and says the answer will be in his own hand, is not an office's, is not signed by a clerk, and has no day on the sheet to be late — **and then says he is not going to be able to say today whether it is going to be a yes or a no, and that he is not going to be in a position to say in three weeks either, and that he would rather the man had it from him in a street than stand there working it out of his face for a month.** On the Thursday **two men of the first lay are saying that this yard has not said no, and one of them says the word *hold* twice, and this party does not go up and correct either of them.** The cistern is charged on the rota day and walked on none, and **the far bench was not occupied on the Wednesday or the Thursday at any hour, and the line is entered with no figure of what came before it: there are days of these three weeks the yard has not entered and is not going up that hill again to enter, and a man who comes up and sees that bench empty and asks what it was the day before is told that they do not know. THE FIRST RECORD SAID THAT THE LAST TIME BEFORE THOSE TWO DAYS THAT THE BENCH WAS EMPTY FOR TWO DAYS TOGETHER WAS IN THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER PAST, AND THAT CLAIM IS WITHDRAWN IN THE CHAPTER AND HERE: THE FIFTEENTH IS UNSTATED IN THE BATCH, AS ARE EIGHT OTHER DAYS, AND NO CHAPTER SUPPORTS THE FIGURE.** The ship's hand says the read-back is deliberately absent, because a thing said in a street is read back by whoever was standing in the street and there were about eleven of them and not one of them is in that shed. **She gives the whole of the reason it cannot be put right: to say no in that street he would have to say the whole of it, including four people of this coast and a limit that does not go into a street, and the second he says that, three men in this town know a thing about four people who did not know it before Friday, and in about four years it will be a thing a man in a city can look up. HE CANNOT SAY NO IN THE STREET AND HE CANNOT SAY YES IN THE STREET AND HE CANNOT SAY HE HAS NOT DECIDED TWICE. The two columns are the reason against the line and the fact that a reason does not travel, and the gap between them is not closed and says so on the page.**

### Chapter 207 — A Counter off the Fish Market, and Two Prices That Are Not the Same Price
Friday the eighteenth and Saturday the nineteenth of December, at a counter in a room off the fish market, and in the shed. **The far bench is occupied on the Friday from ten until about four, not asked, asking nothing, and he was not at that bench on the Thursday at any hour.** At about ten the yard goes down to the counter, which is open to anybody from eight until the market is off the boards, **puts the copy of the record flat on it and reads none of it out, and nobody in that room hears one line of it.** A copyist of fifty-eight sits down on a stool she has not sat on for the last three people of that week and says **nobody has ever said to me at that counter that they did not want a copy.** Two questions, two answers in her own trade's words: **a copy is a copy, and nine copies are nine of the same words and not one of the nine checks anything, and what a man in nine places can check is nine people who each went and got it, and that is not a copying trade and is a fetching trade, and there is not one trade on this coast that does it, and the four people who could do it are alive in this town with no boat and about nine marks between them**; the paper is nine pence and forty of those is two shillings and a threepence, and **the price is nine men's time, and a man's time in a working port in December is a day, and a day at a good trade is about three marks on a board with the eighth and the share off the top, so the price of a page that anybody in nine places could check is the whole of a day's work at a seam.** And the other: **a page that nobody can check is a sheet and a shed and no money at all, and it is the one that cannot be shown to anybody, and a thing that cannot be shown to anybody is a thing that has not been made, and the two of those are the same sentence.** She says she could not tell him in a room which is better because it is not her trade to say. Then the third question, which is not about paper: **what does it cost to write a reason against a line and then to have the reason stop at the edge of the page** — and the answer is that a paragraph is a paragraph, she will write one for a penny like anything else, the good ones are worth about a penny more than the bad ones and that is what a trade is, **and the moment a reason goes on a page it is a paragraph, and a paragraph is a trade, and a trade travels, and a reason can be kept in a shed for nine years and cannot be kept in a paragraph.** And then, about sheets in general and not about this yard's: **a sheet with an office's name at the foot of it and no man's name on it anywhere is the easiest thing in the world for a copyist to sell, because there is nobody on it for her to ask where it came from, and those go out of a shop and into somebody's buyer's book and nobody ever knows.** The yard buys one sheet of her paper at a penny, into her own hand, for its own use and not for a copy of anything, **because this party cannot put a price in a record out of a person's mouth.** 1,196p in the bag.

### Chapter 208 — Two Marks Paid on Saturday and a Man Who Did Not Come on Monday
Sunday the twentieth and Monday the twenty-first of December, at the boards, in the shed, and on the mole. **No day of work booked on the Sunday, and the reason against the line is that a day on which nothing happens still happened, and that the Sunday was a day on which this yard was told a price it had not asked for and entered it before anybody asked it for anything.** At about nine at the boards a man of the second lay tells the ship's hand a thing and tells her and not the holder, and says he is telling her because she writes things down and not because he wants anything out of it. **He lightered alongside that mole on the sixth of November, he hired a man on the Saturday evening for the Monday, and he paid him then, two marks and his victuals, in his own hand out of his own pocket, and the man did not come at eight.** He says he is not going to say it is the hired man's fault and that he has been stood up by better men. **The hired man's reason, in his own words: if everything a yard says in this town goes into a book in a city then a day's work of mine goes into one too, and I have got a girl at a school in a town four days up this coast and I am not having her name read out in a town I have never been to. And I said that is a great deal of fuss about a day's work. And he said it is my day's work, and that is the end of it.** The man will not give the name and neither will the lighterman, and he says that if this party went down to that quay he would be the man who told it. **The price is entered on the Sunday night, in the holder's own hand, at her asking, before anybody asks for anything, and the yard is not going to pay it: a yard which pays a man's day for a thing it said in a street has bought the street, and the yard does not want it and cannot afford it, and the first of those three is the one that is on the page.** **THE CHAPTER NOW ALSO ENTERS, IN ITS PROSE AND IN ITS FIRST COLUMN, THAT THE SATURDAY EVENING OF THE NINETEENTH IS THE SECOND OF TWO DAYS ON WHICH THE SAME TWO MEN OF THE FIRST LAY WERE SAYING A THING ABOUT THIS YARD, THE FIRST BEING THURSDAY THE SEVENTEENTH WHEN THEY WERE SAYING THAT THIS YARD HAD NOT SAID NO AND ONE OF THEM SAID THE WORD *HOLD* TWICE; THAT THE YARD WENT UP ON NEITHER DAY; THAT THE REASON AGAINST BOTH LINES IS THAT A CORRECTION IS THE REASON AND THE REASON DOES NOT GO INTO A STREET; THAT THE FIRST OF THE TWO DAYS IS OUT OF THE YARD'S OWN EYES AND THE SECOND IS OUT OF WHAT THE LIGHTERMAN SAID AT THE BOARDS; AND THAT THE YARD HAS NOT GOT EITHER MAN'S NAME AND IS NOT GOING UP THE HILL FOR IT.** On the Monday the wall comes down bare for the thirty-third Monday, the cistern is charged and walked on none, **the far bench is occupied from ten until about four, not asked, asking nothing, and he was not at it on the Sunday at any hour**, and the two of them go down the hill past the west quay at about eight and the lighter is lying there with one man on it and neither brother says anything and neither stops. The read-back runs.

### Chapter 209 — A Letter With No Threat in It, and the One Place a Man in a City Can Look
Tuesday the twenty-second and Wednesday the twenty-third of December, in the shed, and on the mole. **The wage is not paid, no envelope is made, and the number of weeks fallen due with no envelope standing against them is NINE, all nine in the same breath, and the bag is five hundred and fifty-six pence short.** On the Tuesday the two of them enter that the board has nothing in it for five days after it, **and that a board with nothing in it for five days is a figure anybody can add up, and that a figure anybody can add up is the first one this year that this yard has not been able to stop happening.** At about ten on the Wednesday one sheet comes up the hill in the ordinary post, dated the twentieth: **a printer's letter.** It is not a threat and not a favor and the printer says so himself. **A man who sells ice bought a sheet at a counter off this fish market on the sixth of December, paid a penny, put it in a box of fish and sent it up the coast; it is a half sheet with the name of an office at the foot of it and no man's name anywhere on it; the printer keeps a list of everything that comes into his shop that anybody means to keep; and on the ninth of December a man came to that counter and bought type and nothing else and asked whether he could say where a copy of a record was, and wrote down the name of the town it came from and the day, and said thank you and bought his type.** His one question: **where is the copy of the record.** He is not asking for the sheet, is not asking this party to be examined or licensed or enrolled or paid, is not asking on anybody's behalf, and **is not going to write again until this party writes to him.** The sheet goes onto the bench beside the form with no date on it, and the acknowledgment of the twenty-ninth comes off the shelf, and the three lie in a line a foot apart for about four minutes and nobody says anything. **THE TURN OF THE BATCH: this yard did not write that acknowledgment, did not pay for it, did not ask for it and did not allow it, and it is the one page in this country by which a man in a city can find out where this yard is, and it did the whole of the work in nine days, and no office on this coast could have stopped it and no clerk and no form and no clause.** And: **a reply is a document with this yard's name at the foot of it** — if the holder writes to that printer then this shed has an address it made itself, on this yard's own paper, in its own hand, dated, and the office whose name is at the foot of the form on that bench would find it in about four years in about nine seconds, and everything the printer has done would be done twice and the second time it would be this yard's fault. **SO: NO REPLY. AND THE REASON GOES IN THE FIRST COLUMN, because a man in this harbor can come up this hill and look at that acknowledgment and see the name of an office at the foot of it and no man's name on it anywhere, and can ask a woman of fifty-eight whether she read it out and in what market and on what day, and can ask the post what day a letter came up this road. All three are checkable by any man who can get off a mole, and he is not going to argue with it.** The shape of sentence is said once, about a copy of a record in this yard's hands and this yard's name on a line in a printer's book.

### Chapter 210 — Three Weeks Read Out at the Head of This Dock, and a Day Refused
Thursday the twenty-fourth and Friday the twenty-fifth of December, at the head of this dock, and in the shed. **The cistern is charged on the rota day and walked on none, and the far bench is not occupied on either of the two days at any hour.** At about half past four on the Thursday, at the head of this dock in about eleven people's hearing, the three weeks are read out in about nine minutes, **and not one line of the second column is read out in it**: the bag at seven marks, six shillings and four pence, being one thousand one hundred and ninety-six pence, and the whole of the difference since the sixth of December a day at the second seam and a sheet of paper at a penny, **and a day refused at about three marks on the Friday and that figure is not in the bag and it is the first day in four volumes that this yard has turned money down**; the column at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with the fifth of March the oldest, twenty envelopes, and nine weeks fallen due with no envelope against them given in the same breath, **two of those not paid because there was a sheet of paper and a bone and seven of them not paid because there was nothing**; every debt standing; **the wall bare three times, being the thirty-first, thirty-second and thirty-third Mondays since the first of May, and no sheet gone up on any wall in this harbor in seven weeks and none come off**; the cistern charged on six rota days and walked on none and the charge of the ninth of November standing with no figure against it; the far bench occupied on four days, the seventh, the eleventh, the eighteenth and the twenty-first, and on no other, and neither brother going over on any of the four; **two men of the first lay a morning down on a lighter, two marks and a victual of it paid on the Saturday evening for the Monday, the price entered on the Sunday and not asked for**; **and those same two men saying a thing about this yard at the head of that dock on the seventeenth and again on the nineteenth, the word *hold* twice on the first, about nine people standing there, the yard going up on neither day, the first of the two out of its own eyes and the second out of a man's mouth at the boards, and the reason against both lines that a correction is the reason and the reason does not go into a street**; **the price of a checkable page in nine places and the price of an uncheckable one, both out of a woman's mouth at a counter and not paid for except a penny for a sheet**; and **five papers that none of them can check, being the page and a half, the acknowledgment, the form of the court, the form with no date and no signature, and the printer's letter with one question in it that is going into a drawer and is not going to be answered.** On the Friday morning a man of the second lay comes about a day at about three marks for the Saturday **and the holder says no, in a doorway and not in a market, and gives the reason: a day at a seam is a figure that is earned, and this yard is a party of one and a half with nine weeks of no envelope against it, and it is not turning down three marks in the last week of December because a man came up a hill with a sheet of paper; and the second half of the reason is that he does not know what he is doing on the Saturday morning, and a man who books a day he does not know about books a day with a man in it twice, and this yard is already a day short.** The figure of three marks is entered against that day and not against nothing. The read-back runs, and then: **the turn, in the holder's own left hand, with the date and the hour on it, in the first column — a yard which has spent four volumes saying that a record a man can check is the only kind worth having has found out in three weeks that being checkable is being findable, and that the instrument it built to make itself credible is the instrument that is going to make it locatable, and that it built that instrument on purpose on the seventh of July last and nobody made it do it. It is in the first column and not the second because a man in this harbor can come up this hill on any day of a week and check it: he can ask a woman of fifty-eight what she copied and for how much and on whose account, he can go and count the sheets on a wall in this market, and he can find out whether this yard has said a thing out loud in the open in this harbor this month, and it has said one thing about the answer to that sheet, at the head of that dock on the Wednesday the sixteenth, in about eleven people's hearing, and it did not take it back and is not going to, and the tenth of the month was a question asked and an answer given and is not counted.** The new-volume question is referred to once, in the first column, with its date, its asker, his age and his tonnage, **with the yard's answer in the words already on the page and not improved on, and the entry saying it is not going to answer it in a book either.** The batch's last line is a fact: the bag, the three weeks, the refused day with its figure entered, a sheet with an office's name at the foot of it that has gone nine days from a market in this harbor to a line in a printer's book, and a letter going into a drawer unanswered, **and that every part of it is on that page and anybody in this town can come up this hill on any day of a week and look at it.**

### Chapter 211 — A Board With Nothing in It For Fourteen Days, and the Thing After the Gland
Saturday the twenty-sixth and Sunday the twenty-seventh of December, in the shed, and in the engine house. **No day of work booked on either day, and the reason against the line is that a day on which nothing happens still happened.** The far bench is entered as not occupied on both days, with no figure of what came before it, and with the reason that there are days of this month the yard has not entered and is not going up that hill again to enter. **The compressor is looked at for the first time since the twentieth of October and the shipwright asks what *useless* means, and the answer is the chapter: the part is on the machine and it holds and the pressure does not come out anywhere, and there is no hose in this harbor that is not the fire party's, and the fire party's is dead until the spring. SHE ASKS HIM TO WRITE DOWN WHAT A FOOT OF HOSE COSTS AND HE SAYS NO, and gives the reason, that he does not know and is not going to get the figure out of a shop, and that the answer is not a figure: a compressor in a harbor with no hose is a thing that makes noise.** She writes no figure and writes *engine house* and *looked at* in her own hand. **The working question is who is going to hire it, and the answer is on the page: a day at a seam is a pump, a line, a man on the pump and a slack water, and this yard has the line and two of them and a writ and has not got a pump, and the harbor's gear has no boat of its own, and every day taken in three weeks came up the hill because a man brought a pump up it, and this party has not gone down the hill and asked anybody for a day.** The decision: **the yard will take the next day that comes up the hill**, and the reason is that a yard which is findable has to be seen working and there is no way to be findable and be quiet about it. ### Chapter 212 — The Thirty-Fourth Monday, and a Day That Came In While Four Marks Did Not Go Out
Monday the twenty-eighth and Tuesday the twenty-ninth of December, on the mole's steps, on the face of the second seam, and in the shed. **The wall comes down bare for the thirty-fourth Monday since the first of May, the counter does not restart, the clerk keeps his own page, and no sitting is held. The cistern is charged on the rota day and walked on none.** At ten at the foot of the mole's steps a man of the second lay with a boat of about seventy tons asks about the Tuesday and **is told yes**, and the reason is given in a doorway and not in a market: **on the Friday the holder could not say what he was doing on the Saturday morning and on the Monday he can say, and that is the whole of the change and it is not humility.** The man had a reason for coming back on the Friday morning and says it was the wrong one. The day is worked from eight until half past one, nobody in the water, a hand lead's line over the side and back five times, the board twelve gross and nine paid at the mole and the yard's three, and the board's own device runs at half past one in the daylight. **On the Tuesday afternoon a wage of four marks did not go in and no envelope was made and the number of weeks fallen due is TEN, all ten in the same breath. THREE MARKS CAME IN THAT MORNING AND FOUR MARKS DID NOT GO OUT THAT AFTERNOON, ON THE SAME COLUMN, ON THE SAME DAY, AND THE BAG IS TEN MARKS, SIX SHILLINGS AND FOUR PENCE, BEING ONE THOUSAND SIX HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-SIX PENCE, AND THE FIGURE IT IS SHORT OF THE WAGE IS ONE THOUSAND AND THIRTY-SIX PENCE WHERE IT WAS FIVE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-SIX PENCE THAT MORNING. THE REASON IS ENTERED HERE, ONCE, IN THE HOLDER'S OWN LEFT HAND, IN THE FIRST COLUMN: a wage is a week and not a payment, one week out of ten leaves a bag that pays one week and no other, a man paid in the last week of December and nothing in the second week of January has been given a figure and not a wage, this yard has a page for a figure and does not want one, and a column with the fifth of March still the oldest and the twenty-ninth of December newest is nine weeks out of order and this yard is not going to begin it.**

### Chapter 213 — The List of What a Thing on the Water Is Made Of, and a Year Nobody Noticed
Wednesday the thirtieth and Thursday the thirty-first of December, in the shed, and on the crown of the mole. **The holder writes the cost of that day against that day, in his own hand, in the first column, before the day is spent, and gives the reason: the day is going to be spent whether they agree to a thing at the end of it or not, and a day agreed to and not spent would be a lie with a date on it.** They go up the crown, stand at the two objects of nobody's, touch neither, and look at the mouth of the harbor for four minutes. **THE SHIPWRIGHT WRITES NINETEEN LINES ON THE BOARDS WITH HER BACK TO THE WIND AND READS THEM OUT ONCE, AND EVERY ITEM IS A FIGURE THIS YARD CANNOT PAY OR GEAR IT DOES NOT OWN: a body of iron, a chain and not rope, a weight, something to be seen from a boat in the dark, a mark and not a name, a place to put it that is not a berth and not somebody's room, and a hand that goes out and looks at it. THE SEVENTH IS THE ONE THAT STOPS HER AND SHE WROTE IT LAST ON PURPOSE, and a hand is a person and a person is not a figure and is not going on that page. THE ONLY OTHER NAME THIS YARD HAS IS NOT ON THE LIST, and if his name went on a thing in the water it would go on a thing that owes him more than any other thing in this harbor, and no man alive is going to put a boy's name on a buoy to make a list look finished. A LIST IS NOT A PLAN; A PLAN IS WHAT YOU DO WHEN SOMEBODY IS GOING TO PAY FOR IT.** The cistern is charged on the Thursday and walked on none. **No agreement is made and the reason is entered: not one of the nineteen is a thing this yard can pay for, not one is gear it owns, and the seventh is a person, and this yard has not got a person and is not writing that down in a book that goes in two columns because it can be checked every morning by counting.** The day's three marks is entered as the cost of a day spent and not as a price of anything. **On the Thursday afternoon at the head of this dock a man says out loud that this was the last day of the year and that a man ought to be able to say what he had done in it, and neither of them answers him, and neither of them says the day of the month, and that is entered because a day on which a thing is said in a street is a day on which a thing was said in a street. THE BATCH CROSSES A YEAR BOUNDARY HERE AND IN CHAPTER 215 AND NOT ONE CHARACTER NOTICES.** **Item eleven is said out loud in this yard's own book as a thing this yard cannot put in front of anybody, and it is not off the list and is not going to be.** No buoy went into any water and no stage was taken.

### Chapter 215 — The Thirty-Fifth Monday, and a Date on a Half Sheet That Arrived and Nothing Happened
Sunday the third and Monday the fourth of January, in the shed, and on the mole. **The wall comes down bare for the thirty-fifth Monday and the cistern is charged and walked on none, and the far bench is entered as not occupied on both days with no figure of what came before it.** On the Sunday morning the ship's hand says the only thing anybody in that shed says about the month, which is that the month is out, and the holder says the month being out is the whole of the news in that room, and she says that is all she has got and does not get past it, and **the entry says a thing said in a shed is a thing that happened, and that neither of them noticed anything else.** The read-back runs. **AND ON MONDAY THE FOURTH THE DATE ON THE HALF SHEET ARRIVED AND NOTHING HAPPENED, AND A YARD WHICH HAS SPENT FOUR VOLUMES WRITING DOWN EVERYTHING THAT HAPPENS TO IT WRITES DOWN THAT, IN THOSE WORDS, WITH THE DAY ON IT, AND DOES NOT IMPROVE ON IT. THE YARD DID NOT PRODUCE THE COPY. NO COURT IN THIS HARBOR SAT. NO CLERK OF THAT COURT CAME UP THAT HILL. NOBODY WAS CHARGED WITH ANYTHING. NOBODY WAS FINED, BECAUSE A COURT DOES NOT FINE A POOR MAN AND THE MATTER SIMPLY GOES ON. NOBODY WAS REFUSED ANYTHING, BECAUSE THAT COURT FINDS AGAINST NOBODY.
