### Chapter 281 — *The Word Is Named Once in a Shed and Goes in No Column, and a Counter Off the Fish Market Is Decided On*

**Sunday the twenty-fifth of April. The shed on the mole.** Nothing in, nothing out, the far bench not occupied at any hour. **MARA VENN, A PERSON OF NO OFFICE OF THIS HARBOR, THIRTY, NAMES THE WORD *QUIETENING*, AND SHE NAMES IT ONCE, AND IT IS THE ONLY TIME THE WORD IS SPOKEN IN THE WHOLE OF VOLUME 06 UP TO THIS CHAPTER.** It is a name for a practice and not for a person, a place, an office or a title: two people bring what they have each read out of the same piece of work, the two readings cannot both be true, and the office requires one of them to be asked in writing, in a room with a second person in it, **to withdraw the reading and not to change it.** She filled in the forms and asked the questions for nine years. **She says out loud that nobody she ever asked said who wanted it, not one in nine years, and that she stopped asking in about the fifth year, and that the yard is not to fill that gap, and she is right.** It goes in no column of that yard's own book and on no wall in that harbor, and the fourth column takes its twelfth line. And the decision of the day: **he is going down that hill on Monday to the copyist's counter off the fish market, because it is the only counter in this country that copies anything without asking what it is for, and he does not know what sheet he is going to buy, and the reason against the line of the going is that he has had no better plan since the sixth of March.** Cost: nothing in and nothing out.

### Chapter 282 — *The Fifty-First Time That Wall Came Down, the Forty-First Charge Walked on None, and a Woman of Fifty-Eight Who Does Not Read What She Copies*

**Monday the twenty-sixth of April. A room off the fish market, and the shed.** The wall comes down bare for the fifty-first time and the cistern is charged and walked on none, being the forty-first, and the far bench is not occupied. **PERNEL SAYE, FIFTY-EIGHT, A COPYIST OF THIS HARBOR WHO HAS KEPT THAT COUNTER FOR THIRTY-ONE YEARS, HAS NO OFFICE ABOVE IT, IS NOT OF THIS PARTY, IS NOT ON A LADDER AND IS NOT A VILLAIN, TELLS HIM OF HER OWN ACCOUNT AND UNASKED that she has one sheet on the top shelf at the back of her room, made nine years ago for a man who was buying a house and wanted the oldest paper that came with it copied, and that he paid and did not come back.** The question he asked was where in this town a copy of a thing out of the drowned city would be, and he said out loud at her counter that he was not asking what was on one. **Her rule is the volume's argument in an ordinary person's mouth: she does not read what she copies, because the day a copyist finds out what a thing is she is a person who knows what it says, and a person who knows what a paper says is somebody's to ask, and a copyist cannot have a counter on a street and know what is on the shelf behind her own head.** She asks one thing for herself and he gives it: **if you take it off the shelf, do not come back and tell me what is on it.** **He asks her nothing else and he does not buy it on that day, and both refusals are in the second column with reasons, and the reason he did not buy is not money.** And the sentence the whole batch stands on, said by the ship's hand: **a set is a pressure house's set on a book and it goes where the book sends it, and there is no book on that coast that sends it four hundred miles west, and there is no yard on that coast that rents one, and there is nothing in this country a man can hire that will go and stand in a room seventy fathoms down and hold a lamp in it; and we cannot go and we will not go are different words and only the first of them is true.** Cost: nothing in and nothing out.

### Chapter 283 — *The Twenty-Seventh Week With No Envelope, a Penny Off a Counter, and Fourteen Marks Three Shillings and Fourpence Named in a Shed Before Anybody Agreed to It*

**Tuesday the twenty-seventh of April. A room off the fish market, and the shed.** The wage Tuesday: a wage of four marks is not paid, no envelope is made, the column does not move, the twenty-seventh week falls due. **He buys the sheet at eight in the morning for one penny and she puts the penny in the box and does not look up, exactly as she said she would, and the transaction takes about eleven seconds.** The sheet is one sheet about sixteen inches by eleven of a heavy rag paper gone the color of a wet pipe, folded twice across and once down with the middle fold soft and parting at one corner, and **it is a copy**, in a hand nine years old, copied entire on both sides with no lines ruled and no blot, and at the head of the face there is a name of a chamber. The rest of the day is the price: **between ten and two the holder of that writ names out loud at the bench, before anybody has agreed to it, the cost of a descent for the following day — nine marks for the compressor, the housing, the pipe, the gauges and one man off a Crown house book, two marks and eightpence for the ship's hand's man, a mark and two shillings for a hand on the hose, the same three figures as the fifth of April in the same order — and a second man off that book at two marks and eightpence, making fourteen marks three shillings and fourpence, — the identical figure the eighth, ninth and tenth of April past came to, component for component, the same man off the same book on both days, and the reason a second man is on that book at all is not that the figure is higher and is that he cannot hold a slate and read a figure at the same time and is not going to find out which of the two he loses on the bottom.** Garrow Fisk has the set out of Ternwatch by six in the morning and the book will send the second man. The far bench is occupied from ten until four and is not approached. Cost: one penny out.

### Chapter 284 — *The Second Descent Off the South End at About Forty Fathoms, a Second Man Off a Book, and Eighty-Four Pounds on a Face of a Hundred and Fifty*

**Wednesday the twenty-eighth of April. A mile and a quarter off the south end of that mole, and the shed.** Two thousand two hundred and eighty pence out. **The six conditions of a first entry are read aloud at the boat in order, there is no first entry, there is no harbor authority's book to go in, and this yard's own book is not that book; the bar of four hundred yards off the outer marks is named out loud at the boat, the ground is off the south end and round the corner from it, and no person, no boat and no lead of that yard is inside the bar on that day or any day, and the bar has not been narrowed by anything and was not asked to be.** The pot goes down at about twenty past nine and comes up at about ten to twelve. **The gauge is a pressure gauge on a face of a hundred and fifty and reads eighty-four pounds, as it read on the eighth, ninth and tenth of April past, and the pencil mark where the needle stood on the tenth is not moved, and that is the only reason the two books are the same book.** The pot is landed on the top course, in the empty socket the bar of square iron came out of on the ninth of April. **AND ITS LEAD WEIGHT COMES DOWN ACROSS THE BELLY OF A HERRINGMAN'S NET, AND ABOUT SIX FATHOMS OF THAT NET IS NOW FLAT ON A COURSE OF CUT STONE UNDER A WEIGHT AND IS NOT CUT AND IS NOT MENDED AND WILL NOT COME UP WHOLE**, and nobody in that boat cut it, and the ground is that man's by first refusal, and this yard was on it without him and had named the price the day before and had done all of it right. **The finding is a join: the figure at the near end of the top course is the forty-second and is cut about a quarter of an inch deep where the other forty-one are cut about an inch, and its strokes are laid cross-stroke first, and that says the stone was made in two hands at two times and says nothing whatever about which of them is right, or why, or by whom.** The holder of that writ said out loud that it was to be written down as what it is and not as what it means, **and he could not hold the slate and gave it across the thwart at about four o'clock, and the ship's hand's man wrote the entry.**

### Chapter 285 — *The Forty-Second Charge Walked on None, and a Copy Read Under a Lamp by Two People and Not by the Third*

**Thursday the twenty-ninth of April. The shed on that mole.** The cistern is charged and walked on none, being the forty-second. **AT ABOUT TEN AT NIGHT, WITH THE LAMP LIT AND TURNED ROUND AND THE DOOR SHUT AND THE MARKET OFF THE BOARDS, THE HOLDER OF THAT WRIT AND THE SHIP'S HAND READ A COPY OF A MUNICIPAL SHEET OF A CHAMBER OF A DROWNED CITY. THERE WERE TWO OF THEM IN THAT ROOM AND NOBODY ELSE. THE THIRD PERSON IS NOT IN THE ROOM AND IS THE ONE WHO MOST WANTS TO BE:** a woman of no office was asked on the Wednesday evening, said yes before he had got to the end of the sentence, and was then told she was not to come, and gave the second half of the reason herself — **she was not being left out because she was not able, she was being left out because she is the only one of the three who could say whether it is true, and if she said it then in about four years a man in a city would write *she said so* on the back of a sheet.** **The order is nine lines and there is no tenth: the fleet is ordered down; the order is of the fleet and not of a master of it; the masters are not to be asked which of them made it; the order is carried by the masters and not by any office; no copy of it is to be made, and a copy of it is not it, and a man holding a copy has not got an order; and it is to be carried out in one tide. THE FOOT OF THE SHEET CARRIES NINE MARKS — SIX OF A CIRCLE WITH ONE STROKE, SAME SIZE, SAME HAND; TWO OF A CIRCLE WITH TWO STROKES, SMALLER, OFF THE CENTER, NOT EVEN WITH EACH OTHER; AND A NINTH OF NINE SHORT LINES, CUT AND NOT STRUCK, A THIRD OF THE DEPTH OF THE OTHERS, AT AN ANGLE NONE OF THE OTHERS IS AT — AND UNDER THEM, IN THE SHEET'S OWN HAND, ONE LINE SAYING THE NINTH IS NOT ONE OF OURS AND IS NOT TO BE COUNTED WITH THE NINE AND IS NOT TO BE ASKED ABOUT. THE TWO MARKS DO NOT AGREE AND THE DISAGREEMENT IS THE FINDING AND IS NOT A DEFECT IN THE EVIDENCE.** Cost: nothing in and nothing out.

### Chapter 286 — *The Thirtieth of April, a Far Bench Occupied From Ten Until Four, and a Disagreement About Which Column a Penny Belongs In*

**Friday the thirtieth of April. The shed on the mole.** The far bench is occupied from ten until four and is not approached. **He wants the sheet in the first column and the ship's hand will not have it, and a person of no office says what both of them are actually arguing about: the first column is what a man can go and look at, and no man alive can go and look at that, and it is exactly the size of the truth, and the big thing is on a shelf in a room off a fish market.** And then the turn, out loud: **the thing this yard has been calling an office's fear was real, it happened to real people in real water, it was not one man's vanity and it was not a lie and it was not a weapon, and it was ordered by more than one of them, together, and they argued about it afterwards and left the argument on the paper — AND KNOWING THAT DOES NOT MAKE ANYBODY SAFE, and this yard has five marks in a bag and twenty-eight weeks of no envelope and a form on a step two days down that coast, and now it knows the drawer matters, which is worse.** And the other half: **the sheet is incomplete, and a party that says false about a record that is incomplete has stopped being the party that says what it is not, and the office's three hundred years is not withdrawn and not softened.** And the hole, which stays: **we are not going to know who wanted it, the reason against the finding is the reason of the second of April last about a trade and a price, no letter is to be written to any town and no man sent to any town, and a second-column fact with no name in it is not a document.** The whole of the sheet goes in the second column with a reason against every line. Cost: nothing in and nothing out.

### Chapter 287 — *Saturday the First of May, Six Fathoms of a Herringman's Net Told on the Mole Steps, and Six Doors and a Seventh One That Is a Drawer*

**Saturday the first of May. The mole steps, and the shed.** **ELIAS VOKE, FIFTY-ONE, OF THE HERRING BOAT OF THE SECOND LAY, IS TOLD ON THE STEPS AT ABOUT HALF PAST TEN IN ABOUT NINE PEOPLE'S HEARING that a pot was landed on his ground on the Wednesday at about forty fathoms and that its lead came down on the belly of his net, and that about six fathoms of it is now flat on a course of cut stone and will not come up whole. HE SAYS THE FIGURE IS SIX AND NOT ABOUT SIX, because about is what a man writes when he wants to be argued with, and that entry is six and not about six. He asks for nothing, is given nothing, and says he would rather be a man this yard has not paid, and that not being thanked is the arrangement. The reason this yard did not ask him on the Tuesday is the standing reason about a man this yard has paid, and it was not improved on, and he says out loud that the same sentence is going round forty people and nine steps and that this yard does not have a speech, it has a sentence.** Then the doors, and six are ruled out — the tin, a wall, the ordinary post, the four people of that coast, the copyist's counter, and a fire, and the burning is the keeping and it is the same door — **and the seventh place is a drawer in that shed, and a drawer is a house, and this yard said all of that out loud on the twenty-fourth of April past and meant it, and on the twenty-seventh it went down the hill and put a penny on a counter.** Cost: nothing in and nothing out, and six fathoms of another man's gear.

### Chapter 288 — *Sunday the Second of May, Two Instruments and Two Hands, a Morning That Carries No Figure, and Nine Short Lines That This Yard Is Not Going to Count*

**Sunday the second of May. The crown of that mole, and the shed.** **HE IS ON THE CROWN FROM ABOUT HALF PAST SEVEN UNTIL ABOUT ONE WITH A COMPASS IN HIS HAND AND HE CANNOT USE IT, and at ten past eight he says the only sentence anybody in that harbor has ever used for it, and nobody asks him about it, and the morning goes in the second column with a reason against the line and no name in it and carries no figure because there is no figure for a morning.** The entry of the figure in the top course is written in the ship's left hand from the slate, and **he does not touch the slate and does not check the entry.** And then the temptation, and the refusal: **the ninth mark on the copy is the same shape as the nine-line mark already in that yard's own book, and the two are not to be counted together, and this yard refuses out loud to go to a pressure house at Ternwatch and ask a man there whether his foreman cut cross-stroke first, to write to a town four days up that coast, and to put the two of them in one line together, and the reason against all four lines is that a shape is not a thing and nobody in this country can go and look at either of them.** The chain is on a nail and the bar is in the drawer and neither can be sold nor given away, **and this yard went back down to the socket the bar came out of on the Wednesday and was not able to say one word about whose the bar is.** Cost: a day, and no figure.

### Chapter 289 — *The Fifty-Second Time That Wall Came Down, the Forty-Third Charge Walked on None, and a Question Asked at a Mole Head and Not Answered*

**Monday the third of May. The mole steps, and the shed.** The wall comes down bare for the fifty-second time and the cistern is charged and walked on none, being the forty-third, and the far bench is occupied from ten until four and is not approached. **It is decided in that shed that no part of the sheet is to be said out loud in about forty people, and the reason is standing about thirty feet away: a certificate of method in the reading of worked glass and its faults has already had the standing of it spent in that fish market in about forty people's hearing on the twenty-second of April past, it cannot be given back because there is no office in this country to take it from her, and that price is not being paid a second time because the sheet is better.** And then **a person of no office asks a question out loud at a mole head in about nine people's hearing and says in advance that there is no person in it and wanted it written down that there is no person in it: who was the first one to use a mark like that to keep a thing in an emergency instead of holding it. NOBODY ANSWERS. The holder of that writ says he does not know and that there is nobody in this country he could ask and that he is not going to write to a town to find out. The question goes in no column of that yard's own book, is on no wall in that harbor, and carries no figure.** And the fourth column's seventeenth line takes it, and the batch enters the convergence — about sixty boats on this coast with a sheet that says where every other copy is, and a word in a market, and about seven weeks, and this yard is not going to be the one that moves them along. Cost: nothing in and nothing out.

### Chapter 290 — *Tuesday the Fourth of May, the Twenty-Eighth Week With No Envelope, and Twenty-Two Entries and Eighty-Eight Lines Read Back From a Leaf With Four Columns*

**Tuesday the fourth of May. The shed on the mole, and the bench outside it.** **The wage Tuesday: the column does not move and twenty-eight weeks have now fallen due with no envelope, the second wage Tuesday in these ten days on which the column did not move.** The read-back at about four: **twenty-two entries in the first column at the hour of the read-back and twenty-three at the close, being thirteen before the batch, nine from the twenty-fifth of April to the third of May and one this evening; eighty-eight lines in the second, being forty-eight before and thirty-one in the nine days and nine this afternoon; none in the third, with the boy's hand at the head of it and the four nameless lines above his named line still four and still not struck out; and eighteen in the fourth, the last of them the last thing in that book.** The ship's hand says the one thing that went wrong: **nine refusals in ten days, four things that cost money, and one of them cost a man of fifty-one six fathoms of his gear, and there is still no column in that book for the saying of any of it.** **And then three people say three things and all three are right and they differ in what they are about and not in whether they are correct: the words, by the holder of that writ; the marks, by the ship's hand; the house, by the woman of no office — and hers is that none of the three of us is a keeper and all three of us are, and that is a chair, and the chair is in a house, and there is no handle on the inside of any of the three of them.** And then the turn, out loud a second time in ten days with the reason for the second time given first, entered in the first column in the words of the Friday, without addition, in two halves: **the office's fear was real and it does not make anybody safe, and the opacity was expensive for a reason, and a reason is not a warrant, and this yard does not get to be the one that says that office was right, and the sheet is incomplete.** Cost: nothing in and nothing out. **THE BAG CLOSES AT FIVE MARKS, ONE SHILLING AND FOURPENCE, BEING EIGHT HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN PENCE, and the whole of what went out in the ten days is two thousand two hundred and eighty-one pence, being a penny and a day's set.**

### Chapter 291 — *Wednesday the Fifth of May, Six Hundred and Forty-Nine Pence In, a Man of Sixty-One With a Boat, and a Crown Seal Named Out Loud in a Shed*

**Wednesday the fifth of May. The shed on the mole, and the water off the face of the second seam in the morning.** **SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY-NINE PENCE COMES IN AND NOTHING GOES OUT, being three marks for a day's work at the standing rate, one mark and eightpence for a boat and a man in her, and a penny of line, on a private person's account and for a private person's purpose, not salvage and not a claim and not work under any instrument, and the party was never in the water.** It is the first money into that yard since the eleven marks of Elias Voke on the sixth of April, and it makes the whole of what has come in since the sixth of December two thousand four hundred and nine pence. **And the hire is closed inside itself: a man of about fifty-five states the question out loud before he is asked — whether the thing along his boat's starboard side is his or was there before he bought her — and gets his answer on the page. They go down in a hired pan at about ten and get a line to the ground, and there is a cut in the rock about nine feet long and about two inches across, with dressed sides and square at both ends, counted twice and got nine feet twice; she tells him it is not his, because a thing a man puts into the ground is not square at both ends, and that it was cut before she was built and will be there after she is sold, and that she cannot tell him whose it is and neither can anybody in that harbor; it goes in the first column because a man can go and look at it with a pan and a line and not because anybody knows what it is. He puts the whole of it on the bench without arguing with a figure, says he had not expected to be told anything at all, and does not ask what it meant and does not ask to have his boat up again.** Then **a retired salvage foreman of sixty-one, half deaf, with a boat of about nineteen tons that is not the yard's and a hand of about forty he cannot do without, comes up the steps unasked and is asked for the boat and for nothing else, and sets one condition: his boat goes and he takes her and nobody stands in her but him at the wheel.** He says out loud that he has seen the chamber's name cut in the cheek of a stair more than sixty years ago, is asked nothing further, and **NAMES THE CROWN SEAL FOR THE FIRST TIME IN VOLUME 06 IN A CHARACTER'S MOUTH: a round of glass the size of a saucer in a metal collar with a wheel in the collar and a screw through it, sitting in a bed cut in a sill, the screw taking a load off a thing made of the same glass, the mark of its name cut into the round — a machine and a seal at once — and a term and not a lock, because whoever cut it wanted a thing held for so long and no longer and cut the figure on the sill so the next man would know when, and nobody in this country ever looks at one.** The yard does not enter that word in the first column, and the reason is that a man's memory of a thing he saw a long time ago is a thing a man can go and look at exactly once. **Then the price of a descent to be made on the Thursday is named out loud before anybody agrees to it at fourteen marks, three shillings and fourpence, component for component, the same four figures the eighth, ninth, tenth and twenty-eighth of April came to, and THE YARD CANNOT PAY IT: there are five marks, one shilling and fourpence in the drawer.** A day's set goes off a book at a pressure house at Ternwatch because **a man of sixty-one asked for it**, and the holder of that writ says out loud, before agreeing, that **he has a rule about a man this yard has paid and has not got a rule about a man this yard is being paid by.** And last, the decision, taken in advance, on a Wednesday at four o'clock, before anybody has agreed to anything: **if there is a chamber down there and if it is open enough to be read, this yard will not read it and will not take one piece of it out, and the price of that is named in the same breath — the only proof this yard will ever have of anything about a drowned city will be in a thing that closed, and a proof nobody can check is worth less than nothing.** Cost: six hundred and forty-nine pence in, nothing out.

### Chapter 292 — *Thursday the Sixth of May, the Forty-Fourth Charge Walked on None, Fourteen Marks Three Shillings and Fourpence Off a Book That Is Not This Yard's, and a Doorway at Seventy Fathoms*

**Thursday the sixth of May. Off the south end of that mole, and the shed in the evening.** **THE CISTERN IS CHARGED AND WALKED ON NONE, BEING THE FORTY-FOURTH.** The set is on the mole at six. **The book sends Amos Searle and the yard says no out loud, and the reason is that book on the ninth and the twenty-eighth of April and is entered as a book and not as care of a man, and the second name on it is sent at the same figure, two marks and eightpence a day.** The six conditions are read at the boat, the bar is named in the same words since the seventh of April. **The pot is down at about twenty past eight and up at about half past eleven, about three hours and ten minutes, and the gauge reads eighty-four pounds on a face of a hundred and fifty and the pencil mark is not moved.** **AT ABOUT SEVENTY FATHOMS THE GROUND IS CUT AS A FACE OF THIRTY FEET AND THERE IS A DOORWAY IN IT, five feet of dressed jambs and one dressed stone across the top, and a room about nine feet across, and a sill with a bed cut its whole length and, under the lip of the sill, a second groove, deeper and wider, which is a rebate and not a bed; and a plate of glass about the width of the doorway and a hand and a half high stands in the bed and not in the rebate, and the bed is empty.** Nobody puts a hand in and nobody goes in, and the not-going is said out loud in the boat so that it is a record and not a story. **In the inner face of the sill to the left of the bed there is a row of two hundred and nine marks, cut in the same hand as the figures at the near end of every course on that mole's own floor, with one further cut below the row, deeper and not the same cut, and the row was counted three times and all three counts were the same; and beside the row there is a day cut in the same hand and the same stroke, being the eleventh of May.** Both figures go in the first column because a man in a boat can go and look at them and not because anybody knows what they mean. **He is on the crown of that mole from one until five and loses the afternoon; there is no figure for an afternoon and the reason against the line has no name in it; and he writes the entry himself in his own right hand, slowly, in about twenty minutes, and nobody helps him.** Cost: nothing in, nothing out. Fourteen marks three shillings and fourpence went off a book four hundred miles off.

### Chapter 293 — *Friday the Seventh of May, a Far Bench Occupied From Ten Until Four, a Round of Glass Out of a Bed, and About Six Hours of Weather in That Harbor*

**Friday the seventh of May. Off the south end, and the shed in the evening.** **THE FAR BENCH IS OCCUPIED FROM TEN UNTIL FOUR AND IS NOT APPROACHED.** The reason for going out again is said out loud at eight in the morning before anybody is asked: **the plate stands in the bed, the bed is empty, and on the eleventh the plate goes into the rebate, and a plate the width of a doorway does not come down on a stone floor and stay off it — so the round comes up, or the plate grinds it into about nine pieces in a room at seventy fathoms and nobody in this country ever hears of it again.** The man of about thirty-four reads the price off the paper and adds that **the round goes on the crown of that mole and does not go into that shed, because the second clause of the notice of the thirty-first of October keeps recovered transparent mineral out of every shed in this harbor, and this yard did not write that clause and cannot lift it.** The man off the Crown house book goes down. **What comes up is a round of glass the size of a saucer in a metal collar with a wheel in the collar and a screw down about two turns and stopped, and on the collar a chain of eleven links about a finger long, every link stamped and a date stamped on every link, the last link thicker than the others with something struck on its face under the shadow of the collar which nobody scratched at to read; and under the round a piece of worked glass the size of a hand that will not come away from it and goes up with it.** The crate goes on the crown under a tarpaulin and not into the shed. **Then the weather comes up out of the south-west at about four in the afternoon and does not stop until about ten that night, and no cause is named for it in any column of any book.** The skylight, the door light, a pane of plate out of a shopfront, the running glass of two boats, eleven windows and the lens of the mole-head light all go, and about a hundred people are out in the rain and nobody is hurt. **The storm is entered in two hands on two pages that are not on top of each other**, and the second hand is not the ship's and the second page is not in that shed and is in a man's own book four streets off the front of that harbor, the two pages being a mile and a quarter apart. Cost: nothing in, nothing out.

### Chapter 294 — *Saturday the Eighth of May, a Pane of Plate Glass on a Mole, a Mark and Four Shillings to a Bonesetter, and Until the Second of June*

**Saturday the eighth of May. The crown of that mole, a room over a chandler's, and the shed in the evening.** **TWO HUNDRED AND EIGHT PENCE GOES OUT TO A BONESETTER.** The injury in three parts. **The hand:** a pane of plate about four feet by three, lying on the mole stones since the evening before, and two men lifting it and the wind coming round the head of the mole and putting it over on the crown across the right hand of a man of sixty-one — **the right hand, and the left shoulder and ribs belong to a man of twenty-eight in a bed at Ashtide until the fifth of June and are not this**. **The bill:** a bonesetter of about sixty with thirty-one years and about four hundred things, who comes down the hill because he does not go up one, who says the palm and not the back and that the line along the little finger has not gone near the bone, and **who does not say no and who is not going to be asked twice and says he is not going to hear a word about who brought him** — a mark and four shillings, two hundred and eight pence, paid at a counter over a chandler's at about twenty past ten. **The absence and the consequence:** the hand will grip again by the middle of June and about two-thirds of what it gripped on Friday, and nine parts in ten by Christmas; **a man of sixty-one states the figure himself and will not be argued out of it — he will not be on the water until the second of June — and says that the job on the north bar on the nineteenth of May is not going to happen.** And **his boat of about nineteen tons, which he built himself fifty years ago or near it, has taken a stove on the Friday night in the weather, nobody saw it and nobody has said what caused it, and eleven pieces of her frame came out of her on the Saturday and are on that mole and are not going back in.** He is not thanked and says he is not going to be, and the yard enters that it has a rule about a man it has paid and has not got a rule about a man it has hurt. Cost: two hundred and eight pence out.

### Chapter 295 — *Sunday the Ninth of May, Four Marks and a Shilling to a Glazier, One Man's Own Book Four Streets Off, and the Figure the Bag Is Short of the Wage of Four Marks Coming Back*

**Sunday the ninth of May. The shed, and a room four streets off it.** **SIX HUNDRED AND SIXTY PENCE GOES OUT TO A GLAZIER, being two lights and a skylight, and that is the whole of the glass this yard owns in that harbor; the rest of the front is other people's and the yard paid none of it and was offered none of it.** A man of about nineteen out of the second lay put the running glass into the man of about fifty-five's own boat out of his own pocket for sixpence and nobody in that shed has been told his name and it is not going in that book. **Then the other page of the weather: a man of sixty-one brings his own book up the steps unasked and puts it on the bench, and it is the same account in his own hand in the house of his own boat, four streets off, and in about four years it is the only record in the country of what that front looked like on the seventh, and nobody asked him for it and he is not going to be thanked.** And then the figure that has had no subject since the seventh of April comes back with one: **the bag holds five hundred and ninety-seven pence, the wage of four marks is six hundred and forty, and the figure this bag is short of the wage of four marks is forty-three pence, being three shillings and sevenpence — IT CAME BACK ON THE PAGE AS A FIGURE WITH A SUBJECT AND THE CHAPTER SAYS IT CAME BACK AND NOT THAT ANYBODY IS GOING TO PAY IT.** Nobody is asked what they thought of the weather, and not the man of about fifty-five, and not the boy, and not the four people four days down that coast. Cost: six hundred and sixty pence out.

### Chapter 296 — *Monday the Tenth of May, the Fifty-Third Time That Wall Came Down, the Forty-Fifth Charge Walked on None, and a Thing Said Twice in a Room With Two People In It*

**Monday the tenth of May. A room in this harbor, and the shed in the evening.** **THE WALL CAME DOWN BARE FOR THE FIFTY-THIRD TIME AND THE CISTERN WAS CHARGED AND WALKED ON NONE, BEING THE FORTY-FIFTH.** **The concealment, told once and once only, in a room with two people in it and nobody else in the room and nobody in the passage and nobody sent.** She names the price before he starts: **say it twice.** The first time it was told was in a shed at half past ten at night in about nine seconds in a voice he told her he could not have repeated, and she has never once been able to use it, and **a thing relearned off a sheet in ninety seconds is a record and not a story.** The price of that is hers: in about four years there will be nothing in any record about tonight, and the only thing that will be true of it is that a man of thirty-two and a woman of thirty were in a room on the tenth of May, and she has decided she can live with that and he has not. **And then it is said twice, in his own voice, out loud, in a room, and the first time is: there is a mark on it; it is a sound, not a crack and not a number; it comes up out of the bottom of this harbor in a ground line's delay, three marks and a flick, in a call a boy on a quay used to answer him with when they were eleven; it has been known since the fourteenth of October; it is his brother's; it is Oren's; it is the reason he went into that shard on the thirteenth of October; it is in no record, in no office, in no book and not in any chart.** Four things she will not do: **it does not restore the standing of a certificate of method in a market, which was spent on the twenty-second of April and cannot be given back; her forty marks first after food are not reduced and not paid and were not paid by a thing said in a room; he is not going to be forgiven and did not ask; and she is not going to be able to do it again, and he has known that since the second of January and has said nothing for four months, and she is not going to give him the fifth thing.** **Neither of them calls it a reunion and neither of them is going to.** Cost: nothing in, nothing out.

### Chapter 297 — *Tuesday the Eleventh of May, the Twenty-Ninth Week With No Envelope, a Round of Glass Carried Down to a Boat and Not Put Back, and a Sheet of Glass at Seventy Fathoms Going Down Into a Rebate and Stopping There*

**Tuesday the eleventh of May. Off the south end, and the shed in the evening.** **THE WAGE TUESDAY: THE COLUMN DOES NOT MOVE, NO ENVELOPE IS MADE, AND TWENTY-NINE WEEKS HAVE NOW FALLEN DUE.** **THE FAR BENCH IS OCCUPIED FROM TEN UNTIL FOUR AND IS NOT APPROACHED.** **THE LETTING.** The crate comes off the crown at ten and the round comes out about two feet from the top of the mole steps at about eleven in front of about nine people, and a man of sixty-one with two stitches in his right hand carries it down three steps and hands it over. **The exchange is on the stone of the mole steps from about eleven until the boat goes out at about half past eleven, with the ship's hand asking for it from the boat, and nothing is written on the day.** The ship's hand makes the holder of that writ say the whole of it out loud so that it is a record and not a story: **on the Wednesday before last, at four o'clock, before anybody had agreed to a day, this yard said it would not read the chamber and would not take one piece of it out, and named the price; and on the Friday the round was taken out of the bed with the plate standing in it with nothing behind it, and the round was taken out because the plate is going into the rebate on the eleventh.** The woman of no office says *then you are going to put it back*. **He says no, and gives the reason, and puts it down on the stone of the mole steps: because putting it back holds the plate up and opens that room, and they would go in and read it, and the proof would be in a thing that closes, and a proof in a thing that closed is a proof nobody can check, and this yard has said in six movements out loud that such a proof is worth less than a record a man can look at.** A man of sixty-one says one thing about a term and is not asked and does not say what he thinks of it. **The sentence is: the chamber closes whether it is read or not, and we are letting it close.** And: **that is not a surrender, and it is not a proof, and nobody in this boat is going to say this yard was right about it, because it does not know that it was right about it, and what it costs and what it is worth are not the same figure and the second one is zero.** Then the pot goes on the top course at twenty past twelve, is lifted straight off, and comes up at a quarter past two, and the slate says **THE PLATE IS DOWN IN THE REBATE AND IT IS NOT COMING UP, AND NOTHING IS HOLDING IT UP.** And that nobody in the boat saw the beginning of it, and a man in a boat could see the end of it, and **that is what a figure cut in a sill is for** — the same sentence as **the whole of what has happened in about three hundred years on the coast of this country**. Cost: one mark and eightpence out.

### Chapter 298 — *Wednesday the Twelfth of May, a Lead and a Slate at Seventy Fathoms With No Name on the Slate, Eleven Stamped Links With a Date on Each of Them, and Nine Lines He Cannot Say Any More*

**Wednesday the twelfth of May. Off the south end in the morning, and the crown of that mole in the afternoon.** **A LEAD OF ABOUT FOURTEEN POUNDS MARKED AT EVERY FATHOM GOES OVER THE SIDE WITH A SLATE TIED TO THE LINE, AND THE SLATE HAS NO NAME ON IT, because nobody signs anything in that yard and nobody has since the third of April past.** The entry, in the ship's own left hand, is that the plate is in the rebate, the bed is empty, the round is out, and **there are two hundred and nine marks in the sill and a day in the sill, being the eleventh of May, and the day is the same day it was on the Thursday preceding and has not been cut again** — checkable by anybody with a lead and fourteen pounds, in about nine minutes. Then, alone on the crown at about one, he reads the eleven stamped links twice out loud and, **holding a flat piece of glass to the light so as not to scratch at it, reads the mark on the last link: *Sealed and entered at the Morrow circuit office by order of Magister Ilya Serr, senior Registry examiner.* He is in no room, on no mole, in no market and not in this harbor, was not sent for and was not asked anything, and the name is a line, and the name is not spoken out loud in that shed on the said day and is spoken exactly once in these ten chapters, by the ship's hand, on the fourteenth, reading a column back, and by nobody else.** A date struck on the collar is later than the strike on that link, and the collar is the work of the same office named on the seal line, and **the difference between the two is a difference in two made things and says nothing whatever about which of them is right, or why, or by whom.** And then, at half past two, the ship's hand asks him for the third line of the order and he cannot say one of the nine. **THE PERMANENT LOSS: he read them under a lamp on the twenty-ninth of April and cannot say one of them now, and the sheet is in a drawer in that shed, and she reads them out and he has them again in about ninety seconds, and a thing relearned off a sheet in ninety seconds is not a thing remembered. THE RECORD OUTLIVES THE MAN AND THE MAN DOES NOT OUTLIVE THE RECORD, AND THIS YARD HAS BEEN SAYING THAT FOR SIX MOVEMENTS AND HAS NOT ONCE BEEN TOLD IT WAS A RULE ABOUT RECORDS.** It goes in the second column with the twelfth of May against it and a reason against the line and no name in it, and there is no figure for it. Cost: nothing in, nothing out.

### Chapter 299 — *Thursday the Thirteenth of May, the Forty-Sixth Charge Walked on None, Two Marks on the Bottom Four Hundred Yards Apart, a Name Said Out Loud Once, and Three People Saying Three Things That Are All True*

**Thursday the thirteenth of May. The shed, and the water inside the harbor line in the morning.** **THE CISTERN IS CHARGED AND WALKED ON NONE, BEING THE FORTY-SIXTH, AND THE FAR BENCH IS OCCUPIED FROM TEN UNTIL FOUR AND IS NOT APPROACHED.** A boat is hired at a mark and eightpence on a private person's account, the man of fifty-one is not in her and was not asked and his ground is not in it, and nobody goes inside the bar. **THE TWO MARKS ARE FOUR HUNDRED YARDS APART ON THE BOTTOM OF THIS HARBOR'S OWN GROUND: this yard's own, fouled about four inches on the twelfth of March and about a foot and a half on the thirteenth of May; and one that carries a line and a shackle of a make nobody in this harbor makes, whose season of nine marks is not paid and is not going to be asked for.** A man of sixty-one goes in the boat unasked, stands on the thwart, looks at the second mark from about ten feet off the bottom for about four minutes, says **I have seen that make and I have not seen one in this harbor in twenty years and there are two things I could say about it and I am not going to say either of them, because a man of sixty-one does not get to be right about a thing he has only seen once.** And then, at about eleven with the boat lying still: **the name at the head of the third column is said out loud once, and it is Mara Venn, and it is not the boy's and it is not the holder of that writ's, and it had not been said out loud before and it is said once.** Then the three statements, about three different things, all three true, none improved on: **about the sill**, by the ship's hand — two hundred and nine marks and a day, a chamber was held and the holding had a term and no man read it, and nobody is going to write *because* anywhere near any of it; **about the round**, by the woman of no office — a machine that holds a room open for a term so that somebody has to go and look at it is the most sensible thing she has ever heard of, and they were right, and a reason is not a warrant, and this yard does not get to be the one that says that office was right; and the two figures, nine communities and six centuries, and three hundred years of the office that answers it, are not in one another's sentence; **about the room**, by the holder of that writ — nine communities' votes held in one room that could not all be true together, a hazard and not an archive, and the proof this yard has is physical and labor-based and about half of it is unreadable, and a man of thirty-four at Ternwatch asks whether the proof was made and is told that the yard has proved that the thing the offices say they are guarding against is a room, and has not proved what was in it. Cost: one mark and eightpence out.

### Chapter 300 — *Friday the Fourteenth of May, a Leaf With Four Columns Read Back, Thirteen Things That Are the Answer, and a Working Harbor Poorer on the Last Page Than on the First*

**Friday the fourteenth of May. The shed, and the mole steps in the afternoon.** **THE READ-BACK: thirty-two entries in the first column at the hour of it and thirty-three at the close, being twenty-three on the fourth of May, nine from the fifth to the thirteenth and one this evening; a hundred and twelve lines in the second at the hour of it and a hundred and fifteen at the close, being eighty-eight on the fourth, twenty-four in the nine days and three this afternoon; none in the third, with the boy's hand at the head of it and a name beside it that is not his and not the holder's; twenty-four in the fourth at the read-back and twenty-five at the close, the last of them the last thing in that book.** **Then thirteen things, read out in the flat voice she uses for a column, and entered without addition, and the fourth and the thirteenth are the two the yard is held to.** The fourth: **a seal on the last link of the old evidence chain, dated in the chain and older than the collar of the same office, reading *Sealed and entered at the Morrow circuit office by order of Magister Ilya Serr, senior Registry examiner*, and he is in no room.** The thirteenth: **a working harbor poorer on the fourteenth of May than on the twenty-third of February, and the four returns are four and there is no fifth, the five drawers are five drawers, the plate in eleven feet is in eleven feet with its note open, the forty marks stand twice, the wage column stands, and a yard has two hundred and sixty-one pence in a drawer on a mole.** And then the round of glass: **a person of no office goes up that coast on the seventeenth in a drawer in her own hand, and it will be on the eighteenth a thing in a house that this yard cannot reach, and her forty marks are not reduced and are not paid, and a man who has put a round of glass in a drawer in her hand has not bought a shilling of it. The round is a separate object and is NOT a piece of the plate that has closed — it is the collar-mounted disc that came off the floor of the room on the seventh and is bedded in a separate piece of worked glass, and the plate is still in the sill and went down into the rebate on the eleventh.** Cost: nothing in, nothing out. **THE BAG CLOSES AT ONE MARK, EIGHT SHILLINGS AND FIVEPENCE, BEING TWO HUNDRED AND SIXTY-ONE PENCE, and the figure the bag is short of the wage of four marks is three hundred and seventy-nine pence, being two marks, four shillings and eleven pence, and it is not going to be paid.**

### The batch's money, re-derived from the ten chapters and closing once

**THE BAG OPENS AT FIVE MARKS, ONE SHILLING AND FOURPENCE, BEING EIGHT HUNDRED AND SIXTEEN PENCE, AND CLOSES AT ONE MARK, EIGHT SHILLINGS AND FIVEPENCE, BEING TWO HUNDRED AND SIXTY-ONE PENCE. THE WHOLE OF THE BATCH IN ONE LINE: 816 + 649 − 1,204 = 261.** In: **six hundred and forty-nine pence on the fifth of May only**, being three marks for a day's work (480), a mark and eightpence for a boat and a man in her (168) and a penny of line (1) — **THE FIRST MONEY INTO THAT YARD SINCE THE SIXTH OF APRIL PAST, so the whole of what has come into it since the sixth of December past is now TWO THOUSAND FOUR HUNDRED AND NINE PENCE and not the one thousand seven hundred and sixty the four state files carried, and the figure of the eleven marks of Elias Voke on the sixth of April last is unchanged and is not superseded.** Out: **one thousand two hundred and four pence in four things** — two hundred and eight to a bonesetter on the eighth, six hundred and sixty to a glazier on the ninth, a mark and eightpence for a boat on the eleventh and a mark and eightpence for a boat on the thirteenth. **AND NOT ONE PENNY OF THE TWENTY-EIGHT MARKS, THREE SHILLINGS AND EIGHT PENCE OF PLANT AND AIR ON THE SIXTH AND THE SEVENTH WENT OUT OF THAT YARD AT ALL, because a man of sixty-one asked for the day at a pressure house at Ternwatch and the book sent the man and the house paid the man; that figure is entered in the first column and the fact that it did not touch the yard's own book is entered in the second, with the reason that the yard could not pay and has a rule about a man it has paid and none about a man paying for it.** **The whole of what has gone out of that yard since the sixth of December past is thirteen thousand nine hundred and five pence, being eighty-six marks, twelve shillings and one penny, in twenty-seven transactions at ten counters.** The wage of four marks is six hundred and forty pence: **the figure the bag is short of it had no subject from the seventh of April to the ninth of May, came back at forty-three pence on the ninth, and stands at three hundred and seventy-nine pence at the close, and it is not paid.**

### The batch's costs, in the order they were spent, and none of them paid twice

Six hundred and forty-nine pence of a day's work bought by a stranger; twenty-eight marks, six shillings and eightpence of plant and air on a man's name and not on the yard's; **an afternoon lost to the body on the sixth, with no figure because there is no figure for a day; a right hand of about forty in a man of sixty-one, a mark and four shillings, and an absence until the second of June; a boat of about nineteen tons in eleven pieces on the crown of a mole; a glass storm that cost the yard two lights and a skylight and cost the man of about fifty-five his own running glass and cost the man of about nineteen sixpence of his own; a permanent loss out of the holder's own recall with no figure for it; the only proof this yard will ever have of anything about a drowned city, gone into a plate of glass in a rebate; and a round of glass going up that coast in a drawer in a hand that is not the yard's.**

### The chapter summaries

**Chapter 301 — Saturday the fifteenth of May. A crate on the mole steps for a fourth day, the last of six hundred and sixty pence going into one front, and a tender of about sixty tons lying off the south end from ten at night until first light.** A crate under a tarpaulin that about nine people a day walk past; a glazier of about forty-four on a street four streets off the front who has paid a boy of nineteen every Friday since the sixth of March and is not going to be the man who does not; a boat's owner of about fifty-five up the hill at about eleven asking whether a man is coming to his boat on the slip on Monday, and told, twice and in the same words, why this yard is not going to go and look; and at about half past four the man in a blue coat who has been, a line on the ring bolt, a book on the tail of her, a minute looking at the water with his face to it, and no question asked of anybody. **Cost:** a boat's week and a copper pipe, on a slip at three shillings a week, and a rest out of a man who has not slept since Tuesday. **Opens:** the tender, and the refusal that is going to be the volume's method. Nothing came in and nothing went out.

**Chapter 302 — Sunday the sixteenth of May. A shipwright of about sixty, a copper pipe at Ternwatch, three shillings a week for a slip, and a boat's man of about forty who went out to a tender at five and came back at half past five with nine words in his mouth.** A green length of copper under a housing that wants replacing and a day's water with about four hours in a month; a chandler who gave nine words and no list on Saturday and says out loud that the same nine words would have been given on any Tuesday in the year, and who can no longer be certain which of eleven boats he could have named was out; a tender of about sixty tons lying off the north side with about forty people on the mole; a boat's man of about forty sent out in a dinghy and back in an hour and a quarter with nothing in his head but a question and an answer. **Cost:** nine words in nine people's hearing, and the boat's man counted them because he came off the water with nothing else in it. **Opens:** *then you will want to hear it again from the man who wrote it*, and the rule that a man who does not tell owns a piece of an answer and this yard has no standing to take it off him.

**Chapter 303 — Monday the seventeenth of May. The fifty-fourth time that wall came down, the forty-seventh charge walked on none, a crate going up that coast on the deck of a coal boat, and a notice going up at nine on a wall that was bare at eight.** The wall bare at eight; a crate up a hundred and forty feet of stone on a woman's own back with her reason given once on the steps and not again; **eight clauses of the closed-sea squadron put up at about a quarter past nine over the top of a sheet, with two naval notices already on that wall that this yard did not take down**; a reading in a market in about forty people's hearing by a man of about thirty-four who says he cannot tell what four of the lines mean and will not guess; a woman of about fifty-eight with the end stall saying the sentence of the whole notice, being that a closure has a door in it and this has got a door in the sixth line and no handle on the inside; a barrel of lamp oil at thirty-one shillings and sixpence in February and a mole-head light out in October. **Cost:** a crate this yard cannot reach, and a question asked in a market — *where is that?* — with no answer. **Opens:** the first clause's missing office.

**Chapter 304 — Tuesday the eighteenth of May. The thirtieth week with no envelope, a clerk with a quarter owed him for two months, and a boat of about seventy tons that went out at eleven without a piece of paper.** **A wage Tuesday, four marks not paid, and thirty weeks fallen due.** A properly made declaration, made before two witnesses at a desk in Ternwatch, carried to the west basin and refused by a clerk of about sixty who has been a clerk twenty-two years, for three true reasons, ending with the words *I do not know* out loud in a room with one man in it, and a request that the man not decide about his boat there. Then the boat goes out at eleven with no declaration, is not asked, not stopped, not followed, lies off the south end four hours and comes in at six and takes her berth. **Cost:** a Tuesday on which nothing happened, in a harbor that will hold a record of it that nobody can check. **Opens:** the two true sentences four lines apart, and the round of glass in a house four days up the coast.

**Chapter 305 — Wednesday the nineteenth of May. A man with two marks and one shilling and nine days on a prescription, one mark and eightpence and a penny of line, three soundings inside the harbor line, and a mark fouled to about a foot and seven inches.** **The far bench occupied from ten until four and not approached.** A plasterer of about thirty-eight asking for a boat to carry a chest up that coast for his wife, in about nine people's hearing, with his figure said out loud, and refused with the reason in two parts: a party with no instrument cannot give a hirer a paper to produce, and a man of this yard carrying a thing for a person in a house makes this yard a man in that house's business. Then the yard's last hireable money: **a boat of about thirty tons, a mark and eightpence, a penny of line, on this yard's own account, and three soundings, and the mark on the face of the second seam fouled about a foot and seven inches on the weather side and nothing on the other, and sand under the crown and not rock.** **Cost:** two marks and one shilling against eight marks and a day, and a boat that is not going to be repaired, and nine days on a chest that ran out about a week before the chapter. **Opens:** the fouling ladder, which is in a man's own book and which nobody is going to explain.

**Chapter 306 — Thursday the twentieth of May. The forty-eighth charge walked on none, nine things on the back of a slate in a fish market, and a tenth figure that is the price of a sheet of paper.** **The cistern charged and walked on none.** Nine February figures, none of them a quotation, none of them set in that market, every one of them off a manifest out of an agent at Ternwatch whose price is set in a city four hundred miles off by people who have never come to this quay; and then the tenth figure, a sheet of paper at a penny and forty for a shilling, which has not moved in nine years, and one person in that market asked to look at it. And in the shed that night, a question about the woman of about fifty-eight with a drawer under her bed, refused, on the ground that this yard has one address in this country, **with the reason given as worse than in April and not better, because in April the yard did not know her and now the yard knows she is frightened.** **Cost:** a second address, considered twice in sixteen days, for two different reasons, both of them somebody else's.

**Chapter 307 — Friday the twenty-first of May. Eleven boats of the herring third lay lying off with about fourteen men in them, fourpence a candle, and a man of about sixty of the first lay who has three things and will not say the rest of them in a shop.** Eleven boats inside the harbor line doing nothing wrong; a candle burned and not earned; a chandler who says he has not lost a customer, they are out there; **and a man of about sixty of the first lay, forty-one years on that water, who asked a question in this harbor twice and was answered neither time, saying that he has had three things since Tuesday, naming three honest targets — a man with a book, a chandler, and the harbor authority of this harbor — and saying all three are wrong, AND THEN STOPPING ON PURPOSE AND SAYING WHY OUT LOUD, being that a sentence said in a chandler's on a Friday morning is in eleven markets by Sunday and comes back with a man's name on it that the man did not put there, and that he had watched that happen twice on this coast and once it was fair and once it was murder and he could not tell afterwards which was which.** He is asked for a name and has not got one and will not go and look, and says the correct number of times to ask a question is three and not four. He takes two candles at fourpence and goes down to the water and says he will come back into that shop on Monday. A boy of seventeen carries nine words up the hill from the *Anna Ray* and is taken up the front street instead. **Cost:** eleven boats, fourteen men, and a sentence that was not said. **THE VOLUME'S GOVERNING SENTENCE AND THE CAPTAIN ARE NOT ON THIS PAGE AND ARE MOVEMENT 2'S; the first draft of this chapter spent both and they are withdrawn.**

**Chapter 308 — Saturday the twenty-second of May. The far bench occupied from ten until four and not approached, a copy of a notice bought for a penny in a room off the fish market, two hundred and eleven of one nine-line sheet of a drowned city since the twenty-seventh of April, and a woman who says she is not going to stop.** **The far bench occupied from ten until four and not approached.** The notice copied for a penny out of the ship's own hand and not out of the yard's book; a copyist of about fifty-nine with twenty-two years in that room who has never once asked what she is copying, who says out loud that she has made **two hundred and eleven** copies of **one nine-line sheet about a chamber in a drowned city** since the twenty-seventh of April — **a different sheet from the naval notice, of which not one word is in it, and the two share nothing but a counter and a penny** — and is not going to stop, **because a copyist who stops copying is a copyist who has admitted she copied something, and a trade can be put in a schedule and a confession cannot**; who names the four buyers she knows, of which the first is this yard on the twenty-seventh of April at about half past two, a man of about thirty-two with split hands who did not sit down, and the third is a woman who bought nine at a penny each on the ninth of May and carried them out in a cloth against her chest with both arms, and about whom nobody in that market knows what a person does with nine. **Cost:** two hundred and eleven copies in a town and a reason for not stopping that this yard has no argument against, and a book in her own hand that this yard did not ask to see. **Opens:** the woman with the cloth, which is not followed and will not be.**

**Chapter 309 — Sunday the twenty-third of May. A man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a Crown chart in a bag who says the can was there in the spring, a herring skipper of about fifty-one with a stove out of his wheelhouse, and a season of nine marks that is not going to be paid.** A man of about thirty-one says three things in a market in about nine people's hearing: **the can upon a stake at the outer marks is not on a Crown chart of about nine years standing, not on the outer marks, not on the mole-head approach and not in the approaches table at the back; it was there in the last week of March; and he is not going to say where he got the chart and nobody in that market is going to ask him.** The chart is not opened. **The holder of that writ stood in that market for about four minutes and asked him nothing, and said out loud that he used the four minutes on the not-asking and that this is the second time in a month and both of them were the same mistake.** Elias Voke comes ashore and says he is not going to ask this yard for a stove, and that the harbor authority's clerk took his letter and said he had no season, **and that it has been the best answer he has ever been given and the worst one he has ever been given.** **Cost:** a second time in five volumes this yard could do nothing about a man who is cold, and no figure that tells unable and decided-not-to apart.

**Chapter 310 — Monday the twenty-fourth of May. The fifty-fifth time that wall came down, the forty-ninth charge walked on none, a leaf with four columns read back, three true things said about three different objects, and a man of about thirty-four of a screw-steam packet out of Bramble Strait standing on the mole steps with a copied line in his hand.** **THE CLOSE. The wall bare for the fifty-fifth time and the cistern charged and walked on none, being the forty-ninth, and the far bench occupied from ten until four and not approached.** The read-back: **forty-two entries in the first column at the hour of it and forty-three at the close; one hundred and thirty-nine lines in the second at the hour of it and one hundred and forty-three at the close; none in the third; thirty-four in the fourth and thirty-five at the close, and the thirty-fifth is the last thing in that book.** **The three true things, about three different objects, all true, none improved on: the notice, which has two true sentences four lines apart and which the holder of that writ will not reduce to a design in either direction; the copies, which cannot be made a conspiracy, and the third part of which is him saying out loud that he wanted to put the woman with a cloth in front of a person with a pen and is not going to, because the only reason he could do it is that he is good at finding things out; and the wall, said from the top of the steps by a man of about sixty who was not asked up there, being that about eleven people on this coast cannot read a notice and that nobody in this town has said one word about that in seven days.** Then the last thing done that day: **a man of about thirty-four of a screw-steam packet out of Bramble Strait comes ashore at about five, does not go up the hill, and reads out loud on the stone at the top of the mole steps, in about nine people's hearing, the line off a sheet folded in four, being *a page in a shed on the mole at Morrow Quay, in a drawer, fourth of five*;** and says he came four days up a coast to say it out loud rather than have it found quietly, that he is not going to say who he works for, and that he does not work for anybody, and that the market four days up this coast would not take the sheet down — **and that the line is on that wall and in a drawer in this shed and on about sixty boats, and it is on those boats because a yard printed it in its first year with a place for every copy of itself on the face of it, and he has not got anything against that.** **Cost:** the yard is findable in ten days, and nobody in it wrote, sent, thanked or asked. **Opens:** the volume.

### What the batch paid, in one line

**NOTHING CAME INTO THAT YARD IN TEN DAYS AND ONE HUNDRED AND SIXTY-NINE PENCE WENT OUT, SO THE BAG WENT FROM TWO HUNDRED AND SIXTY-ONE PENCE TO NINETY-TWO, AND THE FIGURE THE BAG IS SHORT OF THE WAGE OF FOUR MARKS WENT FROM THREE HUNDRED AND SEVENTY-NINE PENCE TO FIVE HUNDRED AND FORTY-EIGHT, AND THIRTY WEEKS STOOD FALLEN DUE WITH NO ENVELOPE. THE BATCH'S OTHER COSTS WERE A CHANDLER'S NINE WORDS, A COPYIST'S TWO HUNDRED AND ELEVEN COPIES OF A SHEET ABOUT A DROWNED CITY, ELEVEN BOATS LYING OFF INSIDE THEIR OWN HARBOR LINE, A PLASTERER'S TWO MARKS AND ONE SHILLING AGAINST EIGHT MARKS, NINE DAYS ON A CHEST, A MOLE-HEAD LIGHT OUT IN OCTOBER, AND A STOVE ON AN AFTERDECK. NONE OF THEM WAS PAID BY THIS YARD AND NONE OF THEM WAS OWED TO IT. AND THE ONE THING THIS BATCH DID NOT PAY IS THE VOLUME'S OWN GOVERNING SENTENCE, WHICH A MAN OF ABOUT SIXTY OF THE FIRST LAY HAS THREE THINGS ABOUT AND DID NOT SAY IN A SHOP.**

## Volume 07, Batch 0002 (Chapters 311–320) — complete. Movement 2, a thing that cannot be declared, and a harbor that begins to arrange itself wrongly. **MOVEMENT 2'S TURN IS PAID AND THE VOLUME'S NEW-VOLUME QUESTION HAS NOW BEEN ASKED ONCE AND IS NOT ANSWERED. THE VOLUME IS NOT CLOSED.**

NO CARD FILE EXISTS FOR ANY VOLUME 07 BATCH AND NONE WAS INVENTED, AND `outline/batches/` IS UNCHANGED.**

**Batch 0002 as written, AS RE-MEASURED AFTER THE REPAIR OF 28 SEPTEMBER 2026 AGAINST `logs/batch-0002.review.log`: 32,804 words across Chapters 311 to 320** (Ch311 2,987 · Ch312 3,015 · Ch313 3,170 · Ch314 3,333 · Ch315 3,149 · Ch316 3,339 · Ch317 3,312 · Ch318 3,180 · Ch319 3,278 · Ch320 4,041), measured with `wc -w` including headings, against the 2,200–3,200 guideline. **TEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS FROM TUESDAY THE TWENTY-FIFTH OF MAY TO THURSDAY THE THIRD OF JUNE, ONE DAY TO A CHAPTER, NO DAY MISSING AND NO DAY IN TWO CHAPTERS; THE ONE DAY THAT HAD BEEN IN TWO CHAPTERS WAS PUT BACK INTO ONE, SEE `state/continuity.md` ITEM 1.0a. FIVE CHAPTERS ARE INSIDE THE GUIDELINE AND FIVE ARE PAST IT, being 314, 316, 317, 319 and the close at 320; the shape as first written was nine inside and one past, and the change is the cost of the repair and is recorded rather than trimmed away: item 11 of the review asked for a line of dated work the scene did not do in three second-column entries and those three entries took six hundred and eighteen words, and Chapter 315 took sixty-nine on the repair of the day, and no scene was cut to put a number back.
