## Volume 08, Batch 0004 (Chapters 381–390), Movement 4, a patrol and a transport, and boats that were not a fleet — complete

### Chapter 381 — Wednesday the Fourth of August, the Fifty-First Day of the Ninety. A lighter of about thirty tons broken up in nine foot of water against the wall of that quay with nothing landed out of her at any hour; one hundred and sixty-eight pence in at a berth; four masters asked one question in one morning and four answers that were all things and not one of them a man

A lighter of about thirty tons is broken up against that quay's wall in nine foot of water, which is not the four foot at the edge of the fairway, with a man of about thirty on a staging, a man of about twenty-five in the water to his waist and a man of about thirty-eight on the wall with a saw. Her frames are out by eleven and set along the wall one at a time, the whole of what came out of her goes onto that wall, and nothing comes off it: no sack, no barrel, no chest. The two tons of flour in her bottom went to a paste weeks ago and was pumped over the side and went down the harbour and nobody in that harbour saw it go. A man of about fifty-three who was in her is on the wall at nine, does not help, says nothing and is not said to, and goes down the quay at eleven. No figure and no claim goes against her in any book and the clerk of the office on the west basin is not sent for. **One hundred and sixty-eight pence comes in, being a day's work with a boat and two men at a berth, at the figure in chalk on the slate at the end stall, and the bag is three hundred and seventy-two pence, being two marks four shillings and fourpence, short of the wage of four marks by two hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark nine shillings.** The holder goes down the third lay at one with a leaf and asks four men one question in the same words four times: what does your boat want before she can lie in company with another boat for a day out and a day back. A master of about fifty-five answers a spare warp and says every boat in that harbour has the one warp she carries and no second one, and that the day a boat cuts her warp is the day she is in the water with the company coming down on her, and that he has had that happen once and did not lose the boat and has not stopped thinking about it. A master of about forty of the second lay answers a man who can read a clock and not a watch, because a watch is a man's own and a man in the water is not going to be told the hour by his own watch. A man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no municipal papers answers somebody awake ashore at the other end at the hour, and says a dog would do it, and that he has been in eleven boats in the last year and not one had a dog in her and one had a man in her who was asleep. **A shipwright of about sixty with a bench in his own front door and a strip of leather in his hand refuses the question outright: if what is wanted is a boat that can lie alongside another boat for a day and a day back then what is wanted is a boat that has been kept, and he does not know how anybody prices being kept and has never had a customer who wanted to buy it and is not going to write it on a board and chalk a day beside it.** Three answers go on the leaf and no name and no man. The ship's hand prices two of the three out loud before anybody agrees to them and says the third cannot be bought at any figure and that that is not a fault in it. **THE CONDITION IS ON THE FACE OF IT, IN HIS OWN MOUTH, OUT OF FOUR ANSWERS: a company of boats is no use at all except in the water somebody is looking after between it and the next tide. It is not a secret and it is not a discovery and it is not his, and he has said it because four men answered a question he asked and one of them told him he had come to the wrong bench.** The standing inventory is entered in full once, on this day, and is carried by a short pointer on the other nine.

### Chapter 382 — Thursday the Fifth of August, the Fifty-Second Day of the Ninety. The seventieth time the cistern was charged and walked on none, and a man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a chart in a bag who came up the hill and was not cited in anything

The cistern is charged at about eight and walked on by none of it at about half past nine, being the seventieth, and the top name on the rota board is still off it. A man of about thirty-one of the third lay comes up the hill at eleven with a bag in his hand, stands in the doorway, is not asked to come in, says he heard at the market that the holder went down a lay and asked four men a question and had not heard it, and says he is not there to be put on anything and was not sent. The holder says he did not send for him and has not asked anybody who told him and is not going to ask anybody who told him. The same question is asked in the same words and the man answers **a hand lead, and not the boat's line and not a knotted line with a stone on it, and a lead and a line and somebody in her who can use one, and that is two things and not one**, and that a boat of about twenty tons in company on a flood is a boat being asked to find the same water three times in an hour and there is no way to do that with the eye. The answer goes on the leaf with the other three and with no name against it: four things and no men. **The holder says he is not going to want to know which boats in that harbour have a hand lead, and gives the reason out loud in the same words he gave a man of about thirty-two about a hose in a return on the twenty-sixth of July and about a man's name on a leaf in a drawer on the first of August: a figure against a man in a return of that office or a list in that yard follows the man. One man of that harbour keeps the whole fouling ladder in his own book and said on the first of August that if he were asked he would put the book in his pocket and go home, and he was not asked then and is not going to be asked now and not by anybody in that crew.** The man says that is a list of what is in that harbour and the holder says it is both, and that the one that can be bought is written down and the other one is left where it is. The bag is put down on the step and taken up again and not opened, and nobody asks what is in it. The holder says he looked in it once in June, did not see anything in it he could use and did not see anything in it he was entitled to, and has not looked at it since. **The man asks whether the holder would say so in the room in the front street if anybody in that town ever asked in there whether a man with a chart came up the hill, and the holder says no: the day anybody in that town asks that question in a room with a clerk in it is the day that man is a person in a matter, and the clerk of that room is about sixty and has been in it twenty-two years and is owed a quarter and has no book and no power and is not going to be the reason a question is put to him on that man's account.** The man goes down the hill at noon with the bag still shut, is not paid, is not asked to pay, and is not written down by name in any column of that yard's leaf, and no person in any room in that harbour is told he was up the hill at all. The holder stands at the counter of the office on the west basin at half past four and says nothing, the clerk of about sixty says nothing to him, and the two of them stand there for the length of a pipe and neither puts a hand on anything.

### Chapter 383 — Friday the Sixth of August, the Fifty-Third Day of the Ninety. A counter walked past, a bonesetter's door, and the fifth answer, which is a man

The holder goes up the front street at half past ten and goes past the chandler's counter without stopping and without slowing down. The chandler of about fifty is behind the counter with a paper in his hand and his wife doing the counting and neither looks up, no figure is said out loud in that street, nobody in that street asks the man who sells it anything, and he is not asked a third time; the February figure is still above the June one and both dates are on the board and neither moved. At about eleven a bonesetter of about fifty has his door open and the man of about forty-four of the six is on his step with the top of two fingers of his left hand gone since the twelfth of July past, stiff across them and not a bonesetter's hand and never having been. The bonesetter looks at it from inside his own doorway and does not come out and does not hold out his own hand. **He says he has told that hand what it is twice, once to a man on a Saturday in July in front of two other people on a step in that street, and that he is not going to say it a third time to a person who has not asked him and is not the one he said it to.** The holder says the man is not asking him, and that that is why the bonesetter is saying it and not waiting. The bonesetter says the holder goes up and down that street every day of the week and has never once brought anybody to his door, that he does not know what the holder is doing and is not asking and would rather it went on being a thing he did not ask about, and the holder says then it goes on being a thing he did not ask about, and the bonesetter shuts the rest of the door. Nobody took that hand to a bonesetter on that day and nobody took it anywhere else either. The five shillings and sixpence paid for setting it in July came out of that man's own hand and is not paid twice. **At about one the holder goes down the third lay and asks the question a fifth time of a master of about forty-one with an anchor over his own stern, and the answer is somebody in this harbour who is there on the day.** The master says that is the answer and he has got nothing after it, and that he has been in company three times in his life and twice it went wrong and it went wrong both times because there was a day when somebody who was going to be there was not there, and that the boats did not know it and did not stop and did not turn round and found out at about four in the afternoon in about a mile of water where nobody had told them to look. **The holder does not write it down, and gives the reason out loud: the day a yard writes down who turns up that yard has a list, and a list is the boat, and everybody not on it is not asked and everybody on it has a figure.** The master says the holder has understood that wrong on purpose, and the holder says he has understood it in a shed with three hundred and seventy-two pence in a bag, and has understood it since the twenty-sixth of July, and was wrong about it before in front of about forty people and is not going to be wrong about it again quietly in a doorway.

### Chapter 384 — Saturday the Seventh of August, the Fifty-Fourth Day of the Ninety. Six masters of the third lay taken in at the outer water on a papers question, and a yard that did not go out

A boat of the second lay of about twenty-six tons comes in past the outer marks at two on the sixth clause and a man of about twenty-nine comes up the hill on foot. Six masters of the third lay are lying off the point at about a mile and a half, on the other side of the point from the flour boats, with a small boat of about twelve tons alongside the outside one of them, a boat's boat in her, and a man of about nineteen at her tiller, and nothing flying on her and no gun that could be seen at close enough. She was there at ten and at two and the six had not moved and had not hailed. **She is putting them in one at a time, about half an hour in her each, and what she is asking is whether their papers are in order, and she is writing on something when they hand them over, and no officer in her was seen.** Four of the six hand their papers over and come back in their own boats and say nothing to anybody; the fifth is the master of about fifty-five, who hands his over, sits in her about a quarter of an hour and comes back in his own boat and comes up the hill. The sixth is a master of about thirty-three who says he has no papers on him, says where they are, being a locker in a house in another street, and says he went out on the Saturday morning without going in first; the lever of about nineteen writes that down and puts him in her last, at about one, and he has not come out. **THE HOLDER DOES NOT GO OUT AND GIVES TWO REASONS IN A DOORWAY: this yard has one boat and one man at the tiller and the hundred and sixty-eight pence that paid him on the twenty-seventh is still in the bag and there is no second such day in the month, and the last time he lay alongside a boat of theirs on a paid day he lay there four hours, said nothing, and came off into a tow of eight and cut his own line and lost eight fathoms of his own line and a lighter of about thirty tons with a foot and four inches of water in her and about two tons of flour in her bottom, broken up against a wall in nine foot of water on Wednesday past with nothing landed out of her at any hour; and a papers question is not a thing a boat can answer, and a boat of that harbour going out with no declaration and no paper of any kind would either have a room in that small boat, which nobody has any reason to suppose, or would not, and in the second case this yard's name would be put against a boat of theirs at a mile and a half in front of a man of about nineteen with a list, and a name against a boat follows the boat.** Six berths on the third lay are empty at five, with a coil of line on the second boat's bollard and a hand lead on the third boat's thwart and a lamp in the wheelhouse of the fourth and no man in her. The master of about fifty-five says he will not be going out for the man of about thirty-three and will not be going out for anybody, and that there is one spare warp in six boats and it is a spare warp for his own boat, and he has not given it away and has not promised it and nobody has asked him for it, and he is not going to bring it up a ladder to a boat of about twelve tons and hand it to a man of about nineteen who will write his name on something. Nobody says anything to that either. And before he goes off the lay he says the other half of it, flatly, to that lay and not to the man of about twenty-nine who is of the second: the thirty-three has no papers on him and is not lying and is not a smuggler, he has a boat of his own and a wife in the second lay and a locker in a house in another street with three things in it that are not paper, where there are no papers there is no door, and that is not an opinion of his and is not a hard thing about the man.

### Chapter 385 — Sunday the Eighth of August, the Fifty-Fifth Day of the Ninety. A page of six names on a mole, three men of that lay who said the thing about it and the man of about fifty-one who did not, and a man of sixty-one who said one true sentence and was not asked a second

Three men of the third lay come up the crown at about four and stand in front of a page of six names and a boat and no figure that has stood there since the eighth of July past, and none of them was asked to and none came for it. **The master of about fifty-five says it is a good page and that he has always said that, and then says he has a board in his own boat of what she wants and what he has not got and what he has got twice of, that it has been in that boat eleven years and is painted and nearly all gone, and that he has never shown it to a living soul and it is the one thing in that boat he would be sorry to lose, and that he has never once been asked for it and is not going to be.** The master of about forty-seven says to the water that you cannot read that page and there is nothing on it, and that he has got a list of what he owes in his own head since he was nineteen and it has never been on anything and nobody on this coast can check one hair of it, and that both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other, and that he has had thirty years to want a page of his own and has not put one up and is not going to tell that man he should have. **THE MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-ONE IS ON THE CROWN THE WHOLE OF IT AND SAYS NONE OF IT AND IS NOT ASKED TO EXPLAIN HIS PAGE, and he is not one of the six masters off the point and owns five sixths of a boat on the foul off the south end of that mole and has not had a boat to put it in since the nineteenth of June past, and no figure is put against him by anybody and no boat is given to him and no wage is promised to him and his page is not going into any return.** Tobias Wren, sixty-one, with eleven pieces of a boat behind him and a boat's hook in his right hand, works the hook into a seam at the other end of that crown and says one sentence without stopping: the one that was kept was kept by somebody who came on the days he was not needed. Nobody asks which one, nobody says anything to him about it, he does not say it again, it is not written down, and the holder does not improve on it and does not repeat it. At about half past four the man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no municipal papers of any kind is at the shed door and says he did not go and lie off the point to look at the line as he was told not to on the twenty-eighth of July, and that he is not here about the line; and he says six masters of the third lay are lying off the point with a small boat alongside them and that she is asking them whether their papers are in order, and that he has had no papers for four years and has not wanted any and has said so out loud in that shed before, and that the sixth clause of that notice does not ask anybody a question and he has been in on it twice, and that he is not asking for anything and is telling, because somebody is going to be standing off that point telling a man with a list about a line he has never read. The holder asks him for nothing and sends him for nothing and pays him for nothing. At ten past five the mole head: the light out, the two objects of nobody's at four hundred and twenty-three days, the bench under the pump bare for the hundred and eighty-ninth night, two lights off the point unmoved in seven days, six boats on the other side of the same point with a small boat alongside the outside one of them, and the second seam not looked at.

### Chapter 386 — Monday the Ninth of August, the Fifty-Sixth Day of the Ninety. The sixty-sixth wipe, the seventy-first charge, a boat with no paper of any kind in her going out on a breach of the first clause, five masters in on a line that asked them nothing, and a clerk who decided by himself

The wall comes down bare for the sixty-sixth time and goes up at the angle since the twelfth, and the cistern is charged for the seventy-first time and walked on by none of it, and the top name on the rota board is still off it. **The man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no municipal papers of any kind goes out past the outer marks at about half past seven in the morning on a breach of the first clause, alone, and nobody sent him and he was not paid and was not asked to pay and was not told terms, with a fold of the notice of the seventeenth of May in his own inside pocket that nobody in that harbour wrote and that had been in his own coat since before the spring.** He is alongside the outside of the six at about nine, a mile and a half off the point, and does not go aboard the small boat, and lies off her with his own bow on her quarter and holds on to nothing. A man of about nineteen comes across four of his own feet of water in a dinghy and looks at what is in the man's hand. **He says the notice on the wall in the front street, that he has read it out of that wall twice, that the fifth of it is out and the sixth of it is in and that it does not ask you a question and does not ask him a question and has not asked anybody a question since the seventeenth of May.** The nineteen says he has got no papers and has not had any for four years. The man of about thirty-eight says the small boat is asking five masters whether their papers are in order and that all five are sitting there waiting to find out what a piece of paper is worth, and that it is worth the sixth clause and nothing else and nobody on this coast can put a figure on that, and that the master of about thirty-three has no papers on him and there is no door for him and he is not going to tell him there is one, because he has been in on the sixth and the sixth never once asked him for a paper. **The man of about nineteen looks at him for a while, goes back up his own ladder, brings up a board off the after thwart, being a notice and the same notice and worn at the folds, reads the sixth line of it with his thumb on the line and not his finger, puts the board down and goes down into the dinghy again.** He says nothing to anybody and goes to the five boats in order from the outside one and is in each of them about a minute, and the five of them get under way in the next quarter of an hour without a word between any two of them that anybody heard. **Five masters of the third lay come past the outer marks at about half past four in the afternoon under the sixth clause, which is free, and a lever of about nineteen has put six ticks in a list, and a tick is not a figure.** The man of about thirty-eight comes in at about six with the fold of paper still in his pocket and does not go into that shed and does not go to the end stall and goes home, and the man of about thirty-one with a chart in a bag watches all five come up the third lay from the deck of his own boat and then goes below and shuts his hatch. Nobody in that harbour thanked him and nobody said he had done anything. At about two a man of about fifty from the office on the west basin comes up the hill and says he is not there about a boat, and says the box on his table is for days a boat belonging to that harbour has gone out past the line without a declaration, and that the twenty-seventh of July is the last day in that box, and that the ninth of August is not going into it because a boat that came in again is not a day, and that he has thought about it and decided it and is not asking whether this yard agrees. The holder asks him nothing and he asks for nothing. One hundred and sixty-eight pence comes in and the bag is five hundred and forty pence, being three marks five shillings, short of the wage by one hundred pence, being eight shillings and fourpence.

### Chapter 387 — Tuesday the Tenth of August, the Fifty-Seventh Day of the Ninety. The forty-second wage Tuesday, and a caulker of about twenty-three who was there at four in the morning and was paid one hundred and sixty-eight pence for it

The wage of four marks, being six hundred and forty pence, was not paid on the said Tuesday and the column did not move, so that forty-two weeks now stand fallen due with no envelope against any of them. **At about four in the morning Isaac Fell, a caulker of about twenty-three, of no boat and of no crew and of no lay's crew, not on the stone and not one of the six men of that harbour who are ashore with no boat, is standing on the flat of the bench stone with a maul and a bucket of oakum and has been there since about half past three.** He came on the Tuesday because he heard on the Saturday at the market that the question was on somebody's board and he does not read a board. Asked what that harbour wants for a day out and a day back in company, and told the four answers, he says that is a list of things and it is a good list and he has had it in his head in about four boats and never once on paper, and that none of it works. **HE SAYS THE FIRST THING ANY PERSON IN THAT HARBOUR HAS EVER BEEN ABLE TO TELL IT ABOUT A COMPANY OF BOATS: it is never the warp, and he has never in his life seen a company come apart over a warp, and it is always that there was a Wednesday and a man was at his own bench on the Wednesday, and everybody ahead of him sailed on and everybody behind him sailed on and the boats did not know.** He says he has been on that stone at half past three every morning he could not sleep for nine years and that there has not been one single morning in nine years when anybody in that harbour was on it at half past four, and that that is not a fault of theirs because there is no morning when anybody in that harbour has anything to be on it at half past four for. And that this is the fifth thing and it is not a thing: you cannot buy it, bolt it on, find it in a shop in a street or write it on a board, and the day you do write it on a board is the day a man has a job in that harbour and every other man who was going to be there is somewhere else, and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other, and he has watched a yard try the board about four years ago and will not name the yard because he is not going to talk about a yard that is not this one. **THE SHIP'S HAND PRICES THE DAY OUT LOUD BEFORE ANYBODY AGREES TO IT, being one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, for eight hours of a man who would otherwise be on a bench of his own, with no line and no fathom and no night's food in it, and says the figure is the figure in chalk on the slate at the end stall and is not that yard's figure, and it goes in the second column and not the first with the reason that a man standing on a stone at four in the morning cannot be checked by a stranger with a leaf and a pencil.** It is paid at about four in the afternoon in coin on the flat of the stone. He says the holder did not ask him for a Tuesday after that and that if the holder wants a Tuesday he asks for a Tuesday on a day and pays for the Tuesday, and that the day he does not ask is the day there is not one, and that he is not going to stand there and be thanked for turning up. The holder says he is not going to thank him and is not going to put him on a board, and he says he knows and has been on a board once and would rather be on a day. A master of about thirty asks whether the holder is going to take a company out on the flood and back on the flood. **The holder says no, and says he will not take a company out on a day when the man whose day it is has not been asked for it by name, and will not take one out at all until he has been asked for a Tuesday and has said yes to that Tuesday and has been paid for that Tuesday, and will not take a company out on a flood because a flood is the only tide that harbour can make and he is not going to stand on that quay and pretend those two things are not the same thing.** The master says that is a long way round and the holder says it is four days and a hundred and sixty-eight pence a day and it is a day shorter than what it costs the other way. The bag is three hundred and seventy-two pence again and the figure short of the wage is two hundred and sixty-eight pence.

### Chapter 388 — Wednesday the Eleventh of August, the Fifty-Eighth Day of the Ninety. A box that is no longer empty, six masters asked one at a time, one who said no, and a master of about thirty-three coming in on a line that did not ask him

A man of about fifty from the office on the west basin comes up the hill at eleven without knocking and says it is in: the twenty-seventh of July past in the box on that table in his own hand with his own hour against it, written on Monday morning at about nine, with the boat, the hour, the tide, the eleven minutes and the lighter in it, and the box not empty since the fifth of July past. **He says he wrote what he knows and did not write who was in the boat because he does not know and has not asked, and that he had not come up to be told anything and there is nothing in it this yard is entitled to, and that he was telling because somebody in a room will read it in about a month and he would rather this yard heard the day off him than off a sheet.** He says he had been waiting eleven days to find out whether the holder would ask him and had not, and that the other paper on that table has a box in it which is still empty and is the only box in that office he has never once wanted to fill, and that he said so out loud in a doorway to one person and it does not go any further than that doorway. The holder says it does not go any further, and that he is not going to put it in any column because he could not check a hair of it and would have to write a thing he cannot check with somebody's hand on it. At two the holder stands at the counter of the office on the west basin and says nothing and the clerk of about sixty says nothing to him, and neither puts a hand on anything; the list on the board on that wall is a list and is not a schedule and binds nobody, and the fire party's hose is not on it and the tide gang's want of four men is not on it and there is not one name of any man in that harbour on that board. **At half past three six men of the third lay are asked one at a time, in the same words, what a company of boats out on a flood and back on a flood with the same men in them going out and coming in, and a paper between them with each master's name and each man's name on it, and a man on a mole head at four in the morning and at four in the afternoon, and nothing in it for anybody and nothing in it against anybody and a day and a wage for the man on the stone would be.** Four say yes in the first hour. The master of about fifty-five says yes and then says the second half of it, that a spare warp in six boats is one spare warp and he would have to buy a second one before the day and is not going to be the man who said no to a day he was asked for and then went and did not come. The master of about forty of the second lay, the master of about thirty of that lay and the master of about forty-one, who gave the best of five answers on the sixth of August and was not thanked for it and was not written down, say yes. **THE MASTER OF ABOUT THIRTY-THREE, WHO HAS NO PAPERS ON HIM AND WHOSE PAPERS ARE IN A LOCKER IN A HOUSE IN ANOTHER STREET, SAYS NO, and says it is not because of the day or the wage, and gives the reason: a paper with his name on it says a master and then somebody wants to know what a master with a boat of his own is doing in a company of eleven, and then somebody wants to know where his papers are, and he has not got them and is not going to stand on a quay and say he left them at home. The holder says that is a no and it is on the leaf and he is not going to ask for the reason twice.** The master says what is on the leaf is not a company then, that five of them is five boats, and that he has been in five-boat companies off that coast; the holder says five is a foot and that he had been told so by a man of about thirty-three with no papers on him and is not going to improve on it. Six answers go on a leaf with an hour against each and no name and no figure. **And the master of about thirty-three comes past the outer marks at about half past four in the afternoon on the sixth clause, which is free, alone in his own boat, and does not hail anybody and nobody hails him, because the small boat of about twelve tons was at that hour at the other end of the tow of seven flour boats a mile off the point and there was nobody at that harbour's outer water at all, and he put his boat on the third lay at about five and did not go up the hill and did not go into that shed and nobody thanked him and nobody asked him where his papers were, because there was nobody in that harbour who had been asked to ask him.**

### Chapter 389 — Thursday the Twelfth of August, the Fifty-Ninth Day of the Ninety. The seventy-second charge, a man of about forty-four back on the water at a tiller, forty-four pence for a loaf and a half and a candle, and the name he asked for still refused

The cistern is charged for the seventy-second time and walked on by none of it, and the top name on the rota board is still off it. **The man of about forty-four, the second of the six men of that harbour who have been ashore with no boat since the nineteenth of June past, with the top of two fingers of his left hand gone since the twelfth of July past and the binding off for the first time on the first of August and the hand stiff across the stumps and unable to close on a maul or to hold a caulking iron, went out on the Wednesday in a boat of about twenty-one tons of the third lay with a master of about thirty in her, and stood at her tiller from about half past five in the morning until about six in the afternoon, and was not paid and was not asked to pay, and the terms were said out loud on that quay by the master of about thirty and not by this yard.** He asked and was asked, and neither of those is a favour and neither of them is a debt. He is a boat's man and not a master and is put to a tiller and not to a caulking iron, because a man who can steer with two fingers gone is worth more on that boat than a man who can caulk with two fingers gone, and the caulking on that boat is not caulked and will not be done in this month. **He was fed before he went and the pot came back empty and clean at about six, and he brought the pot back to that shed himself and stood in the doorway with it and did not come in, and said forty-four pence came out of that bag and that he knows what is in that bag because he has read it off the bench stone like everybody in that harbour does, and that there is no figure against him and he is not going to ask what is left in it.** The holder says there are three hundred and twenty-eight pence in it, being two marks and eightpence, and the figure it is short of a wage of four marks is three hundred and twelve pence, being one mark twelve shillings and eightpence, and that none of that is his business and all of it is on a board in that shed which is not the market wall. The man says he knows it is not the market wall and that this yard has not put anything of its own on a wall in that town in three months and that everybody has noticed and nobody has said so. The holder says nobody has said so because nobody in that town is going to do a thing for nothing and a thing that is not asked for is a thing that is not owed, and says the forty-four pence is not a wage and is not against the man's name and is not going in a return and that there is no return, and that he would not have told him at all if the man had not brought the pot back. **And the man says this yard still has not written his name on a leaf in a drawer, that he asked on the first of August and was refused and has thought about it for eleven days on the water and on a stone and has come to tell this yard it was right and not to ask again; and the holder says he said no and is going to keep saying no and the reason has not changed and has not been improved on, and that he is not going to thank him for coming up a hill to be told he was right, and that if there is a day and a boat and a wage one day he is going to come and find him and he is going to say no, and that will be the third time and it will be a no like the other two.** The man says that was fair and goes down the hill. Forty-four pence, being three shillings and eightpence, goes out for a loaf and a half and a candle and a pot, and the bag is three hundred and twenty-eight pence, being two marks and eightpence, short of the wage by three hundred and twelve pence, being one mark twelve shillings and eightpence. Two lights off the point unmoved in eleven days, about twenty-six tons of flour in seven boats of a tow of eight which has not come in and has not been hailed once in eleven days, and no sack of it in that harbour and no figure against it and no claim.

### Chapter 390 — Friday the Thirteenth of August, the Sixtieth Day of the Ninety. The sending, the occasion, the timing he chose, a route out he knows and does not have, the shape of a thing on a board said in a shed, the read-back, and the mole head

A master of about fifty-five comes up the hill at about two with his own boat's painter over his shoulder and says that a small boat of about twelve tons came round the point at about eleven that morning with two boats in her and went down-coast, and that before she went round the point she came to the six of that harbour on the water and a man in a dinghy put a question into his boat asking where the company out of that harbour sails and on what day, and that he told him the flood, and that he did not say the holder's name and nobody said the holder's name, and that he is not taking his yes back, and that he would rather the holder heard it off him than off a sheet and that he had not found a better reason in three hours. **The holder goes into the shed and shuts the door, which he does not do, and says the thing: a flood is the only tide this harbour can make and a flood is the only hour a loaded transport can come down that reach going that way, and he chose the day, and he named it out loud in front of a master of about thirty and in front of about nine men of that third lay over four days, and he said no on Tuesday to being asked whether he was going to take a company out on the flood and back on it; and nobody made him name the day and nobody put it in his mouth and he did not ask what else goes down a reach on the flood because he did not ask.** **HE KNOWS A ROUTE OUT AND DOES NOT HAVE IT:** a reach below the foul that comes out a mile and a half inside the point, a channel in it he has never been down, three soundings off a hand lead in a leaf a stranger with a lead could take again, a third channel that is three iron rings on a pinger on an adrift buoy and is nobody's measurement, a pinger that went back up that coast on the Tuesday of the thirteenth and has not come down, and the one thing in the man of about thirty-four's own book that he did not name and was not asked for and is not going to be; and the reason he has not got it is the same reason there is no spare warp in six boats and the same reason the man whose day it is is a caulker of twenty-three who was on a stone at four in the morning because he cannot sleep, and not an arrangement and not a list and not a person anybody in that harbour is paying to be there except on a Tuesday for a day at a mark and eightpence. **And in that shed he says what a thing on a board is, about a shape and not about a sheet: a board of about a yard wide under a sloping canvas on an after thwart, with one word at the head of it in block capitals, being UNSEALED, two ruled columns under it, eleven marks in the right-hand one against dates from the eighth of May to the twenty-second of July, two impressions struck side by side at the foot of which he read neither, and a date cut into the timber above the head, being the fourteenth of February, ninety-two days before the notice went up on a wall in a different street. He has not got the form, he has not got a copy of it, and no document of anybody's changed hands on the water, and what he has got is a shape, a date, two impressions he did not read and a word, and he said it out loud once and is not going to say it again in that shed.** The leaf is read back at about four with three of them in the shed: **at the hour of the read-back one hundred and twenty-two, four hundred and eighty-seven, none, one hundred and fourteen; at the close one hundred and twenty-three, four hundred and eighty-nine, none, one hundred and fifteen, the hundred and fifteenth the last line in that ledger and the column not closed. Both definitions are on the face of the reading: the first column's and the fourth column's figures at the hour are counts of entries and of lines and are checkable by a stranger with a leaf and a pencil, and the second column's is that ledger's own and is not checkable from a mole, and it is the close less the two entries that go in after the reading.** The third column is none and nobody has been appointed to it, the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it with a name beside it that was said out loud once in a boat on the thirteenth of May past and is not said again, and his surname is on no page, and there is now a fifth week in which nobody in that crew has said one word about the three nots. The woman of no office asks the only question asked in that shed that day, being whether he will take them out on the day he named, and he says no, and says he will not take them out on it or on any day until a caulker of about twenty-three has been asked for that day by name and has said yes to it and has been paid for it, and that if it comes to it he will not take them out on a flood and will say why on the quay in front of the boats and not in that shed, and that the reason will be the tide and will be true and will not be the whole of the reason. She says that is a decision and not a finding and that she will write it in the second column with the reason against the line, and the reason is that he knows the hour and is not going to be at it, and he says that is the reason. **The whole of what came into that yard in the ten days is three hundred and thirty-six pence on two days and the whole of what went out of it is two hundred and twelve pence on two days, and the bag is three hundred and twenty-eight pence, being two marks and eightpence, short of the wage of four marks by three hundred and twelve pence, being one mark twelve shillings and eightpence, and the wage column is unmoved on its forty-second Tuesday and the forty-third is not going to be paid either.** At ten past five the mole head: the light out and its lens out since the seventh of May, the notice at eighty-eight days and not compared with anything, two lights off the point unmoved in twelve days, seven boats of a tow of eight with about twenty-six tons of flour and no sack ashore and no claim, the two objects of nobody's at four hundred and twenty-eight days, the bench under that pump bare for the hundred and ninety-fourth night, the second seam not looked at on any of the ten days and its season and the mark four hundred yards off it nine marks each and neither paid, eight marks and a day of a boat owing to that harbour's own bellwright since the twenty-third of May with the chest shut and it not asked in ninety days and no digit of anything he ever said on a page, and a tender of about ninety tons at the head of eight boats inside the line for eighteen days that nobody in that harbour was told anything about.

**SEVEN REPAIRS, ALL ARITHMETIC, COUNTING, ANTI-DUPLICATION OR HOUSE-FORM, AND NO CHAPTER RESTARTED, NO SCENE CUT, NO CHARACTER MOVED, NO DATE MOVED, NO COST MOVED AND NO FACT ADDED OR REMOVED. MOVEMENT 2 PAID A ROOM WHERE NOBODY WITH A TITLE IS IN IT, A CLAUSE THAT HAS NEVER BEEN TESTED, A DOOR THAT BINDS NOBODY WHO DOES NOT USE IT, A MAN SAYING OUT LOUD WHAT A REFUSAL COSTS, AND AN APOLOGY THAT WAS NOT FORGIVEN AND WAS NOT THANKED AND WAS PAID ONCE.
