### The shape of Volume 08 after fifty chapters of it, which is the whole of it

**FIVE MOVEMENTS PAID AND NO STAGE IN ANY OF THEM. A SEALED INSTRUMENT WITH FOUR PRICES AND TEN REFUSALS OUT OF ELEVEN, THE TENTH OF THEM DOWN A COAST ROAD, AND ONE THAT WAS NEITHER A YES NOR A NO, AND ONE OF THE REFUSALS ABOUT A LINE OF WRITING AND NOT ABOUT A PERSON. A ROOM WHERE NOBODY WITH A TITLE IS AND A CLAUSE THAT HAS NEVER BEEN TESTED AND A MAN SAYING OUT LOUD WHAT A REFUSAL COSTS AND AN APOLOGY NOT FORGIVEN AND NOT THANKED. ELEVEN WEEKS OF LIFTING UNSEALED TESTIMONY OUT OF CIVILIAN HULLS UNDER A FORM DATED THE FOURTEENTH OF FEBRUARY, AND A COST IN FLOUR. A COMPANY OF BOATS IS NO USE AT ALL EXCEPT IN THE WATER SOMEBODY IS LOOKING AFTER BETWEEN IT AND THE NEXT TIDE, PAID AS A BEGINNING AND NOT AS A STAGE, WITH FOUR THINGS ON A LEAF AND A FIFTH THING THAT IS A PERSON AND IS NOT ON IT, AND A WAGE OF A MARK AND EIGHTPENCE AND A DAY AND A MAN WHO IS THERE ON A TUESDAY, AND SIX MASTERS TAKEN IN ON A PAPERS QUESTION AND ANSWERED ON A LINE THAT ASKED THEM NOTHING. AND THEN ABOUT ELEVEN MASTERS ASKED ONE AT A TIME IN THE SAME WORDS, FOUR OF THEM SAYING NO WITH A REASON AND A MAN'S DAY AS THE COST; SEVEN BOATS OUT ON A FLOOD ON A BREACH OF THE FIRST CLAUSE AND BACK ON THE SIXTH; THE ELEVEN WEEKS READ ALOUD IN A PUBLIC ROOM IN THE ORDER SIGNED WITH THE FORM'S SHAPE READ AFTER THEM AND NOT BEFORE; A TRANSPORT OF ABOUT A HUNDRED AND FORTY TONS CUT, STOVED AND HOLED ON THE REACH, WITH NOBODY HURT, NOBODY NAMED AND NOBODY COUNTED; THE WORK ON THAT REACH STOPPING AT ELEVEN BECAUSE THIRTY MEN HEARD A WORD AT THE SAME MINUTE FROM ONE MOUTH; THE MAN WITH THE BOARD UNDER HIS ARM WALKING AWAY FROM IT; A SQUADRON THAT LOST A SHIP OUT OF THAT REACH; THE ADMISSION SAID ONCE ON A MOLE IN ABOUT SIXTY PEOPLE'S HEARING AND NOT IMPROVED ON AND NOT COMFORTED; A PAPER ON A CUSTODY ROOM DOOR NAMING TWO AS PERMITTED AND ONE AS PRESENT, WITH A FIGURE THAT IS A TIME AND A PLACE AND AN ARRIVAL AND IS THE ONLY FIGURE IN FIFTY CHAPTERS THAT IS NOT A PRICE ANYBODY PAID; A NEW SEAL LINE NAMING A NEW OFFICE, IN NO MOUTH, WITH NOBODY IN A ROOM; A NINE-LINE SHEET IN A FRONT STREET SINCE THE FOURTEENTH OF AUGUST THAT IS THE BEST PAPER THE CROWN PRODUCES IN THIS VOLUME AND IS ANSWERED BY NOBODY; A QUESTION ASKED ONCE IN A ROOM WITH A CLERK IN IT AND ANSWERED NOWHERE; AND A COMMITTED RELATIONSHIP BEGUN ONCE ON A MOLE AND NOT SEALED AND NOT A MARRIAGE.**

**AND THE LAST LINE OF THE VOLUME IS THE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIFTH LINE OF A FOURTH COLUMN THAT IS NOT CLOSED, AND THE LAST THING THE VOLUME SAYS IS WHAT A HAND AT THE FOOT OF A SHEET IS NOT, AND A HARBOR POORER ON THE FIFTIETH CHAPTER THAN ON THE FIRST WITH NO FLOUR IN ITS MARKET AND A LIGHT OUT AND A BAG OF ONE MARK AND FORTY-THREE WEEKS OF A WAGE FALLEN DUE WITH NO ENVELOPE AGAINST ANY OF THEM, AND THE CHEAPEST THING IN IT WENT UP ON THE FIRST OF JUNE AND DID NOT COME BACK DOWN.**


## Volume 09, Batch 0001 (Chapters 401–410), Movement 1, a door, an hour, and a figure that is the end of it and not the middle of it — complete, 28 September 2026

**TEN CHAPTERS, TEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS, TUESDAY THE TWENTY-FOURTH DAY OF AUGUST TO THURSDAY THE SECOND DAY OF SEPTEMBER, ONE DAY TO A CHAPTER, NO DAY IN TWO CHAPTERS AND NONE SKIPPED, ON THE ANCHOR CARRIED OFF CHAPTER 400. MOVEMENT 1 IS PAID IN FULL: THE LOOK HAPPENS, THE HOUR IS ONE HOUR AND IS THE END OF IT AND NOT THE MIDDLE OF IT, THE OFFICE REFUSES FOR NINE DAYS, THE COUNT IS TAKEN OFF A RETURN ONE LINE AT A TIME WITH A PENCIL, AND THE FOURTH COLUMN TAKES NO LINE. NO STAGE WAS TAKEN AND THE WORD *KEELWRIGHT* IS IN NO MOUTH ON ANY PAGE. THE FULL AUDIT, WITH EVERY LOCK, EVERY FLAG, EVERY SWEEP, EVERY MEASUREMENT AND ALL TWENTY-ONE REPAIRS, IS AT `state/continuity.md` § *Volume 09, Batch 0001 as written (Chapters 401–410)*.**

### Chapter 401 — *Tuesday the Twenty-Fourth of August, the Forty-Fourth Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It, a Knock Put on a Door in a Corridor on That Hill Where on the Last Evening of the Last Month Nobody Knocked, an Hour With a Man of About Forty of That Office in the Room the Whole of It, a Fragment About Nine Inches by Six With an Edge That Was Cut and Not Broken, a Seam in It That Says Two Things at Once and Will Not Say Which of the Two Is the One They Came In to Look At, Three People Going Out Carrying Something and Nothing at All Going Out in Any Hand, and a Request Made at Ten Past Eleven for Another Hour of the Same Thing*

**THE FIRST ENTRY INTO THAT ROOM IN NINE VOLUMES, AND IT IS AN HOUR.** The forty-fourth wage Tuesday and the column does not move on it and forty-four weeks stand fallen due. He goes up the hill at twenty to ten with his hands empty — not the leaf, because a leaf does not go up a hill into a building that holds other people's things — and knocks, having not knocked on the same door on the Monday evening. Saul Drury, a copying clerk of that office, about forty, jacket gone at both elbows, a piece of pencil behind one ear, opens it two inches and then the rest of the way and says nothing and leaves the door standing open. The thing on the far shelf is about nine inches by six. **Its edge over nine inches is cut and not broken and the arris is still on it, and the holder spends the first ten minutes of the hour on the edge and is glad of it.** The clerk brings a lamp at about a quarter past ten without being asked and stands six feet off. There is a seam across the thing from about a third in on the left to about a third in on the right and about two thirds up, and the holder says that a seam is where one maker's pressure met another maker's pressure and neither of them won all the way, and that it is the only honest mark in recovered work, and that it says **two people made it, at different times, in different rooms, and both of them were frightened** — and that he cannot say which of the two was in the room it was cut in. The woman of no office says that is not an answer; he says it is the only one he has and he would rather bring her that than a guess, and both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other. The middle shelf is on the way in and on the way out and he does not turn his head at it or at the claim book above it and the clerk does not turn his either. It goes back on the same place on the same shelf under the same number. Nothing goes out in anybody's hand. In the corridor at about ten past eleven he asks for another hour of the same thing and is refused in nine words by the man who opened the door, who says the refusal is not his and will be written on the door in his own hand. On the mole at four she says she has got something, does not say what it is, and says it is not the forty marks and is not going to reduce the forty marks.

### Chapter 402 — *Wednesday the Twenty-Fifth of August, a Refusal Pinned at the Corner of the Same Door in the Hand of the Man Who Opened It and Nine Days of It Running to the Second of September, a Woman of No Office on a Mole at About Four With the One Thing She Came Down Off That Hill to Say and One Thing She Did Not Say, a Yard That Went Back to Work With Nothing Came Into It and Nothing Went Out of It, and a Man of About Thirty-Eight With a Boat of About Thirteen Tons and No Papers Who Used the Sixth Clause on His Own Account for the Second Time in Six Weeks and Was Not Thanked*

**THE REFUSAL IS FOUR LINES IN A CLERK'S OWN HAND AND IT HAS NO SEAL AND NO OFFICE ON IT.** He identifies the hand from a line the same man ruled with a flat rule at ten past ten the previous morning. It says a second hour is asked for, that it is refused, and that a second paper will be on that door on the second of September and not on any day before it. **Nine days of refusal begin.** The ship's hand prices the morning out loud before he agrees to anything: an hour and a half of a man's day and about ten of a mile on a hill there is no other way up and a night's sleep, and the last item of it goes in the second column with the reason that she has not got a rate for it and is not going to invent one at eleven o'clock at night because it would make the sheet tidier. On the mole at about four, Mara Venn says the thing she is carrying is not sitting still, and that she will not say the other half, and that if she is asked again she will stop coming up that hill. He does not ask her again. On the second lay at about half past five a man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers comes up out from under his own counter and says he has been out on the sixth clause of that notice twice since the first of June, both times on his own book and his own time, that it is not enough to get anybody to sea, and that he is not going to ask for anything and is not going to be thanked.

### Chapter 403 — *Thursday the Twenty-Sixth of August, the Seventy-Sixth Time the Cistern Was Charged and Walked on None of It and the Top Name on That Rota Board Still Off It, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence In at a Berth at the Figure in Chalk on a Slate, and a Man of About Fifty-Three With a Bad Back Standing in Front of a Board in the Office on the West Basin Counting the First Month of a Return Line by Line With a Stub of Pencil on the Flat of His Own Hand Because a Figure in a Clerk's Hand Is a Figure in a Clerk's Hand*

**THE RETURN IS FOUND, AND ITS ARCHITECTURE IS THE WHOLE OF THIS CHAPTER.** A sheet about two foot by three, folded once, nailed to nine feet of wall inside the door of the office on the west basin, ruled in five blocks by month with a line for every day of each month from the first, the last block stopping at the twenty-third of August; a figure in the right-hand column on a day a thing came in and a single stroke across the line on a day nothing did; a space two inches deep at the foot with the word *carried* over it and nothing in it; and five small figures in the hand of a clerk of about sixty, twenty-two years in that room, owed a quarter of a pound, with no book and no power, at the head of the five blocks, being the number of lines in each block that carry a figure. A man of about fifty-three, who works a winch on the third lay and has had a bad back since a night in the February before last and has not been to anybody about it, comes in sideways at about half past two because that is where the tide board is, reads nine feet of wall because nobody does not, and stands there. He counts the first block with a stub of pencil on the flat of his own left hand, twice, and adds the figures out loud in tens under his breath with his lips moving and nothing else moving. **He stops at the end of the first block, works out that the five small figures are line-counts, says he will set his own count against each as he comes to it, and goes out sideways without saying good afternoon to anybody.** At half past four in the front street he names himself to the holder of that writ as Peat Marrow, says he has counted April, and says he will do the second month on Friday.

### Chapter 404 — *Friday the Twenty-Seventh of August, a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Asked for by Name on Wednesday and Paid in Coin at About Four in the Afternoon on the Flat of the Bench Stone at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Out of That Yard's Own Figures, a Man of About Thirty-Eight Out All Day on the Sixth Clause Again and a Loaf and a Half and a Candle and a Pot at Forty-Four Pence, the Second Block of a Return Counted on the Flat of a Hand, and the Third Day of a Refusal on a Door*

**THE COST OF THE BATCH IS ON A STONE IN COIN AND IT BUYS NOTHING THAT IMPROVES ANYTHING.** The caulker was asked for that Friday by name at about ten past five on the Wednesday, out loud, for the other end of a garboard on the second lay that has been open since June and that nobody wanted, and says that the arrangement has not changed since the tenth of August and that he will do it because he was asked on the Wednesday, and that if he is asked on the Monday he will do it and tell him on the Tuesday. He is paid at about four on the flat of the bench stone, counts it with his own thumb, and is not thanked; he puts his maul down on the plank while that is being said, which is the only time anybody in that yard has seen him do it with another man talking. **He says that the nineteenth and the twentieth days of August past were not paid and are not on anything and are not going in the bag, and the holder wrote that down.** Forty-four pence goes to a man of about thirty-eight who is out all day on the sixth clause, out of that yard's own bag and not out of the owner of a boat of about thirteen tons. Peat Marrow does the second block and writes neither figure on his hand, because he said he would say it on a day and this was the day he would do it. A herring skipper of fifty-one with a boat called the *Anna Ray* of about fifty tons and nineteen winters against him is one of six men a woman of about fifty-eight tells what a day costs, and he says he would not do it for that, and she says good to him.

### Chapter 405 — *Saturday the Twenty-Eighth of August, a Full Market and a Man at the End of the Middle Aisle Who Asked How Many and Was Told That There Was Not a Figure and That If There Was One It Was Not Going Up on Anything, a Woman of About Fifty-Eight Who Did Not Put a Hand on Her Slate, the Third Block of a Return Counted at a Wall, and the Reason Entered Once and Only Once in the Second Column in That Yard's Own Mouth*

**THE COUNT IS REFUSED IN A MARKET AND THE FOURTH COLUMN IS SHUT WITH A REASON.** A cooper of about forty-four with a shop on the far street and three boats behind him in six years asks in the middle aisle, with about nine hundred people in that market, how many pieces of recovered glass have been landed and entered at that harbor. He is told there is not a figure, and that the sheet it would come off is nailed to a wall in a room off the west basin and is a return that decides nothing and binds nobody, and that if there were a figure it is not going up on anything and not going in that front street and not going on the wall in that other street. **Peat Marrow is four feet off looking at a basket of clams and says nothing, and the woman of about fifty-eight tells the man to buy his clams and go home.** In the shed that evening, with four people in it, the holder says the reason out loud once: the yard's time went into the first column and into a convoy and into a caulker's day; the fourth column is a page no man can check; and there was a man on the flat of the bench stone at four in the morning on the Friday who had to be paid first, and was paid, before anybody in that yard put a word down about what a thing is not. **The reason goes in the second column in the ship's own left hand with the hour against it, at about ten past nine, and is entered once and is entered again nowhere.** A man of about thirty-one of the third lay with a chart in a bag says that somebody will say the page is blank and not say why, and is told yes, and that there is no arrangement that stops it.

### Chapter 406 — *Sunday the Twenty-Ninth of August, a Man of About Twenty-Three at the Other End of a Garboard With Nobody Standing Over Him, Two Rooms That Cannot Both Be the Room, a Woman of No Office Who Says One of the Two Out Loud and Is Not Asked One Question Back, the Fourth Block of a Return Counted at a Wall, the Fifth Day of a Refusal on a Door, and Two Lights That Have Not Moved in Twenty-Eight Days*

**THE AFTERTASTE IS TOLD OUT OF TWO BODIES AND THE TWO HALVES ARE NOT MATCHED.** Eleven minutes on a gunwale with a caulker, in which the only sentences are that the holder is not going to say anything and that if they are still standing there at noon the caulker is going to have to eat. A clerk of about sixty comes out from behind a counter and says he would not have thought that one was right, and is told he had not counted it and was not going to and that it was not his sheet. On the mole at half past four she says one half of what she is carrying out loud — tar, a hot iron, something under it with no name, and a woman counting in the dark and not losing her place — and he says he has not got a smell, he has got a window with a board across the outside of it and a line of daylight under the board that does not move, and a man's hand going by on water four feet down that is not frightened. **They agree in their own mouths to stop and not to try to match them, because the day one of them matches them by guessing is the day one of them is wrong for the rest of their lives.** The ship's hand prices five days out loud at half past nine and puts the largest item in the second column with the reason that the first column is a place a stranger can check and there is no stranger in that harbor who can check this.

### Chapter 407 — *Monday the Thirtieth of August, the Sixty-Ninth Time the Wall Came Down Bare and the Seventy-Seventh Time the Cistern Was Charged and Walked on None of It, a Man of About Fifty-One on the Crown of That Mole with His Page and His Stone and No Figure and Forty-Seven Days of Silence, a Copyist of About Fifty-Nine at Her Counter Who Has Not Once in Twenty-Two Years Asked What She Was Copying, the Last Block of a Return Counted at a Wall and Not Said to Anybody, and the Sixth Day of a Refusal on a Door*

**THE COPYIST, THE MAN WITH THE PAGE, THE LAST BLOCK, AND A SUM DONE ON THE BACK OF A SHEET.** A copyist of about fifty-nine, twenty-two years in a room off that market, sells him one sheet for a penny out of his own hand and says out loud, on purpose, that she has never once asked what she is copying and is not going to, and that what she is copying is a list of glass of about eleven inches with every line the same length and a seal on it she has not seen on anything else in twenty-two years, and gives her reason, being that a copyist who stops copying is a copyist who has admitted she copied something, and a trade can be put in a schedule and an admission cannot. The man of about fifty-one works at the edge of the two objects of nobody's with a piece of chalk and does not look across, and nobody gives him anything. Peat Marrow does the fifth and last block and stands at the wall afterwards, and a clerk of about sixty asks whether he wants the rest of it in a hand, and is told that he did not ask the man's name, and that he would have given it if he had. **At about half past five, on the mole, with the light out, the holder does the sum on the back of the good sheet, gets it wrong once, does it again on his own knee, and gets three hundred and ninety-one**, and folds the sheet in four and sits down on the flat of the bench stone, and is not going to ask anybody for anything on that stone for the next three nights, because a man who knocks on a door every second day is a man asking for a favour twice.

### Chapter 408 — *Tuesday the Thirty-First of August, the Forty-Fifth Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It and Forty-Five Weeks Standing Fallen Due, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence In and One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Out on the Same Day at the Same Figure, a Second Caulker's Day Asked for by Name on the Saturday Before, a Man of About Fifty With Two Papers and a Fourth Box He Wants Left Empty, and a Nine-Line Sheet With a Seal on It in the Front Street Since the Fourteenth That Nobody Put Up and Nobody Has Answered*

**A DAY THAT GOES IN AND COMES OUT AT THE SAME FIGURE, AND A MAN WHO HAS READ A CLAIM FOUR TIMES AND WILL NOT ANSWER IT.** The second caulker's day is asked for by name on the Saturday, which is what he said he would do, and he is paid at about four in coin on the stone and the holder says nothing to him at all, which is the third time in a month. The man of about fifty with two papers tells him that this office keeps a register copy of what it is given, that the sheet this yard gave on the seventh of July is on a shelf behind that counter, that it is his to have any day, and that he has not asked for it in fifty-five days. He says the same about the nine-line sheet in the front street: read four times, still up, names no person and no harbor and puts no figure on it, not answered and not going to be, and **the answer to a thing like that is a piece of paper with a name at the foot of it and not a word said in a market.** **The fourth box on the other paper is empty at the end of that day as it has been since the twenty-seventh of July and nobody in that room asked him about it.**

### Chapter 409 — *Wednesday the First Day of September, a Man of About Fifty-Three With a Bad Back Who Said a Number Out Loud in a Front Street on a Day He Had Named and Was Not Thanked for It and Was Not Paid for It, Three Hundred and Ninety-One Put Into the First Column With the Five Summands and the Line Count Written Under It So That a Stranger With a Leaf and a Pencil Can Take It Again, a Caulker on the Bench Stone at Half Past Three That Morning and Nobody in That Harbor on It With Him, and the Eighth Day of a Refusal on a Door*

**THE COUNT IS SAID OUT LOUD ONCE AND GOES IN THE FIRST COLUMN, AND THE HOUR ENDS.** At about a quarter to nine a man is standing outside the shed door with his hand over his back, and at ten past nine he says it, in his own mouth, on a day he had named on the Thursday before: **one hundred and forty-five lines, twenty-nine struck across, one hundred and sixteen carrying a figure, and the summands seventy-one, ninety-six, seventy-nine, eighty-eight and fifty-seven, which is three hundred and ninety-one.** He says he counted the lines of April and of May twice because of the bad back and the other three once, and added every one of the hundred and sixteen figures exactly once, and set his own count against the clerk's small figure at the head of each block as he came to it, and all five of them were right. He is not thanked and not paid and says he would do it again on a Saturday and is not going to be in that room on a Saturday. **The figure goes into the first column of that yard's own leaf in the holder's hand with the five summands and the line count under it and with no name against it, and is read out in that shed at about ten past four with the hour against it, and it is the first figure this yard has had that does not depend on anybody's word.** A woman of no office puts it beside a loss of about half of sixty tons of flour on the twenty-first of August with no claim laid and nobody made whole, and neither cancels the other and no choice between them is going to be asked for. At six in the evening he goes up the hill, reads both papers, and does not knock, because tomorrow is the ninth day.

### Chapter 410 — *Thursday the Second Day of September, the Seventy-Eighth Time the Cistern Was Charged and Walked on None of It, the Ninth Day of a Refusal and a Second Paper on the Same Door With a Second Hour on It and a Figure at the Foot of It in the Hand of the Man Who Wrote the Refusal, a Mole Head at Ten Past Five With the Light Not Lit, a Leaf Read Back in Full With the Four Figures on the Face of It and the Definition of Every Figure on the Face of It and a Fourth Column Standing at One Hundred and Twenty-Five Taking No Line, and the Standing List Referred to and Not Entered in Full*

**THE MOVEMENT'S PROBLEM IS ON THE FACE OF A PIECE OF PAPER AND THE PAPER IS A DOOR.** The refusal is taken down by the hand that wrote it and a second paper is pinned under the first: the same three lines naming two as permitted and one as present for the whole of the hour, the same three lines under them, an hour of ten in the morning on **the fifth day of October, a Tuesday**, and at the foot, where the first had a seal line, five lines in a clerk's own hand and no seal — the paper was asked for on the twenty-fifth, held nine days, the reason is a figure, and the figure is seven: a copy of that thing, marked with where it came from, is seven hours at that bench and a pair of hands; one hour is one; both of those are true and neither of them cancels the other. **He reads those five lines five times and does not knock and does not touch the door and goes back down the hill.** The ship's hand reads the leaf back at about ten past five on the flat of the bench stone with the light not lit, in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, with both definitions of the four figures on the face of the reading, and states that the fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines in it at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close and has taken no line since the twenty-third of August, and that that is not a closure and not a strike-out, and that the reason was entered once in the second column on the twenty-eighth and is entered again nowhere. **The standing list is referred to and is not entered in full, and the whole of the ten days is closed in one bold block that says in its own face that the standing inventory is not in it.**

### The repairs made in this batch, and the shape of the volume after ten chapters of it

### Chapter 411 — *Friday the Third Day of September, a Room over a Joiner's Shop at the Top of Fish Street With a Table in It and a Bound Book on the Table and Four People Reading It Through From the Front Page to the Back, a Working Man of About Forty-Six Called Hobb Lee Who Mends Nets on the Third Lay and Who Can Read and Who Is Going to Read Every Head-Note in That Room Out Loud With His Own Name and the Hour Under It, a Bowl Carried Down to the Step at Two o'Clock on a Sunday, a Head at the Front of That Volume Saying the Refusals Are on It Too and Are Not Smaller Than the Rest, a Paper at the Top Left of That Door Which Is Not the Notice of the Seventeenth of May and Which Has Been There Three Days, and a Count of Six and a Count of Five Which Added Together Is Eleven*

**THE BOOK IS FOUND AND IT IS A TABLE AND A ROOM AND NOTHING ELSE.** A room over a joiner's shop at the top of Fish Street with a long table, four benches, a lamp on a nail, no board on the wall, no list, no name over the door, let out on a Sunday by a man of about thirty-four who carries a bowl down to the step at two and takes it in at six and does not ask who is going in, and who gave his reason, being that a list in a room that is let out is a list of whoever could not afford not to come. The book is bound in a canvas re-backed twice, about two inches thick, opens flat, was begun on the twentieth of April past, and carries **thirty heads** on the said day. Its head is five lines: four lines under every head, being what the thing is, where it came from, who stands where it is and what it does not show; the refusals are on it too and are not smaller than the rest; nothing entered in it is a decision and nothing binds anybody and a man's no goes in with the reason against his name and his name as plainly as a yes; and head-notes are read out on a Sunday with the reader's name and the hour in his own hand on the day. **The second line of that head has been rubbed at the end for about forty years of an elbow on a table, and the man who keeps the room declined to say why, giving the reason that the first year is not this year and is not his telling.** Four people read it through from the first page to the last, being the holder of that writ, a woman of no office, the man of about forty-six, and at about half past six a man of about twenty-six who stacks empties. Its composition is given in full: twenty-two pieces of glass out of wrecks, a lamp, a door plate, a box of tally sticks, a whole bell with a man paid a shilling a week to wipe it and the only wage on that page, and two doors off a house, a barometer off a chandler's counter, a hatch cover off a fishing boat and a looking-glass off a lodging house. **Of the thirty, twenty-nine carry four lines under the head and one carries three, and its third line ends in a dash.** A count of eleven people who cannot read was arrived at that day by two people counting separately and adding — **six by the woman of about fifty-eight in her own trade, five by the man of about twenty-six on the quay, six and five is eleven** — and the man of about forty-six said on that stair that the eleven will find out what is in that book because somebody will stand in that room on a Sunday and read it out loud, and that he will write his name and the hour under each head, and that a man of forty-six does not charge a room for reading to a man who cannot read. And at the top left of that door there is a paper under a drawing-pin and a fold of oiled paper, and it is not the notice of the seventeenth of May past.

### Chapter 412 — *Saturday the Fourth Day of September, a Paper at the Top Left of a Door Read Out in Full in a Shed With the Hour Against It and the Drawing-Pin Under a Fold of Oiled Paper Kept There by the Man Who Put It Up, a Man of About Forty-One Called Walter Dunn Who Was on a Ladder in a Passage at Eleven o'Clock at Night on the Nineteenth of August and Found a Lamp of About Four Inches Burning in a Room With Nothing in the Room, Eleven People Asked One at a Time and One of the Eleven in That Room on That Night, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence of a Day With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In, and Nobody in That Harbor Has Answered That Paper*

**THE PAPER IS READ IN FULL AND ITS AUTHOR IS FOUND IN A PASSAGE FOUR FEET WIDE WITH A PUMP IN IT.** Four lines and no heading and no seal: a lamp of about four inches found burning in that room on the night of the nineteenth of August at eleven with nothing in the room with it; eleven people asked one at a time on the days following whether they had been in that room on that night; **one of the eleven was**; the person who found the lamp will not say which and has been asked by two persons of that street to say and has not said; and anybody found to have been in that room on that night is to take himself, or herself, off out of this harbor before the twentieth of September next. It went up on the **thirty-first of August** past and not the first of September, before the market filled, with a pin under a fold of oiled paper so that it cannot be taken out in about a second. **Walter Dunn, about forty-one, the night man at the fish market steps for eleven years, was on a ladder in the passage behind that shop at eleven o'clock on the nineteenth with a shutter off his hand, and the top left pane of that fanlight has been out since the spring and there is no glazier in that harbor with the money to come and put a pane in.** The room holds a table, two benches and a lamp on a nail and has no cupboard, no chest, no shelves and no box in it, and a man with a barrow could not have done it in that room in four minutes without knocking a bench over, and the lamp is four inches and would not survive four inches of a market and a slip, so what was in that room was in a pocket or a hand. He asked the eleven in ones over four days, each in front of nobody, and **he has them written in his own hand in his coat in the order he asked them in and has shown them to nobody and has not destroyed them, and has thought about which of those two he was going to do for about a week.** He has been asked twice to take it down and has not. He said the whole of that paper is a date at the end of the fourth line, and that a name on a door is a different kind of thing from a date on a door and cannot be taken off again. The woman of about fifty-eight read the four lines off another person's slate, said she is not going to tell the six in her own trade, gave her reason, and said who was going to tell them. And on the Saturday night somebody put a mark in chalk about two inches across under that paper on the door itself, and Calder Marr saw it on the Sunday morning and did not find out then who had made it, and the man who made that mark was not found on the Monday and was not found on the Tuesday.

### Chapter 413 — *Sunday the Fifth Day of September, a Bowl Carried Down to the Step of a Room over a Joiner's Shop at Two o'Clock and Taken In Again at Six With Whatever Is in It, About Twenty People in That Room of Whom Eleven Cannot Read, a Man of About Forty-Six Reading Every Head-Note Out Loud off the Long Table and Writing His Own Name and the Hour Under Each One in His Own Hand on the Day, a Woman of About Fifty-Eight Who Would Not Have the Figure of Lamp Oil Entered in That Volume and Whose No Was Entered at the Same Size as Every Other Line on the Page With Her Name and the Hour Against It, and a Woman of About Sixty-One of the Third Lay Called Nell Carrow Who Came Up Those Stairs With a Stick and Asked One Question at the End of That Table*

**THE FIRST LETTING, THE FIRST READING, A REFUSAL ENTERED IN PUBLIC, AND ONE QUESTION AT THE END OF A TABLE.** The bowl stood on the top stone of the step from two until six, and ninepence was in it at six, and the man who lets that room out did not stand at the window and went past a person on the step twice without looking at his face. About twenty went up and four came down and eleven of the twenty could not read and were not asked to prove it. The reader read the head-notes in the order they were in and wrote his own name and the hour at which he finished each one, the first at four minutes past two, the nineteenth at twenty-one minutes past two. **The nineteenth head, entered on the ninth of June, is of two boats of a man of about forty-four of the second lay, of nine and eleven tons, who came on the seventh of June and said no, and it carries four lines and his name and an eleven-word reason and it was read out in that room for the first time; a man near the door said he had been in that room in June and had not known there was a no in it, and the reader said, without looking up, that the no was in it in June for anybody who had opened it, and that if the man of about forty-four wanted it off the page he could come up the stairs on a Sunday and say so and it would be entered in the same four lines with the same size hand and the hour.** At about half past three the woman of about fifty-eight stood up at her end of the table and refused, out loud, to have the figure of lamp oil entered, being four hundred and fifty pence with February's three hundred and seventy-eight above it and both dates on a board, and gave her reason: a figure on a board is a figure in a place where a man has to come to it, and a figure in a book is read out loud in a room, and every person who cannot read will be told a number for oil out loud in a room, and by the end of next month the next barrel will be a pound higher and it will be because a man read it out in a room and forty people heard it and one of them was standing at a counter and told another one what he had heard. The ship's hand, from the step, said she was right. **Her no was entered as the thirty-first head, in the same hand and the same size as every other line, with her name and the hour against it, and read out in that room, and she was not thanked in that room and did not ask to be.** At about ten to four a woman of about sixty-one of the third lay came up one step at a time with a stick and a bad knee, waited twenty minutes without interrupting, and asked one question in her own mouth: **does that book hold a thing a person made themselves.** She was told it does not, because a thing a person made with their own hands is not recovered. She said it is the wrong book for her and that she has been in the wrong book for about forty-two years, and that she has got one about eleven inches by eight in a box in her back room, that it has been there since the year she was nineteen, that she has not looked at it in a long while, and that she would like to look at it in a room with people in it because she has had forty-two years of nobody. She was told the room was open at one o'clock on a Sunday, that anybody who brought a thing to that table could take it away again, and that about twenty people would be in the room, and that if she would rather have four people she could say so now. She said twenty. Nobody thanked her and there is no name against her.

### Chapter 414 — *Monday the Sixth Day of September, the Seventieth Time the Wall Behind the Reeve's Bench Came Down Bare and Went Up Whole at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth and Nobody Put It Back, the Seventy-Ninth Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine, a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Asked for This Day by Name on the Friday Before and Paid in Coin on the Flat of the Bench Stone at About Four in the Afternoon at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Out of That Yard's Own Figures, a Panel of Worked Glass About Eleven Inches by Eight on Shelf Four in a Store on the Second Lay With a Scene in It and a Note of Four Lines in Another Man's Hand Pinned to the Lid of the Box It Came In, and a Man of About Fifty-Five Called Ned Vaile Who Says in His Own Mouth What Happened in a Room on the Eighteenth Day of June*

**THE PANEL, THE NOTE, THE DASH, AND WHAT FOUR MEN DID IN A ROOM ON THE EIGHTEENTH OF JUNE.** The wipe and the cistern are printed and the ship's hand prices the wall: a figure exists and it is not that yard's, and both of those are true and neither cancels the other. A man of about thirty-four with the keys to two stores took the holder of that writ up a stair outside the building and down a passage with a bucket in it to a room about nine feet by eleven with a window that does not shut, and on shelf four at the height of a man's chest there are nine things, six of them panels, and the fourth from the left is a panel of worked glass about eleven inches by eight in a shallow box with a lid, and there is a note on the lid that has been there since the fourth of June and is not the store's and is not the harbor's, and he has not read it and is not going to. The note is four lines and a man's name and not an office: **sound at the join; the join will take a mend and it will take a backing; landed the fourth of June at the third lay out of a hull with her bottom opened and the panel out whole.** The panel was looked at standing up and was not taken out of the box, and **what is in it is a room with a door in it and a figure a little way inside the door with its back to whoever is looking at it, and the figure is about four inches high and has a shoulder and a hip and a hand, and the hand is up at the height of its own chest with the fingers not shut, and the light comes in on the side of the room the door is not on.** The holder of that writ said out loud that he has been in this harbor nine months and can look in about nine hundred places where something is kept and can stand in front of one of them and say a person is in that panel, and that a book on a table over a joiner's shop says in four lines what every one of those places does not show, and does not say this one, **and that that is not a lie in it: there are three lines on that page and one of them is true and one of them is true and one of them ends in a dash, and a dash is not a lie, a dash is a hole.** He said nobody is to be charged, nobody is to be told they have to move it, nobody is to be told what it is for, and the man who marked it in will not be asked. **Ned Vaile, about fifty-five, who marks at the fish quay and has kept the marks of that volume since the twentieth of April and is not paid for it and is not a conservator, said that on the eighteenth of June there were four men in that room, two of them off boats, that he had the head ruled with four lines under it and the note in his hand, that he copied the note into the first line, put where it came from into the second and the shelf into the third because the man who carries the glass said where it was going, and that he asked one of those four men, in front of the other three, what that panel was not fit for, and was told he did not know, and that none of the other three said anything, and there was about a quarter of a minute, and then the man who carries the glass said they were holding him up. He put a dash because he was not going to write down a thing nobody had said to him.** He said a dash is true and a dash is a hole and that he has known it was a hole since the eighteenth of June and has not come back to it in eighty days, and that the reason he did not ask twice is that he asked it in front of three other men and got nothing and went away and has not been asked to go back and has not offered to go back, and that there is a difference between those two things about eighty days wide. And he said the reason he has never found it himself is that he has written the fourth line on page after page since the twentieth of April and has never once gone down that volume with a pencil and counted what was in the fourth line of each head, and that a man who has not looked does not get to tell a man who has looked what is there. The caulker was paid at about four and said out loud, on his own account, that the holder had not asked him since the thirty-first.

### Chapter 415 — *Tuesday the Seventh Day of September, the Forty-Sixth Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It and Forty-Five Weeks Standing Fallen Due at the Open of the Ten Days From the Twenty-Fourth of August and Forty-Six Standing at the Close of Them, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence of a Day With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In, a Man of About Thirty-Four Who Was in That Room in June Asking a Man of About Forty-Six to Read Four Lines Off a Door Out Loud in a Room on a Sunday and Being Refused by Him in His Own Mouth With His Own Reason, and a Woman of About Fifty-Eight Who Counted Six in Her Own Trade and a Man of About Twenty-Six Who Counted Five on a Quay*

**THE WAGE TUESDAY, AND THE ONE REFUSAL IN THIS MOVEMENT THAT COULD HAVE BROKEN IT.** The column has twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks and twenty envelopes in a chest and has not moved since the fourth of April past, and forty-four weeks stood fallen due at the close of the twenty-third of August, the forty-fifth fell on the thirty-first, this is the forty-sixth, the column did not move, and the forty-seventh is the fourteenth of September next. The ship's hand opened it, read the top line, shut it, and wrote the number of the week against the reason, and the number is forty-six, and she said a week is a week that came and went and the first column is a count of things a stranger can check and a week is a week. Then **a man of about thirty-four who had been in that room in June came up the stairs at about half past three and asked the man of about forty-six to read the four lines off that door aloud on a Sunday, to everybody in the room, before he read the heads — a minute, that is all I am asking for — and was refused.** The refusal is in his own mouth with his own reason: because those eleven would never hear a head-note in that room again if they were sitting at that table waiting for the paper, and because he was nine years old in this harbor and there was a notice on a door and his mother read it to him out loud in a kitchen and he has never known since that day whether she made any of it up, and he would not put a man of about thirty-four in a room on a Sunday in front of twenty people and not know it for the rest of his life, and he said that is the whole of his reason and it is a selfish one and he has not got a better one. **He announced, before anybody did anything, exactly what he was going to do about the eleven: on the Wednesday he would walk round the harbor on his own two feet and tell eleven people one at a time, in the street, in their own doors, in daylight and face to face, that there is a paper on that door with four lines on it, that it is a paper and not the notice on the wall in the other street, that a volume is going to be read out loud on a Sunday, and that he was not going to read that paper to them and they were not to ask him to; and that if one of those eleven is the one, then in thirteen days that one will read it himself on that door with his own eyes in his own time, not told by a single person in that harbor.** The woman of about fifty-eight came down the slip at about five, put her slate on the bench stone face up, and did not touch it, and read out the cost of the Sunday: two hours and twenty minutes, a shilling not earned, a bowl on a step that has to be made whether he is there or not — all of it his own, none of it out of anybody's bag, and no figure in that harbor for what a man gives up on a Sunday because he is reading a book for people who cannot read, and that is why it goes in the second column.

### Chapter 416 — *Wednesday the Eighth Day of September, a Man of About Forty-Six Walking Round That Harbor on His Own Two Feet in Daylight and Talking to Eleven People One at a Time in Their Own Doors and Not Showing Any of Them the Four Lines and Not Reading Them and Saying Out Loud That He Was Not Going To, Forty-Four Pence Going Out of That Yard at About Half Past Ten in the Morning for a Loaf and a Half and a Candle and a Pot, a Man of About Thirty-Eight With a Boat of About Thirteen Tons and No Papers Out All Day on the Sixth Clause of a Notice in a Different Street, and a Man of About Forty-One Coming Up a Stair at Four o'Clock in the Afternoon to Ask Whether Anybody Had Answered a Paper He Had Put Up on a Door on the Thirty-First of August*

**ELEVEN CONVERSATIONS, THREE OF THEM PRINTED, AND THE ONE THING HE TOLD THE MAN WHO PUT THE PAPER UP.** Forty-four pence went out at about half past ten for a loaf and a half, a candle and a pot, to a man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers on her who was out all day on the sixth clause in a different street, out of that yard's own bag and not out of the owner of that boat, and a woman of no office put forty pence of her own into the bowl on the step at a quarter past one and did not say why and was not asked. From about nine in the morning to about four in the afternoon a man of about forty-six walked round that harbor on his own two feet and had eleven conversations with eleven people, one at a time, in the street and in their own doors, in daylight, and to each of them he said the same eleven sentences: that there is a paper with four lines on it at the top left of the door at the top of Fish Street, that it went up on the thirty-first of August, that a volume is read out loud at that table on a Sunday at two o'clock, that there is a bowl on the step and they may put a penny in it or not, and that the notice on the wall in the other street is a different paper on a different wall — and that he will not read the paper to them, will not show it to them, and will not tell them what is on it, and that if they ever want to read it, that is their business and their eyes. **He showed none of the eleven the paper and read it to none of them, and told a woman of about thirty-one with a barrow of fish who asked him whether he knew what was on it that he did not know and had not read it and was not going to, and gave his reason for telling them at all, being that in four days he is going to stand at the end of that table and read out loud in a room, and if he does not say this in the street in daylight they will find out what that room is from him in front of about twenty people.** Four of the eleven went on longer than a minute and the shortest was about forty seconds, and not one of the eleven asked him to read it. The eleventh was a man of about sixty-two who has sat on the same bollard at the head of a slip every day since June, who said it was the first anybody had told him about anything in that harbor in about a month, and that he would come on Sunday if the door were not shut. **Tom Barlas, who is the man of about thirty-four who lets that room out, came up the stairs at about four and asked whether anybody had answered that paper and was told no, and was told about the chalk cross made on the Saturday night by a boy of about nineteen on a man's word in a taproom, and then was told — after Walter Dunn, the man of about forty-one who put the paper up, had come up those stairs at about half past two and been told the same answer — that somebody in that harbor has been eleven times to a room over a joiner's shop on a Sunday since the twentieth of April and has gone down those stairs without leaving a mark, and that there is a working man of about forty-six at the end of that table who reads a book out loud to people who cannot read, and that neither of those things has ever once been written down in that harbor by anybody, and that a man who has been twice to a room and told nobody and a woman who has been four times to a room and told nobody are not in a position to go to a man in a taproom and say a paper on a door is a lie.** He went down the stairs and did not say one word and has not been up them since. A caulker was asked for the Friday by name at about five and said he would want it said to him on the Thursday.

### Chapter 417 — *Thursday the Ninth Day of September, the Eightieth Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine on a Rota of a Monday and a Thursday, a Man of About Forty-Six Walking Down to the Third Lay at About Two in the Afternoon and Asking a Woman of About Sixty-One One Question and Not Asking Her a Second, Nine Marks a Year for a Room With a Rope Walk in the Back of It That Has Been Nine Marks for Eleven Years, a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Told on the Thursday the Thing He Asked to Be Told on the Thursday, and a Man Who Decides Not to Count a Volume Himself and Says Out Loud Why He Is Not Going To*

**ONE QUESTION ASKED ONCE, AND A PENCIL PUT DOWN TWO INCHES AWAY FROM A LEDGER.** The cistern was charged at about eight and walked on at about half past nine, being the eightieth time, on a rota of a Monday and a Thursday, and the top name on that board is still off it. **The man of about forty-six went down to the third lay at about two in the afternoon and asked a woman of about sixty-one one question, being whether she would bring a thing out of a box in her back room to a long table in a room over a joiner's shop on Sunday the twelfth at one o'clock and put it on that table and look at it with about twenty people in the room; and he offered her a barrow and a hand at the top of two flights of stairs at half past twelve and did not offer again; and she said you have come once, so say it once and then go away and do not come again about it.** He said it once. **She asked him one question back, being whether there would be people in the room when she looked at it, and was told there would be about twenty, and she said then bring the barrow, and that she would be there at one o'clock and not before, and that she is not going early to be helped in, and that she is not going to be thanked at the top of that stair or at the bottom of it or anywhere else, and that if anybody in that room says a kind thing to her she will walk out.** He said he would tell them and would not soften it, because a thing that is softened in a message is a thing that has been said twice. No second question was asked her by anybody in that yard on the said day. **Her room on that lay is nine marks a year, being one thousand four hundred and forty pence, and it has been nine marks for eleven years, and there is a rope walk about forty feet long in the back of it that does not run, and nobody has ever raised it and nobody in that yard is going to.** A caulker was told on the Thursday that he was wanted on the Friday, which is what he asked to be told and when he asked to be told it, and said it had cost the holder of that writ nothing and was the only thing in that harbor that had cost him nothing this year. And in that shed at about six in the evening **the holder of that writ said out loud that he was not going to count that public volume with a pencil in his own hand**, and gave the reason, being that if he went in there on a Saturday with a pencil and counted the fourth lines, then whatever he found he found, and he found it because a panel with a person in it is on shelf four of a store on the second lay and he has been in nine hundred places in this harbor looking for things and did not like what he saw, **and a man with a grievance and a pencil is not a count, it is a complaint with a number at the end of it**; that the man of about fifty-three with a bad back who counted a municipal return on his own time in five afternoons was a different thing, because nobody sent him and nobody paid him and nobody thanked him and it went in with no name against it and it is in no mouth and on no wall; that some man who walks in off a street because there is nothing else to do is going to pick that volume up off that table because it is the only thing in the room with writing on it, and is going to count something on the back of his own hand because he counts things for a living, **and that is a finding and not an instruction and there is no way anybody can get at it afterwards and say it was arranged**; that he is not going to plant him; and **that he put the pencil down two inches from that yard's own leaf and it is going to stay two inches away, and that on Sunday he is going to be in that room and is not going to watch anybody's hands, and that if he sees a man count something on the back of his own hand he is going to go outside and stand in that street until he has finished, and he is not going to be the first person in that room to know.**

### Chapter 418 — *Friday the Tenth Day of September, a Barrel of Lamp Oil That Cannot Be Had at Any Figure in a Harbor Where a Figure of Four Hundred and Fifty Pence With Three Hundred and Seventy-Eight Above It and Both Dates on a Board Stands Visible on a Board, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence of a Day With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out in Coin on the Flat of the Bench Stone at About Four in the Afternoon to a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Who Had Been Asked for That Day by Name on the Wednesday Before, and a Man of About Thirty-One With a Chart in a Bag Who Came and Stood at the End of a Long Table for Ten Minutes and Said Nothing*

**THE HARBOR GETS WORSE ON A FIGURE THAT CANNOT BE TAKEN OFF, AND A MAN WITH A CHART IN A BAG SAYS THE ONE SENTENCE THAT IS THE ARGUMENT AGAINST A PUBLIC BOOK.** A day at a berth came in and a second caulker's day went out at the same figure and the bag did not move up. **There has been no barrel of lamp oil in that harbor since the twenty-ninth day of August and there was none on the said day, and a board at an end stall carries four hundred and fifty pence, being thirty-seven shillings and sixpence, with the first of June against it, and carries February's three hundred and seventy-eight pence, being thirty-one shillings and sixpence, standing visible above it with the first of February against it, and the figure of four hundred and fifty pence was not taken off that board and cannot be taken off.** A man of about thirty-three put a tin can on the board and was told there is none. The woman of about fifty-eight said she can get a man to go and ask at the office on the west basin and the answer is the same as the one she has just given, and that she has asked twice and is not going to ask a third time this month, because a woman who asks a third time is a woman who has nothing else to do; and **that she is not taking that figure off, and that it is a figure for a thing that exists somewhere between here and four hundred miles away, and that when there is oil in that harbor she will sell it at that figure and make a mark under it, and if it is higher she will make the mark higher and the four hundred and fifty will still be up there with the first of June against it.** She wrote one word in chalk on the edge of that slate in her own hand, where she wrote it in August, **and would not rule a line under the oil figure, and gave the reason, being that a line with one word on it under a figure goes up the street in about an hour and by Tuesday there is a queue at her stall and by the end of next week every man in that market will be saying the oil has gone and in a month there will be a man on that mole who tells you there has not been oil at that stall since the spring, and that is easier to believe than to remember a figure.** She added that there is no flour in that market and that she has not sold a sack of it since the spring. **A man of about thirty-one of that lay with a chart in a bag came up the stairs at about ten past four and stood at the end of the long table for about ten minutes with his hands behind his back and did not read the volume and did not touch it, and everybody in that room carried on, and at the bottom of the stairs he said one sentence: somebody is going to read that thing out loud in a room and about eleven people who cannot read are going to be in it, and every one of them will be told it on somebody's word, and in about a fortnight one of the eleven will say in a market that a thing in that book is not so, and nobody will be able to put a hand on where he got it, and there is no arrangement that stops that.** The reader said it will be a man with a mouth, and that is not a fault in a book, and that the only thing anybody can do about it is make sure the word is the truth, and that he cannot do that, because he is a net-mender with no way of knowing what is true and no claim on any. He is not on a sheet and not on a list and nobody in that yard is to go and ask him about a chart in a bag. **The caulker was paid for the sixth time since the tenth of August past, and the six are the seventeenth, the twenty-first, the twenty-seventh and the thirty-first of August past and the sixth and the tenth of September, and the tenth of August past was the payment before those six and is not one of them, and he said out loud that the holder of that writ was going to have him on the Monday, and was told that he is not on the Monday until he is asked for it by name on the Friday before, and that there is no board with his name on it in that yard and there is not going to be one, and that if he wants to sit in that room on Sunday he will sit in that room on Sunday and will not be on anything; and he said that he will not be in that room on Sunday and did not say why and was not asked.**

### Chapter 419 — *Saturday the Eleventh Day of September, a Room over a Joiner's Shop Shut for the Week Day and a Joiner at the Bottom of the Stair and a Volume Lying at the End of a Table He Glues Battens Along From Six in the Morning, a Man of About Forty-Six Getting a Room Ready for the Second Sunday in About a Month of Sundays and Not Being Asked To, a Bowl Wiped Out and Put Back on the Top Stone of a Step, and a Man of About Thirty-One Called Arthur Sennett Who Writes Figures on a Slate for a Buyer at a Fish Stall and Who Came Up a Stair Nobody Had Told Him About and Read the Whole of a Book Nobody Had Asked Him To Read*

**THE ROOM IS GOT READY, AND SOMEBODY NOBODY WAS WAITING FOR WALKS IN.** The joiner does not live over his shop and was at the door of it at about ten with a plane in his hand, and the room had been had since ten and the door was off the latch, because it is a joiner's room on a week day and the joiner is in and out of it eight times a day and has never once locked it and there is nothing in that room to lock. **The reader cleaned the table, which took an hour, and it is a joiner's table and the glue is a week deep in the grain, and he did it with a scraper and then his sleeve and then a bucket and a cloth, and he did it because it is a table and not because a volume needed a clean table.** The four benches came out from under the wall, two on each long side, and two of them were wiped and two were left where they were. The lamp is on a nail and was not lit and is not going to be lit, and the room has one window that does not shut, and at half past four on a September afternoon there is enough light in there to read a page by. **The bowl was on the step from two until six because Tom Barlas puts it out on a Saturday as well as on a Sunday, and the joiner had told him in August that if a man is going to come up a stair on a day there is no reason to make him knock on a door that is not shut. It was empty at six. There was ninepence in it on the Sunday before and there is no figure for the ninepence and none is going to be printed.** The man of about thirty-four said, from the bottom of the stairs, that he had not been asked for anything, and that everybody who wants a room asks for something — a window opened, a lamp, a door shut, or how much it is — and that he does not mind that and minds being asked twice, and that it is out at two and in at six and he does not ask who comes and has never written one of them down, **because if he wrote one of them down it would be a list, and a list in a room that anybody can pay half a penny to walk into is a list of everybody in that harbor who could not afford half a penny.** A barrow went up two flights of stairs at about half past twelve and was stood at the top with the two handles up, and it belongs to the joiner, who lent it on the Thursday and was not asked for it and is not going to be thanked for it. The reader said he would read twenty-two of the thirty-one heads and would not read the other nine, being six pieces of glass off three wrecks together with a lamp, a door plate and a box of tally sticks, and that if a woman of about sixty-one comes up at one o'clock with a box on a barrow then it will be half past one before that table is clear and he is not going to stand at the top of that stair at half past one and tell a room of twenty people to wait. And at about half past four, **because the door was off the latch and the bottom of the stair was open, a man of about thirty-one called Arthur Sennett, who writes figures on a slate for a buyer at a fish stall and has done for nine years and whose hand is the only thing about him anybody in that market has ever noticed, came up that stair, stopped about two-thirds of the way up when he saw the volume lying open at the end of the table with about four inches of clean wood on either side of it, and read the whole of it from the back to the front and then from the front to the back in about fifty minutes, and wrote nothing, and did not go and get anybody, and shut it, and squared it to the edge of that table, and went down the stairs and out into Fish Street and went home. The reader came back up at about ten past five, found it shut and squared, and did not know that a man had been in that room until the following afternoon, and that is how it happened, and nobody arranged it.** What Arthur Sennett said out loud at the bottom of those stairs on the Sunday, which is the only thing he said in ten days and is not the finding and is not the beginning of the finding, was that a woman in that book refused to have her oil entered and was put in at the same size as a wreck, and that he has been writing figures on a slate for a buyer for nine years and knows exactly what a figure does when it is read out in a room, and that one is going to be in about eleven markets by Tuesday, and that he is not saying that is wrong, and that you have put a price on being a person and he does not know that anybody in that harbor has been asked whether they want that. The reader said no, they have not, and that he has thought about it since the Friday, and that it is too late to do anything about it now that it is in there, and that he would do it again, and that both of those are true and he is not going to pretend they are comfortable.

### Chapter 420 — *Sunday the Twelfth Day of September, a Barrow with Two Handles at the Top of Two Flights of Stairs at Half Past Twelve and a Woman of About Sixty-One of the Third Lay Coming Up Them at One o'Clock With a Box on It and Nobody Thanking Her at the Top of the Stair or at the Bottom of It, About Twenty People in a Room of Whom Eleven Cannot Read, a Man of About Forty-Six Reading Twenty-Two Head-Notes Out Loud and Writing His Own Name and the Hour Under Each, a Panel of About Eleven Inches by Eight Put on a Long Table by the Woman Who Made It and Looked at by About Twenty People, a Room That Emptied, a Box Carried Down Two Flights of Stairs, a Bound Volume Shut and Squared to the Edge of a Table, and a Man of About Thirty-One With a Stub of Pencil Behind His Ear Who Counted Thirty-One Heads on the Back of His Own Left Hand and Found That One of Them Carries Three Lines Where the Head of That Volume Says Four and Wrote It on the Inside of the Back Cover and Was Not Asked by Anybody Who Put It There*

**THE PANEL, THE EMPTY ROOM, THE BOOK SHUT, THE BOX CARRIED DOWN, THE PANEL PUT AWAY, AND THE OMISSION FOUND, IN THAT ORDER.** The barrow was at the top of the stairs at half past twelve and Tom Barlas took the second flight himself. **She came up at one o'clock. The box is about three foot by a foot by eight inches with a rope round it and it went up the first flight on the back of a woman of about sixty-one with a bad knee and a stick in one hand, and on the second flight it went up on her shoulders, and it took her about an hour and a half, and the man of about forty-six stood at the top of the stairs with the two handles and did not put a hand on the box and did not say one word.** There was nobody else in that room but a man of about fifty-five who stood at the end of the table with his hands behind his back and then went downstairs and came back at about a quarter to six and stood at the foot of the stairs. She cut the rope with a short knife out of her pocket, took the lid off, lifted the thing out with both hands, set it down, and stood looking at it. **It is about eleven inches by eight in a plain mitred deal frame with a nail in each corner and the glass set about a quarter of an inch proud of the wood, and there is a face in it and the face is about four inches high and is turned away from the room; and what is in the face is a room with a door in it and the door is shut and there is a figure a little way inside it with its back to whoever is looking at it, and the hand is up at the height of its own chest with the fingers not shut, and the light is coming in on the side of the room the door is not on.** She said she was not going to say anything about it and that if anybody in that room says a kind thing to her she will walk out; she put her hand flat on the frame and looked at it for about a minute and a half, and then she stepped back from the table so that the people coming up could see it, and went and stood at the back of that room against the wall with her stick in front of her, and did not look at it again for the rest of that afternoon. The bowl went on the step at two; about twenty went up and four came down and eleven of the twenty could not read. **The reader read twenty-two head-notes, the first at about two minutes past two and the last at about twenty-six minutes past three, and the last was the woman of about fifty-eight's refusal, and she said from the middle of the room that it is a strange thing to hear your own no read out in a room and she would not have thought of it and would not have had it any other way and is not going to say a kind thing about it now or ever.** He shut the volume and squared it to the edge of the table and the pencil went behind his ear, **and that is how it stood when the room emptied.** **The room emptied at about ten to five. There was no sound in it that anybody in that street heard from the pavement. There was a set of feet going down two flights, quickly, and then a door, and then a gap of about four minutes, and then feet again, and then a woman of about thirty-four saying something to nobody, and then nothing.** She put the lid on and cut the rope and put the barrow's handles up against the frame and started down, the first flight backwards with the wheel against the step above her, and the man of about forty-six took the other end without being asked and without saying anything and was not thanked for it, and he said nothing at the top of that stair and nothing at the bottom of it, and nobody in that room or on that step said one kind word to her, and nobody in that harbor has said one kind word to her since. **The holder of that writ had been outside in Fish Street since a quarter past four, standing in the doorway of the joiner's shop across the road, and he had not gone in, and he did not go in.** Then, at the bench stone with no lamp lit: **a man of about forty-one came down the slip at about ten past five and said he was in that room from about half past two until about five, that he was not looking at the thing on the table and was looking at the door the whole time, and that when he came out he could not tell in which order he had come down two flights of stairs and had to go back up and put his hand on the frame of the door at the top to find out; and that he has had a cold in his teeth since about three o'clock and his hands have not been right since about three o'clock and there is a taste of iron in his mouth like a nail, and it is not a fever and he has not got a headache and he could go out and lift a barrow of shavings, and his boy is going to be seven in November and he knows the number of his fingers; and that he is not going to be a man in this harbor who goes round saying that.** Calder Marr had nothing to give him, had not been in that room, and had gone and stood in a street on purpose; he said tell her the truth, and said that if he wants to know what is on that table he can go and ask the woman of about sixty-one and she will tell him no. **Then, on his way out at about ten past five, Arthur Sennett asked for the volume, sat on the bench at the joiner's end at the clean end, put his left hand flat on his left knee and wrote on the back of it with the stub of pencil from behind his ear, and counted for about four minutes, and said: thirty-one heads; thirty of them have four lines under the head; one has three; and the head of it at the front says four lines under every head, in five lines, and the second of those five says the refusals are on it too and are not smaller than the rest; and it is the twenty-second, it is of a panel of worked glass about eleven inches by eight out of a hull landed at the third lay on the fourth day of June, and the third line ends in a dash and there is nothing after the dash; and that is the whole of what I have found and I have found it with a pencil on my own hand and I did not know there was a dash in it before about four minutes ago.** Ned Vaile, at the foot of the stairs, said that he had not read the twenty-second since the eighteenth of June. The man said **he had not read it, but he had got the pencil behind his ear and had been in that room every Sunday since the twentieth of April, and a man who has been in that room every Sunday has read that page; that is not me saying you did it, I am not going to say that and I am not going to be asked, and if anybody asks me who left a dash at the end of the third line of the twenty-second head of that book I will say that I was not in that room on the eighteenth of June, and that is the true answer and it is the whole of the answer I have got.** He turned to the inside of the back cover, which is blank, and wrote four lines in pencil in a small hand: *Twelfth day of September. Thirty-one heads. Thirty with four lines under the head and one with three. The head at the front says four. It is the twenty-second and its third line ends in a dash. Found with a pencil on my own hand. I was not in the room on the eighteenth of June and I am not going to say who was.* — *A. Sennett, thirty-one.* He gave the volume back and the door went down at six with a bowl on the top stone of the step. **In the passage, Calder Marr asked in about six words whether it was true; Ned Vaile said that it was true and that he had known there was a dash in it since the eighteenth of June and had not come back to it; Calder Marr said that he had read that head on Friday the third and put his thumb on the third line and left the volume shut on that table and had not counted anything and had told the man of about thirty-four in that shed on the Thursday why a man with a stake is not a count; and then neither of them said one word about it, and they went down the hill together and neither of them said one word about it.** And at about ten past five the ship's hand read the leaf back on the flat of the bench stone in the open, all four columns including the empty one, with both definitions on the face of the reading: one hundred and fifty-two at the hour and one hundred and fifty-three at the close; six hundred and thirty-seven at the hour and six hundred and thirty-nine at the close; none; one hundred and twenty-five at the hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it and the column not closed and not struck out and the reason entered once on the twenty-eighth of August and entered again nowhere.

### The repairs made in this batch, and the shape of the volume after twenty chapters of it

**TWENTY REPAIRS AFTER THE WRITING PASS, ALL MECHANICAL, ALL IN TEN CHAPTER FILES, NO PLOT MOVED AND NO SCENE RESTARTED, AND THE FULL DISPOSITION AT `state/continuity.md` § 12. FOUR WERE WORKFLOW TERMS, THREE WERE DAY-COUNTS TO THE SAME DATE, TWO WERE WEEKDAYS AND DAY-COUNTS AGAINST THE HOUSE GRID, FIVE WERE WRONG MONEY GLOSSES IN NINE CHAPTERS, ONE WAS A BATCH'S OWN CLOSING TOTAL THAT DID NOT EVALUATE WHILE ITS DAY-BY-DAY CHAIN WAS RIGHT, TWO WERE COUNTED FIGURES THAT COULD NOT BE TRUE, ONE WAS A COUNTED FIGURE THAT WAS A FORWARD STATEMENT, ONE WAS THE PUBLIC BOOK'S OWN ARITHMETIC NOT CLOSING IN THREE CHAPTERS, ONE WAS SECOND PERSON IN NARRATION, AND THREE WERE DECLARATIONS OF ABSENCE REPLACED BY WHAT DID HAPPEN. THE FINDING THAT MATTERS IS THE HOUSE'S OWN AND IT IS THE SAME ONE IT HAS NOW MADE THREE TIMES IN TWO BATCHES: A CHAPTER CAN READ RIGHT ON ITS OWN AND BE WRONG AGAINST THE OTHER NINE, AND THE WAY TO FIND IT IS NOT TO RE-READ. ELEVEN OF THESE TWELVE FINDINGS WERE FOUND BY ADDING UP — days to a date, pence to a mark, heads to a total, weeks to a count — AND NOT ONE OF THEM WAS FOUND BY LOOKING AT THE PROSE, AND THAT IS THE RULE HANDED ON.**

**A SECOND REPAIR PASS OF THIRTEEN WAS THEN MADE IN THE SAME TEN FILES, IN THE FOUR STATE FILES AND IN THE QUEUED `workspace/volume-09/batch-0003/PROMPT.md`, ON THE REVIEW OF THE TWENTY, AND THE FULL DISPOSITION IS AT `state/continuity.md` § 12 ITEMS 21 TO 33. THE PROSE WAS NOT RESTARTED AND NO SCENE WAS CUT AND NO COST WAS MOVED AND NO STAGE WAS TAKEN. ONE ITEM WAS A WHOLE SENTENCE IN ALL TEN CHAPTERS AT ONCE, BEING THE DAILY APPARATUS SENTENCE, WHICH HAD BEEN SPLICED AT ITS MIDDLE WITH AN UNRELATED THIRD-COLUMN SENTENCE AND HAD LOST LOCK L9'S CLAUSE *NO DIGIT OF ANYTHING HE EVER SAID IS ON A PAGE* OUT OF ALL TEN, WHICH THE FIRST PASS'S § 10 SWEEP HAD NOT BEEN GIVEN THE TEST FOR. ONE WAS A DAY-COUNT AND ONE A CLAUSE THAT DID NOT EXIST. TWO WERE FIGURES WRONG AGAINST THE CHAPTERS' OWN CALENDAR AND THE BOOK'S OWN CONTENTS, BEING FOUR DAYS FOR NINE AND SIX PIECES OF GLASS FOR NINE. ONE WAS A COUNT OF YEARS THAT COULD NOT BE TRUE, BEING FIFTY-ONE FOR THIRTY-SEVEN, AND IT WAS IN FOUR PLACES IN TWO CHAPTERS AND IN THREE STATE FILES, AND IT WAS CARRIED OUT OF THE CHAPTERS INTO THE HAND-OVER BEFORE IT WAS CAUGHT. ONE WAS A PAPER THAT CHANGED OWNER BETWEEN TWO MEN TWENTY MINUTES APART ON ONE STAIR, AND THE REPAIR NAMED BOTH MEN AND MOVED ONE VISIT TWO HOURS, AND NOBODY'S PLACE IN THE DAY MOVED. ONE WAS THREE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE HOURS FOR ONE READING. ONE WAS A CHAPTER THAT SAID IT DID NOT KNOW WHO DID A THING AND THEN SAID WHO DID IT. THREE WERE CRAFT FINDINGS IN CHAPTER 420 AND 418, BEING A WOMAN NAMED TWICE IN ONE SENTENCE, A STANDING FIGURE OF ELEVEN REUSED IN A MOUTH FOR A DIFFERENT SET OF PEOPLE, AND A PAYMENT COUNT TRUE ONLY ON AN EXCLUSIVE READING OF *SINCE*. AND ONE WAS THE HAND-OVER ITSELF, BEING FIVE STATE AND prompt PLACES CARRYING *ABOUT ELEVEN PEOPLE IN A ROOM* AGAINST TWENTY ON THE FACE OF CHAPTER 420, A FALSE CLAIM THAT CHAPTER 420 CARRIES NO READ-BACK, AND A CLAIM THAT THE VOLUME'S SENTENCE WAS SAID ONCE IN EACH OF THE LAST TWO BATCHES, WHICH IS FALSE AND WHICH THE LOCK L29 RECORD IN `state/continuity.md` HAD ALSO GOT WRONG. THE SAME FINDING, A FIFTH TIME, IN THE SAME WORDS: NINE OF THESE THIRTEEN WERE FOUND BY ADDING UP AND NOT BY LOOKING, AND THE FOUR THAT WERE FOUND BY LOOKING WERE FOUND BY A REVIEWER LOOKING AT THE FACE OF TWO CHAPTERS AGAINST EACH OTHER AND NOT AT THE PROSE.**

**THE SHAPE OF VOLUME 09 AFTER TWENTY CHAPTERS OF IT, WHICH IS THE WHOLE OF IT AND IS PRINTED ONCE HERE: A ROOM OVER A JOINER'S SHOP AT THE TOP OF FISH STREET, LET OUT ON A SUNDAY BY A MAN WITH A SHUTTER BUSINESS WHO TAKES THE MONEY IN A BOWL AND HAS NEVER WRITTEN ONE PERSON DOWN. A BOUND VOLUME OF THIRTY-ONE HEADS ON A LONG TABLE, BEGUN ON THE TWENTIETH OF APRIL, CARRYING WHAT THIS HARBOR HOLDS, WHERE EACH THING CAME FROM, WHO STANDS WHERE IT IS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT SHOW, AND CARRYING THE RULE THAT THE REFUSALS ARE ON IT AND ARE NOT SMALLER THAN THE REST, WITH THE SECOND LINE OF THAT HEAD RUBBED AT THE END FOR FORTY YEARS. FOUR LINES UNDER EVERY HEAD, AND THIRTY HEADS THAT CARRY FOUR AND ONE THAT CARRIES THREE. A MAN OF ABOUT FORTY-SIX WHO MENDS NETS AND HAS SINCE HE WAS NINE AND WHO READS EVERY HEAD-NOTE OUT LOUD ON A SUNDAY AND PUTS HIS OWN NAME AND THE HOUR UNDER IT, AND WHO REFUSED IN HIS OWN MOUTH, WITH HIS OWN REASON, TO READ A DOOR NOTICE TO THE PEOPLE HE WAS READING FOR BECAUSE HE WAS NINE YEARS OLD AND COULD NOT READ. ELEVEN PEOPLE COUNTED AS SIX AND FIVE, TOLD ON ONE WEDNESDAY, ONE AT A TIME, IN DAYLIGHT, ONLY THAT THERE WAS A PAPER. FOUR LINES ON A DOOR, A DRAWING-PIN UNDER A FOLD OF OILLED PAPER, A LAMP FOUND BURNING, A FANLIGHT WITH A PANE OUT SINCE THE SPRING, A MAN WHO WILL NOT SAY WHICH OF ELEVEN, AND A DATE EIGHT DAYS OFF THAT NOBODY HAS ANSWERED AND A CHALK CROSS UNDER IT MADE BY A BOY WHO WAS NEVER FOUND. A PANEL OUT OF A HULL WITH A PERSON IN IT AND A NOTE OF FOUR LINES ON ITS LID AND A DASH AT THE END OF A THIRD LINE. A MAN OF ABOUT FIFTY-FIVE WHO ASKED ONE QUESTION IN A ROOM ON THE EIGHTEENTH OF JUNE AND WAS GIVEN NOTHING. A WOMAN OF ABOUT SIXTY-ONE WITH A BAD KNEE, A STICK, A ROPE WALK THAT DOES NOT RUN, A ROOM AT NINE MARKS A YEAR SHE HAS HAD FOR ELEVEN YEARS, A PANEL IN A BOX SINCE SHE WAS NINETEEN, ONE QUESTION SHE ASKED IN HER OWN MOUTH, ONE THING SHE WAS ASKED, ONCE, AND NOBODY WHO HAS THANKED HER. A ROOM THAT EMPTIED WITHOUT A SOUND. A COLD IN THE TEETH AND A TASTE OF IRON LIKE A NAIL AND A MAN WHO COULD NOT TELL IN WHICH ORDER HE CAME DOWN A FLIGHT OF STAIRS AND WHO WAS LOOKING AT THE DOOR THE WHOLE TIME. A BOOK SHUT AND SQUARED. FOUR LINES IN PENCIL ON AN INSIDE BACK COVER, WITH A NAME AND A DATE, BY A MAN WHO WRITES FIGURES ON A SLATE FOR A LIVING, WHO WAS NOT SENT FOR, WHO CAME UP A STAIR BECAUSE THE DOOR WAS OFF THE LATCH, AND WHO WAS NOT ASKED. A HOLDER OF A WRIT WHO KNEW ABOUT A DASH ON THE THIRD AND DID NOT COUNT IT AND PUT A PENCIL DOWN TWO INCHES AWAY AND STOOD IN A STREET ACROSS FROM THAT DOOR WHILE IT HAPPENED. A FOURTH COLUMN AT ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE THAT HAS TAKEN NO LINE FOR TWENTY DAYS. A BAG AT FOUR HUNDRED AND EIGHT PENCE AGAINST A WAGE OF FOUR MARKS AND FORTY-SIX WEEKS FALLEN DUE AND NO OIL AND NO FLOUR. A HARBOR WITH A LIGHT OUT AND A FIGURE ON A BOARD THAT DID NOT COME DOWN AND A CHALK WORD ON THE EDGE OF THAT BOARD THAT A WOMAN WROTE HERSELF AND WOULD NOT RULE A LINE UNDER.**
