## Volume 09, Batch 0003 (Chapters 421–430), Movement 3, a real terror and a false story, and the date at the head of the notice — complete, 28 September 2026

### Chapter 421 — *Monday the Thirteenth Day of September, the Seventy-First Time the Wall Behind the Reeve's Bench Came Down Bare and Went Up at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth and Nobody Put It Back, the Eighty-First Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine on a Rota of a Monday and a Thursday, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence of a Day With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In at the Figure in Chalk on a Slate at an End Stall, a Man of About Thirty of the Third Lay Called Emmet Slade Who Cannot Read Coming Up a Slip at Two in the Afternoon to Ask Whether There Is a Paper Against Him and Being Told Out Loud That There Is One and That This Yard Knows Nothing About What Is On It, and a Man of About Thirty-Four Off a Screw-Steam Packet Out of Bramble Strait Landing a Sack of Printed Sheets at That Quay at About Four in the Afternoon*

**THE SEVENTY-FIRST WIPE, THE EIGHTY-FIRST CISTERN, A DAY AT A BERTH, AND THE MAN THE WHOLE MOVEMENT IS GOING TO BE ABOUT.** A hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at the figure in chalk on a slate at an end stall and nothing went out, and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence, being three marks eight shillings, and is short of the wage of four marks by sixty-four pence, being five shillings and fourpence. The wall came down bare and went up at the angle it has been at since the twelfth and nobody put it back; the cistern was charged at about eight and walked on at about half past nine for the eighty-first time and the top name on the rota board is still off it. **Emmet Slade, of about thirty, of that lay, with a boat of about nine tons and a claim window on a wreck off the point since the end of July, came up that slip at about two in the afternoon and said in the first half minute that he cannot read, and said he had heard there was a paper against him and would not say from whom.** He was told by the ship's hand that there is a paper, that it is at a counter in an office off the west basin, that it is not that yard's and is not in that shed and has not been seen in that shed, and that what is known of it is four things. He asked whether it could be read to him and was refused in his own mouth, being that a man who cannot read and a man who has not seen the paper together produce a third thing which is the reader's head, and that a version of a paper in a head gets into a market in about a week with that yard's name at the bottom of it. He was told that if there is nobody to take he should stand at that counter and say out loud in front of the man behind it that he cannot read and that he has asked him to read it, and take a man with him who can hear him say he has done it, and that this costs an afternoon and is the only thing in that harbor that costs a man nothing. **He asked whether it was against his boat and was told that nobody in that yard knows, and that being told it was not would be a kindness and not a finding.** He was told to bring the words and not what he made of them, and he went down the slip. **And at about four in the afternoon a screw-steam packet put her hook on and a man of about thirty-four came ashore with a sack heavier than paper ought to be, and said out loud that the lot had been given to him at the top of a gangway by a man behind a counter with a book open who did not ask his name and did not ask what it was for and did not ask who it was for, and that he was going out on the evening tide and was not going to be asked about it again by anybody in that harbor.** The paper at the top left of that door in Fish Street is thirteen days old and its fourth line ends on the twentieth of September next, which is seven days off.

### Chapter 422 — *Tuesday the Fourteenth Day of September, the Forty-Seventh Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It and Forty-Six Weeks Standing Fallen Due at the Open of These Ten Days and Forty-Seven Standing at the Close of Them, a Boy of About Seventeen Called Dill Cardew Carrying a Message Ashore on the Second Lay at Ten in the Morning and a Man of About Forty-Four Off the Water With Two Fingers of His Left Hand Stiff Taking It Out of His Hand in a Street and Not Giving It Back, and Twenty-Four Sheets Going Through a Copyist's Counter in a Room Off That Market at a Penny a Sheet With Nobody Asking the Woman of About Fifty-Nine What She Was Copying*

**THE FORTY-SEVENTH WAGE TUESDAY, A MESSAGE OUT OF A BOY'S HAND, AND THE WHOLE OF THE LEAK.** The chest is in a front room and has been on a bench since the fourth of April past, and there are twenty empty envelopes on a shelf above it folded the same way by a woman of about fifty-eight about eleven weeks ago. **The column did not move and forty-six weeks stood fallen due at the open of these ten days and forty-seven stand at the close of them.** The ship's hand wrote the number of the week against the reason and said a week is a week that came and went and that is not a complaint; and she said out loud, standing in that room with the holder of that writ, that nobody in that crew has asked him one word about the three nots standing against the eighth of June past in an eleventh week, and that she is not going to put a figure on it and not going to put his name on it, and that both of those are decisions and not oversights. **At about ten in the morning Dill Cardew, of about seventeen, came off a cart at the top of the slip at the second lay with a folded paper in his right hand, and a man of about forty-four off the water with two fingers of his left hand stiff took it out of his hand, read it standing up in about the time it takes to read four lines, said it was a thing a man does not carry in a street, put it inside his coat and went up the slip.** The boy lost the paper and lost the hour he was going to be somewhere else in, and a boy who loses a message loses that hour and cannot get it back with a second paper, because a second paper would have a reason in it and he has not got the first reason. He stood on a step for about twenty-five minutes and a woman of about forty came out of a shop and asked if he was all right and he said he was waiting for somebody. **The man he was going to was told at about eleven and said he was not going to send it again, and asked the boy what the man in the street looked like and the boy told him and the man nodded and put nothing down.** Nobody charged the boy and nobody gave him anything and nobody asked him one word about the second lay. **Twenty-four sheets went through a copyist's counter in a room off that market at a penny a sheet, being twenty-four pence, being two shillings, out of the hand of a woman with a stall and not out of that yard's bag, and the woman of about fifty-nine did not ask what she was copying and was not asked and did not stop.**

### Chapter 423 — *Wednesday the Fifteenth Day of September, a Sheet of Six Lines With a Date at the Head of It and a Charge at the Foot of It Going Up on a Wall at the Back of an End Stall at Ten in the Morning on the Outside of a Figure of Four Hundred and Fifty Pence That Was Not Taken Down First and Cannot Be Taken Off Again, a Man of About Thirty-Four Who Says in His Own Mouth That He Was Given the Lot at the Top of a Gangway and Was Not Asked His Name and Could Not Say That What Was On It Was a Lie, and About Thirty People Standing in Front of That Wall by Twelve o'Clock and Not One of Them Knocking It Down*

**THE NOTICE, ITS SIX LINES, ITS DATE, ITS CHARGE, AND THE FIGURE IT IS PUT UP ON THE OUTSIDE OF.** Nothing came into that yard and nothing went out of it and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence. **At about ten in the morning the man of about thirty-four pasted a sheet on the wall at the back of that end stall, on the outside of and about four inches to the left of the slate that hangs on a nail on that wall and carries four hundred and fifty pence with the first of June against it and February's three hundred and seventy-eight pence standing visible above it, and that figure was not taken down first and was not taken down and cannot be taken off again.** The woman of about fifty-eight asked whether there was anything in the sack worth money to anybody, was told it was paper, said then it is not my sack, and had it carried three feet and set against the back boards of her own stall with a stone on it. The sheet is printed and reads: a date, **the eighth day of May**; then a piece of worked glass that has had a scene taken from a living person in it keeps what the scene was, and what the scene was stands off the piece into the air of a room and settles on the people in that room and is taken home in the clothes and is not a thing that comes off in an afternoon at a tub; then that it is not a fever and not a disease and that no physic has ever charged for it and that it will sit in a market the same as it sits in a room; then that every person who has been in a room with such a piece, or carried one, or stood within a man's arm's length of one on a table, is to be entered in the claim book at the counter of the harbor authority of the town where he stands under his own name and is not to be at work on glass in that town until he has been entered and the entry has been read out to him where he can hear it; then that a book is not a court and a claim in a book decides nothing and a man may say no in it and his no goes in at the same size as everybody else's; then that no person and no town is named and that it is put up on the outside of this figure; and then that the charge for lodging one claim is one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, and that a claim so lodged is read out in the room where the public book of that town is kept, on a Sunday, by a man at the end of the table, and a man who cannot read may be there and hear it. **He said he did not write it, that he was not going to say who did and not going to be asked twice, that he read the first four lines standing at a counter four hundred miles away and has not been able to put them down since, and that he could not say it was a lie and that if anybody wants it said that it is a lie they will have to say it themselves.** The woman of about fifty-eight turned her slate about so the oil figure was showing again and said it is not coming off for a piece of paper with a date on the top of it, and said she wrote one word on the edge of that board in August and would not rule a line under the oil figure, and that she is not going to write a new answer in chalk because whatever she writes on that wall goes out of it in a morning. **About thirty people stood in front of that wall by noon. A man of about thirty-three with a hand like a winch said out loud that the first of the six lines was a lie because there are men in that harbor who have had glass in their hands since they were boys, and a woman who was in the room said he was not in the room, and he said counting people going down a stair is not the same as saying a piece of glass can do a thing to a room, and she said no, it is not, and that she was not going to say a thing she did not know either.** Nobody put a hand on that sheet at any hour of the day. **Calder Marr read it twice, found no name in it and no town in it, stood in front of the date at the head of it and did not go up the hill, and did not take a paper out of the inside pocket of his coat and did not tell anybody in that market that there was one in there.**

### Chapter 424 — *Thursday the Sixteenth Day of September, the Eighty-Second Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine on a Rota of a Monday and a Thursday, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out of That Yard in Coin on the Flat of the Bench Stone at About Four in the Afternoon to a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Asked for That Day by Name at About Five o'Clock on the Friday Before and Told on the Wednesday That He Was Wanted, a Man of About Forty-Six Reading Six Lines Out Loud in the Middle of That Market at About Eleven in the Morning With His Own Name and the Hour Against It in Front of About Thirty People, and a Man of About Thirty-Six Who Says Out Loud That He Has Stood in a Room With Glass off a Wreck and Come Out of It All Right and Is Not Answered*

**THE EIGHTY-SECOND CISTERN, THE CAULKER'S SEVENTH DAY SINCE THE TENTH OF AUGUST, AND SIX LINES READ ALOUD ONCE.** A hundred and sixty-eight pence went out of that yard in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four in the afternoon and nothing came in, and the bag is four hundred and eight pence, being two marks seven shillings and fourpence, and is short of the wage by two hundred and thirty-two pence, being one mark six shillings. The cistern was charged at about eight and walked on at about half past nine for the eighty-second time and the top name on that rota board is still off it. **A man of about forty-six read the six lines off that wall out loud in the middle aisle of that market at about eleven in the morning in front of about thirty people of whom about nine could not read, and wrote his own name and the hour under it on the back of a crate in his own hand and no man helped him with it**, and he had said in his own mouth on the morning before that if a thing is going to be said in a market it is going to be said once and properly and not three times slightly wrong by three men. **Four men in that market said out loud that they had been in the room over the joiner's shop on the twelfth, being a man who stacks empties at a quay, a woman who sells fish off a barrow, a man who cuts weed off a mooring chain and a man of about forty-one, and there were about twenty people in that room and nobody counted who was in it and no sheet carries the name of anybody who was.** A man of about thirty-six said out loud that he had been in a shed with glass off a wreck off the point in April with about six men in it and had come out and eaten his supper, and the man of about forty-one said he had not been near a piece since the fourth of June and had had a cold in his teeth and hands that had not been right since about three o'clock on the Sunday, and said out loud that he did not know which of two things was the thing that does it and that a man who does not know ought to say so in a market and not after it. **And Hobb Lee said out loud in that shed at about half past one that he is not going to read a claim out at that table on a Sunday, and gave the reason twice, being that the head of that volume says four lines go under every head and a claim is not a head and has no where it came from in it and no who stands where it is in it, and that the day he reads one out in there he has turned that table into a court with a net-mender at the head of it — and when the ship's hand put it to him a different way, being whether a poor man's claim with no fee is a different claim, he said it is different and it is the same and that he is not going to invent a rule about it, and that what will happen is a man in that harbor with a pencil in his hand standing at the top of that stair saying no one at a time on a Monday, which is one man and not a court and not a rule and not a sheet, and that he knows that is not a system and is not going to pretend it is.** Isaac Fell was paid the seventh time since the tenth of August past and said out loud that he has four days of his own account in the third week of September that nobody is going to ask him for.

### Chapter 425 — *Friday the Seventeenth Day of September, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence of a Day With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In, a Chandler's Counter Shut to a Man Called Nate Pry of About Forty-Four Who Carried a Piece Out of a Boat's Hold in June and Was Not Asked Why He Was Carrying It, Four Shillings for Eight Fathoms of Tarred Rope That He Did Not Get, and a Paper Going Up on the Counter of the Office off the West Basin at About Four in the Afternoon With a Hand on It and No Name on the Paper*

**A COUNTER SHUT TO A MAN WITH A REASON THAT IS NOT COWARDICE, AND A PAPER WITH NO NAME ON IT.** A day at a berth came in and nothing went out and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence. **A chandler of about fifty whose wife keeps the count refused at about eleven in the morning to sell eight fathoms of tarred rope at four shillings, being forty-eight pence, to Nate Pry, of about forty-four, of that lay, who carried a piece of worked glass about the size of two hands with a border round it out of a boat's hold in the middle of June past on his own back to a store on the second lay and was given a shilling and a half for it and has not been near a piece since and was not asked why.** He gave the reason in his own mouth: there is a sheet on a wall at the back of that end stall since the Wednesday, and he is not going to stand in his shop and ask a man whether he has been in a room with a piece of glass, and he has a wife and a girl of eleven behind that counter and would rather be wrong about himself than about her; and if he asked any other man the same question he would have had to give the same answer and the shop would have shut to everybody. He took fourpence on an old account and gave the rope back onto the man's arm. At the end of that street a man mending a net said he has bought candles off that counter since he was nineteen and has never had him not sell him a candle, and the man said that is where we are and went on down the slip. **There is no other rope seller in that harbor and the eight fathoms went back onto that third lay on his own shoulder and lay in the bottom of his boat until the middle of October, and his seine was still open where it had been open since June.** **And at about four in the afternoon a man of about fifty, who works at a table with two papers on it in an office off the west basin, came out with a four-line sheet and put it on the counter, and it has no name on it and no seal at the foot of it and no office at the end of anything**, and says that a claim has been entered under a sheet that went up in that front street on the fifteenth, that a person who has been in a room with a piece of worked glass with a scene in it is to be entered in the claim book of that harbor under his own name, that until he has been entered a claim window held by him is held, and that a claim window is not ownership and expires on the day it says it does. A man of about twenty-six asked the man of about fifty one question about it, being what a claim book was and where it was kept, and was told it is a book, it is in that building, and that the man was not going to say what room it was in and he did not ask and would not have been told. **Nobody in that yard asked the man of about fifty one question about it. And nobody in that harbor has lodged a claim and nobody has paid a penny of the charge at the foot of that sheet, being one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, which is the figure in chalk on a slate at an end stall for a day's work with a boat and two men — and the ship's hand put that figure and her reason in the second column with no name against it, being that a man with nothing can put a sheet up on a wall and can pay a penny for a sheet of paper and cannot pay a mark and eightpence for a claim.**

### Chapter 426 — *Saturday the Eighteenth Day of September, a Berth Held on a Man of About Thirty-Eight With a Boat of About Thirteen Tons and No Papers at the Head of the Third Lay at About Six in the Morning, a Man of About Thirty of the Third Lay Called Emmet Slade Standing at a Counter in an Office off the West Basin at About Eleven o'Clock and Being Told Something by a Man Behind That Counter That He Cannot Read and Cannot Check, and a Man of About Thirty-One With a Chart in a Bag Who Says Three Things at the Foot of a Slip and Is Not Asked About the Chart*

**A BERTH HELD FOR THREE HOURS, AND THE WORD *OFF* READ TO A MAN WHO CANNOT READ.** Nothing came into that yard and nothing went out of it and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence. **A sheet tied to the peg of a berth at the head of the third lay with a piece of line and dated the seventeenth day of September past held a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers**, and her owner stood at it until about half past six in the morning and then took her round to the hard at the back of that lay and lay there from about seven until about ten with about four other boats, and at about eight a man of about fifty-two whose engine has not turned over since the spring put a kettle on his own stove and gave him a cup without saying why. He said out loud to a man of about twenty-nine with a hod of lime that the sixth clause lets me in and does not give me a berth and does not say anything about a sheet of paper on a peg, and he went out on the sixth clause at about half past six that evening and came in past the outer marks at about five the following morning. **A berth is not a price and there is no figure for a day on a hard at the back of a slip.** And Emmet Slade, who cannot read, was at a counter in that office at about eleven with his name written at the top of a sheet lying under the sheet of the seventeenth, and a man behind that counter read him the sheet out word for word and told him in his own mouth that the word on it is off, and that he is not to be at work on glass in that harbor until he has been entered and the entry read out to him where he can hear it, and that when it has been the window stands again. **He said that off is a different word to held, and was told that off is the word on the paper and that he was not going to be given another one, and that he could go and get somebody to read it and that the somebody would read him the same word because it is the word that is on it.** He asked whether it was against his boat and was told that his boat is nine tons and lies at the head of that lay and is not on that counter and is not in that room, and that nobody has written a word about taking it in front of that man. He went out at about ten past eleven, stood at the head of that lay with his hand on his own stem, said **nine tons, and I have not lost the wreck yet and I have not lost the rails and I have not lost the window at the office. I have lost a word**, and did not take his boat out on the said Saturday and did not take it out on the Monday either. And a man of about thirty-one of that lay with a chart in a bag said one sentence at the foot of that slip: that he was in that room on the twelfth, that he has had a cold in his teeth and hands that have not been right since about three o'clock on that Sunday, that he has not been near a piece of glass since the fourth of June, and that he is not going into that market to say that a glass did it or did not do it, because there is a piece of glass in about nine boats in that harbor and eight of those boats went out this week with their owners in them. **He said out loud that he is not on a sheet and is not going to be, and told the ship's hand that five men had walked down past him that week and looked at him like that, so that there is one man in that harbor who knows what it looked like on the days it was there and there is not going to be a sheet with it on.**

### Chapter 427 — *Sunday the Nineteenth Day of September, a Room over a Joiner's Shop Let Out for the Third Time With a Bowl on the Step at Two o'Clock and About Sixteen Going Up and Three Coming Down and Nine Heads Read Out Loud and No Claim in Any of Them, a Man of About Fifty-Eight Who Takes the Rents in Two Houses on the Third Lay Standing at a Door at About Eleven in the Morning Giving a Woman of About Sixty-One a Reason in His Own Mouth, a Box Carried Down a Slip on a Bad Knee Between One and Half Past Two in the Afternoon, and Nobody Charged and Nobody Made Whole and Nobody in That Harbor Told*

**THE ROPEMAKER IS FOUND OUT BY A MOUTH AND IS PUT OUT OF A ROOM SHE HAS HAD FOR ELEVEN YEARS, AND NOBODY IS CHARGED AND NOBODY IS TOLD.** Nothing came into that yard and nothing went out of it and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence. **On the Friday before last, at about two in the afternoon at the head of a quay, a man of about twenty-six who stacks empties said out loud to about four people that the woman who carried a box up two flights of stairs to the room over the joiner's shop on the Sunday before is a woman of about sixty off the third lay and has a rope walk in the back of her room; he was not asked where he got it and said he got it from a man who had been on the second lay, and by Saturday there were people in that harbor who knew which lay she was on, and on Sunday morning when she opened her door there were two men she had never spoken to standing on the stones opposite it.** **At about eleven in the morning Ruben Priest, of about fifty-eight, who takes the rents in two houses on that slip and has taken this one for eleven years at nine marks a year, being one thousand four hundred and forty pence, paid out of rope in every one of those eleven years, told her the room is not hers after the end of the quarter.** He gave the reason in his own mouth: there is a sheet on a wall in that front street and there are people on that slip who were in that room over the joiner's shop on the twelfth, and there is no way on that coast for him to go and stand in a room and ask a person face to face whether they have been in a room with a piece of glass, and he has a wife and a girl of eleven in that house; and he said he was not going to ask her because if he asked then she would answer him and he would never get it out of his own head, and that he would rather have asked nothing and be wrong than have asked and be right. She asked him one question, which was when, and was told after the quarter, and that she had paid to the end of it and he would not have it out of her and would not give it to anybody else, and that he had no other room and was not going to look for one for her, because a room found for her now would be a room somebody stood at in a month asking why she was in it. **That was the whole of what was said in that doorway.** She cut the rope off her box at about one o'clock, took the panel out and put it back in and knotted the rope the way she knots it, and carried the box down the slip on her own bad knee backwards with the wheel of the barrow against the step above her between one and half past two, and nobody on that lay carried anything for her and nobody offered. The rope walk in the back of that room is about forty feet long and about five feet wide and does not run and there is not another rope walk in that harbor. **Nobody was charged and nobody was made whole and no figure in that yard's leaf stands against that room or that rope walk or those eleven years or that box or that knee, and nobody in that harbor has been told that anything was done for her and nobody in that harbor has thanked her and nobody in that yard went up that slip on the said day.** In Fish Street the bowl went on the step at two and about sixteen went up and three came down and eleven of the sixteen could not read, and nine of thirty-one heads were read out loud from about two minutes past two to about twenty-one minutes past three with his own name and the hour under each, and there was no claim in any of the nine and no claim on that table and nobody asked him to read one, and the woman of about fifty-eight came up those stairs with her slate and said out loud that a sheet on a wall is not on that table and that she is not going to ask anybody to read it out in there.

### Chapter 428 — *Monday the Twentieth Day of September, the Seventy-Second Time the Wall Behind the Reeve's Bench Came Down Bare and Went Up at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth and Nobody Put It Back, the Eighty-Third Time the Cistern Was Charged and Walked on by None of It, the Fourth Line of the Paper at the Top Left of That Door in Fish Street Ending on the Said Day and Being Answered by Nobody, a Man Going Down in a Bell at About Eleven Foot on a Berth at the Third Lay at Ten in the Morning Beside a Crate of Three Pieces of Recovered Glass and Coming Up at About Twenty Past Eleven With a Cold in His Teeth and a Taste of Iron Like a Nail, and a Ship's Hand Who Says Out Loud That She Has Got No Figure for It and Is Not Going to Make One Up*

**THE SEVENTY-SECOND WIPE, THE EIGHTY-THIRD CISTERN, A DATE THAT ENDED AND WAS ANSWERED BY NOBODY, AND ONE DIVER.** Nothing came into that yard and nothing went out of it and the bag is five hundred and seventy-six pence. **The fourth line of the paper at the top left of that door in Fish Street says that anybody found to have been in that room on the night of the nineteenth of August is to take himself, or herself, off out of that harbor before the twentieth day of September next, and it is the twentieth day of September, and the paper is on that door, has been there twenty days, has a drawing-pin under a fold of oiled paper, and has been answered by nobody.** The room was let out on the Sunday before and about sixteen went up and three came down and eleven of the sixteen could not read, and whether one of the eleven was in that room on that Sunday is not a thing anybody in that room looked for. **And a man went down in a bell at about eleven foot at a berth on the third lay at ten in the morning with a man of about twenty-nine on the rope and a boy of about fifteen on the pump, and about nine feet off his left shoulder under that boat's fore peak there was a crate about four foot by two with boards across the top of it and some straw in it and three pieces of worked glass in it, being a border, a panel about the size of two hands and a piece of a hatch cover with a hinge still on it, which the owner bought off a man off a lighter on the Friday for four shillings and is sending up-coast on the Tuesday.** He put a mend in a garboard with oakum and a marlinspike and paid it round and did it twice, and at about half past ten the boy on the pump stopped for a moment and started again and his hands went to the ladder frame before his head had told him anything. **He came up at about twenty past eleven and sat down on the stones at the head of that berth for about a quarter of an hour and then said three things and no more: a cold in his teeth that was not there at eight o'clock, a taste of iron in the back of his mouth like a nail and hands that were not right, and not being able to tell for about half a minute which of two hatches in that boat he had come up out of.** He said that he has had that taste of iron three times in nine months and that on each of those three times he was within a foot of a piece of worked glass for about as long as it takes to boil an egg, and **that he has got no reading out of it and is not going to say that he has, and that nobody in that harbor has to take notice of it and nobody is going to and that includes him.** A man of about twenty-nine said it is a thing off a bell that he has had nine times in eleven years and that it has been cold coming in off the water every one of the nine and that he has never once had a taste of anything out of his mouth, and said that to the ship's hand and not to him. **The ship's hand came down that slip at about half past twelve and was told the same three things and said out loud that she has got no figure for that and is not going to invent one, and that if she put a mark against his name in the first column he would be a man on a page for the rest of his life over a bad lunch, and wrote one line in the second column against a reason with no name against it; he is not on the page.** The crate was still under that fore peak at about four in the afternoon and nobody in that harbor has told the eleven people anything about any of it.

### Chapter 429 — *Tuesday the Twenty-First Day of September, the Forty-Eighth Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It and Forty-Seven Weeks Standing Fallen Due at the Open of That Day and Forty-Eight Standing at the Close of These Ten Days, Forty-Four Pence Going Out of That Yard at About Half Past Ten in the Morning for a Loaf and a Half, a Candle and a Pot, a Boy of About Seventeen Telling a Man of About Thirty of the Third Lay Something at About Two in the Afternoon That He Was Told in Turn at a Counter in That Market and That Man Going Home and Not Taking His Boat Out, and a Holder of That Writ Saying Once Out Loud What He Wrote Down on the Twenty-Second Day of August Past and Why*

**THE FORTY-EIGHTH WAGE TUESDAY, A BOY WHO TELLS A MAN SOMETHING WRONG, AND A LEAF WITH ELEVEN DATES ON IT THAT HE DOES NOT READ OUT.** Forty-four pence, being three shillings and eightpence, went out at about half past ten in the morning for a loaf and a half, a candle and a pot, to a man of about thirty-eight with a boat of about thirteen tons and no papers, out of that yard's own bag and not one penny of it out of the owner of that boat; and that man said out loud that he was told on the eighteenth that his berth was held, that he put his boat on the hard for about three hours and took her off in the evening when the paper was off the peg and the peg was still there, that he does not know who took it down and did not ask, and that he is not going to stand at an office and ask a man about a sheet four days old when he has got a tide on the sixth clause. **The forty-eighth wage Tuesday came and the column did not move on it and forty-eight weeks stand fallen due at the close of these ten days and the forty-ninth falls on the twenty-eighth of September next.** And at about two in the afternoon Dill Cardew came down that slip for the second time in eight days, having been sent by a man behind a counter in that fish market to tell Emmet Slade two things, being that his window is stopped and that he is to hand in a third of anything landed in that harbor. He told him in about eight words and the man cannot read, and said out loud that there is no third of anything because there has been nothing landed in that harbor since June past that anybody has a claim on, and that the boy was told to say it by the man at the counter, and that on the eighteenth a man behind a counter in the office off the west basin read him the sheet out word for word and told him the word on it is off, and that he said then that off is a different word to held and was told that off is the word that is on the paper, and that he has now got it twice and both times a bit different and the next market was the following morning. **He went home and did not take his boat out. Nobody in that yard asked that boy where he was on the fourteenth at about ten in the morning and nobody in that yard is going to**, and the reason is in his own head and is that a boy who cannot account for an hour is a boy who does not get sent anywhere again. **And at about half past nine in the evening the holder of that writ put a leaf on the bench stone and said out loud, once, that he wrote eleven dates on it in his own hand in a room over a fish market on the twenty-second day of August past in the order he read them off a board about a yard wide under a sloping canvas on an after thwart, with no name and no figure against any of the eleven and a column ruled at the left of them with nothing in it; and gave the reason in his own mouth, being that in July he had a thing in his head that only he had and in August two other men had things that only they had, and that one of those was a shape he had seen with his own eyes and one was a shape he had heard described in a room, and that he has not had a use for it since and is not going to look for one.** He said he is not going to tell anybody in that harbor what is on it unless it is read out in that room on a Sunday with his name and the hour under it in the hand of the man at the end of that table. She asked him why the column was ruled and left empty, and he said he did not draw it because a man counted thirty-one heads on the back of his own hand on the tenth day of September and found one of them carrying three lines where the head of that book says four and wrote it on the inside of the back cover with his own name and the date, and nobody has asked him who left the dash, and that he wants it said out loud that he put a pencil down two inches from his own book and left it there.

### Chapter 430 — *Wednesday the Twenty-Second Day of September, a Leaf Read Back in Full on the Flat of the Bench Stone at That Mole Head at About Ten Past Five in the Evening in the Open in the Ship's Own Left Hand All Four Columns Including the Empty One With Both Definitions of the Four Figures on the Face of That Reading, a Fourth Column Standing at One Hundred and Twenty-Five Where It Stood and Taking No Line and a Third Column None, the Bag at Five Hundred and Thirty-Two Pence Against a Wage of Six Hundred and Forty Pence, and a Harbor With No Flour in That Market and No Oil in It Since the Twenty-Ninth Day of August and a Light Out of a Mole Head and a Figure on a Board That Did Not Come Down*

**THE READ-BACK WITH BOTH DEFINITIONS ON ITS FACE, THE FOUR FIGURES, THE BAG, AND THE STANDING CONDITION, AND NOTHING PREDICTED FOR THE DAYS AFTER IT.** Nothing came into that yard and nothing went out of it and the bag is five hundred and thirty-two pence, being three marks four shillings and fourpence, and the figure it is short of the wage of four marks is one hundred and eight pence, being nine shillings. **The whole of what came into that yard in the ten days that ended on the said Wednesday is three hundred and thirty-six pence on two days and the whole of what went out of it is two hundred and twelve pence on two days, and four hundred and eight plus three hundred and thirty-six minus two hundred and twelve is five hundred and thirty-two, and the equation on the face of the chapter evaluates.** Nessa Pike read the leaf back on the flat of the bench stone at that mole head at about ten past five in the evening, in the open, in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, with the mole-head light not lit and its lens out since the seventh of May past. **She said that the first column has one hundred and sixty-two entries at this hour and one hundred and sixty-three at the close of the day, being one hundred and forty-three at the close of the second day of September past and twenty going in since, one against each of the twenty days, with not one day in two of them, and that a day of the first column carries one entry against it whatever else that day printed; that the second column has six hundred and eighty-seven lines at this hour and six hundred and eighty-nine at the close, being five hundred and eighty-nine at the close of the second and five a day since, three before the hour of each day's reading and two after it; and that that figure is that book of that yard's own and is not a count of anything anybody can check from a mole, while the first column's figure and the fourth column's are a count of entries and a count of lines and can both be taken with a pencil, and those are the two definitions and they are printed so that a later writer with a pencil knows which of them they are counting and at which of the two moments.** She said the third column is empty and nobody has been appointed to it and the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it with a name beside it that was said out loud once in a boat on the thirteenth of May past and has not been said since, and that there is now an eleventh week in which nobody in that crew has said one word about the three nots standing against the eighth of June past. **And she said that the fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines at this hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, that it has taken no line since the twenty-third day of August past and has taken none on any of these twenty days, that there is no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, that that is not a closure and not a strike-out and nobody has closed that column and nobody in that yard is going to, and that the reason was entered once in the second column at about ten past nine in the evening of the twenty-eighth of August and is entered again nowhere.** **Mara Venn said the one thing she said on that mole head, four feet off the stone: that there is a sheet on a wall with a date at the top and a charge at the bottom and four men in that market have said out loud they were in a room and a man of about thirty-four has got a cold in the teeth off a bell at eleven foot on the third lay, and there is not one figure in that harbor that puts the two of those together, and neither of those is going to be settled in that shed this month, and neither of them cancels the other, and she is not going to stand on a Wednesday evening and pretend that one of them is a comfort. The holder of that writ did not answer that and did not improve on it.** Then the standing condition in full: no flour, no barrel of lamp oil since the twenty-ninth day of August, four hundred and fifty pence on a board that is not cleared with the new sheet on the same square of wall above it, the paper of four lines in Fish Street on that door and answered by nobody, the nine-line sheet with a seal on it on the front street wall for thirty-nine days, the chandler's note at thirty-one with its three counts at twenty-two, thirteen and eleven and not re-written, the delayed note at eleven logged occasions and two of them with no call, the mole-head light out, the north berth out, the hose dead until the spring, the tide gang four men short, the hard at Ashtide unanswered and the three marks against it on an anchor date out of an earlier volume, one berth short on the third lay, nineteen winters disputed, and forty-eight weeks fallen due. **And the ten days' cost in people at the end: a man of about thirty-eight who went out on the sixth clause and will come in at about five tomorrow morning, a man of about thirty who did not take his boat out yesterday and has not taken it out today, a man of about forty-four without eight fathoms of tarred rope, a man of about thirty-four off a packet who has gone out on the tide and is not coming back to that harbor this month, three pieces of worked glass going up-coast out of a crate for four shillings, a woman of about sixty-one not in a room at nine marks a year, and a boy of about seventeen who cannot account for an hour of this month and is not going to be asked. This harbor is poorer on the twenty-second day of September than it was on the thirteenth and poorer than on the fourteenth of May, and nothing taken in these ten days has been given back.**

## Volume 09, Batch 0004 (Chapters 431–440), Movement 4, a convoy, a maintenance rota, and a wreck that has to be looked after between it and the next tide, in which the Keelwright stage is taken in the last four of them — complete, 29 September 2026

### Chapter 431 — *Thursday the Twenty-Third Day of September, the Eighty-Fourth Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine on a Rota of a Monday and a Thursday, a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Named the Alewife Taken Up the Foul Off the South End in the Night With Nobody in Her and Lying With Her Port Bilge Up in About Five Foot of Water, Nine Men Unstepping and Landing Her Mast in About Fifty Minutes Before the Flood at About Half Past Six in the Evening, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out of That Yard at About Ten in the Morning for Oakum and Iron and a Length of Three-Inch Stuff, and a Day's Work With a Boat and Two Men at a Berth Coming In at Four in the Afternoon, and the Bag at Five Hundred and Thirty-Two Pence at the Close of the Day as It Was at the Open of It*

A warp round a bollard that had been on her since March parted at about two o'clock in the morning and a boat of about nineteen tons of the third lay named the *Alewife* went up the foul off the south end of that mole with nobody in her. Jos Lund, of about forty-four, found her at about twenty past five from the top of the mole by the smell of her. She lay with her port bilge up in about five foot, eleven foot off her port rail, her starboard side out of the water as high as her garboard strake, and her garboard open about two foot forward of the keel. **Nine men unstepped and landed her mast from about a quarter to seven until about twenty past seven, being about fifty minutes, and it split a piece out of the coping at the corner where the mole steps come up.** Her chain came off in about eleven minutes, her wheel went into a boat, both anchors were let go and left in nine foot on a foul with no survey against it. Calder Marr packed the open garboard from the inside with oakum and a canvas patch at about eleven foot and said out loud that it would hold until the flood, and Nessa Pike asked how long and was told that, in those words, in her hearing, at about eleven o'clock. **The flood came at about twenty past six, set her beam ends in about four minutes, put her port rail against the mole's footing stones for about an hour and ten minutes, and at about half past seven she came off and took the ground on a bank about four hundred yards down that foul in about nine foot.** Nobody was paid for that morning, because a morning on a wreck is neither a day's work at a berth nor a caulker's day and that harbor has no figure for one. One hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about ten in the morning for oakum and iron and three-inch stuff and canvas and nails and one hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at about four in the afternoon, and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two pence where it stood at the open of the day. **Nessa Pike told the holder of that writ in the open that she had two figures in that harbor and nothing at all for a man in the water at four in the morning and would not make one up, and that the person is the thing that costs, and that a day for a person has to be written on a paper and asked one man at a time.**

### Chapter 432 — *Friday the Twenty-Fourth Day of September, a Bell Down to a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Lying in About Nine Foot on a Bank Four Hundred Yards Down a Foul at a Quarter to Four in the Morning and Up Again at About Twenty Past Five, Two Hours and Thirty-Five Minutes of Air and Pumping With a Boy of Fifteen on the Pump and the Owner and a Man Hauling on the Fall, a Shore of Two Baulks of Oak Faired to a Keel in the Dark With a Light and a Hand and Made Wrong Once and Made Again, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out of That Yard at About Nine in the Morning for a Pump Leather and a Coil of Marline, and a Man of About Thirty-Four of the Second Lay Who Keeps the Whole Fouling Ladder in His Own Book Saying Out Loud in a Shed How a Heel Is Fitted Where the Reeds Move the Ground, and a Packet Going Down to a Coast Where the First Public Route Codes Are Kept*

The ebb at the bottom of that bank is about a hundred and five minutes and the bank comes up under a hull about a foot and a half on the flood. Calder Marr went down off the starboard quarter at about a quarter to four with two men of the crew on the rope, a boy of fifteen on the pump, Jos Lund on the fall, and a man of about twenty-six holding a light over the side for about two hours and forty minutes without being asked to move it. He shored her with two baulks and got them to bear and she came down about two inches and stopped dead. **He went thirty feet along the garboard with his hands on it and found about nine feet of soft plank nine feet aft of the shore and put his thumb through the veneer of it about the size of a shilling, and said out loud that a shore does not stop soft plank and a patch does not stop soft plank, and that he cannot get a light on a keel in nine foot of water in the dark and would be guessing.** The pump leather went at about half past four and about fifty minutes of fresh water came over the side. One hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about nine in the morning and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four pence. **Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, who keeps the whole fouling ladder in that harbor in his own book and has never shown it to anybody, came in at about half past ten, did not open the book, and said out loud that they do not do it that way in Lowfen, where a man takes the mould off a piece of the old keel with the boat still floating in about two foot of water with two men on a pole and a third with the battens and lets it down onto the marks as she comes off, and that the ground under a Lowfen hull is not the ground there next year because the reeds put it out and pull it back, and that a mould there is kept in a head and not in a book, and that he has never been to Lowfen in his life and that is how he knows and nobody in that shed asked him where he got it.** The woman who prices things told him he was not on any sheet. A packet went down the coast at about four in the afternoon offering one day at the figure in chalk and telling whoever came, in the packet, that the figure being offered was not the figure anybody ought to take.

### Chapter 433 — *Saturday the Twenty-Fifth Day of September, Eleven Masters Asked One at a Time in the Same Words and Not One of Them Asked Twice, a Page With a Name and an Hour Against Each of Eleven Lines and Ten of the Eleven Said Yes and One Said No With a Reason in His Own Mouth and Was Not Asked Again on Any of the Six Days After It and Was Not Given Another Job and Was Not Thanked, a Boat of About Fourteen Tons Out of Lowfen Among the Seven and a Man of About Sixty There Who Puts a Bundle of Hazel Out on the Point of the Shoal Every Spring, About Thirty Men in Seven Boats and a Woman of About Fifty-Eight With a Slate Who Says That the Figure on That Page Is Her Figure and That She Is Not Going to Be Told What to Do With It, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming in at the Figure in Chalk on a Slate at an End Stall, and the Bag at Five Hundred and Thirty-Two Pence*

The words were written at the head of the page before anybody was asked and were the same eleven times and were read out of the page and not out of a memory. **Eleven masters of that harbor were asked one at a time between about nine in the morning and about twenty past five in the evening and every line carries a name and an hour.** Ten said yes with a reason each: Ormond Kettle at about nine with her heel off since June and eleven weeks waiting for anybody to tell him it was a mould problem; Ham Birt at about ten with a question back about who pays for the damage; Silas Pride at about half past ten; Alban Pree at about eleven, out loud, in front of his own mate, that he was told in July he would get nothing and has got nothing and is saying yes anyway and is not going to be thanked for it; Sedge Rundle at about half past eleven; Jens Ower at about two in the afternoon; Jos Lund at about three on his own boat's ground in the rain; Elias Voke at about four with no reason at all, saying that if anybody wanted one they could ask the nineteen winters; Iver Sallow at about half past four with a chart of about nine years standing in a bag for nine years; and a man of about twenty-nine who asked his master's leave first. **Nessa Pike said yes at about twenty past five on her own deck, gave her own hours from about seven until the last of the ebb, and said that her hours are her hours and the bill for the whole of it comes to her own table and not to anybody else's. Rowan Teel, of about fifty-one, of the second lay, whose right forearm is set out of his own hand, said no at about a quarter to six and said in his own mouth that he would be the ninth man on a line of eight and that he would rather say it then than have somebody come to his door about it on the Tuesday, and he was not asked again on any of the six days after it and was at his own bench from about eight until about six on each of them and nobody came in there with a piece of paper.** Sedge Rundle said out loud that he goes by three things and none of them is on a paper. A woman of about fifty-eight with an end stall said the figure on that page is her figure and that she wrote it up in chalk on the first of June and is not going to be told what to do with it. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at about eleven in the morning and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two pence.

### Chapter 434 — *Sunday the Twenty-Sixth Day of September, a Twelfth Week Beginning With the Three Nots of the Eighth of June Past Standing Unasked in It, a Room over a Joiner's Shop at the Top of Fish Street Let Out for the Fourth Time With a Bowl on the Step at Two o'Clock and a Man of About Forty-Six Reading Heads off a Long Table With His Own Name and the Hour Under Each, a Bellwright of About Thirty-Four off the Western Reef Line Coming Down off a Coast at About Half Past Ten in the Morning With Her Own Tools in a Box and a Paper of Lead Cuts in the Lid of It, Five Shillings Named Against One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Said Out Loud Once, and a Mould Taken off a Keel on a Hard With Battens and a Pitch, Two Baulks of Oak Planed at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence, and the Bag at Three Hundred and Sixty-Four Pence*

A twelfth week began and the three nots of the eighth of June past stand in the first day of it unasked. **Mina Kett, of about thirty-four, a bellwright of Tidewatch on the western reef line, came down at about half past ten with her own tools in a box and paid her own passage out of her own hand, and took eleven battens off the keel of a boat of about nineteen tons lying on that hard since June with her heel off, in about two hours and ten minutes, with a drawknife and a mallet and a piece of belaying pin and with nobody talking, and numbered the ends in pencil with her own marks and not with figures, and said that the new piece goes on to that and that it is not a drawing and is a bit of that keel, and that it is still a guess and it is a guess with a curve in it instead of a straight one.** She was told she would be paid at the figure in chalk and **said out loud once that that is a caulker's figure, that she is not a caulker, that a bellwright off that line gets five shillings, being sixty pence, and that she has been getting five shillings for nine years and has never asked anybody for more because she has never been in a room where she could, and that she was saying it once so that it would be in somebody's head and was not going to say it again and was not going to be thanked for it.** The room over a joiner's shop was let out at two o'clock with about twenty going up and three coming down and eleven of the twenty unable to read, and Hobb Lee read the head-notes out loud until about twenty past three with his own name and the hour under each, and there was no claim in any of them. The woman of about fifty-eight came up with her slate and said out loud that the sheet on the wall in the front street is not on that table and is not in that book. **At about four o'clock about forty small pieces of lead came out of the lid of the box and she said there is a nail in the door frame of her workshop at Tidewatch with about forty of them on it and a woman of about sixty-one there who copies a cut onto a paper for a penny to anybody who walks in, and that nobody has ever been refused at that door in twenty-six years, and that these are not for this coast and she is not going to say which marks they stand for, and that the sheet was to go to the woman who prices things and was not to be put on a wall.** Two baulks of oak planed went out at one hundred and sixty-eight pence and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four pence.

### Chapter 435 — *Monday the Twenty-Seventh Day of September, the Seventy-Third Time the Wall Behind the Reeve's Bench Came Down Bare and Went Up at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth and Nobody Put It Back, the Eighty-Fifth Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine, a Rota Written on a Sheet of Good Paper From a Counter in a Room off That Market at a Penny Out of the Holder's Own Hand and Not Out of That Bag, a Young Man of About Twenty-Three off a Small Steam Tender of About Forty Tons Who Is Not a Cruiser and Not an Officer and Whose Own Hours Run From About Seven Until About Five and Whose Own Rate Is His Tender's and Not This Yard's, Fifteen Fathoms of Chain Off His Quarter Round a Spurle and Back With a Weight on It, and a Foot of Water on the Flood With About Two Hours of It in Every Twenty-Four*

The wall came down bare for the seventy-third time and went up at the angle it has been at since the twelfth and nobody put it back. The cistern was charged at about eight and walked on at about half past nine for the eighty-fifth time and the top name on that rota board is still off it. A sheet of good paper came from the counter in a room off that market at about nine in the morning at a penny out of the holder's own coat and not out of that bag, with four days on it and one figure on it: one person on the water in company from about seven in the morning until the last of the ebb, one hundred and sixty-eight pence out of that yard's own figures, not out of any boat and not out of any owner of a boat, and a person may refuse and will not be asked again. **Mara Venn read it off the wall of that shed and said one thing about it: that it has got a person in it and that there is no column in that yard's book for a person who has been asked to turn up and that she would put it in the second column with the hour against it and not in the first, because a man on a mole can count the first column and cannot count this, and nobody thanked her for it.** **Halvard Ness, of about twenty-three, second hand on a small steam tender of about forty tons, came down the slip and asked what the steam tender was wanted for, was told that a man who is paid by nobody in the boat is the only man in the boat who can stop the working without asking anybody, laid fifteen fathoms of chain with a swivel in it from his tender's quarter cleat to the bitt of the boat on the bank, round a spurle and back with a weight on the tail, and said out loud that he would not ask anybody's leave to pull it and that nobody in that boat had any standing to tell him not to, and that his own hours run from about seven until about five and he is paid by his tender at eight o'clock on a Saturday and by nothing else.** The woman of fifty-eight was told that the figure on her slate is the same figure as the charge at the foot of the sheet on the wall of her stall and said it has been the same figure since the first of June, that she did not have anything to do with that sheet and is not going to be asked about it, and that two figures on two pieces of wood nine feet apart is no more than that, and asked for her tobacco to be paid for. Seven boats and about thirty men went out at about half past six for a turn of the leg and came in at about eight, inside that harbor's own line, and no paper went out with them. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at about two in the afternoon and the bag stands at five hundred and thirty-two pence.

### Chapter 436 — *Tuesday the Twenty-Eighth Day of September, the Forty-Ninth Wage Tuesday and the Column Not Moved on It and Forty-Nine Weeks Standing Fallen Due at the Close of the Day, a Day on the Water Paid at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Out of That Yard's Own Figures at About Four in the Afternoon, a Bellwright's Day at the Same Figure, Seven Boats and About Thirty Men Out From About Seven in the Morning Until the Last of the Ebb, Fifteen Fathoms of Chain Off a Tender's Quarter With a Weight on the Tail of It Coming Up Over a Rail at Half Past Two With the Reason Written Down, a Boat of About Twenty-Two Tons Striking a Baulk of Oak That Was Laid Down Without a Light on It and Opening About Nine Foot of Her Garboard, and the Bag at Three Hundred and Sixty-Four Pence*

The forty-ninth wage Tuesday did not move the column and forty-nine weeks stand fallen due at the close of the day. Seven boats and about thirty men went out at ten past seven with the steam tender ahead of them, got a keel of about nineteen feet about two feet clear of the mud by about eleven, and took the water over her from nine foot at the top of the water to about seven foot and a half by about two in the afternoon. **Mina Kett came down in the tender's boat at about eleven, stood on the mud in eight foot of water on that boat's port bilge and put eleven battens down that keel in about eleven minutes, and a man of about forty-four who has been planing forty-one years cut the new piece out of two baulks of oak in about fifty minutes and it came off in three pieces and it did not fit, and nobody in that company said a word about it for about ten minutes, and then she put her thumb into the end of the middle piece and said out loud to about thirty men in seven boats that it is a guess with a curve in it and that she had told them it was a guess with a curve in it.** About a sixteenth came off the whole length and not off one end and it went on in about two hours and was faired at the after end and was done at about twenty past two with the water down to about seven foot and a half and the mud coming up to her. **There is nine foot on that bank at the top of the water and about seven foot and a half at the bottom of it, and that foot and a half is the whole of what a man has got, and it comes back every twelve hours and a bit.** The chain weight came over the rail at twenty-two minutes past two and every man in that bank was in the boat in about nine minutes, and the reason was written down at about half past four with the hour against it. **At about ten past two a boat of about twenty-two tons struck a baulk of oak that that yard's own hands had laid down at about half past eight in the morning with about nine inches of it out of the water in a sea and no light on it and no flag and nothing on it at all, and opened about nine foot of her garboard and put a hole in her lee rail about the size of two hands, and about thirty men got a line to her in about four minutes and she was under about two feet by the time she was fast, and nobody was hurt.** The owner said in his own mouth that the baulk is that yard's and that the bill is that yard's and that it is not going to be charged to the owner of any of the seven boats. Two payments of one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being three hundred and thirty-six pence, went out and one hundred and sixty-eight pence came in and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four pence.

### Chapter 437 — *Wednesday the Twenty-Ninth Day of September, the Keel of a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Rebuilt About the Shoe and Painted and Caulked in Company Between Her and the Next Tide, Seven Boats and About Thirty Men on the Water From About Ten Past Seven Until the Last of the Ebb, a Chain Weight Over a Rail at Twenty-One Minutes to Two in the Afternoon With the Reason Written Down, One Man in a Bell at a Quarter to Four in the Morning and Then Another Man in That Bell One at a Time With the Same Tender and the Same Cutoff and a Reason Against Each of Them Written Down With the Hour, a Bill for Damage Done in Company That Comes to This Yard, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out at About Eleven in the Morning for Iron and a Plank and Roves and Copper, and the Bag at One Hundred and Ninety-Six Pence*

The new piece was caulked in about two hours by Isaac Fell, of about twenty-three, of no boat and no crew and no office and on no sheet, who was asked at about ten in the morning whether he would take the joint on that afternoon and who said the figure he works to out loud before he was asked for the day. **The chain came over the rail at about twenty-one minutes to two and he was out of that boat and on the tender's deck with his iron and his oakum and his maul in his hand before the weight had stopped swinging, and the reason was written down at about half past four with the hour against it.** At about a quarter to four in the morning Calder Marr went down off the port quarter, and **Nessa Pike put the first other man in that bell behind him, one at a time and not two at a time.** Tam Sparre, of about twenty-nine, went down at about half past five, was in about twenty-five minutes and came up and said that there is a hole in her about two foot aft of where the shore is and that it is not open and that it is soft, and that he put his hand flat on it and it went in about the depth of a thumb and came back with a smell off it that was not tar and was not oil, and that he has not been in her in June and was not going to give anybody anything else. The first man said he had put his thumb through the veneer of that plank about the size of a shilling at nine foot on the Friday before last and that they had found it and had not stopped for it. **Both accounts are in that book in the order they were said and neither agrees with the other and neither was settled before the end of the day.** One hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about eleven in the morning for iron clamps and a plank of white oak four inches by nine and eleven feet long and roves and copper, and that plank is for the lee rail of the boat that struck the baulk, and the owner said out loud that the baulk was ours and that nobody marked it and that he has got a hole in his boat and a man of about thirty-one in that harbor who went over her side and held his own hat, and that he is not going to be told what that costs by a woman with a slate and is not going to be thanked for saying so, and that he is going to hold that baulk next time and the yard has written that down with the hour against it. Four pence and eighteen pence went out of a man's own coat for biscuits and a coil of new manila. The bag stands at one hundred and ninety-six pence, being one mark and three shillings.

### Chapter 438 — *Thursday the Thirtieth Day of September, the Eighty-Sixth Time the Cistern Was Charged at About Eight in the Morning and Walked on by None of It at About Half Past Nine and the Third and Last Charge in These Ten Days, a Second Man Put in That Bell One at a Time With a Reason Written Down Against It Before He Went Down and a Tender of About Forty Tons and Fifteen Fathoms of Chain and a Weight on the Tail of It, a Cutoff Pulled at Nine Minutes to Three in the Afternoon, a Word for the Thing Asked Out Loud by a Man of About Forty-Six and Given an Answer in Nine Words, Not One Penny Charged to the Owner of Any of the Seven Boats on Any of the Three Days, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming In at About Two in the Afternoon, and the Bag at Three Hundred and Sixty-Four Pence*

The cistern was charged and walked on for the eighty-sixth time and the top name on that rota board is still off it, and that is the third and last charge in these ten days. **The reason a man is put into the water was written down before he went down, which had not been done before and was done from that day on, and the reason for it is that a reason written after a man comes up is worth nothing.** Sedge Rundle went down at about half past five and was in about thirty minutes and came up and sat on the tender's deck with his back against a steam pipe and said that he had been in that boat once in ninety-five for a day and a half laying planks in her bottom and remembered where the ballast was, and that a piece of about two foot of that bottom two foot aft of the shore is not soft and is as sound as anything in her, and that he put his whole hand flat on it and could not get his thumb into it and did not try to force it, and that he was not going to change it because somebody else had been in there and he had not. **That is the third account of about two foot of plank and one of the three men is wrong and nobody knows which one and this yard has entered all three in the order they were said and has not settled them.** The chain came over the rail at about nine minutes to three with about twenty-five men in that boat and they were out on the tender's deck in about eleven minutes. **Hobb Lee came down the slip at about eleven in the morning in daylight and asked what the man who keeps a keel right in between tides with a chain and a weight on it is called, and was told that there is a word and it is not taken by being said and that he would not be given it in a shed or have it off anybody in a market, and he said in his own mouth that he would not ask again and would not say it at his table and that he would not read anything out in that room that is not a head in that book.** The woman of fifty-eight said three days had gone by and not one penny of any of it had come off anybody's boat and would like that written down somewhere and not on her slate. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at about two in the afternoon and the bag stands at three hundred and sixty-four pence.

### Chapter 439 — *Friday the First Day of October, a Man of About Forty-Four Asking at About Eleven in the Morning for a Line to Be Struck Out of the Convoy's Own Sheet and a Woman of About Thirty-Four Asking at About Half Past Eleven for a Line of Hers to Be Struck Out of the Same Sheet and Two Men on the First Lay Asking at About Two in the Afternoon for a Line to Be Struck Out of That Yard's Own Leaf, and the Same Nine Words Given to All Three of Them, a Word Said Out Loud Once in a Shed and Not Taken by Being Said, a Fourth Man in That Bell With a Reason Written Down Before He Went Down and a Chain Weight Over a Rail at About Twenty Minutes to Two in the Afternoon, a Tender of About Forty Tons Whose Own Hours End at About Five in the Afternoon and Whose Own Rate Is His Tender's, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out at About Eleven in the Morning for Canvas and Tar and a Spare Bight of Line and Copper, and the Bag at One Hundred and Ninety-Six Pence*

**Four people asked for a line to be struck out and were refused in the same nine words, being that that line stays, that nothing comes out of this book once it is in, for any reason, to anybody.** Jos Lund at about eleven, against a line carrying his name and an hour and eleven minutes of lateness. Mina Kett at about half past eleven, against a line carrying her name and an hour and the figure in chalk on a slate at an end stall, on the ground that she was not underpaid on that line, she was paid the wrong figure on it, and the line is what happened. **She asked for a second line under it and got one, and that line is in the second column of that yard's own leaf and names her own figure of five shillings, being sixty pence, against the one hundred and sixty-eight pence she is paid, and says she has said so once out loud and has been underpaid by it and has not stopped work and has not asked for it a second time.** Two men off the first lay at about two in the afternoon against a line in the first column carrying about nine foot of garboard and a hole in a lee rail. **At about half past two in the afternoon Ormond Kettle, of about forty-four, said the word out loud for the first time in that harbor and was told it is a trade and not a power, that it settles nothing, that it prices nothing, and that it makes nobody better off than he was on the Thursday before, and Mina Kett said that on her coast it means a man who keeps a keel right and not a man who fits one, and Sedge Rundle said from the doorway that the asking is not the work and that eleven masters asked one at a time with one of them saying no and not being asked again is a keelwright, and nobody repeated it after him and it is on no sheet in that harbor.** A man of about fifty-eight who sweeps out the Fish Street room went down in that bell at about half past five with his reason written down before he went down and came up at about twenty past six and said he could not tell anything at all and that a man of his age in a bell in eight foot goes down to be a second pair of eyes and not a pair of hands. The chain came over the rail at about twenty minutes to two and Halvard Ness put his chain away at about five and his own pay was eight o'clock on the Saturday out of his own tender and there is no figure of it on any sheet in that harbor. One hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about eleven in the morning and the bag stands at one hundred and ninety-six pence.

### Chapter 440 — *Saturday the Second Day of October, a Leaf Read Back in Full on the Flat of the Bench Stone at That Mole Head at About Ten Past Five in the Evening in the Open in the Ship's Own Left Hand All Four Columns Including the Empty One With Both Definitions of the Four Figures on the Face of That Reading, One Hundred and Seventy-Two and Seven Hundred and Thirty-Seven and None and One Hundred and Twenty-Five at the Hour of That Reading and One Hundred and Seventy-Three and Seven Hundred and Thirty-Nine and None and One Hundred and Twenty-Five at the Close of the Day, a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Paid in Coin on the Flat of the Bench Stone at About Four in the Afternoon at the Figure in Chalk on a Slate at an End Stall, a Room over a Joiner's Shop Let Out for the Fifth Time With a Bowl on the Step at Two o'Clock, and a Harbor With No Flour in That Market and No Oil in It Since the Twenty-Ninth Day of August and a Light Out of a Mole Head and a Figure on a Board That Did Not Come Down*

The leaf was read back at about ten past five in the evening on the flat of the bench stone at that mole head, in the open, in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, **with both definitions on the face of that reading: one hundred and seventy-two entries in the first column at the hour and one hundred and seventy-three at the close, being one hundred and forty-three at the close of the second day of September past and one entry against each of the thirty days since with no day in two of them; seven hundred and thirty-seven lines in the second at the hour and seven hundred and thirty-nine at the close, being five hundred and eighty-nine at the close of the second and five a day since, six hundred and eighty-nine plus fifty at the close and six hundred and eighty-seven plus fifty at the hour; none in the third with the boy's hand at the head of it and his surname on no page; and one hundred and twenty-five in the fourth with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it and the column not closed and the reason entered once on the twenty-eighth of August and entered again nowhere.** **The woman of no office said the one thing she said on that mole head and said it four feet off the stone: that what is hers and what is anybody's has to be written down and is not that yard's book, that that yard's four columns and that yard's figure and that yard's method do not go on the table in Fish Street and are not going to on any wall in this harbor, that her name does not go on a sheet for any of this, and that forty marks first after food is not reduced by a chain and a weight and a bellwright from off the reef line, and that none of those three things has been paid and none of those three things is going to be paid in this harbor in her lifetime.** He did not answer that and did not improve on it. **A caulker of about twenty-three was paid one hundred and sixty-eight pence in coin on the flat of the bench stone at about four in the afternoon, asked for by name at about ten in the morning on Wednesday the twenty-ninth of September past, on no other day of these ten, and nobody thanked him.** The room over a joiner's shop was let out for the fifth time and about seventeen went up and three came down and eleven of the seventeen could not read, and about twenty went up on the twenty-sixth, which is about thirty-seven across the two Sundays, and there was no claim in any of them. One hundred and sixty-eight pence came in at about ten in the morning and one hundred and sixty-eight pence went out at about four in the afternoon and the bag stands at one hundred and ninety-six pence, being one mark and three shillings, short of the wage of four marks by four hundred and forty-four pence, being two marks ten shillings and fourpence. There is no flour in that market, no barley in that market since the middle of the month, no oil in that harbor since the twenty-ninth of August, the light is out, the sheet of six lines is on that wall for the seventeenth day on the outside of a figure that did not come down, the nine-line sheet with a seal is on that wall for the forty-ninth day and is answered by nobody, and the paper of four lines in Fish Street is on that door for the thirty-second day.

### The repairs made in this batch, and the shape of the volume after forty chapters of it

**TWELVE REPAIRS, ALL AT `state/continuity.md` § 12, THE TWELFTH OF THEM MADE IN A SECOND PASS AFTER THE WHOLE OF THE VOLUME WAS WRITTEN, NONE OF THEM A DATE, A CHARACTER, A SCENE, A STAGE OR THE PLOT: the word *fleet* cut from a mouth in Chapter 436; a second person in narration cut from Chapter 434 and a second one cut from a closing block in Chapter 433; the one instance of the fuller shape of the house's fault form, in Chapter 433's body, rewritten to say what happened; a declaration of absence cut from Chapter 433's subtitle and replaced with what a woman of fifty-eight said; a surname cut from Chapter 432's disambiguation and carried descriptively; the house's own name *this volume* cut out of a mouth in Chapter 440 and rephrased; two hundred and eighty-four pence glossed and a tide that went from nine foot to seven foot in twenty minutes repaired to a tide that can happen and a day's work repaired to end before the cutoff that ended it, all in Chapter 436, and that same figure of two hundred and eighty-four then found in a second pass not to be the sum of the two halves itemised beside it in the same sentence, and repaired in three places in Chapter 436 and in two state files to two payments of one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being three hundred and thirty-six, which is what Chapter 440's own ten-day total of eight payments already required and which makes the ten-day chain close on all ten of its days; three unglossed money figures in Chapter 440 and one in Chapter 437; a real reason put into nine ledgers; and a money gloss typed wrong in the draft of `state/current.md`. TWELVE FIGURES, ALL FOUND BY SWEEPING OR BY ADDING AND NONE BY LOOKING, AND THE ONE THAT A GLOSS SWEEP CANNOT CATCH IS THE ONE WHERE THE GLOSS WAS RIGHT ABOUT A FIGURE THAT WAS WRONG.**

**THE SHAPE OF VOLUME 09 AFTER FORTY CHAPTERS OF IT.** Forty days, one day to a chapter, from Tuesday the twenty-fourth day of August to Saturday the second day of October. One custody room entered once. One public book that is wrong on its own face by an omission a stranger with a pencil can find. One panic that is real in its witness and false in its story, with the two halves on the page and nobody resolving them. **One stage taken, in the last four days of this batch, on the water, in company, at a wage out of that yard's own figures, under a consent asked for one man at a time, with a named tender and a cutoff that a man who is paid by nobody in the boat is the only person who can pull.** The four columns stand at one hundred and seventy-three, seven hundred and thirty-nine, none, and one hundred and twenty-five, and the fourth has taken no line in forty days and nobody has closed it.
