The bag stands at one hundred and ninety-six pence against a wage of six hundred and forty and has been short of that wage on every hour of every one of the forty days and nobody is going to write one word under it. The third column is empty and unappointed and the boy's surname is on no page. **A harbor poorer on the fortieth day than on the first, with no flour, no barley, no oil, a light out, a figure on a board that did not come down, a sheet of six lines on a wall for the seventeenth day that nobody answered, a nine-line sheet for the forty-ninth, a paper of four lines on a door for the thirty-second, forty-nine weeks fallen due with no envelope, and a hundred and forty days in which the bellwright of that harbor has not been asked.** Three of the volume's costs are paid with figures and none of them is a payment of anything old. **THE PARTIAL CONFESSION IS NOT PAID IN FORTY DAYS AND THE FOURTH BOX IS STILL EMPTY, AND BOTH ARE OWED TO THE LAST MOVEMENT.**

## Volume 09, Batch 0005 (Chapters 441–450), Movement 5, the copy, the account, the charter, and the cost, in which the custody room is entered the second time and once only, at the hour named on the second paper, and in which the charter is written in a room over a fish market and the title the series file has named is said once by a working man on the day it is written — complete, 29 September 2026

### Chapter 441 — *Sunday the Third Day of October, a Day on Which No Charge Was Placed on That Cistern and on Which That Wall Came Down and Went Up Whole, the Last Day of a Twelfth Week in Which Nobody in That Crew Has Said One Word About Three Nots, Six Things Named Out Loud in a Shed as What Any Account of Anything in This Harbor Has to Carry and the Refusals Named Among the Six, a Woman of No Office Told in That Shed at About Four in the Afternoon That Her Name Is Going on a Public Sheet and Her Not Asking for It to Be Taken Off, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming Into That Yard at About Ten in the Morning and One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Going Out of It at About Four in the Afternoon, a Room over a Joiner's Shop at the Top of Fish Street Let Out for the Sixth Time on a Sunday, and a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Still on a Bank About Four Hundred Yards Down That Foul in Nine Foot of Water With Eleven Feet of Caulked Joint in Her That Has Been Wet Once*

The boat of about nineteen tons was still on the bank four hundred yards down that foul with about eleven feet of caulked joint in her that had been let into the water once. **Nessa Pike, from the bow of a boat of about eleven tons, said at about seven in the morning that she is not coming off this tide and she is not coming off the next one either, and that a joint of oakum and tar goes soft the second time it soaks and sets hard the second time it dries, and that a joint that has done one of each is not a joint yet, and that she has to be wet twice and dry once between and that is about four days of tide whatever the weather does, and that she is coming off on the Monday and that she will put that in the second column in a reason against the line and not in the first, because a man on a mole cannot check what a joint feels like.** Halvard Ness had a kettle on his tender's galley for about nine men and none of them is paid by that tender and none of them is paid by that yard, and he had not pulled the chain and said at about eight o'clock that a chain weight is a thing for a man who has a reason and that he had not got one this morning. **At about eleven in the morning the holder of that writ put six things on the bench stone and said them out loud while three people were standing up, because in three days it is going to be on a piece of paper and he will not be able to change a word of it after that: what a thing is, what a thing is not, where it came from, what it does not show, the refusals, and the people — and the sixth is the seam, of which this yard has no copy and is not going to get one.** Nessa Pike made the sixth go on a page of its own, in her own mouth, because a person who cannot read is going to be told that page by a man with it in his own hand and a page that carries both will get the other one shrunk. **At about four in the afternoon, in that shed, with the door open on the slip, he told a woman of no office that her name is going on a public sheet for the first time since she came to that harbor, and she said she had had about six hours to work out that this was what he was going to do, and that a thing that has not been asked for is not on anybody's sheet and the only way it comes on a sheet is if somebody puts it there, and she said I am not going to ask you to take it off and you are not going to offer to take it off, and that forty marks first after food is not reduced by her name being on a piece of paper in an office on a hill, and that she is not going to be restored by it and is not going to be thanked, and that a person who asks to be taken off a piece of paper is a person who has been on it, and that was the whole of what was said about it in that shed.** The room over a joiner's shop was let out for the sixth time on the Sunday; about twenty went up and three came down and eleven of the twenty could not read, Hobb Lee read the head-notes out loud with his own name and the hour under each, there was no claim in any of them and no claim on that table, the twenty-second head carried three lines and a dash and nothing was said about it, and a man of about sixty-one asked at the door whether a person could put a thing in that book that they had not seen with their own eyes and was told no, and said that was fair, and went down the stairs.

### Chapter 442 — *Monday the Fourth Day of October, the Seventy-Fourth Time That Wall Behind a Reeve's Bench Came Down Bare and Went Up at the Angle It Has Been At Since the Twelfth, the Eighty-Seventh Time That Cistern Was Charged and Walked on by None of It With the Top Name on That Rota Board Still Off It, a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Off a Bank About Four Hundred Yards Down That Foul at About Half Past Two in the Afternoon With Eleven Feet of Caulked Joint in Her That Held, a Chain Weight Over a Rail at About Ten Past Three With an Hour and a Reason Written Against It, a Man of About Fifty Standing in Six Inches of Water on the End of a Baulk of Oak That the Same Hands of That Same Yard Laid Down a Week Before With Nothing on It, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Going Out at About Nine in the Morning and Coming Back at About Ten and Going Out Again at About Four in the Afternoon, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence, Against a Wage of Six Hundred and Forty*

The wall came down bare for the seventy-fourth time at about eight in the morning and went up at the angle it has been at since the twelfth and the man who laid the last course of it on the Friday put the same course on the Monday and did not put it back, and has not since the twelfth of August and is not going to. **The cistern was charged for the eighty-seventh time and about half of it went over the stone lip, and the man who charged it wrote the date on the board and then looked at the top of that board for about as long as it takes to write a date, and the top name has been off it since before the middle of the month, and it was off it at eight in the morning and it was off it at half past nine when he put his boot on the stone and the water went over his boot.** The *Alewife* came off that bank at about half past two in the afternoon, upright, on her own third attempt, with her new piece of keel going into the water first and about four inches of it under before the rest of her followed, and about eleven feet of caulked joint going under together and holding. Halvard Ness brought the chain over the rail at about ten past three and the reason was written down in the ship's left hand at about half past four with the hour against it. **They took her up to the head of the third lay on the flood and put her alongside the stone between about four and six boats, and a caulker of about twenty-three came out and looked at about eleven feet of joint that had been in nine foot of water for five days and said it was the only caulking he had ever seen that had been asked to do that and that he was not going to be paid for looking at it, and nobody paid him for looking at it.** Nine men got the mast in in about forty minutes and were not paid. Jos Lund, of about forty-four, stood in his own boat at about five and said she had got off and that nobody had got her wetter and that this yard's new piece on her keel was still on her and about eleven feet of a caulker's work was still in her and that both of those things were still true at six o'clock on a Monday in October and would be true on Wednesday. **At about half past eight in the morning two of that yard's hands laid a baulk of oak down across the same run of hard water that the baulk of the twenty-eighth of September had been laid across, and Ham Birt, of about fifty, whose boat that baulk opened about nine foot of garboard and a hole in her lee rail, stood in six inches of water at the end of it holding the top of it with both hands from about half past eight until about ten past eight, and about thirty men from seven boats went past him and about twenty of them said his name. Nobody thanked him at six o'clock or at seven or at eight and he did not ask, and that baulk was still on that run of hard water at dark and on the twelfth day of October.**

### Chapter 443 — *Tuesday the Fifth Day of October, the Fiftieth Wage Tuesday, and the Wage Column Did Not Move on It and Fifty Weeks Stand Fallen Due With No Envelope Against Any of Them at the Close of the Said Day, Four People in a Room at the Back of a Corridor in a Building on a Hill Under a Paper on a Door That Names Three of Them, a Bellwright of About Thirty-Four With a Piece of Worked Lead About the Size of a Man's Palm and a Knife and a Straight Edge, a Seam in a Fragment About Nine Inches by Six That the Cut Will Not Carry and That Is the Reason the Cut Is a Route and Not the Thing, a Clerk of About Forty Going Back to a Table at Eleven o'Clock Because the Hour Named on That Paper Is the End of It and Not the Middle of It, One Thing Out of Three and Nothing Going Out of That Room in Any Hand, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming Into That Yard at About Ten in the Morning and One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Going Out of It at About Half Past Eleven in the Morning, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence*

He went up the hill at about twenty to ten with nothing in his hands and read the foot of the first paper for the eighth time, and the seal line told him the same it had told him on the twenty-fourth of August, and he knocked. **There were three things in that room and the middle one was a fragment about nine inches by six whose edge was cut and not broken and in which there is a seam about three inches long where the pressure on one side is not the pressure on the other, and nobody in that room can say which of the two witnesses it is.** The copying clerk was about forty and put a fourth stool at that bench and said, before anybody asked, that there were four people in that room and the paper names three of them, and that he had not written the fourth one in his book and was not going to, and that if anybody wanted to make it an irregularity then it was an irregularity and he would write that down at the end of the day in a book that is not this one. **Mina Kett was asked one question and the question was whether she could cut a lead, and she said she could and that it was nine years of it and that she would do it in that room in about forty minutes and would do it badly at the ends because she cannot see a line through her own thumb, and that what she could not do was copy that, because that is nine inches by six with a whole scene in it and she is not a painter and there is no painter on that coast, and a scene is not a cut, and a cut is one line and a mark at the end of it and the same line in a hundred years, and you cannot cut a scene without deciding what it was about, and she is not going to decide what that is and she has not been in that room.** She did not touch the fragment for the first twenty minutes and then said there was a change in it about the length of her hand, and that it was not a crack and that somebody had worked on one side of that for longer than somebody had worked on the other, and that she could feel where it was with her hand on the cloth and could not tell anybody what it meant and neither could anybody else who was not a fool, and that she was telling three of them and a clerk, in front of that bench, that her cut was not going to carry it — **because a cut is a line, and a line cannot carry a place where the pressure changed, and a cut that carried it would be an opinion cut into a piece of lead that would go on saying it for two hundred years after everybody who could tell you it was an opinion is dead, and if she cut round it there would be a hole in the lead about the size of her thumb that a man with a pencil in a hundred years could see and could go and ask what was there.** She cut the line in about thirty-five minutes; the ends were thicker than the middle by about the width of a hair and she said that was how it is and that a man in a hundred years could see which end was made first. It went nine notches, the second, fifth and eighth deeper than the others. The marks cut into it were a letter at the head that was the office's own mark and not a number, a hand the size of a thumbnail, and an arm with a notch in it and a hole through the head cut small and off to one side, and **no figure and no number of any kind, and when the holder of that writ looked at the bellwright to ask why, she said tell them, and the clerk said, without looking up, that a number cut into a thing is a thing that can be asked after, and that he has three things in that room under three numbers and is not putting one of them on a piece of lead that is going to sit in a drawer for a hundred years, and that she would not have done it either, having left a hole in the line rather than cut something she did not know.** The fragment went back on its shelf under the same number at about twenty to eleven, the third of the three was not looked at and was not named, its claim in a book in that building was not withdrawn and no request for its withdrawal was made by anybody, and at eleven the three people named on that paper came out and the fourth came out behind them, and the door was shut and nothing went out of that room in any hand, including a piece of worked lead about the size of a man's palm. The clerk said at the steps, once, that seven is the right number for a bench, that it is not the right number for a knife, that he was never asked about the seven and is not going to be, that his book says a thing was cut at that bench at ten in the morning with a mark, and that his book does not have her name in it and is not going to.

### Chapter 444 — *Wednesday the Sixth Day of October, a Long Sheet of a Copyist's Hand About Four Feet Long With a Head at the Top of It and a Rule Under the Head and Nine Boundaries Printed on the Face of the Same Sheet and Not on a Separate Paper, Three Names Against the Head of Custody and Four More Against a Line That Says a Rotation and Not an Office, a Man of About Twenty-Nine of No Lay and a Man of About Forty-Four Who Carried a Piece of Worked Glass Out of a Boat's Hold in June Having Asked to Be on That Rotation, a Sheet of Four Refusals With Four Names and Four Hours on It Put Into the Fourth Box on a Table in an Office off the West Basin Against the Word of a Man of About Fifty With Two Papers on That Table, a Caulker of About Twenty-Three Asked for by Name at About Ten in the Morning and Paid at About Four in the Afternoon, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence*

The sheet was copied at a counter in a room off that market at about a quarter past nine in the morning by a copyist of about fifty-nine who has been at that counter for twenty-two years and did not ask what she was copying, and the penny came out of the holder's own coat and is not a figure of anything. He wrote the head himself at about ten and stopped, and said there were three people who would have their names against it and that two of them had not asked to be on it and that this was the part where somebody had to say something in a room, and Mara Venn said the thing she had said on the Sunday about a person who asks to be taken off a piece of paper, and he wrote her name against the head of it. Nessa Pike put hers there in her own hand and was not thanked. **Jens Ower, of about twenty-nine, of no lay, who lightered about eleven tons, came up that slip at about a quarter to ten and said he had heard there was going to be a sheet with three names on it and wanted to know who the other people on it were before he put his name under it, and having been told the two, put it under it; and Nate Pry, of about forty-four, put his name under it too and said one thing when he did, which was that he had been in a chandler's shop four weeks ago and had walked out of it, and that a sheet that says three names is a sheet he could stand behind.** Four names are under a line that does not say office and does not say deputy and does not say member and says only that they asked for a turn of four weeks from the sixth of October, and a stranger with a pencil can count that on the face of the sheet. The head-rule went on the top in the ship's own hand in four lines, and under it the nine boundaries were printed, and they are the reason the community can stand behind four names at all: what the copy is and is not and where it came from and what it does not show; that the thing does not show the place about the size of a thumb and that place was left out on purpose and this account does not say what was in it and cannot; that the thing is a made thing and not a transcript and every mark on it can be seen and none of them is a number; that it may be used for a route and not for a scene; **that four lines are missing from the twenty-second head of the public volume in Fish Street, being the clause that would say what that panel is not fit for, and that clause is not on that page and is not being put on it, and a person with a pencil has found the place it should be in and that finding is on this account because that page cannot carry it; that a panel in that harbor holds a scene that a living person was made to settle at about nineteen years old in a room with a prepared frame and an anchor in it, and that person is alive and is not named on that account and is not on any other sheet in that harbor and nobody in that harbor is to ask that person about it again; that a berth was held on a man of about thirty-eight and a claim window is off on a man of about thirty who cannot read the paper it is on, and neither the berth nor the window is given back by anything on that account, and a man behind a counter read him that paper out in September and told him in his own mouth that the word on it is off, and off is a different word to held, and nobody in that harbor is going to read it to him again; and that a charge of one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, stands at the foot of a sheet of six printed lines on a wall at the back of an end stall, on the outside of a figure of four hundred and fifty pence that was not taken down first, and that no claim has been lodged under that charge and no penny of it has been paid.** Under the nine, a rule that any person in that harbor may put his own words against any line in the room where the account is read out, with a name and an hour, and both are printed, and the person who entered it does not get to strike his. **At about half past three in the afternoon Mara Venn went down the west basin with a sheet of good paper carrying the four refusals, the four names and the four hours, and put it into the fourth box on a table in an office off that west basin, and the man of about fifty who works at that table said there is no name on that, and she said there is no name on that, and that there are four names at the top of it and an hour against each of them and four sets of the same nine words under them, and that it went through a counter at a penny a sheet out of a man's coat, and that she put it in that box because a refusal that stands on a wall in a shed is a thing a person can be told did not happen. He said he had wanted that box left empty, and she said he said it once in a shed and she heard him and that he has not been asked about it since and is not going to be asked now, and that it is on the face of that sheet in the last line, which names her, and his word, and the date. He read that last line twice and put the sheet into the fourth box and shut it, and he was not asked about it.**

### Chapter 445 — *Thursday the Seventh Day of October, the Eighty-Eighth Time That Cistern Was Charged and Walked on by None of It, a Room on the Premises of That Office on the Hill With a Chair and a List at the Door and About Thirty People in It of Whom About Eleven Could Not Read, a Net-Mender of About Forty-Six Reading an Account of About Four Feet Aloud From Two o'Clock Until About Half Past Three With His Own Name and the Hour Under It in His Own Hand, the Foot of That Sheet Read Aloud Once in That Harbor and the Office Named Once in a Working Man's Mouth, a Man in a Coat of an Office in a City Entering a Claim Against the Copy at a Counter off the West Basin at About Four in the Afternoon and Neither Granting It Nor Refusing It, and the Original and the Copy Both Staying in the Building They Were In*

There was a chair at the door of that room and a woman of about forty-four in it who keeps the key to that corridor with a list on a board, and she wrote every name that went past her and the hour against it and did not read the list to anybody and did not ask anybody what they had come for. **Hobb Lee, of about forty-six, who mends nets on the third lay and can read, stood at the end of the middle table and read the sheet out loud from about a quarter past two until about half past three and wrote his own name and the hour under every page of it in his own hand, and the head of that sheet says in four lines that any person in that room may stop him at any word and put his own words against it, and nobody in that room stopped him for about an hour and a quarter, and then a man of about thirty-eight stood up and said one word, which was which, and the reader said it was the seventh of the boundaries, and the man said that was the one he was asking about and sat down again.** About eleven of the people in that room could not read, and eleven of them were in that room on the seventh of October and every one of them heard the whole of that sheet from the middle of that table, and Hobb Lee did not turn a page round to face himself while he was reading it, and one of the eleven kept his own thumb on the line he was on until the reader had finished that line, and that is what that room did for the people in it that afternoon. **The foot of that sheet is the foot of a paper of that office and the same seal line has been at the foot of the first paper on the door of the custody room since the twenty-second of August, and it was read out loud for the first time in that harbor at about a quarter past three on the seventh of October, and it is thirteen words long, and the office at the end of it went into that room in a working man's mouth for the first time since the twenty-second day of August, which is the day that first paper went up on that door: *Recovered accounts, circuit of this town. Magister Ilya Serr, Registrar of Recovered Accounts.*** There was a silence of about the length of two breaths, and then a woman of about forty who sells milk in that harbor and who has a boy of eleven said, in her own voice and to nobody, that she had been told since the summer that that name could take a harbor's records whole, and then said that it is a name at the foot of a page and that she had been told a thing about a name and not about an office, and then asked the man beside her whether the milk was still outside. The reader said the sheet was going on the desk at the door on its way out and that anybody in that harbor could take it up and read the whole of it, and then said he was going to put his own name under the foot of it, which he did, with the hour. Nobody thanked him. **The original did not move that afternoon and did not move on any of the ten days after it, and the piece of lead cut on the fifth of October is in a drawer in the same building under a drawer of its own, and neither of them came to that harbor.** At about four in the afternoon a man in a coat of an office in a city came into that harbor at a counter off the west basin, four hundred yards from that building, and was not named to anybody and was not asked anything and did not stop for more than a quarter of an hour, and put a sheet with a mark on it that was not a seal into a book at that counter, and what he put in was a claim against the copy, being that a copy of a record of recovered accounts made in that building is a record of recovered accounts and is to be held against it until somebody in authority has looked at it. **The man of about fifty at the table read it and did not grant it and did not refuse it and wrote in the register copy that it was entered at four o'clock and not granted and not refused, and told the man in the coat that a claim entered is a claim entered, and that a thing entered in a book in that office is a thing that can be pointed at by anybody who comes in with a pencil, and that that is the whole of what this harbor has got to do about it and the whole of what it is going to do about it.** That claim is not withdrawn.

### Chapter 446 — *Friday the Eighth Day of October, a Line of Nine Soundings Taken Off a Sheet of Paper in a Room on a Hill and Carried Out in a Pocket by Hand, and Not the Lead, Which Did Not Come Down That Hill, Three Accounts of the Same Stone at the Fifth of Those Nine Soundings in About Four and a Half Fathoms That Do Not Agree With Each Other and Are Kept in That Order and Are Not Settled, a Man of About Forty-Four Going Against a Line of That Account With His Own Name and the Hour Under It and the Account Not Being Changed, a Diver Going Down Once on That Line at About Two in the Afternoon Under a Tender of About Twenty-Three and Fifteen Fathoms of Chain and a Weight on the Tail of It That Came Over the Rail at About Ten Past Three, and What He Was Able to Put a Name to When He Came Up and What He Was Not, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence*

**The line went out of that harbor in three pockets on the Friday morning and it was not the lead, and that is the whole of what a boundary is for and the first time a thing has gone out of a drawer in a building on that hill as written words rather than as a thing.** What came down was a sheet of about four feet with a line of nine soundings on it, **written in the ship's own hand at about half past six in the morning on the Friday out of the account of about four feet that was read out in a room on that hill on Thursday the seventh, and not out of any drawer in any building, and no person in that harbor has seen the thing it describes.** **THE SHEET CARRIES ITS OWN NAME, ITS OWN HOUR AND ITS OWN AUTHORITY ON ITS FACE: IT SAYS AT THE HEAD THAT IT IS A DESCRIPTION OF A MADE THING AND NOT THE THING, IT SAYS WHERE IT CAME FROM, AND IT CARRIES THE FIFTH OF THAT ACCOUNT'S NINE BOUNDARIES IN THE SAME SIZE AS THE REST OF IT, WHICH AUTHORIZES A LIMITED USE OF THE ROUTE BY THE FOUR PEOPLE WHOSE NAMES ARE ON THAT ACCOUNT AND NAMES THOSE FOUR, AND THERE IS NOTHING ON IT THAT WOULD PUT A FIFTH NAME THERE. A COPYIST OF ABOUT FIFTY-NINE WROTE IT OUT AT A PENNY A SHEET, THE PENNY OUT OF A MAN'S OWN COAT AND NOT OUT OF ANY BAG, AND THE HOLDER READ IT AGAINST THE ACCOUNT BEFORE IT LEFT THE BUILDING.** It notes which three of the nine were shallow, and it notes at the foot that the lead has an office's mark and a hand and a person's own mark and no figure at all. **Jens Ower had it in a fold of oilcloth at about seven in the morning and had copied the nine soundings onto the back of his own hand with a bit of charcoal, and said on the quay, to nobody, that he had done that because he could not read the numbers and could count nine of anything.** The line runs between the point and the north end of that mole and about two miles and a quarter offshore, and the second, fifth and eighth of the nine are shallow, and the fifth is on the top of a stone in about four and a half fathoms. Three accounts of that stone, in one afternoon, in the order they were said, all in the second column in the yard's own mouth with the reason against the line, none taken back and none settled. **The first was the holder of that writ's, at about half past ten in the morning: a stone about the size of a kitchen table lying with its long side across the tide, and a piece of iron standing out of the middle of it about nine inches, square and not rusted through, and he is saying that because he has seen it twice, once in June and once on the twenty-fourth of August, and both times he was in a bell at about ten feet looking down at it, and a square thing nine inches out of a stone at four and a half fathoms does not grow. The second was Nate Pry's, in his own boat of about nine tons, at about one o'clock in the afternoon: a stone about the size of a kitchen table, and nothing standing out of the middle of it, and he lay off it and looked at it for as long as it takes to boil an egg and there is nothing on that stone at all, and he has been in a lot of holds in thirty years and knows what a piece of iron in a stone looks like from underneath. The third was Jens Ower's, in his lighter, at about a quarter past two: a stone, and two things on it, and one of them a square piece of iron about the size of his hand standing up out of it, and the other a bottle with a cork in it, and the cork is not in and the bottle is not empty and there is a paper in the bottle and he has not read the paper and has put the cork back in it as far as it will go and put the bottle back on the stone where it was because he does not know whose it is.** Nobody in those three boats could say the other one was wrong, and all three were written down at about half past five and nobody was asked a second question, and **the three accounts of about two foot of soft plank in a boat of about nineteen tons entered in the last ten days stand in the same leaf in the same order and are not settled either, and there are now six accounts in that book that do not agree with each other and not one of the six has been settled and nobody in this harbor is going to settle any of them.** Nate Pry went back up the west basin at about six and put his own words against the fifth line of that account, being the line that says the thing may be used for a route, and what he wrote against it is that a route is a route if it is there twice and that he has been on it once and there was nothing on the stone, and that went under the account the same day and both are printed and the account was not changed. Calder Marr went down in a bell off the port quarter of a boat of about eleven tons at about two in the afternoon, once, with the reason written down before he went down and the hour against the reason, and a man of about fifty-eight who has swept out the Fish Street room on every Sunday since it was let out and had been in a bell once and could tell nothing at all came along in the tender and stood on her after deck with a line in his hand and did not go down. He was in the water about thirty-five minutes. The chain came over the rail at about ten past three and the reason was written down at about half past four with the hour against it, being that the bottom of that stone was not visible in about four and a half fathoms on a west wind and no man was going to hold his breath for a third look at a piece of iron. **He sat on the after deck with his coat off and had a cold in his teeth and a taste of iron in his mouth like a nail, and said the two of those things out loud to about four men on that deck because that is what a body says and a body says it to people and not to a paper, and it is an aftertaste and it is not a fever and it is not a complaint and it is not glass and it is not an illness and it does not tell anybody anything about anything. Then he said the third thing, which was new: I can put a name to the afternoon. I cannot put a name to what was in the boat with me. The twenty-ninth of June, out of that harbor, on the ebb, and I know the day and I know the water and I know whose hand it was that I can see in my own head when I think about it, and there was a second man in that boat and I do not know which of two men it was, and I am not going to stand here and pick one out of the four that it could be, and I am not going to have anybody in this harbor pick one for me.** That went into the second column at about half past six with the hour against it and no name against it.

### Chapter 447 — *Saturday the Ninth Day of October, a Far Bench Occupied from About Ten in the Morning Until About Two in the Afternoon and Not Empty at Four o'Clock, and That Bench Not Having Been Emptied Before Four o'Clock on Any of the Days Before It, a Man of Sixty-One Coming Down a Slip and Saying Four Sentences Out Loud in His Own Mouth in a Shed and There Being No Fifth of Them, the Fact of His Own Signature, the Harbor and the Yard and the Hour, the Weather and Two Marks Nine Shillings and Fourpence in His Pocket and a Day's Pay in Front of Him, and What He Said to His Wife That Night and What He Has Said in That House Every Day for Twenty-Two Years, and Nobody Thanking Him and Nobody Forgiving Him, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming Into That Yard at About Ten in the Morning and One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Going Out of It at About Eleven in the Morning, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence*

Nessa Pike went out to the head of the third lay at about ten past two because the caulked joint in a boat of about nineteen tons wanted looking at in daylight and she wanted to look at it herself, and put her coat on the back of a chair and went down that slip, and that shed was shut from the front and open at the back and there were two people in it at about two o'clock in the afternoon. **The man who came down that slip at about two o'clock was sixty-one and had been on that far bench since about ten and had not asked for anything all morning, and he came down it without anybody in that yard going up to him, and he came down it the way a man comes down a slip he has not come down in twenty-two years, which is that he puts his hands in front of him and looks at the steps. He stood about four feet off the bench stone with his hands at his sides and he said four sentences.** They were these. *I put my name to a paper at Ternwatch on the twenty-second of November, and it was my name, and I have never once said it was anybody else's.* *The harbor was Ternwatch and the yard was two hundred yards inside the third pier and I was at the gate of it at about eight in the morning.* *It was blowing hard off the land and I had two marks nine shillings and fourpence in my pocket and there was a day's pay in front of me and I took the job.* *I came home that night and told my wife it was a survey, and it was not a survey, and I have said that sentence in this house every day for twenty-two years.* And then he stopped, and that was the end of it, and there was no fifth of them, and he did not say another word in that shed for about four minutes. **The holder of that writ was standing at the bench stone when the four sentences were said and did not take a step forward while they were being said, and afterwards he did not go over to him either, and there was nobody else in that shed and nobody came into it and the door at the front was shut the whole time.** What he said, about a minute after, was not a thank and was not a forgiveness and was not a question about a paper: *I am not going to say anything about that here, and I am not going to say it tonight either, and you are going to sit on that bench tomorrow from ten until four like you have.* The man of sixty-one said that was all right and went back up the slip, got back onto that far bench at about ten past three and was on it at four o'clock, and did not speak to anybody in that yard again that day, and nothing was put in his hands at any hour of that day. **Nobody thanked him. Nobody forgave him. A man of about thirty-two did not forgive a man of sixty-one on a Saturday afternoon in a shed and did not say that he had and did not say that he had not, and a woman of no office upstairs was not told any of it, and the second column of that leaf has no line in it about the twenty-second of November and never will, and neither brother has ever said why either of them went into that yard in April or why neither of them has said one word about it since.** What was said in that shed on the ninth day of October was not written down by anybody in that harbor at any hour of that day or after it, and the reason was given at about a quarter to eight in the evening and is this: that a man said four sentences in a shed and nobody asked him for a fifth and nobody asked him for the first of them again, and that this yard keeps what it did and who did it and in what order, and that what a man of sixty-one said once at about two o'clock in the afternoon is not something that yard did and is not something that yard is going to write down, and that if this yard wrote it down then a person in that harbor would find out one afternoon what a man said in a shed, and this yard is not doing that to anybody.

### Chapter 448 — *Sunday the Tenth Day of October, a Room over a Fish Market in a Different Building from the Room over a Joiner's Shop at the Top of That Street, About Twenty-Two People in It at About Ten in the Morning, a Long Sheet With No Name at the Head of It and Nobody Having Asked for One, Four Rule-Heads Written on It and Read Out From Eleven o'Clock Until About Ten Past Twelve, a Master of About Fifty Saying the Name of That Thing Once at About Ten Past Eleven in the Morning on the Day It Was Written and Writing It at the Head of That Sheet Himself, a Rotating Council, a Right for a Community to Withdraw From a Route, Two Standing Rules, a Claim Against a Copy Carried on It and Not Discharged, a Question Asked Once After the Four Heads Had Been Read and Not Answered by Anybody and Recorded in a Minute as Asked, a Remaining Question Asked Once and Carried by No Rule, and a Room over a Joiner's Shop Let Out for the Seventh Time on the Same Sunday*

The room was over a fish market and it was not the room over a joiner's shop and it was not four hundred yards from it, and anybody in that harbor who has heard the two of them spoken about in the same week has heard the wrong one about the other. **There is a difference that matters: the room over a joiner's shop keeps a public volume of thirty-one heads with four lines under every head, and a claim is not a head and is not read at that table, and a man of about forty-six reads what is on a page in that room and will not read anything that is not a head in that volume. The room over a fish market has a long table, a stove that does not draw, and about twenty-two people in it at about ten in the morning, and nothing in that room on that day was a claim.** The sheet was bought blank for a penny out of the holder's own coat and it is about three feet long, and the first thing anybody said about it was said at about half past nine by Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, who keeps the whole fouling ladder in that harbor in his own book and has never shown it to anybody: *There is a head of paper at the top of that thing and it is empty, and I am not going to be the one who writes on it.* Nobody wrote on it for about forty minutes. **At about ten past eleven a man of about fifty, master of the boat of about twenty-two tons whose garboard that yard's own baulk opened on the twenty-eighth of September and who was not charged a penny for that bill and did not offer and was not thanked for saying he would hold that baulk next time and held it on the fourth for about an hour and ten minutes and was not thanked for that either, picked up the pencil and said the name of the thing once, and wrote it at the head of that sheet himself in a hand that is not a clerk's hand, and put the pencil down.** He said it once and did not say it again that day, the two people nearest him did not take it up, and the twenty-two people in that room were about eleven working people and their families and one bookbinder's apprentice of about seventeen and the holder of that writ and three people who have asked to be on the rotation, and that sheet went on the wall of that room at about one o'clock and has hung there since with nothing written on it above those four heads, and eleven names are at the foot of it and there is no seat and there is no roll and there is no seal, and a person in that harbor who wants to know who belongs to that sheet can go up that stair and read the eleven names on it and count them. **Four heads were written on the sheet under the name and read out loud from about eleven until about half past twelve, with the reader writing his own name and the hour against each as he came to it, and about four people in that room could not read and heard all four. One, Claims: a claim is a thing somebody wants and has not got, put in their own words with their own name and the hour on it, and it is not decided by anybody on that sheet or off it, and a name on a claim is not a finding. Two, Refusals: a refusal is a thing this harbor has been given and is on this sheet at the same size as the rest of it and is not a footnote, and the same words are used for a refusal about a claim and a refusal about a panel and a refusal about a person. Three, Restricted records: some things are closed and stay closed, and a thing that is closed is not a thing anybody has to explain, and the closing of a thing is written in the same hand as the opening of it. Four, Public correction: when a thing turns out to be wrong it is corrected in the same place it was printed, with the wrong thing left where it is and readable, and a correction is not a removal and a removal is not a correction, and anybody in that harbor may make one and nobody may take one away.** Then four standing lines: no route, panel or account is represented by anybody who has not asked to be represented; the refusals are on it and are not smaller than the rest; a community may withdraw from a route, and it takes one person of that community to say it and it does not take a vote and nobody on that sheet can ask a community why it wants out; and the council turns, four names, asked for, four weeks from the tenth of October, no turn to be given to anybody who has not asked for it, and a person whose turn it is may be asked once and not twice. **And then a fifth thing which is not a rule: a claim against the copy entered in a book at a counter off the west basin on the seventh of October, not granted, not refused, not withdrawn, written on that sheet at the same size as the four heads, and that sheet does not discharge it and does not refuse it and does not pretend to be able to.** And under that, four lines saying what that thing is not, which a stranger with a pencil can take and hold against the rest of the sheet and find that the sheet bears out. **The question was asked at about twenty past twelve in the afternoon by a woman of thirty of no office, and she is Mara Venn, and she has forty marks first after food standing against her and is not restored, and it was asked after the four heads had been written and read out, and she named no person: can a thing like this speak for people who cannot speak safely, and for people whose own account of what happened to them is being held under a lie? A man of about thirty-three said that it could not, because of the first of the four standing lines, and then he stopped. A woman of about forty-three who keeps a store on the second lay said that it could, because of the second, and then she stopped. Ollum Trevask said that he did not know, and that not knowing is a thing a man can put in a minute.** The minute says the question was asked at about twenty past twelve in the afternoon of the tenth of October in a room over a fish market, that nobody answered it, that three people began to and stopped, and that a man of about thirty-four said he did not know, and it does not say what the answer is, because there was not one, and the four heads were not changed by the asking and would not have been changed by any answer. **The other question was asked at about half past twelve by a man of about forty-four who crews in no boat and holds no office, and it is a question and it is the whole of what he said: who is it that gets into the big ones, the big wrecks that are the Crown's own, is it the same for everybody or is there a list? Nobody answered that either, and it is in the same minute in the same hand at the same table, and no rule was written on that sheet about it and no office was made for it and no seal line was cut for it.** At two o'clock the room over a joiner's shop was let out for the seventh time, about twenty went up and three came down, eleven of them could not read, there was no claim in any of them and no claim on that table, and nothing written in a room over a fish market that morning was read out in that room that afternoon, and the eleven people on a paper of four lines at the top left of that door have been told nothing further by anybody in that harbor.

### Chapter 449 — *Monday the Eleventh Day of October, the Seventy-Fifth Time That Wall Came Down Bare, the Eighty-Ninth Time That Cistern Was Charged and the Last Charge Before the Last Day of the Ten, an Account of About Four Feet and a Man's Words Against One of Its Lines Read Out Aloud a Second Time in the Same Room at the Same Stated Hour With the Same Custodian at the Door and the Account Not Being Changed, Five Costs of Ten Days' Work Set Down One Under Another and Not One of Them a Payment and Not One of Them a Victory, a Man of About Thirty-Three Reading Six Printed Lines Aloud to Two Men Who Cannot Read and Then Reading Them the Figure of Four Hundred and Fifty Pence Off a Slate Underneath, and Nobody Answering That Sheet and Nobody Knocking It Down, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence*

The account was read out a second time at about a quarter past two in the afternoon in the same room on the first floor of that office on that hill, with the same woman of about forty-four in the chair at the door and her list on the board and the same hour written on it; about twenty-four people were in that room and about eleven of them could not read, and when the reader came to the fifth line he read the words that a man of about forty-four had put under it on the Friday evening, with his own name and the hour against them, the same as the rest. Nobody stopped him for about an hour. **At about half past three a woman of about thirty-one of that harbor stood up and said that she had been in a room in that town in the summer of the year before last and had been asked to hold a sheet of paper flat on a table while a man copied off it, and that she was not going to say anything else about it in that room, and that she was saying it because that account is about a piece and because a man of about forty-four had put his words against a line of it on Friday, and a person who is not going to say anything else should at least be the kind of person who turns up. Nobody asked her a question and nobody asked her to say it again and the reader wrote her name and the hour on the back of the sheet, and the sheet went back on the desk at the door on its way out. The account was not changed, it says at the head of it that the person who entered it does not get to strike a line out of it, and four words have been added under the fifth line since the seventh of October and the head has not been touched.** Then the five things, set down one under another the way Nessa Pike read them off a slate at about five in the afternoon and not the way they would read on a wall. **One, the copy and the original are both in the building on that hill, the original is on a shelf and has not moved, the piece of worked lead is in a drawer in the same building under a drawer of its own, and neither came to this harbor and neither went anywhere. Two, the account was read out at a stated hour on the seventh and again at a stated hour on the eleventh, in a room on the premises of the office that holds the original, with a custodian of that office in a chair at the door and a list of names and hours on a board, and about eleven people in that room on both days could not read and heard the whole of it both times. Three, a claim against the copy is in a book at a counter off the west basin, entered on the seventh of October, not granted, not refused, not withdrawn, and carried at the same size as the four heads on a sheet of about three feet in a room over a fish market, and that sheet does not discharge it. Four, a woman of no office has her name on a public sheet and on that sheet of four heads, and the account says at the head of it that nobody is put on it who has not asked to be on it, and she did not ask to be on either of them and is on both of them, and nobody took her name off either, and nobody thanked her, and nobody has offered to take it off, and forty marks first after food stands whole against her. Five, a diver went down once on the eighth of October under a tender of about twenty-three and fifteen fathoms of chain and a weight on the tail of it, with the reason written down before he went down and the reason written down after the weight came over the rail, and he was in the water about thirty-five minutes, and he came up with a cold in his teeth and a taste of iron in his mouth like a nail, and he can put a name to one afternoon in June and cannot put a name to what was in the boat with him, and that afternoon is in the second column of that leaf in the yard's own mouth with the reason against the line and no name against it.** Beside those five, and not part of them and not smaller than them, a ropemaker of about sixty-one of the third lay is not in that room and does not get that room back at any page of anything, no one has been made whole and no one has been charged with anything, a man of about fifty stood in six inches of water on the fourth holding a baulk for about an hour and ten minutes and has not been thanked and did not ask, a man of about thirty-eight whose berth was held on the eighteenth of September has not been given that berth back by anything that happened in these ten days, and a man of about thirty whose claim window is off cannot read the paper it is on, and the word on that paper was put into his own mouth once at a counter off the west basin in September and off is a different word to held, and nobody in that harbor is going to read it to him again. **At about half past four in the afternoon a man of about thirty-three stood in a front street in front of the wall at the back of an end stall with two men beside him who cannot read, and read the six printed lines out loud to them twice, and then one of the two asked him what the number under it was, and he turned round and read the figure off a slate on the same square of wall, and it is four hundred and fifty pence, being thirty-seven shillings and sixpence, quoted on the first of June, with February's three hundred and seventy-eight pence, being thirty-one shillings and sixpence, standing visible above it and both dates on that board, and the figure of the first of June was not taken down first and cannot be taken off. He said that he could not say it was a lie and he did not say it was not, and one of the two said he had a brother in a boat that went for pieces in April and did not say anything else, and the other said nothing at all, and they did not take the sheet off that wall and nobody in that street knocked it down and nobody wrote anything on it and nobody in that harbor has answered it in twenty-six days, and the charge at the foot of it of one hundred and sixty-eight pence, being one mark and eightpence, has not been paid by anybody and no claim has been lodged under it.**

### Chapter 450 — *Tuesday the Twelfth Day of October, the Fifty-First Wage Tuesday, and the Wage Column Did Not Move on It and Fifty-One Weeks Stand Fallen Due With No Envelope Against Any of Them at the Close of the Said Day, One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence Coming Into That Yard at About Ten in the Morning and a Bellwright of About Thirty-Four Paid One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence in Coin on the Flat of the Bench Stone at About Four in the Afternoon, and Twenty-Eight Pence in the Bag, Being Two Shillings and Fourpence, Against a Wage of Six Hundred and Forty, a Mole Head at Ten Past Five in the Evening With the Light Out and Its Lens Out Since the Seventh of May, a Leaf Read Back in Full With Both Definitions on the Face of That Reading and the Fourth Column Standing at One Hundred and Twenty-Five Where It Stood and Taking No Line, Three Statements About the Water and the Harbor and This Yard in Three Voices, the Whole of That Harbor's Standing Condition Once and Nowhere Else, and a Book on a Table in a Room With One Line in It Left Blank, Being a Place Where Nobody Was Asked*

At about ten past five in the evening, on the flat of the bench stone at that mole head, in the open, in her own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, Nessa Pike read that leaf back and the holder of that writ stood on the other side of it and did not touch it. **The first column has one hundred and eighty-two entries in it at this hour and one hundred and eighty-three at the close of the day, being one hundred and seventy-three at the close of the second of October past and one entry against each of the ten days since with no day in two of them, and a day of the first column carries one entry against it whatever else that day printed, so that a stranger with a leaf and a pencil can count it. The second column has seven hundred and eighty-seven lines in it at this hour and seven hundred and eighty-nine at the close, being seven hundred and thirty-nine at the close of the second and five a day since, three before the hour of each day's reading and two after it, and three of this day's went in before this reading and two went into it in this evening after it, and seven hundred and thirty-nine plus fifty is seven hundred and eighty-nine at the close, and seven hundred and thirty-seven plus fifty is seven hundred and eighty-seven at this hour. That figure is that book of that yard's own and it is not a count of anything anybody can check from a mole; the first column's one hundred and eighty-two and the fourth column's one hundred and twenty-five at this hour are a count of entries and a count of lines, and both of them can be taken with a pencil; those are the two definitions and they are printed here so that a later writer with a pencil knows which of them they are counting and at which of the two moments. The third column is empty and nobody has been appointed to it and the hand of a boy of twenty-two is at the head of it with a name beside it that was said out loud once in a boat on the thirteenth of May past and has not been said since, and nobody in that crew has said one word about the three nots standing against the eighth of June past and there is a fourteenth week in which that has not been said. The fourth column has one hundred and twenty-five lines in it at this hour and one hundred and twenty-five at the close, and it has taken no line in these ten days and there is no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, and that is not a closure and it is not a strike-out and nobody has closed that column, and the reason it has taken no line was entered in the second column at about ten past nine in the evening of the twenty-eighth of August in that yard's own mouth with the hour against it and is entered once and is not entered again, and the reason it is in the second column and not in the fourth is that a man on a mole cannot check the second column and a man on a mole can check the fourth.** She shut it and put it under her own coat and neither of them said one word about the figure it gave. Then three people said one thing each about that mole head, in that order, and none of it was said twice and none of it was written down. **Jens Ower, of about twenty-nine, about the water: the water is the only thing in this harbor that has not gone up since the first of June, and the reason is that nobody has ever managed to put a figure on it, and there is nine foot on a bank four hundred yards down that foul and seven foot and a half at the bottom of it, and a foot and a half is the whole of what a company of seven boats is worth, and that has not changed since the twenty-third of September and is not going to change this winter. The woman of about fifty-eight with the end stall and her slate, about the harbor: this harbor is the cheapest thing in it, and I have got a figure on a slate behind me that has been up since the first of June and it is the price of a barrel of oil and there is not a barrel of oil in this harbor to price, and that figure is not coming off, and I have been asked three times in a month to take it off and I am not going to take it off, and that is the whole of what I have to say about this harbor. The holder of that writ, about this yard: this yard is a shed, a bench stone, a leaf with four columns in it, a hundred and sixty-eight pence a day at a figure in chalk on that slate, and twenty-eight pence in a bag at the close of today, and three of the four columns in that leaf are mine and the first is a count anybody can take with a pencil and the second is a count nobody can, and I have been printing that on the face of it for ten days so that a stranger knows which one they are holding, and that is what this yard is, and it is not an office and it decides nothing and it is not a member of anything, and a master of about forty-six out of Lowfen told me from a doorway on Friday the first day of October that the asking is not the work, and he was right about that before I was, and this yard is still the same yard.** Then the whole of that harbor's standing condition, once and nowhere else: no flour and none coming this month and no barley since the middle of the month; no barrel of lamp oil since the twenty-ninth of August and a board carrying four hundred and fifty pence with February's three hundred and seventy-eight above it and both dates and the figure of the first of June not taken down and cannot be taken off; physic at fourteen pence, being one shilling and twopence, and none of it; the mole-head light out and its lens out since the seventh of May; the north berth out; the hose dead until the spring; the tide gang four men short; the hard at Ashtide unanswered; the third lay fills on the first of April and one berth is short; nineteen winters disputed and unpaid; the chandler's note at thirty-one with its three counts; the delayed note at eleven logged occasions and two with no call in them and the call not named; the wage column at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with twenty envelopes in a chest and fifty-one weeks fallen due; the cistern charged on the fourth, the seventh and the eleventh and walked on by none of it and the top name still off the board and the seven other days putting no charge on it; the six-line sheet on that wall for the twenty-seventh day on the outside of the figure, answered by nobody, and the nine-line sheet with a seal on a different square of a different wall for the fifty-ninth day, naming no person and no harbor, putting no figure on it, answered by nobody; the paper of four lines on that door for the forty-second day with the eleven people named on it told only that the paper is there; the notice of eight clauses on its own wall in a different street for one hundred and forty-eight days; **the twenty-second head carrying three lines and a dash, and four lines in pencil on the inside of the back cover with a name and a date against them, not to be repaired, explained or named against; a ropemaker of about sixty-one of the third lay, with a bad knee and a stick and a rope walk about forty feet long that does not run, put out of a room on the nineteenth day of September and not back in it, and nobody has been thanked for that and nobody is to be, and nobody has been made whole and nobody has been charged with anything;** the far bench occupied from ten until four with a shoe on the floor beside it that is not his and has been there since the third of May past; the two objects of nobody's four hundred and eighty-eight days old and about nine feet apart with a corner off one of them since the seventeenth of June past and not lashed back; two lights off that point not moved in seventy-two days; **a man of about fifty-one on the crown of that mole who has said nothing to anybody about a page of six names for ninety days, has a stone in his own pocket that he put there himself, and has been given nothing;** three marks to a man of Ashtide on an anchor date out of an earlier volume ruled not repaired; seven pence to that yard's own shipwright; eight marks and a day of a boat to that harbor's own bellwright, chest shut, not asked for a hundred and fifty days; eight shillings and tenpence to a woman of that harbor with her name on the figure; forty marks first after food to a person of no office; forty marks whole to a boy of twenty-two, with the three nots a fourteenth week unasked and the third column unfilled and unappointed and his hand at the head of it; a municipal claim on the third of three things in a custody room on a hill not withdrawn and no request for its withdrawal made by anybody; a box in an office off the west basin not empty and a fourth box on the same table not empty either, and a man of about fifty who wants that fourth box left empty not asked about it; a slip of paper with a figure on it and no name on it in a drawer with a sheet in it not looked at, priced or headed; a claim against a copy in a book at a counter off the west basin not withdrawn and carried on a sheet of four heads that does not discharge it; a belt of a coast road unlicensed and the thirty marks on it not paid; and a line cut in lead about the size of a man's palm in a drawer in a building on that hill that did not come down that hill. **At about half past five in the evening, in the room over a joiner's shop at the top of Fish Street, Hobb Lee put his hand on the long table and looked at the public volume on it and did not open it at the back cover, and then he turned back to the page he had left open and ruled a line under the last head on that page and left it empty, and wrote his own name and the hour against it in his own hand. The head at the top of that line is a page of six names on a mole with a boat as a price and no figure against it. The line under it is empty. The reason is written at the foot of that page in the same hand and it is: there is nobody in this harbor I can ask for this line, and I am not going to write one and put a name against it, and I have left it ruled and empty so that anybody who comes in here can see that there is a place on this page where nobody was asked. The twenty-second head of that volume was on a different page and carries three lines and a dash, and it was not touched on that evening, and the four lines in pencil on the inside of the back cover were not looked at by anybody, and the bowl on the top stone of that step was still on the step where he had put it at two o'clock.**

### The repairs made in this batch, and the shape of the volume after fifty chapters of it

**SEVEN REPAIRS, ALL AT `state/continuity.md` § 12, NONE OF THEM A CHARACTER, A SCENE, A STAGE OR THE PLOT, AND ENUMERATED HERE IN THE SEVEN OF THAT SECTION SO THAT THE TWO COUNTS AGREE: the word *plate*, the word *compartment* and the word *manifest* cut from Chapter 447's closing block and apparatus, being two of each before the pass and zero after; the house's own name *in this volume* cut out of Chapter 443's closing block; the word *fleet* cut from Chapter 448's closing block and a list of things that are not turned into a sentence of what is; two declarations of absence in Chapter 448's body and first column rewritten to say what happened, and a counted figure in the same passage that did not match the room it was in repaired; A MONEY CHAIN THAT DID NOT RUN ACROSS NINE DAYS RE-DERIVED BY HAND, EVERY FIGURE ON EVERY PAGE REPLACED, AND THE BAG'S CLOSE CORRECTED FROM ONE HUNDRED AND NINETY-SIX PENCE TO TWENTY-EIGHT; TWO UNGLOSSED FIGURES IN CHAPTER 450; AND ONE MUDDLED PASSAGE IN CHAPTER 450'S READING, WHERE THE SECOND COLUMN'S RUN WAS FIRST GIVEN AS SEVEN HUNDRED AND FORTY-TWO PLUS FORTY-EIGHT IS SEVEN HUNDRED AND NINETY, REWRITTEN TO SEVEN HUNDRED AND THIRTY-NINE PLUS FIFTY IS SEVEN HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-NINE AT THE CLOSE AND SEVEN HUNDRED AND THIRTY-SEVEN PLUS FIFTY IS SEVEN HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SEVEN AT THIS HOUR. ALL SEVEN WERE FOUND BY SWEEPING OR BY ADDING AND NONE BY LOOKING, AND THE FIRST PRINTING OF THIS PARAGRAPH SAID *SIX FIGURES* AGAINST A LIST OF SIX, WHICH WAS BOTH WRONG AND THE HOUSE'S OWN FAULT FORM, AND IS CORRECTED ON ITS FACE HERE.**

**THE SHAPE OF VOLUME 09 AFTER FIFTY CHAPTERS OF IT.** Fifty days, one day to a chapter, from Tuesday the twenty-fourth day of August to Tuesday the twelfth day of October. **One custody room entered twice and twice only, at ten in the morning on a Tuesday in August for a look at one thing out of three, and at ten in the morning on a Tuesday in October for an hour under a paper on its door with a clerk in it the whole time and four people in it and a made thing cut in lead that does not go out of that building in any hand.** One public book that is wrong on its own face by an omission a stranger with a pencil can find, and still wrong, and not repaired. One panic that is real in its witness and false in its story, with the two halves on the page and nobody resolving them and the date at the head of the notice never put beside the eleven dates in fifty chapters. One stage taken, in Movement 4, on the water, in company, at a wage out of that yard's own figures, under a consent asked for one man at a time, with a named tender and a chain and a weight that a man who is paid by nobody in the boat is the only person who can pull, and its three costs on the face of the pages and not summarised. **An account of about four feet in a desk at a door, with nine boundaries on its face, a rule that a line can be answered and not struck, four words under one of its lines that are not the yard's four words but the same rule, and a woman of thirty of no office on the head of it who did not ask to be there.** A charter of about three feet in a room over a fish market with four heads and four standing lines and a claim on it that it does not discharge, and a title said once by a working man on the day it was written. **The four columns stand at one hundred and eighty-three, seven hundred and eighty-nine, none, and one hundred and twenty-five, and the fourth has taken no line in fifty days and nobody has closed it. The bag stands at twenty-eight pence, being two shillings and fourpence, against a wage of six hundred and forty, and has been short of that wage on every hour of every one of the fifty days, and nobody is going to write one word under it. The third column is empty and unappointed and the boy's surname is on no page. A harbor poorer on the fiftieth day than on the first, with no flour, no barley, no oil, a light out, a figure on a board that did not come down, a sheet of six lines on a wall for the twenty-seventh day that nobody answered, a nine-line sheet for the fifty-ninth, a paper of four lines on a door for the forty-second, fifty-one weeks fallen due with no envelope, and a hundred and fifty days in which the bellwright of that harbor has not been asked.** Three of the volume's costs are paid with figures and five more of the climax are set down one under another, and none of the eight is a payment of anything old and none is a victory. **The partial confession was paid once, in four sentences, in a shed, on the ninth day of October, and there was no fifth, and nothing was written down, and nobody thanked him and nobody forgave him. The fourth box is not empty and the page says who put a sheet in it and why it went in against a man's word, and that man was not asked. A person of no office's name is on a public sheet for the first time since she came to that harbor and nobody took it off and nobody thanked her and nobody offered, and forty marks first after food stands whole. Six accounts in that yard's own leaf do not agree with each other and not one has been settled. And four questions were asked once each, and none of them is answered anywhere in fifty chapters, and the four thousand words this book has spent on a thousand small voices have not answered one of them, and that is the shape the volume closes in and it is not a resolution and it is not a cliff.**

**AND TWO FIGURES THAT THE AUDIT'S RE-DERIVATION ADDS TO THE RECORD, WHICH NO SUMMARY AND NO STATE FILE CARRIED BEFORE.** **The whole of the fifty days is four thousand and thirty-two pence in and four thousand one hundred and sixty-four pence out, being 160 + 4,032 − 4,164 = 28**, and it is now at `state/continuity.md` § 3 and `reviews/volume-09/volume-09-close.md` § 20 Item 7. **And the volume measures 205,204 words by `wc -w` on each of the fifty files and the fifty results added**, in five batches of **39,216 / 42,857 / 40,360 / 41,921 / 40,850**.

### The volume's own figures at the last page, and the five parts of its closing image

**THE FOUR COLUMNS AT THE CLOSE OF CHAPTER 450: ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-THREE / SEVEN HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-NINE / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE, AND AT THE HOUR OF THE LAST READING ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-TWO / SEVEN HUNDRED AND EIGHTY-SEVEN / NONE / ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY-FIVE.** **Both definitions are on the face of that reading and of the other four read-backs, at Chapters 410, 420, 430, 440 and 450, and on no other page.** The third column is empty and unappointed and nobody has been appointed to it and the boy's hand is at the head of it and **his surname is on no page of the fifty.** The fourth has taken no line in fifty days, there is no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it, the count of the italic fourth-column line across the fifty chapters is zero, and the reason was entered once, in the second column, on the twenty-eighth day of August, and is entered again nowhere.

**THE MONEY AT THE LAST PAGE: THE BAG IS TWENTY-EIGHT PENCE, BEING TWO SHILLINGS AND FOURPENCE, AGAINST A WAGE OF FOUR MARKS, BEING SIX HUNDRED AND FORTY PENCE, AND THE FIGURE IT IS SHORT BY IS SIX HUNDRED AND TWELVE PENCE, BEING THREE MARKS ELEVEN SHILLINGS, AND IT IS NEVER ZERO AND NOBODY IS TO WRITE ONE WORD UNDER IT SAYING ANYBODY IS GOING TO PAY IT.** No day's balance was ever at or above six hundred and forty at any hour, and the highest close in the fifty days is five hundred and thirty-two.

**THE FIVE PARTS OF THE FINAL CHAPTER IMAGE, ALL ON THE FACE OF CHAPTER 450, AND THE COUNT IS FIVE AND NOT SEVEN:** the mole head at ten past five in the evening with the light out; a leaf read back in full with both definitions on the face of the reading and the fourth column standing at one hundred and twenty-five where it stood and taking no line; three statements about the water and the harbor and this yard in three voices; the whole standing inventory once and nowhere else; and a book on a table in a room with one line in it left blank, being a place where nobody was asked.

**AND THE ONE LINE THE AUDIT END ON, WHICH IS THE VOLUME'S CONDITION AND NOT A STRIKE-OUT AND NOT A CLOSURE.** A thousand small voices is a name and the count of recovered panels this volume arrives at is three hundred and ninety-one, being pieces landed and entered at that harbor since the first of April, and the two are not the same thing and no chapter says they are. A seal line went into a working man's mouth once. A sheet of about four feet went on a desk at a door. A sheet of about three feet went on a wall over a fish market with four heads on it and no jurisdiction under them and a claim on it that it does not discharge. Four questions were asked once each in fifty chapters and none of them is answered on any page. Six accounts in one yard's own leaf do not agree with each other and not one of them has been settled. A figure of four hundred and fifty pence is still on a board in a front street and did not come down. There is no flour in that market and the light is out and the harbor is poorer on the fiftieth day than on the first.
