NOTHING BELOW IS REWRITTEN BY THE REPAIR EXCEPT WHERE A LINE SAYS SO.**

### Chapter 451 — *Wednesday the Thirteenth Day of October, Eleven People Asked One at a Time in the Same Eleven Sentences, Nine of Them at Four Marks and Two at One Mark, Two of the Eleven Saying No With a Reason in Their Own Mouths and Not Being Asked Again, a Woman of Thirty Saying Out Loud That a Sheet of Money Is Not a Sheet of Rules, and the Bag at Twenty-Eight Pence*

A trip to a shelf under the drowned city is named at about ten to six in the evening, after nineteen people have gone, by a man of about thirty-four of the second lay who keeps the whole fouling ladder in that harbor in his own book, has never shown it to anybody and is not asked for it. **The trip itself was named on that page in one of the eleven sentences at about ten in the morning; what was new at ten to six in the evening was the place.** *Repaired on the second pass: the chart is taken off this man's mouth and given back to a man of about thirty-one of the third lay, who was not in that room and was not brought into it and says it out on that slip with the door shut behind him, per `outline/volume-10.md` L29; the minute no longer says the trip was unnamed, and the clause at the eleventh sentence that had cancelled itself is repaired.* **Eleven people were asked one at a time in the same eleven sentences, written at the head of a page before anybody was asked and read out of the page, with a name and an hour against every line; nine wrote their names and two wrote their names and NO FIGURE WAS WRITTEN ON THE WEDNESDAY, the figures going on against those same nine and two names on the Thursday, and six of the eleven said out loud what the money was for before they wrote a name. A master of about thirty-three said no at about a quarter to five in front of five people, giving a reason about a boat of about seventeen tons, a mortgage standing until the spring and four men unpaid since the summer.** *Repaired: the figures are dated to the fourteenth, being the day the sheet existed, and the eight marks, the one mark and the mark and a half are no longer dated to the thirteenth or the sixteenth in this chapter.* A woman of thirty of no office read the eleventh sentence twice to a man of about thirty-eight who cannot read before he wrote a mark against his own line, and that mark is not a name and is not a figure. **Mara Venn put the batch's first rule on the record: a sheet of rules and a sheet of money are two things, and a harbor that cannot tell them apart will be told what to do by whichever is written in the larger hand, and the two are never to be in one room without both being named out loud.** Opened the thread that a piece of paper is about to be carried somewhere it has not been carried.

### Chapter 452 — *Thursday the Fourteenth, a Rota Day, the Ninetieth Charge on That Cistern Walked on by None of It, a Sheet Bought Blank and Blank at the Head of It for Forty Minutes, the Head Written Afterwards, Six Thousand and Eighty Pence Against Two Lines, a Pump Hand of About Forty-Four Named Ivo Skell Asked What a Compressor Wants, and a Second No*

A second sheet of good paper is bought for a penny out of a man's own coat and stands blank at the head of it for forty minutes, because the last blank page in that harbor stood blank for forty minutes four hundred yards away and a man of about thirty-four said the same sentence in both rooms. **The head is written in the holder's own hand and says what the money is for, that it promises nobody a find, that no penny comes out of the bag, that the four heads are not changed by it, that the refusals stand on it at the same size as the figures, and — in a line under all the rest — that the sheet carries no count of persons.** Six thousand and eighty pence, being thirty-eight marks, is against two lines by the close of the day, and the six who had said out loud what the money was for say it again before they write the figure and the other five of the nine say nothing. *Repaired: the head of the sheet is written at about ten past ten, being forty minutes after half past nine, and not at twenty past ten.* **A pump hand of about forty-four with nineteen years of compressors is asked what a compressor wants and answers the question nobody asked him, which is that being wrong has to be cheap, at four fathoms and not forty, and that a figure of money is not a thing you do to a boat.** A woman of about thirty-one who crews a lighter says no in front of nine people, names three men in a coat and a Tuesday in August, and is not asked again. Cost: ninety-six and two hundred and four.

### Chapter 453 — *Friday the Fifteenth, No Barrel of Lamp Oil in That Harbor, a Figure of Four Hundred and Fifty Pence on a Board That Is the Price of a Barrel That Does Not Exist, a Barrel Bought off a Coasting Boat at Four Hundred and Eighty-Six Pence, and a Sheet of About Four Feet Put in an Inside Pocket and Said to Nobody*

A woman of about fifty-eight with an end stall does not get up and says four hundred and fifty pence is the price of a barrel of lamp oil and that she has never once said anybody could buy one at that figure, and those are two different sentences. A barrel is bought off a coasting boat on the quay at four hundred and eighty-six pence, and the thirty-six pence between the two figures is named out loud and is the price of nothing. **At about four in the afternoon the owner of a boat of about twenty-two tons of the second lay comes down the slip and puts eight marks, being one thousand two hundred and eighty pence, against a line, and nobody asks him one word about the figure.** *Repaired: the eight marks are dated to the fifteenth, being lock L4's day for them, and were moved here out of Chapter 454, and the second column's phantom man of about thirty-one at the end stall is now the man who keeps the leaf.* **And at about five in the afternoon, alone, with four men talking, the holder of that writ reads the head of a sheet of about four feet in fifteen seconds and puts it in the inside pocket of a coat and tells nobody. It is in neither column of that leaf. He does not soften it and the chapter does not explain it in his own mouth.** The reason he gave himself is that a hundred years from now a man with a paper and a bell and no time at all might open a thing that took nine people nine bells to open.

### Chapter 454 — *Saturday the Sixteenth, Two Days' Money In and Two Days' Money Out, a Boat of About Nineteen Tons Hired for Six Days at Two Hundred and Fifty Pence a Day, a Master Who Asked Two Questions Before He Took the Money, Bread and Salt Beef Because There Is No Flour, Four Men Paid a Day Apiece in Advance, and a Mark and a Half That Was for Flour*

A master of about fifty-one named Simeon Roke, out of a coast town four days down that road, asks who is paying and is told nobody, with the FIRST standing line off another sheet given as the reason, and then asks what happens if there is already somebody on that shelf and is told that nobody knows. **Five of the six days of hire, being one thousand two hundred and fifty pence, went onto the sheet on the said day and the sixth day is to be paid on the twenty-second, which is the day the lease ends.** Provisions are bread and salt beef for nine men for four days and there is no flour and none is bought, and the reason there is no figure against flour is on the sheet with the hour against it. Four men are paid a day apiece in advance and one of them asks to be paid on the second day and not the sixth and gets it. **A woman of about forty-three who keeps a store puts in one mark and a half and says out loud that the money is for flour, and there is no flour in that market, and nobody said a word to her about it, once, on one day, against one figure.** *Repaired: the answer to the master no longer counts eleven people or says the sheet has no head on it, the eighth of the four hundred and twenty-two pounds of the party is no longer put in on this day, and three hundred and thirty-six pence each way on this Saturday is the only double day of the ten.*

### Chapter 455 — *Sunday the Seventeenth, the Seventy-Sixth Time That Wall Came Down Bare, and a Disagreement Said Out Loud on That Quay in Front of Nine Men and About Thirty Passing People and Put in a Minute and Not Answered by Anybody*

The batch's turn, and it is not resolved. **A man of thirty-two says on a quay that he is going to carry the sheet of about four feet down the coast in his inside pocket. A woman of thirty of no office says no, out loud, in front of everyone, and gives the reason: a route is a way boats go and a description is not a way anything goes, and if a paper can stand in for the thing it describes then every one of the four heads has a hole in it and the hole is the size of a boat.** He answers with the fifth of the nine boundaries, which authorizes a limited route use by four named people; she answers with the other half of the same boundary, which says a route and not a scene, and that what he wants is neither. Four people say one thing each, and one of the four is the man who proposed carrying the sheet, who says he does not know what a thing answering a description means and is not going to be the man who guessed; a man of about thirty-four says he does not know and that not knowing is a thing a man can put in a minute; three other people on that quay begin and stop and are not asked what they began to say. *Repaired: the third of the four voices is the holder of that writ and the phantom man of about thirty-one is cut out, because the account of the eighth of October and the afternoon in June is his own and not another man's.* It goes into a minute with the hour. **Nobody was asked to take anything back, nobody thanked anybody, nobody apologised, and no reader is told who is right.**

### Chapter 456 — *Monday the Eighteenth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-First Charge on That Cistern, a Harbor Authority on That Coast Road Whose Coal and Water Have Been Paid For Twice in a Fortnight by a Name That Is the Name of an Office, a Reeve Who Does Not Know and Says So, a Man Who Will Not Sell What He Knows, and Coal for Two Days at One Thousand One Hundred and Eighty Pence*

A reeve of about fifty-nine has had his coal and his water paid twice in a fortnight by a name that is a name of an office, and he says out loud that he does not know who paid, asks for it to be written in a minute, and the minute is read back to him and he does not ask to change a word of it. **A man of about thirty-eight in that harbor will not sell what he knows about the shelf and gives a reason that names three men out of a coat, nine days, and the fact that he was the second man; he was not asked a second time by anybody in that party and was not shown the sheet.** Coal for the pump for two days is bought off a supply boat at one thousand one hundred and eighty pence, twice what coal is at home, and the figure is said out loud to nine men in a boat. **The holder of that writ is not in that harbor and the woman's wage still comes in and goes out, one hundred and sixty-eight pence each way as on every other day of the ten except the Saturday, and the ship's hand and the woman of thirty are on the water with that party from the Wednesday before,** and the reason — a berth fund pays a day for a day and does not care which coast the day happened on — is entered in the second column and not the first, because a man on a mole cannot check it.**

### Chapter 457 — *Tuesday the Nineteenth, the Fifty-Second Wage Tuesday and the Column Did Not Move on It and Fifty-Two Weeks Stand Fallen Due, a Bell-Shaped Chamber With a Deck Plate and a Stove and a Stove Pipe and a Working Gauge Built on the Bottom of an Exposed Shelf in a Day and a Half, a Gauge Reading Eighty-Four Pounds on a Face of a Hundred and Fifty, and a Mark About Four Inches Long Cut Into the Floor About Three Weeks Old*

The fifty-second wage Tuesday comes and goes in that harbor two days behind the party and the column does not move on it, and the nineteenth is the third day of a run that began on the seventeenth. *Repaired: the harbor is two days behind and not four, the day of the run is the third and not the fourth, the bell is two and a half tons in both chapters that give its weight, and the man of sixty-one on the mole goes home for the fifth time in ninety days.* A bell-shaped chamber with a deck plate, a stove, a stove pipe and a gauge goes down onto an exposed shelf in about nine fathoms and stands on it, and it is a thing and not a building and it has no door on the shore side, and the gauge reads eighty-four pounds on a face of a hundred and fifty and that reading is not a depth reading and the two numbers are on the same slate on purpose. **A man of about thirty-four in a bell about ninety yards off the port bow finds a cut about four inches long with square ends in a flat place where there is no reason for a cut to be, with thin silt on it and bright edges, and puts in that it is about three weeks old.** Nine men look at it and say nothing about it, and one of them asks whether anybody is going to say it out loud in front of the master, and the answer is no, because the master was told on the thirteenth that nobody knew what was on that shelf and that answer is now out of date and will be given again in the morning.

### Chapter 458 — *Wednesday the Twentieth, the First Descent, a Tender of About Thirty-Eight on the Surface and Not in the Boat, an Air Limit of Forty Minutes Written as a Figure, a Gasket That Let Go at About Ten to Three in About Nine Fathoms, a Chain Weight Over a Rail, a Man Out in About Six Minutes, and a Man of About Twenty-Nine Who Came Up and Cannot Hear Out of One Side of His Head*

Everything about the descent is on a slate before anybody goes down. **A gasket in the hatch of that bell lets go at about ten to three in the afternoon in about nine fathoms, a tender of about thirty-eight pulls his own chain weight over his own rail without asking anybody and without speaking to anybody afterwards, and the reason is written down afterwards with the hour against it, being that water was coming in and the man was in it.** Nobody is lost and the bell is recovered and pumped out through the night. **A deck hand of about twenty-nine named Amos Trewin, who asked for the descent and was given it, comes up and about an hour afterwards says he cannot hear out of the left side of his head; it is not a pain, it is not ringing, and the sounds on that side are about nine feet off. He goes on working that evening and the days after, and is not thanked, not made a casualty and not sent home, and no figure is set against it.** He says there was a noise in about nine fathoms that was there before anything that makes a noise got there. **The man who went down first says he heard nothing and will not say the other man did not hear it. Both accounts are in the book in the order they were said, and there are now eight accounts in that leaf that do not agree with each other and none of the eight has been settled.**

### Chapter 459 — *Thursday the Twenty-First, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Second Charge on That Cistern, the Mouth of a Trench in About Twenty-Two Fathoms, the Water at That Mouth Coming Up About Two Feet in the Twenty Minutes After the Flood, a Sheet of About Four Feet in an Inside Pocket That Answered Something, Eleven Square-Ended Marks About Three Weeks Old, and a Piece of Worked Lead in the Same Cut*

The trench is found at about ten past nine in the morning in about twenty-two fathoms and it is a mouth and not an object, and the rule of it is put on a slate: the water comes up about two feet in the twenty minutes after the flood and does not go down again inside the working day, and the working day is the ebb after the flood. **At about half past ten a man in a bell with the sheet in an oilcloth fold in his inside pocket feels a thing in that trench answer the paper, and will not describe it in the boat until Amos Trewin, who could not hear out of one side of his head, has been down and asked the same question, because a man who keeps the only account of a thing because he was in it first will end up with a record of himself.** The answer goes into the second column at about six in the evening and into no other place: a paper cannot answer, whatever answered was answering a description, a record of a man holding a paper is not a record of the thing, and this does not make what came up true. **On the ledge to the left there are eleven square-ended marks about three weeks old, no two the same length, and beside the eleventh on a flat stone is a piece of worked lead about the size of a man's palm with nine notches in it, three of them deep, a thumb-sized place left out on purpose, no figure and no number — and the cut is the cut.** *Repaired on the second pass: the shelf's lead is in the same cut as one **cut on the fifth of October past, being sixteen days before this day, on a hill two days' sail from that boat**, and the sentence in the deck is two days' sail off and not four hundred yards.* A man of about thirty-six named Corwin Tace says he is a setter of marks, that setting marks is what he does, that his warrant has a seal on it and no figure on it, and that a warrant is a piece of paper that says somebody has paid for the coal. He puts the lead inside his coat and is not stopped and is not thanked.

### Chapter 460 — *Friday the Twenty-Second, a Man of Thirty-Two Saying Out Loud Before He Was Asked What He Did With a Sheet of About Four Feet, a Printed Boundary That the Echo May Inform a Public Record and May Not Decide Anything This Party Does, a Fitting-Out Sheet Read Back in Full With Both Totals, a Leaf Read Back at Ten Past Five With Both Definitions, the Whole of That Harbor's Standing Condition Once and Nowhere Else, and Five Hundred and Fifty-Eight Pence Left on a Sheet*

**He tells her, in his own mouth, before she asks, what he did with the sheet and what answered it, and says the fault for her not being told is his and not hers, and neither of them says he was right or wrong and it is in neither column.** She writes the boundary and it is printed and public and it is that the echo may inform a public record and it may not decide anything this party does. The sixth day of the hire, being two hundred and fifty pence, is paid in coin on the deck and nobody says thank you; a master of fifty-one asks for one thing to be put in the book, which is that he was told the truth **on the Saturday, six days before he took the hire money.** **At about half past four, with the lease out and his boat his own again, he says the other half of what he said at the table on the sixteenth, which is that he is going home on that tide, and that he will carry the party up the coast for two days and will not take a figure for it; no line was opened on that sheet for it and none is going to be, and the party is under way home on the twenty-third and sails in on the evening tide of the twenty-four.** *Repaired on the second pass: the master's second day was printed as the Wednesday and is the Saturday, and the return leg is now paid on the page so that Movement 2's first two chapters are reachable; Amos Trewin's depth is twenty-two fathoms and not the nine feet that is the width of the mouth.* The fitting-out sheet is read back in full, twelve lines out and five in on the fourteenth, the fifteenth and the sixteenth, both totals said out loud, and the leaf is read back at about ten past five in the open in the ship's own left hand at **192 / 837 / none / 125** at the hour and **193 / 839 / none / 125** at the close, with both definitions on the face of the reading and the reason the fourth column took no line entered once and not again. Three people say one thing each about the water, the paper and the trip. **The whole of that harbor's standing condition is on that page once and nowhere else, and the batch closes on a party that has lost a hearing, spent other people's money, and found somebody else cutting the same cut.**

## Volume 10, Batch 0002 (Chapters 461–470) — complete, 29 September 2026. Movement 2, *the run home, a rule read out in a room, a second figure asked of the same eleven, and the first thing that comes off that floor that nobody can read*. `workspace/volume-10/batch-0002/PROMPT.md` was the phase. **SATURDAY THE TWENTY-THIRD DAY OF OCTOBER TO MONDAY THE FIRST DAY OF NOVEMBER, TEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS, ONE DAY TO A CHAPTER, NO DAY MISSING AND NO DAY IN TWO CHAPTERS, AND NO CHAPTER STATES A YEAR. THE VOLUME IS TWENTY CHAPTERS OLD OF FIFTY AND IS NOT CLOSED.**

### Chapter 461 — *Saturday the Twenty-Third, a Day at Sea a Day off That Coast, a Small Supply Boat at Six in the Morning, Three Days of Coal for the Pump at One Thousand Seven Hundred and Sixty-Four Pence Said Out Loud on a Deck, and a Man of About Twenty-Nine Who Put Himself in the Middle of That Boat and Said He Did It on Purpose and Not Because Anybody Asked Him*

A passage home with no figure on any sheet, on a boat of about nineteen tons, a day off that coast, the harbor a day behind. **A small supply boat is spoken at about six in the morning and three days of coal for the pump go onto the fitting-out sheet at one thousand seven hundred and sixty-four pence, being eleven marks and fourpence, said out loud by the man who keeps the leaf at about ten past seven and not argued with by nine men before noon; and the reason coal is a price and a price is the figure a person says out loud to somebody else is entered in the yard's own mouth.** A pump hand of about forty-four says out loud that a stove off a supply boat at that figure is the one that has not had a hole in it, and says it because a line is going on a page and two hands are to write it and only one of them can read. **A man of about twenty-nine had moved his bag and his coat and his oilcloth to the middle thwart on the Friday night while four men watched, a tender of about thirty-four says it out loud on the Saturday morning that the man has done it so that he can see everybody, and he says it back, in that order: I did it on purpose, and I did not do it because anybody asked me, and I want the second of those printed louder.** The order of the two clauses is on a slate with an hour against it and the second of them was not written louder. Nobody asked him what the loss of one side of his hearing is like and no figure is set against it. The master says the thing he says every morning of a run. The sheet is read back in full for the first time since that boat left harbor and the man of about fifty-one from the coast town reads the shortfall back twice and suggests nothing.

### Chapter 462 — *Sunday the Twenty-Fourth, the Seventy-Seventh Time That Wall Came Down Bare in a Harbor the Party Was Not In, a Boat Sailing In on the Evening Tide With Nobody Met and Nobody Thanked, a Berth Fund That Carried a Day and Did Not Make a Fuss, and a Man of About Thirty-Four Asking One Question at the Head of a Slip and Not Getting an Answer*

**The wipe happens in a harbor the party is not in.** The boat makes the roads at about five, lies off the point two hours for a north-wester, and goes alongside the dolphin at the end of the second lay at about half past seven with nobody met and nobody thanked. **A second hand's day at the compressor goes onto the sheet at one hundred and sixty-eight pence, paid in coin on the stone, to a man of about thirty-seven who asked for it by name on the Friday.** At about ten past eight the man who keeps the leaf goes up the slip and a woman of about fifty-eight with the end stall tells him the berth fund has carried his day in and out at the same figure at the same hours, that she looked at the book twice on the Friday because it looked wrong and it was not wrong, and that she is not going to be glad about it to a man who has been away; he did not thank her and she said she had noticed. **Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, asks one question on that slip and is not answered: How do you know it was the paper.** He does not ask it twice; he puts his hands in his pockets and waits; the reason is in the second column with the hour and no name, and the fact that he was not answered and did not ask again is the only thing about that question that is entered. A woman of about thirty-one who crews nothing and sells nothing, out of a coast town four days down, is hired on for the second trip and is one of the four men paid a day apiece; the chapter names her as not the woman who said no on the fourteenth, and the two are not to be counted together.

### Chapter 463 — *Monday the Twenty-Fifth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Third Charge on That Cistern, and a Line Read Out Twice in a Room over a Fish Market Before About Twenty-Two People of Whom About Eleven Cannot Read*

**The boundary is read out twice, in a room, and not in a scene of two people.** *The echo may inform a public record, and it may not decide anything this party does.* A name and an hour under it, being Mara Venn and ten past ten in the morning on the twenty-second, in her own hand. The page is a page: it is not the sheet that carries the money, it is not the four heads on that wall, and it does not go on that wall. **A man of about thirty-one who keeps a chandler's store on the second lay says out loud at about ten past eleven that he does not agree with it, and says why — that the line was written by the people on the water and he sells rope to the boats both ways, and that a rule written by the people on the water is a rule about a boat — and is not argued with and not thanked, and his words are on the same line of the same minute as the rule and not under it.** A woman of about forty-three says it is about time somebody said that. A day apiece in advance goes to four men at six hundred and seventy-two pence. The sheet stands at 7,760 in, 9,806 out, short by 2,046 pence, and that figure is said out loud in a shed and is not written in that room and does not go on that wall.

### Chapter 464 — *Tuesday the Twenty-Sixth, the Fifty-Third Wage Tuesday, Fifty-Three Weeks Standing Fallen Due and the Column Not Moving, and Eleven People Asked a Second Time in Eight New Sentences Written at the Head of a Page Before Anybody Was Asked*

**The wage column is at twenty-six lines and one hundred and four marks with twenty envelopes in a chest and fifty-three weeks stand fallen due; it does not move and nobody writes a word under it saying anybody is going to pay it.** A second ask is written at about ten in the morning, before anybody is asked, in eight sentences and not eleven, and the eleventh sentence of the first ask is put at the head of it word for word. Eleven people are asked one at a time and not in front of each other in a loft over a chandler's, where about eleven people cannot read the eleven sentences on the wall. **The page says plainly that the sheet is short and puts the shortfall at the foot of it in words and not in figures: two thousand and forty-six pence, being twelve marks, ten shillings and sixpence.** The two who said no on the thirteenth and the fourteenth are not in that loft and are not asked and nobody goes to either door, and that neither of them was asked again is a line on the sheet and is not a figure and is not a name. **Nine lines are opened against that second ask and not one figure goes in on that Tuesday.** The page also says, in the yard's own mouth, that no list of the people who put nothing in is kept by anybody in that harbor, because such a list is a weapon.

### Chapter 465 — *Wednesday the Twenty-Seventh, Eleven Asked a Second Time and Nine Lines Opened, Five of the Nine Putting In More on Seven Lines and Four of the Nine Putting In Nothing, Two of the Four Saying Why in Their Own Mouths, and Air Cylinders Rented for Three Days at Five Hundred and Forty Pence*

**Five of the nine put in two marks each and two of those five put in a mark each more: one thousand six hundred pence and three hundred and twenty pence on the day, ten marks and two marks, with a name and an hour against each.** Four put in nothing and two of them say why out loud in front of somebody: a man of about fifty-six, that a second time is not a different amount of money but the same money with a different day on it; and a woman of about thirty-eight, that her husband's wage is a figure and a second wage is an opinion, and she would rather be one of the quiet ones than say a thing out loud she cannot hold. **No figure is set against any of the four, no second list exists, and the rule that no such list is kept is printed on the sheet.** A pump hand of about forty-four says out loud at about half past three that he will put in two marks and says why, and that it is not about the money: he can hear a throat in that stove off a supply boat from the top of that ladder and would rather somebody had put in two marks than be right and the trip short. **He puts the two marks in on the twenty-eighth with the day against them and not the Wednesday.** Air cylinders are rented for three days at five hundred and forty pence, being three marks and five shillings.

### Chapter 466 — *Thursday the Twenty-Eighth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Fourth Charge on That Cistern, Four Marks More From the Owner of a Boat of About Twenty-Two Tons, and a Man of About Twenty-Eight Who Will Not Go Again Naming His Own Hand*

**Two marks from the pump hand go on at about nine in the morning, in his own hand, with the day against them; nobody thanks him and nobody asks whether the throat is any better, and he says it is not and that he has decided it does not matter.** Four marks, being six hundred and forty pence, go on at about eleven from the man of about fifty who owns a boat of about twenty-two tons of the second lay, who said the name of that thing once on the tenth of October and has not said it since, and who was asked nothing about it. **At about two in the afternoon a man of about twenty-eight who crews a boat of about nine tons and who went on the first trip says out loud that he is not going again, and gives a reason that names his own right hand, which has not closed all the way since the third of August, and the fear is not the water and not the money but being a man who is pulled up by three people and cannot get hold of anything on the way.** It goes onto the sheet at the same size as the figures. Nobody asks him a second question on any of the three days after it. A woman of about fifty-eight with the end stall, who is not asked and is not a witness, says one thing from a doorway about a figure put on a board. **A man of about twenty-nine asks out loud whether that man has been told what the reason is going to be used for, and is told it is not going to be used for anything, and that if it ever is, the person who uses it is to put it in the second column himself with the hour against it.**

### Chapter 467 — *Friday the Twenty-Ninth, a Day Apiece to the Same Four Men, Two Men Taken Out of a Tide Gang Four Men Short, the Question Asked Out Loud Whether the Trip Is Going Ahead Because the Money Is In or In Spite of It, and a Boat Let Go at Six in the Evening on the Flood With the Sheet Three Hundred and Seventy-Eight Pence Short*

**A day apiece goes to the same four men at six hundred and seventy-two pence, who ask the same question they asked on the sixteenth and are given the same answer by the same man.** Two men are taken out of a tide gang that is four men short and the man who counts it says out loud that he was told and not consulted, that they will be back on the Thursday, and that he cannot count them for anything until then; their days come out of the harbor's own count and are in neither column of that leaf. **A man of about fifty asks out loud, on that slip, in front of about nine people, whether the trip is going ahead because the money is in or in spite of it, and is answered in the yard's own mouth that it is because the money is in, that the money is short, and that the other reason is given separately, being that the first trip brought back a number, a line and a bell.** A woman of about fifty-eight says a figure put on a board cannot be taken off again. **The boat is let go from the dolphin at about six in the evening on the flood with the sheet three hundred and seventy-eight pence short, being two marks, four shillings and tenpence, and there is a line still to go on for a gasket and a patch and stove pipe and it has not been costed yet.** The figure of four hundred and fifty pence is still on a board at an end stall and did not come down.

### Chapter 468 — *Saturday the Thirtieth, the Second Day of the Run Down, a Man Who Makes His Own Bed and a Man Who Does Not, One Thing Said Out Loud About a Silt and a Book Not Shown, and a Figure That Comes Off a Man's Own Book and Goes on No Page*

**A tender of about thirty-four makes his bed; a man of about thirty-four of the second lay does not, and says at about half past five that some men stow a bed and some men stow a book, and that a man who stows a bed has to get up in the dark, and that it is not a virtue and would not want anybody to write it down as one; nobody wrote it down.** He says his one thing at about eleven in the morning, standing at the rail: there is silt on that floor below the step, banked on the left and not on the right, and banked silt does not tell you which way the water goes through a place, it tells you which way it has been going round, and a man who has been in holds for nineteen years knows the difference and a man who has been in books does not. **He says it once and is not going to say another word about it on the water. He does not show the book, has never shown it, has not been asked for it, and says that a man of about thirty-four who has not been asked has time.** A pump hand of about forty-four writes a figure in his own book against a day of compressor's hours holding a bell full of air at the bottom of that trench, which nobody asked him for; **no line is opened on that sheet for it, it is in neither column of that leaf, and the yard does not put a figure on a page for a thing nobody has asked for.** Half of what goes into that stove goes out into the water in about an hour, as it has since the eighteenth, and the coal for it was bought once on the twenty-third and no second load was bought.

### Chapter 469 — *Sunday the Thirty-First, a Chamber Cut Free of Four Corners and Taken Down the Outside of a Trench in About Twenty-Two Fathoms and Seated on Four Pads, a Party Standing on That Floor for the First Time, About Forty Racks in Rows Holding Nothing, and a Worked Blank of Glass About the Size of a Sheet Going Into a Crate on That Deck*

**The chamber is cut free of its four sanded corners in about forty minutes, hung on four slings and taken down the outside of the trench on the ebb, the winch worked off a spar and not off the boom because the master says so and is right.** It is seated level on four pads of sawn fir at about ten past four. The stove pipe cracks nine inches up from the bend and the gauge's gasket goes, and the gauge reads nothing for a quarter of an hour; a gasket and a patch and stove pipe go onto the sheet at three hundred and eight pence. Two men go down under a slate with the reason and the hour and a figure of forty minutes of air and a named tender on the surface with a cutoff he could pull without asking; nobody went into that mouth at the top of a flood and nobody went in twice. **What is on that floor is a yard and not a wreck: forty racks, cut to a pattern, in rows, holding nothing, with the mark in the bottom of each of the thing that was made to sit in it, all the same shape and about the size of a sheet of paper, nothing fallen in from above, and the floor under them swept.** **A worked blank of glass about the size of a sheet comes up off that floor at about ten past five in the afternoon, after the party went down onto it at about half past four, in a hand cradle in a bell and goes into a crate on that deck with a blanket and a batten and the day against it, and a woman of thirty of no office, who has been reading things out of glass for eleven years, says there is nothing on it to read, that the working is good, and that she is not going to write a sentence about it tonight or tomorrow. It is blank in a way that is not an empty vessel, and no word for it is on any page of that harbor, and nobody on the face of that harbor can read it.**

### Chapter 470 — *Monday the First Day of November, a Man of About Twenty-Nine Asking to Come Up at About Half Past Ten and Not Being Argued With, Two Accounts of the Same Thirty Seconds That Do Not Agree and Neither Settled, a Leaf Read Back at Ten Past Five With Both Definitions, the Whole of That Harbor's Standing Condition Once and Nowhere Else, and the Sheet Six Hundred and Eighty-Six Pence Short*

**A man of about twenty-nine goes down at about ten past ten on the ebb into the yard of racks in about twenty-two fathoms, under a named tender on the surface and not in the bell, on an independent line, with forty minutes of air written on a slate with his reason in his own words and the hour against it and a cutoff the tender could pull without asking.** He is in the water about thirty-five minutes and on the bottom about thirty-one of them, and at about half past ten uses the line; the tender pulls and nobody says a word to him about it; the tender would have pulled at about ten to eleven whatever the diver wanted, and he came up at about a quarter to eleven because he asked. **The hour is entered and it is the only line on that sheet in this movement anybody is glad about.** He says he asked to come up because he did not like it and he is not going to dress that up as a symptom. **A woman of about thirty-one says out loud, before anybody has said anything, that a man who cannot hear out of one side of his head has not heard the same thirty seconds that she has, and is not going to be the one who says it to him, and nobody argued with her and nobody told him she had said it.** She goes down at about ten past one and nobody goes down twice that day. **At about half past three the two of them give their accounts of the same thirty seconds of that floor and they do not agree: he heard a noise from below and behind the far row, about thirty seconds, six of something in it at about four-second intervals, stopping all at once the way a thing stops when it is finished; she heard nothing, her left ear shut for about thirty seconds, and when it cleared there was a noise already going and ending, and she does not know whether she missed the beginning or whether there was never one. Both are entered in the order they were said and neither is settled, and there are now ten accounts in that leaf that do not agree with each other and not one of the ten has been settled.** The leaf is read back at about ten past five in the ship's own left hand, in the open, all four columns including the empty one, read twice, **at 202 / 887 / none / 125 at the hour and 203 / 889 / none / 125 at the close, with both definitions in the same words they came out of the same mouth in on the twenty-second of October.** The sheet that carries the money is read back in full at **10,640 in and 11,326 out and 686 short, being four marks, three shillings and tenpence**, carries no count of persons, and no figure has been asked of anybody to make that shortfall be otherwise. **The whole of that harbor's standing condition is on that page once and nowhere else.** The thing on that trench floor is still not identified and is not named, and the word that would name it is in no mouth.

## Volume 10, Batch 0003 (Chapters 471–480) — complete, 29 September 2026. Movement 3, *a hull built to take testimony out of the living, and a tool that was civic before it was the Crown's*. `workspace/volume-10/batch-0003/PROMPT.md` was the phase. **THE VOLUME'S MIDPOINT IS PAID AND IT IS PAID IN CHAPTER 474 AND IN NO OTHER CHAPTER. TUESDAY THE SECOND DAY OF NOVEMBER TO THURSDAY THE ELEVENTH DAY OF NOVEMBER, TEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS, ONE DAY TO A CHAPTER, NO DAY MISSING AND NO DAY IN TWO CHAPTERS, AND NO CHAPTER STATES A YEAR. THE VOLUME IS THIRTY CHAPTERS OLD OF FIFTY AND IS NOT CLOSED.**

### Chapter 471 — *Tuesday the Second, the Fifty-Fourth Wage Tuesday, That Column Not Moving on It and Fifty-Four Weeks Standing Fallen Due, a Slate Written Before Anybody Went Down, a Man of About Thirty-Four of the Second Lay Opening One of the Forty Racks With His Own Two Hands in Front of Every Man on That Deck, a Cut About Two Inches Long Across the Back of a Left Hand Off the Lip of That Rack, and the Shortfall Said Out Loud on That After Deck at Two Thousand Nine Hundred and Fifty-Eight Pence*

**The day is money and nothing else, and a man of about thirty-four opens one of the forty racks with his own hands while nine men watch, and what is in it is a part and not a relic.** The slate carries the reason in his own words with the hour against it, a figure of forty minutes of air, a named tender on the surface and not in the bell, and a cutoff he could pull without asking. He is in the water about fifty minutes and on the bottom about thirty-five and comes up at about ten to ten. What comes up is worked glass about the size of a sheet with a flange down two edges, two squared holes in that flange, and the middle of it worn bright and in one place worn thin enough to see through — and the wear is in the middle and not at the ends. **Two people say one thing each about it and do not agree**: a man of about fifty-one out of the coast town four days down says it came out of a chest in a house four days up this coast and has a figure cut on the flange for the making and not for the worth; Trevask says he can tell what a thing has been *doing* and not what it was for, and that he will give two figures for it on the Thursday and neither was asked for and neither was offered. **The lip of that rack cuts him across the back of a left hand about two inches long at about ten to ten and no figure is set against it and nobody was thanked.** Bread and salt beef for nine men for ten days goes on at one thousand six hundred pence and a day apiece in advance to the same four men at six hundred and seventy-two, and nothing goes on in any hand. The shortfall is said out loud on that deck at about half past four at two thousand nine hundred and fifty-eight pence and nobody argues with it and nobody is asked for the rest of it.

### Chapter 472 — *Wednesday the Third, a Supply Boat at the Reef at the Same Figure, a Second Part Out of a Rack Described Three Ways by Three People Who Do Not Agree, and the Same Sentence Said Out Loud Twice to Two Different Men*

**The supply boat that spoke them on the twenty-third of October puts three days of coal for the pump on that sheet at the same figure, one thousand seven hundred and sixty-four pence, being eleven marks and fourpence, and the man in her says one sentence out loud twice — once to the man who keeps the leaf and once to the master of the boat — and nobody asks him anything about it and it is written on no sheet.** Sabra Loach goes down at about ten with a reason of her own and comes up at about ten to eleven with a cold in her teeth, a taste of iron like a nail and a bruise on her right hip the size of a hand, and works the rest of the day at the winch and is not thanked. **A second part comes up and three people describe it and the three of them do not agree:** a lid of a box with the lip worn bright on one side and not the other, a carrier drawn out of a channel with the wear at the two ends of the channel and not the middle and the two ends not worn alike, and a lap, in the working word of a pump hand of about forty-four who has taken six of them out of machines standing before he was born and says it does not matter in the least what it was for. All three go into the second column in the order they were said and none is settled. The shortfall is four thousand seven hundred and twenty-two pence.

### Chapter 473 — *Thursday the Fourth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Sixth Charge on That Cistern Walked on by None of It, a Frame Past the Last Row With a Maker's Mark and a Count of Six Hundred and Eleven Cut Beside It, Two Figures From a Man of About Thirty-Four and Nobody Arguing, and the One Word in That Boat That Names What a Thing Like That Was Built For*

**Past the last row of forty racks the floor stops being swept and there is a frame: about nine feet long and four wide, made of bar and not of rolled metal, corners cut and not welded, three rivets, two inches of silt banked on the north side and not the south, and nine short lengths of newer metal in nine holes with collars on them.** Amos Trewin goes down at about ten and comes up at about ten to eleven with his hands shaking for two hours and is not asked to write anything and writes nothing. **Ollum Trevask goes down again at about two in the afternoon under his own slate, reads the frame and the nine with a slate held over it, and gives two figures and not one — a very old cut, on which he refuses to put a number of centuries because a man who has been in holds nineteen years knows what a hundred years looks like and not what six hundred looks like, and about three weeks, because there is silt lying in the top of the bright ring round the base of one of the nine.** A mark on the frame is a hammer and a square crossed with a chisel, cut and not stamped, and beside it is six hundred and eleven, and there is no year on that frame and no name, so no man in that boat can turn six hundred and eleven into a year. **A pump hand of about forty-four gives the yard a word once, in one mouth, as the name of a thing built to be worked by more than one person at a time so that one account can be set against another's while it is being given, and says he has never been in one, is in nothing, and do not write it down as mine.** The cistern is charged for the ninety-sixth time and walked on by none of it, nothing goes on that sheet, and the shortfall does not move.

### Chapter 474 — *Friday the Fifth, THE MIDPOINT PAID IN THE CHAPTER IT IS STATED, Fifteen Frames in Rows With Nine Fittings in Each and a Worn Cup Between Every Two of Them, Three People Saying One Thing Each Who Do Not Agree, a Man of About Thirty-Six Still Setting Marks Around It, and the Reason That Party Is There Being a Different Reason From the One It Was*

**The thing on that floor is a machine and it is identified there and then, by its makers' marks, its geometry, its wear and its date, and it is not a monster and not a curse and not a god and not a tomb and not a ghost and no character in these ten chapters says it took anything out of anybody because it wanted anything.** Fifteen frames in rows, every one carrying the same mark and the same six hundred and eleven; nine fittings in each about three weeks old; a channel about the width of a hand between every two frames with a curved thing set into the floor, the shape of a cupped hand with a hole bored through the middle of the cup, worn deep at the rim and bright across the middle. **Three people say one thing each and do not agree:** a man of about fifty-one says it is a machine for taking an account off a living person and standing one account up where nine used to be, built by people who had nine communities arguing with each other about a disaster for two years and who wanted one version everybody could put a finger on, and that wanting one thing is not wickedness, it is an answer, and it is a bad answer and it is still an answer; Sabra Loach says it does not matter in the least whose hands it was in, that she counted the cups from the ladder and said out loud that the counting is on the face of that floor and a man on a mole could have it off a plan, that what she is not going to write down is what the nine were for, and that the difference between a number and a reason is that the number costs nothing to keep, and that there are nine of us on this boat; Calder Marr says the honest reading of the geometry is that it held nine accounts at a height where a man could walk round them, that the frame is the old part and the fittings are the new part, and that he will not write down which of the two readings he hopes for. All three in the second column in the order they were said, none asked to say it again, nobody votes. **Corwin Tace, of about thirty-six, comes up out of the dark with his tool roll at about ten past one, is asked one question about his own work, answers about marks and about a paper that says four inches, is given nothing and thanked by nobody, and goes in again.** And at about half past five on that deck, in front of all nine of them, the holder of that writ says out loud that the reason this boat left that harbor on the twenty-ninth of October — to find out whether a sheet of about four feet answers, and what it is answering — is the wrong reason, that the reason on the fifth of November is to get the shape of that frame up into daylight where a man on a mole can see the same thing he was told about, and that he is not going to use the sheet in his coat pocket to decide where that boat goes tomorrow, and that if he broke that in twenty-two fathoms where nobody could find out, the rule would only ever be a rule for the water somebody could watch. Nobody argues, nobody thanks him, and the question asked on the twenty-fourth of October is neither asked again nor answered.

### Chapter 475 — *Saturday the Sixth, Four Days of Air Hired at Seven Hundred and Twenty Pence, a Grayness in the Middle of a Morning That Did Not Lift Until Two in the Afternoon, the Line of the Twenty-Second of October Said Again in the Open Before All Nine of Them and Reached Exactly as Far and Not One Inch Further, and a Pump Hand Told Out Loud That There Is No Rule for a Machine and That It Is a Hole*

**Four days of air go on the sheet at seven hundred and twenty pence, being four marks, six shillings and eightpence, with three of the four days in front of the party and no line opened for a fifth.** Amos Trewin goes down at about ten past nine, is in the water about forty minutes and comes up at about ten to ten with a cold in his hands that will not come out of them for about an hour and a grayness in the middle of the morning that will not lift until about two in the afternoon, works the winch from eleven until five, and is not thanked. **At about one o'clock on the after deck Ollum Trevask says one of the two figures again in the same words, being about three weeks and not three days, because he said out loud on the Thursday that he would say it on the Friday and on the Saturday; he says that one half only and does not put the other half up a second time, because a number can be said twice to show it has not moved and a thing that is not a number is said once. Nobody argued with him, nobody thanked him and nobody asked him for a third.** **At about two in the afternoon, on that deck, in the open, before all nine of them, Mara Venn says one thing about the line she wrote on the twenty-second of October: that it was written about a piece of paper and about something that answered one, that it does not say one word about a machine on a floor, and that she is not going to stretch it until it does, because the day she stretches a line written for one thing until it covers another is the day it stops being worth the name and the hour under it.** The line stands and reaches exactly as far as it reached on the twenty-second. Calder Marr says one sentence back and does not ask her to move it and does not pretend his new reason came out of that line. **A pump hand asks out loud what the rule is for that thing down there and is told, out loud, that there is not one: nine men decide it with their mouths, the best of the nine wins, nobody on shore finds out which, and when this boat is in a harbor there will be a room with about eleven people in it who cannot read and he is going to stand in it and be told no.** The crate with the blank in it is on that deck, came into the harbor on the twenty-fourth, stood five days in a room off that market unopened, came back out on the twenty-ninth on no line of any sheet, and its batten has not been off since the thirty-first of October; nobody has named what is in it. The shortfall is five thousand four hundred and forty-two pence.

### Chapter 476 — *Sunday the Seventh, the Seventy-Ninth Wipe in a Harbor the Party Was Not In, Four Hands Down on One Ebb One at a Time, and the Fourth of Them Coming Up at About Half Past Twelve on the Air and Saying Out Loud That Nineteen Minutes Under There Felt to Him Like an Hour and a Bit and That He Does Not Know What It Is*

**Four men go down on one ebb, one at a time, under four slates written before each of them went, a figure of forty minutes of air on each, the same named tender on the surface for all four and a cutoff he could pull without asking; nobody goes in twice and nobody goes in at the top of a flood.** The reason for the four is written before any of them goes and is not a reason about any of them. **The fourth is a pump hand of about forty-four who is in nobody's crew, and he comes up at about half past twelve on the air and comes up shorter than he went down**: he says he was in the water nineteen minutes and knows it because the tender had the slate and the slate has his own time on it; it is not what it felt like, it felt like an hour and a bit, and in nineteen years of compressors he has never once come up off a floor thinking a thing took longer than the slate said; he says he does not know what it is and is not going to work it out on a compressor on a Sunday, that if it does it again he will say so again, and that **nothing came up off that floor with him that belongs to anybody else**. **Nobody asks him why, nobody asks what he thinks happened, nobody asks him to describe it again, nobody asks him to write it down and nobody thanks him, and no figure is set against it, and it is not a memory, it is not permanent and it is not something in him that is not his.** He goes back to the compressor at about one and works it until about six and does not go down again that day and nobody asks him to and nobody asks him why he did not. Twenty fathoms of three-inch line at three hundred and forty pence and a second pair of hands for a day at one hundred and sixty-eight go on that sheet, and **neither line has anything to do with what happened to him**. The shortfall is five thousand nine hundred and fifty pence.

### Chapter 477 — *Monday the Eighth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Seventh Charge Walked on by None of It, a Built Thing Under the Water With Two Kerbs and a Gutter a Foot and a Half Wide About Nine Fathoms Off a Line, a Man of About Thirty-Four Who Says It Is a Way and Not a Wreck and Does Not Show His Book, and a Wall Fourteen Feet High With One Doorway in Sixty Feet of It*

**The chamber with a stove in it stays exactly where it was seated on four pads of sawn fir and nobody moves it.** The party goes out on the ebb and there is a built thing about two fathoms off the bottom with about nine fathoms over it, nine fathoms being a figure off a line and on the slate before anybody went down: flat, about thirty feet wide where it is clearest, two kerbs, a gutter a foot and a half wide down the middle running with the fall of it, the fall being to the west, and silt banked against the west kerb and not the east. **Ollum Trevask says one thing about it: it is a way and not a wreck, made for things with wheels, with a gutter because a way without a gutter is a way that rots, and he gives no year and does not give the name of the thing that made it, because a guess wearing a coat is worse than no figure.** His book is not shown, is not asked for and is not offered, and he asks for both of those to stay exactly as they are for as long as the boat is on that coast. A man of about thirty-seven goes down at about ten to sweep the gutter with a slate and comes up at about ten to eleven with a headache that lasted three days and is not thanked. At about half past two the far end of the way runs into a built wall about fourteen feet high with one doorway about five feet six inches wide and six feet two high, the only opening in about sixty feet of it, and the party stops there and does not go through and is back on the trench floor at about a quarter to three. **The cistern at the back of that market is charged for the ninety-seventh time and walked on by none of it and the top name on that rota board is still off it.** The four days of air hired on the sixth have one day left, and the line for them bears the sixth and not the eighth.

### Chapter 478 — *Tuesday the Ninth, the Fifty-Fifth Wage Tuesday, the Column Not Moving and Fifty-Five Weeks Fallen Due, a Day Apiece to the Same Four Men at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two Pence and a Third Question Asked and Answered Honestly, a Long Hall With a Foot of Level Silt in It, Thirty Feet of Hull Planking Set Into a Wall, and a Mark of Nine Short Lines Joined at One Point About Which a Woman of Thirty Says Five Things Before Anybody Can Say Them About Her*

**The fifty-fifth wage Tuesday comes and goes and the column does not move and fifty-five weeks stand fallen due with no envelope against any of them.** A day apiece goes to the same four men at six hundred and seventy-two pence, and **one of the four asks a third question — if this boat goes back up the coast before the four days are up, do I get the day — and is told he gets the days that have been paid and no more, that no promise stands behind them, and that nothing will be said to him about the others until there is a day to say it about**; he says thank you and the man who keeps the leaf says he is not to be thanked for it. Behind the doorway is a long hall with a foot of level silt and nothing fallen into it, two rows of square-ended holes running the length of both walls at shoulder height, spaced and shaped identically, and about thirty feet of curving hull planking set into the north wall on iron brackets, fastened with metal and not with glass. **On the third plank from the head of it is nine short lines joined at one point, each about an inch and a half, cut to the same depth with a graver, with no figure, no year and no name beside it.** Trevask gives no number and says why, and it is the third time he has given that reason — the bar on the fourth, a built way on the Monday, and this — and it is not the same reason as the one he gave about the bar. **At about a quarter to eleven a woman of thirty of no office says five things about that mark out loud before anybody could say them about her**, being that it is a builder's mark and not a name; that it was cut before any claim was laid over that ground, no claim in that yard's own book and no warrant any of them has seen standing in front of that plank, no man on that boat able to say by how much earlier it was cut, and nobody having put a number of years on that mark this week and she not going to be the first; that it is not a seal, being pressed and rimmed and put on by somebody saying out loud they are answerable for it; that it is not a limit of anybody's consent, no person put it there and it says nothing about what any living person agreed to; and that it is not proof that anybody agreed to anything, nine lines in a point meaning a maker and a yard and a contract between a man who wanted a boat and a man who built one. Nobody argued, nobody agreed, **nobody thanked her**, and nobody in that boat compared it with anything, because there is a drawing of a mark in a book in a shed two days' sail off and a drawing is not a mark. The shortfall is six thousand six hundred and twenty-two pence.

### Chapter 479 — *Wednesday the Tenth, a Fitting Cut at the Neck Because There Are Older Holes Under the Nine and a Hole Under a Fitting Cannot Be Read While the Fitting Is On It, a Man Going Down on an Independent Line and Coming Up on the Bell's Line, and the Holder of That Writ Saying Out Loud That He Had Just Taken the Only State That Floor Will Ever Be In Off It*

**There is an older hole under each of the nine fittings and a hole under a fitting cannot be read while the fitting is on it.** A man of about fifty-one out of the coast town four days down goes down at about ten on an independent line to cut one off at the neck, having said out loud on the deck that a piece of three-inch iron with a collar on it does not go through a round hatch in a bell-shaped chamber with a stove in it, and that cutting it smaller would leave a piece nobody could ever read again, and that he would not do that. **He is in the water about fifty minutes and on the bottom about thirty-four and comes up at about ten to eleven on the bell's line and not on the independent one; he is not hurt, nobody has named him a casualty, no figure is set against him and nobody was thanked.** The fitting lies on that floor with its neck cut a third of the way down, the hole under it open and the silt in the bottom of it disturbed by a thumb, and it is not coming up on this trip. **At about two in the afternoon on that deck the holder of that writ says out loud, in front of all nine of them, that he has just taken the only state that floor will ever be in off it**, and gives his reason — that if there is an older hole under those fittings then those fittings were put in over something and somebody had a reason — and the man who did the cutting answers that that is the reason the other man did it for, that it is a good one, that he did the cutting and will not have it put on either account, that a thing done for a reason is a thing somebody has to be answerable for, **that it is not a thing that gets to be done because a reason sounded well at half past five on the Friday**, and that what is lost is lost whether he was proud of the cutting or not. A second stove pipe and a bracket to carry it down a ladder go on at three hundred and ninety-two pence, being two marks and six shillings. The shortfall is seven thousand and fourteen pence.

### Chapter 480 — *Thursday the Eleventh, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Eighth Charge Walked on by None of It, Two Slates Left Inside a Doorway With a Date on Them and No Name on Them, a Man of About Fifty-One Writing Out Four Measurements From Memory on a Deck Because a Piece of Three-Inch Iron Will Not Go Through a Hatch, Three Statements in Three Voices Said Once Each, a Leaf Read Back at About Ten Past Five With Both Definitions and Its Own Derivation, and the Chamber Still Standing on That Trench Floor With a Crown Man's Marks Set Around It*

**A man of about thirty-four goes through the doorway at about ten under a slate whose reason is that a room under the water written on no slate is not a room to the next man who comes here, and leaves one slate on the second plank of that hull planking and one on the floor inside the doorway, and comes up at about ten to eleven with a cold in his teeth, a taste of iron like a nail and a cough that came on him about two hours after he came up and was still going on that deck when the leaf was read back at about ten past five, on air out of that boat's own bottles off her own compressor and not out of the four days hired on the sixth of November, which ended on the ninth; nobody thanked him, he is not a casualty, and the two slates say nothing at all about who put them there.** **A man of about fifty-one sits on that after deck from about two in the afternoon until dark with a slate and a pencil and writes out the diameter of the older hole and the depth of it and the length of the collar and the way the silt lay in the bottom of it; that is what he did instead of bringing the piece up, it is work, nobody has checked it, nobody can, he did not read it out, and he is not named in the column.** **Three people say one thing each about what is on that floor and each is said once and nothing is explained a second time:** Corwin Tace, still setting marks, says the warrant has a seal and no figure and he stopped asking for one the second week, because a man who asks for a figure gets a figure and then the figure is on him, and that he is not going to be there on Monday if they are and that is not a threat, it is a Thursday; Mara Venn says she has written down what three people saw and what one man said and what five things she said about a mark, has not written down what any of it was for, and that if somebody asks her on Monday what that floor is she is going to say that she does not know, and that that sentence is going on a page in her own hand with an hour against it; and the master of the boat of about nineteen tons says he has a boat and two men and a boy, that he is going to take them up that coast, that nobody has asked him to and nobody has thanked him, and that he would have taken them on the Thursday before they came out, and that he is not being brave or careful about it. **At about ten past five on that deck, in the open, in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, read twice because about four men cannot read, the leaf is read back and both definitions come out of the same mouth in the same words as on the twenty-second of October and the first of November**, **and the closing sentence of that second definition is the same one the read-backs of Chapters 460 and 470 now carry, being that the two definitions are said out loud in the same words and in the same order every time that leaf is read back, so that a man with a pencil taking either figure off a page knows which of the two he is holding and at which of the two moments — the earlier form of that sentence, which named a later writer with a pencil, is out of this volume and is not to be reproduced in Chapter 490** — with the derivation printed on its face: 183 + 30 = 213 at the close, 789 + 150 at the close, a hundred and forty-five of those on the twenty-nine days before and three this morning, a hundred and fifty less two is a hundred and forty-eight, 789 + 148 = 937 at the hour; the third column empty and unappointed with a boy's hand at its head; the fourth column at one hundred and twenty-five with no hundred and twenty-sixth line in it and no closure and no strike-out. **The sheet is read back in full with the day against every line and stands at ten thousand six hundred and forty pence in, being sixty-six marks, six shillings and eightpence, and seventeen thousand six hundred and fifty-four pence out, being one hundred and ten marks, four shillings and sixpence, and is seven thousand and fourteen pence short, being forty-three marks, eleven shillings and twopence**; it carries no count of persons, the three refusals stand on it at the same size as the figures and none of the three was asked again on any of the ten days, nothing went onto it in any hand in the whole of those ten days, and no figure has been asked of anybody to make that shortfall otherwise. **The chamber with a stove in it is standing on a trench floor in about twenty-two fathoms with a second pipe and a bracket carrying it down a ladder; there are forty racks holding nothing and fifteen frames beyond them and a cut fitting and two slates inside a doorway at the far end of a built way; a man of about thirty-six is still setting marks round all of it and will be there on Monday; nobody in that harbor has been given the machine and nobody in that harbor has been stopped from knowing about it; and the word that would name the seal on that warrant is in no mouth on that boat and in no mouth in that harbor.**
