## Volume 10, Batch 0004 (Chapters 481–490) — complete, 29 September 2026. Movement 4, *a cache, a strip, and a crew that comes up different*. `workspace/volume-10/batch-0004/PROMPT.md` was the phase. **SATURDAY THE THIRTEENTH DAY OF NOVEMBER TO MONDAY THE TWENTY-SECOND DAY OF NOVEMBER, TEN CONSECUTIVE DAYS, ONE DAY TO A CHAPTER, NO DAY MISSING AND NO DAY IN TWO CHAPTERS, AND NO CHAPTER STATES A YEAR. THE MOVEMENT IS CLOSED AND THE VOLUME IS FORTY CHAPTERS OLD OF FIFTY AND IS NOT CLOSED. THE STRIP, THE ANCHOR, THE PROOF AND THE QUESTION ARE ALL AHEAD OF THE MANUSCRIPT.**

### Chapter 481 — *Saturday the Thirteenth, Bread and Salt Beef at One Thousand Six Hundred Pence and a Day Apiece in Advance to the Same Four Men at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two, Nothing Going In on Any Line, Three Descents on the Boat's Own Air, a Second Opening in a Wall at the Far End of That Floor About Four Foot Wide, and a Room Behind It That Was Dry*

**Three descents on air out of that boat's own bottles and on no line.** Ollum Trevask, of about thirty-four, of the second lay, goes down at about ten past nine under a slate with a figure of forty minutes and a named tender on the surface and not in the bell, is in the water about fifty minutes and on the bottom about thirty-four, and comes up at about ten saying that there is a second opening in a wall at the far end of that floor, about four foot wide and five foot high, past the last of the fifteen frames and not the doorway he went through on the eleventh, and that there is a floor behind it and racks on that floor — **and that he did not go through it, because his air was at about eleven minutes and he is not a man who goes through a door he has not looked through.** A man of about fifty-one out of a coast town four days down goes down at about ten past ten and comes up at about eleven with a woven basket about the size of a water butt that had been standing in that room, full of brown folded paper, and a man of about thirty-seven goes down at about twenty past eleven and comes up at about ten past twelve with two more baskets, the third not full. **The holder of that writ says out loud in front of all nine of them that he is sending a second man down on air he did not own, that the air is the master's, and that this is not his to give and that he is doing it in front of nine people rather than at night on his own.** The paper is brown and folded twice and stiff at the folds with a parted string through two holes, a head ruled on it, a column of figures ruled under the head, a small cramped hand that is not a hand any man on that boat has seen before, and no name and no year on the face of it. **It is the best thing this party has ever had in its hands, and nobody on that deck said so on that day and nobody was thanked.** The master says out loud at about half past twelve that there is nowhere on that boat to put it, that the only dry flat place is under the stove-pipe bracket, that the boy keeps the forepeak, that a box is not free and that he is not buying one. The shortfall is nine thousand two hundred and eighty-six pence.

### Chapter 482 — *Sunday the Fourteenth, the Eightieth Wipe, Nothing Going Out on Any Line, and a Woman of Thirty of No Office Reading the Head of One Page Out Loud and Saying Out Loud Before Anybody Could Say It About Her That a Record Is a Thing Somebody Wrote*

**A man of about thirty-seven goes down at about ten past ten under a slate of his own and comes up at about eleven with the count of what is in that room: four racks against the back wall and one long one down the side, the four alike and the long one not, every shelf of every one of the five with a raised lip about two inches deep along the back of it, a lip for stopping a thing sliding off backwards.** At about two in the afternoon a woman of thirty of no office reads the head of one page out loud in the open in front of all nine of them — a word naming what the sheet is for and a figure, the same figure at the head of every sheet in that bundle, a column ruled down with a figure to a ruled line and a short stroke of the same length beside each — and says there is no name on it and no year on it and nothing on the face of it that says what any of the figures are counting. **And then she says the rest of it before anybody can say it about her: that a record is a thing somebody wrote, that it does not consent, that it cannot be asked anything, that it does not testify, that it is not a witness and not a verdict and not a voice, and that a thing somebody made can be described, cut, copied, carried and put on a shelf; and that she has wanted that paper since about eleven o'clock that morning as much as anybody on that deck.** It goes in the second column and not the first, because a stranger with a pencil can check what a page looks like and cannot check what it was meant to do. Nobody thanked her. A man of about thirty-four gives one figure, about three weeks, once, and does not put the other half up again.

### Chapter 483 — *Monday the Fifteenth, a Rota Day, the Ninety-Ninth Charge Walked on by None of It, Three Slates Written Before Anybody Was Asked, Three People Asked for One Thing Each That They Can Carry, Three Tethers On Before Anybody Asked Anything at All, and a Page in a Woman's Own Hand With an Hour Against It*

**Three slates carry one sentence at the head of a page before anybody is asked anything**, asking in the same words whether a person is told they may go down into that room on the seventeenth, one at a time, under a slate, with a named tender on the surface and a figure of forty minutes of air and a cutoff that tender can pull without asking, and come up with one thing they can carry in their own hands, and say it out loud on that deck, and give it up when it has been said. One asks for a sound, one for a movement, one for what was in the air. **At about ten past eight in the morning, before anybody had said a word to any of the three, a short line goes off a belt at the waist of each of them to a ring on the outside of that bell, and the man who keeps the leaf says out loud that it is thirty feet of three-inch line and a ring and a belay, and that nobody is going to be holding the other end of it, and that it is not a man and not a person.** The three are asked one at a time with the door shut, are told before they are asked anything that they may stop it, are asked what they intend to do about stopping it, and answer that out loud before they answer anything else. Ollum Trevask says he intends not to stop it and will take one sound, not the one he expects — there is a thing in that room he has been hearing in his own head for four days. **Amos Trewin says he intends not to stop it and will take one movement, and asks that it be written on a slate that he cannot hear out of the left side of his head.** Sabra Loach says she intends not to stop it and will take what was in the air, and says out loud that she counted the cups on the fifth and said then that the number was on the face of that floor, and that she is going to be wrong on the seventeenth in a way no plan can be checked against, and asks that the page say she knew it on the fifteenth and went anyway. **At about two in the afternoon the woman of thirty of no office writes her promised page in her own hand with the hour against it, one sentence — if somebody asks her what that floor is she is going to say that she does not know — and it goes in the first column, and nobody asked her and nobody thanked her, and she says out loud once that it is the first sentence of that kind she has written in eleven years.** A man of about thirty-six named Corwin Tace sets more marks on that floor in the morning and is off it by the middle of that day, as he said he would be, and says nothing about it.

### Chapter 484 — *Tuesday the Sixteenth, the Fifty-Sixth Wage Tuesday, the Column Not Moving and Fifty-Six Weeks Standing Fallen Due, Four Days of Coal at Two Thousand Three Hundred and Fifty-Two Pence, and a Man Asking What He Is Owed if the Boat Goes Home Early*

**Four days of coal for that pump at the same figure as the last two loads.** A man of about fifty-four out of a supply boat off that reef says, for the third time this trip and in the same words, that coal off that boat goes up at the end of the month, and **the man who keeps the leaf opens no line for it and says so out loud.** At about half past ten one of the four men paid a day apiece, of about thirty-eight, asks the master in front of the whole party what a man is owed if the boat goes home early, and is given the same answer for the third time — that a day in advance is a day in advance and is not taken back, that it is not a promise of a day after it, that his boat is not this party and the man was never in it, and that he cannot be asked to stay and is not going to be asked. **He thanks him and is told again that he is not to be thanked for it.** A man of about thirty-seven goes down at about ten under a slate of his own and comes up at about ten to eleven with the long rack's four shelves against the other four racks' three, and a fourth shelf a foot lower than the other three, and does not go into it past the second shelf and nobody asked him to. **The fifty-sixth wage Tuesday comes and goes, the column does not move, and fifty-six weeks stand fallen due, and a wage Tuesday does not pay a wage.** The shortfall is eleven thousand six hundred and thirty-eight pence.

### Chapter 485 — *Wednesday the Seventeenth, a Crate and Matting and a Lid at Two Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence and Four Fresh Days of Air at Seven Hundred and Twenty, Three Descents One at a Time on That Hired Line, and Three Things That Do Not Agree*

**Four fresh days of air are hired off that supply boat and the line bears the seventeenth of November and no other date, and the four days are the seventeenth, the eighteenth, the nineteenth and the twentieth.** Ivo Sark, of about twenty-four, one of the master's two men, is the tender on the surface for the whole of the three and is not in that bell at any hour, with the pump hand of about forty-four on the compressor. The three go down one at a time, were asked on the fifteenth one at a time and not in front of the other two, and are asked nothing at all on that Wednesday. **Ollum Trevask, down at about ten past nine and up at about ten, gives a sound:** a knocking of about nine strokes of about the length of a heartbeat and not even, the eighth shorter than the other eight, not from that wall and not from that floor and coming from further off than that room. **Amos Trewin, down at about ten past ten and up at about eleven, gives a movement:** something on the far side of that back wall came down about a foot and stopped, heard and not seen, not the water, late on the knocking with a space in between, and he does not know what was in the space. **Sabra Loach, down at about twenty past eleven and up at about ten past twelve, gives what was in the air:** water in the air in that room, not sea and not a drain, the smell of a stone floor that has had a roof over it for a very long time and has never had a fire in it, and a sweetness that came and went about four times while she stood there, and she does not know that the sweetness is the paper and the man of about fifty-one does not know it either and has not offered. **The three do not agree and they were not made to, and put together they have a clock — about nine strokes, then a space, then something settling, then a change in the air, inside about two minutes — and not one of them knew at the time that the other two were carrying the other two parts of it. That is not a finding and is not a recording and is not a verdict and no part of it can be taken off a page by a stranger with a pencil.** All three went into the second column in the order they were said and none was asked to give it better. The shortfall is twelve thousand six hundred and twenty-six pence.

### Chapter 486 — *Thursday the Eighteenth, a Rota Day, the Hundredth Charge Walked on by None of It and the Figure of a Hundred Said Out Loud Once, Thirty Fathoms of Line at Five Hundred and Ten Pence, a Crate Filled, the Cost of It That Nobody Was Warned About, and a Page That Will Not Sit Flat and Was Not Cut*

**The hundredth time that cistern was charged, at about eight in the morning, walked on by none of it, and the figure of that hundred is on a slate in that market and nowhere else and is said out loud on that deck once and is not going to be said again.** Thirty fathoms of line at five hundred and ten pence, paid for a day after it was bought on purpose. A man of about fifty-one goes down at about ten and comes up at about a quarter to eleven and the four baskets come up one at a time on that line. **And the crate is filled and it will not go under the stove-pipe bracket, and the after deck has to be cleared, and the man who has slept under that bracket for three weeks goes into the forepeak with the boy, and the boy gives up his bunk without being asked — and nobody was warned about that, because nobody had any idea what was in that room until a basket came up out of it on the Saturday.** Nobody thanked anybody and no figure is set against any of it. **A page that is old and damp at one edge will not sit flat and cannot be folded and was not cut**; the woman of thirty of no office names it out loud once as the third thing off the second shelf of the rack against the back wall on the north side of that room, and says she is not writing that down on anything, and that the only way anybody will know where it is is if somebody on that boat remembers it; and the man of about fifty-one says he has cut about four hundred pieces of paper in nineteen years and cut every one of them because the man who owned it was standing there telling him to, and that nobody on that boat owns a page out of that room, and that a man who cuts a thing nobody owns is a man who has decided what the thing was. **Nobody was asked to decide it and nobody voted and nobody put it in a column and the man who keeps the leaf said no to putting it in the second one.** The shortfall is thirteen thousand one hundred and thirty-six pence.

### Chapter 487 — *Friday the Nineteenth, a Day Apiece in Advance to the Same Four Men at Six Hundred and Seventy-Two Pence, a Man of About Thirty-Eight Coming Up at About Twenty Past Eleven With Something in Him That Is Not His, and Nobody Asking Him for It*

**A man of about thirty-eight, one of the four paid a day apiece, goes down at about half past ten under a slate with his own reason — that he has never in nineteen years of stands been in a room with a floor in it that was swept, and that he wanted to stand on one — and comes up at about twenty past eleven on the air.** He is not hurt, nobody has named him a casualty, no figure is set against him anywhere, and no sheet that carries money carries any line against him. He sat on the edge of that hatch with his boots off and worked that compressor's second shift from about one until about six. **At about two in the afternoon on that after deck, in front of all nine of them, he says one thing about it, once, in about half a minute:** there is a woman in that room who has put a bowl of water down outside a door on the off side, and a man has gone past it and gone in without stopping, and the handle of the bowl is turned to the left as a person goes in and the rim is chipped on the left and the chip is old — and he has never seen any of it and does not know what it is, and he has worked out that a man who says a thing like that and then argues about it spends the rest of his life arguing about it, so he has said it and he is keeping it, and nobody is to ask him for it. **It goes into the second column with the hour against it and not into the first, and the man who keeps the leaf says out loud that no figure will be set against the day of it and that the man is not a casualty and has not been thanked and will not be thanked.** A man of about thirty-seven goes down at about half past eleven, after the man of about thirty-eight is up and out of the water, and comes up at about twenty past twelve with nothing at all and says so, and nobody was in that mouth at the same time as anybody else at any hour. The shortfall is thirteen thousand eight hundred and eight pence.

### Chapter 488 — *Saturday the Twentieth, a Second Pair of Hands for a Day at One Hundred and Sixty-Eight Pence, a Crown Man Still Setting Marks and Given Nothing, and Three Accounts of That Floor That Do Not Agree*

**A second pair of hands for a day off that same supply boat at one hundred and sixty-eight pence, the fourth and last of the four hired days of air, and no line opened for the twenty-first or the twenty-second and nobody asked why.** A man of about fifty-one goes down at about ten and comes up at about ten to eleven. **A man of about thirty-six named Corwin Tace has been on that floor since before that party came out here in October and is setting marks**; he comes up at about eleven, goes down again at about half past two, is on the bottom about thirty of them and comes up at about a quarter past three, and the one question he is asked is how many he is putting in on that side, and he says four, two at the ends and two a fathom in, four inches apart, because there is a paper that says four inches and he has it in the roll and nobody else does, and he does not open the roll. **Three people say one thing each about what is on that floor and none of them is asked to say it again:** the man of about thirty-seven says there is a bar about the height of his own chest running about nine foot on the far side of the last frame, worn bright along the top for about two foot in the middle, and that he has been in that room four times since the Saturday and is telling them that is a rail; the pump hand of about forty-four says a floor is for a man to stand on while he does a thing that takes a long time, that this one has fifteen long things on it and no roof and nowhere to sit down, and that a rail on a floor like that is for a man to stand beside while something heavy comes past him; **and the master of that boat says a rail is for moving a thing, and that there are rails under his own forepeak where a man cannot get at.** Nobody picked one, nobody wrote down which he thought was right, and the party does not know. The shortfall is thirteen thousand nine hundred and seventy-six pence.

### Chapter 489 — *Sunday the Twenty-First, the Eighty-First Wipe, Nothing Going Out on Any Line, the Party Off That Floor for a Working Day, and a Crate That Is Not Opened in Front of Nine Men Because Nine Men Is Not a Room*

**No descent, no line, and the reason said out loud once at about eight in the morning:** four days of air were bought on the seventeenth for the seventeenth to the twentieth, and a boat lying still over that trench burns more coal than a boat working, and the coal was bought at fourteen marks, nine shillings and fourpence for four days. The boy is up the after masthead with a caulking iron, the man of about fifty-one counts the drying bundles and reads the count out once, the man of about thirty-eight works the compressor the whole of that day and says no word about the Friday to anybody, and the pump hand sleeps for four hours in the middle of the day. **The crate stood on that after deck with the matting in it, the lid on it, a batten across the lid and a line round the whole of it, and was not opened, and at about half past ten in the morning a woman of about thirty-one who crews nothing and sells nothing put her hand flat on the lid, did not lift it, and said out loud that a crate is for a thing that has to be somewhere and is not for a party being proud of itself, and that a thing opened where the nine people who filled it are standing is a thing that has been opened in public, and that this one is going into a room over a fish market four hundred yards from a shed where about eleven people cannot read, so the lid comes off in that room or it does not come off at all.** Nobody thanked her and nobody argued and nobody had proposed opening it, and she said afterwards that she had put it out loud on purpose so that it could not be said that nobody had ever said it. The other crate, with the batten on it since the twenty-ninth day of October and no word on any page of that harbor for what is in it, was on the other side of that deck and was not opened either, and the two are not the same crate and were not opened on the same day.

### Chapter 490 — *Monday the Twenty-Second, a Rota Day, the Hundred and First Charge Walked on by None of It, a Crate Not Carried in a Hand, a Leaf Read Back at About Ten Past Five With Both Definitions and Its Own Derivation, and the Sheet Thirteen Thousand Nine Hundred and Seventy-Six Pence Short*

**The cistern is charged for the hundred and first time and walked on by none of it, and the figure of that hundred is not said again.** The master of that boat is still on that deck, was asked by nobody for a date, gave none, and his boat was not put to sea. Corwin Tace is not on that floor and his tool roll is not on that deck. **At about half past ten in the morning a woman of about thirty-one who crews nothing and sells nothing says out loud what is in that crate and what is not in it, without opening it:** what is in it is the best evidence this party has ever had in its hands, and it is the best evidence because it is a record made at the time by somebody who was there, kept dry in a dry room, standing in racks in a wall behind that thing on that floor, and because three people have said what that thing is and the three of them do not agree and she did not pick one of them, and none of it can be read by anybody on that boat — **and it is going into a crate and not into anybody's hand**, because a thing carried in a man's coat is a thing one man has and a thing a room has is a thing about eleven people can be told a thing about, and the day it is carried to that harbor by a man with a coat on his arm is the day it becomes something else. What is not in it: **the third column, which nobody has filled, nobody has been appointed to, and that she says out loud nobody is going to fill**, and one damp page lying flat under a weight on a tarpaulin, on no sheet in that boat and on no sheet in that harbor. **At about ten past five in the evening the leaf is read back in the open in the ship's own left hand, all four columns including the empty one, twice, and both definitions come out of the same mouth in the same words as on the twenty-second of October and the first and the eleventh of November, and the reading prints its own arithmetic on its face: 183 + 40 = 223 at the close, 789 + 200 at the close, a hundred and ninety-five of the two hundred on the thirty-nine days before and three this morning, two hundred less two is a hundred and ninety-eight, and 789 + 198 = 987 at the hour, and the forty days are forty days of the forty-one from Wednesday the thirteenth of October to this day, the twelfth day of November being the one day in between that is a day nobody is in.** The sheet is read back in full: ten thousand six hundred and forty pence in, twenty-four thousand six hundred and sixteen out, **thirteen thousand nine hundred and seventy-six pence short, being eighty-seven marks, four shillings and eightpence, against that yard's own book, said out loud in that yard's own mouth and not answered by anybody.** The four columns at the close stand at two hundred and twenty-three, nine hundred and eighty-nine, none and one hundred and twenty-five.
